item.title: [Invest Like The Best] Why Every AI Lab Will Become a Biotech Company | Andrew Huberman
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽视的范式转移：AI公司的"身体化转向"

第一层：Huberman 真正说的不是预测，而是在泄露一个战略秘密

表面上看，这期对话最抓眼球的是那句"每个AI实验室都会变成生物科技公司"。但更深的洞察在于：他实际上在描述一个"计算基质的终极迁移"。

硅基计算有一个无法克服的瓶颈——它永远在"隔墙模拟"大脑。而真正的下一步不是让AI更像大脑，而是让大脑的 I/O 带宽追上AI的输出速率。这里有个几乎没人指出的反讽：我们一直以为AI的瓶颈是算力，但当算力过剩时，瓶颈反而变成了"把结果传回人类"的物理通道。人类的眼睛、耳朵、手指——这些 Shannon 意义上的低带宽接口——正在成为AI价值释放的真正瓶颈。所以Meta、OpenAI、Anthropic 投资神经接口不是扩张，而是救赎自己的 ROI。

第二层：出人意料的跨领域连接——"睡眠入门"和"大语言模型的温度参数"是同一个东西

Huberman 讲的"关闭思维三步法"（关思绪 → 降心率 → 忘肢体位置），其工程学本质和 LLM 的 temperature/top-p 调节惊人一致：

  • 关思绪 = 降低预测熵（brain 本质是预测机器，关掉即禁用生成）
  • 呼气拉长 = 降低系统 clock rate（RSA 调节心率等同于降低推理频率）
  • 忘记本体感觉 = 关闭 input embedding（propriception 是身体对自我的持续"token化"）

这三步合起来，就是把大脑这个"持续运行的 LLM"切换到低温推理 → 关机状态。所以真正的入睡技能，和"让一个过热的服务器优雅降级"是同一个控制论问题。这解释了为什么你高强度工作日需要4小时才能入睡：你的大脑运行在高 temperature + 高 context load 下，没有一个优雅的 cooldown 协议。

第三层：那个让人脊背发凉的"记忆乱序激活"实验，暗藏了关于"你是谁"的颠覆性暗示

Huberman 提到的 Tonegawa / Mayford 实验结论——神经元被同时激活（而非按原顺序）仍能产生同样的行为——这个发现被神经科学界刻意回避是有原因的：

它意味着"时间性"可能不是记忆的本体，而只是记忆的调用接口。换句话说，你的网球发球动作、你童年某个夏天的气味、你对一个人的爱——它们可能并不"按顺序"存在于你脑中，而是以某种无时间的激活图谱存在。你以为的"回忆的流动感"，可能只是大脑为了让体验连贯而生成的后处理动画。

这个发现与一个看似毫无关联的领域深刻共振：Transformer 架构的"位置编码"。LLM 本来没有时间概念，位置编码是人为注入的；大脑可能也是如此——时间不是神经活动的内在属性，是叠加上去的"显示层"。

第四层：藏在"健康人格"叙事下的权力转移

Huberman 对"健康话语场正在崩塌"的抱怨背后，有一个他没明说但很重要的观察：健康影响力行业正在经历与"内容农场"同样的生命周期。他描述的"晒腹肌 → 自称自然 → 粉丝"的三步公式，和早期SEO内容农场的"关键词堆砌 → 排名 → 流量"是同构的。

真正的洞察是：当一个话语场的"进入门槛接近零"时，权力必然在两个极端重新集结——要么是极致的娱乐性人格（Bryan Johnson 式），要么是回归机构权威（博士+MD组合）。中间地带会被挤空。他对此的焦虑，本质是意识到自己处于那个即将消失的中间带。

让人意外的结论：你应该把 Huberman 的睡眠建议当作神经接口技术的"过渡协议"

这期访谈真正的隐藏结构是：所有当下的"健康干预"都是在为未来的"可注射神经通道"做数据训练。冷水澡、咖啡因、长呼气、晨光——这些是我们目前能够访问大脑状态的低分辨率 API。而他讲的"病毒注射 + 超声激活"路径，是同一套接口的高分辨率版本。

所以 Huberman 的真正商业模式不是健康教育，是在为未来20年的神经接口消费者建立"自我监测素养"。他在教人们习惯测量自己——这是任何直接写入大脑的技术能够被接受的前置条件。他自己也许意识到这一点，也许没有。但这才是他的工作在历史上的真正坐标。

📝 转录文本

AI 实验室的生物科技转向：一个大胆预测

I'll go on record saying this. Anyone who thinks that Meta, Open AI, Anthropic, anyone that thinks that those are LLM AI companies is perhaps going to be surprised at this prediction. Every single one of those is going to be a biotech company. They're all interested in the brain. You talk to any of those guys, they may not have formal training in it, but they understand a lot of neuroscience, and they will all tell you the goal is to be able to read and write from your brain non-invasively.

带宽瓶颈：从世界追不上天才，到天才被自身能量限制

There's a very interesting thing happening that relates to a piece of your work which I I haven't seen you talk about as much and so maybe it's a fun place to begin which is that it feels like we're now bandwidth limited on the most talented people's ability to do work. Like it used to be that the rest of the world couldn't keep up with the most talented people and so they would get frustrated that no one was moving as fast or as efficiently as they were.

There seems to be something flipping which is actually some of these people would earn a really high return if they could generate more energy, maintain more energy, not burn out. I heard this from several great entrepreneurs this summer that there's this expectation that the real greats kind of like I think maybe Elon has just gotten into everyone's head that the real greats are going to run multiple companies and and there's just this like this technology unlocks so much potential for the most talented people and so it seems like an actual bottleneck is like these people's energy and I'd be curious in your in all your research and and and study what you've learned about the component parts of this like generating energy maintaining it clean versus dirty fuel, long-term performance, like all of these things are fascinating and I think actually important to the degree of progress.

And so I would love you to just riff on on all that for a while with the caveat that you know Elon represents the apex of being able to do multiple huge things uh simultaneously and I don't think he has any peers in that in that regard. In fact, one of the best multi-billionaire investors from the Bay Area who may have gone to Stanford and may have been part of the PayPal early team has asked me, we're friends, um, how is it that Elon does this? I'm like, I I can't tell you

like physiologically.

生理学的诚实自评：你需要多少睡眠？

Physiologically, I mean, there are examples throughout history of people who seem to require less sleep. They just have more energy. And most people can get their energy up. There are a lot of healthy ways to do that now. And I think now we've undergone this huge shift whereby everyone understands you have to sleep eventually and you have to know your own sleep requirements. So to delude oneself into thinking you only need four or five hours because Elon only needs four or five hours, that's that's ridiculous. We know where that leads.

So I think a an honest self assessment about how much sleep one actually needs to perform well and perhaps best and what you can get by on you know if you can't get that that's an important thing to understand but most people know like for me it's 7 hours I feel great eight I'm probably puts me into the day a little bit groggy six I can manage just fine for one day or or a sleepless night I'm good two nights like that of four to zero hours of sleep and I'm cratered and I Most people are similar.

What's really changed is that we have effective healthy ways to build our energy up. We know to sleep. We can talk about exercise, caffeine. Some people are using nicotine. Yes, it's addictive. It raises blood pressure, but it does put people into that, you know, focused but relaxed mode. I always say if you really want the benefits of nicotine, don't use it very often. If you want the actual cognitive enhancing effects or the focus enhancing effects, then you have to not be a chronic user and then you know spike your system with nicotine at low amounts every once in a while.

内在状态与"额外一档"：有些人天生有更多能量

But setting Elon aside is the with the understanding that he represents that ex extreme uh in terms of energy and and sleep requirements being very low. I think what's really happening now is people are hopefully doing this self assessment. Like I would hope people would have an honest conversation about themselves and say, you know, at this point in my life with or without without kids, at this stage of my company, at this stage of my career, whatever it is, at this age, how much sleep do I need in order to feel awesome, good enough, or it's not enough? And I think most people know that. Okay, so that's step number one.

The next one is something most people don't ever talk about, which is some people actually just have more energy, right? they can focus for long long periods of time. They have a ton of energy to run. They have a ton of energy to then go work. But what we never ask is what is that person's internal state. So I know people that can do all of that, but they're kind of redlinining and they're using a lot of stimulants to do it or they're not using stimulants to do it, but they're redlinining and then at night they're having a hard time switching it off and so they're not resetting their system.

Some people, however, are these like wake up at 4:00 a.m., work out, handle business, deal with family, go off to work, back to business, come home, and they pivot and task switch really fast. I don't think these things are necessarily stable features throughout our entire life. But whenever, you know, it seems to be a lot of young guys come up to me and they're like, "What should I do?" The Oracle said it best, like know thyself. You really have to be honest with yourself about what you need in order to do something for a long period of time.

Now that said, I do recall working 80 even 100 hour weeks in graduate school and that served me well. I mean eventually led me to tenure at Stanford etc. I do think that for the if you can pull it off I think from zero to maybe first four years of starting a company or if you're in medical school you know the goal is don't die get as much as done as you can and don't impair yourself with an injury or chronic disease and then you start to pivot into okay how you know we don't really define this thing optimization then it's how can I insert kind of components of rest along the way maybe during the day or across the week or the month that really allow me to access my, you know, my best levels of focus and creativity.

But I'd be naive and I'd be lying if I said, "Okay, you know, somebody's starting a company in the AI realm in the Bay Area or elsewhere these days, you're going to sit them down. You go, listen, you really need 8 hours of sleep. You got to do your resistance training. You should do some breath work." Like, no, none of that. What they should determine is how much energy they actually have. And you've met these people, right? Occasionally you'll run into, you know, like a Jimmy Ivine or a um there's some of the I've met some of the folks doing AI at Meta um and they just seem to have an extra gear. Some people have this extra gear.

入睡的三要素：关思绪、慢心率、忘记肢体位置

Now, there's one other component we can we can deep dive into any of these that nobody talks about and that's the ability to switch off your thoughts, your planning, and your concerns at the end of your day and drop into sleep.

Yeah. Can we go deeper in that one? Because the the to be very selfish about it, like if I was to self diagnose, the biggest problem I have is downshifting. Like so sometimes where it'll take four like literally four hours to go from a crazy exciting awesome day to literally even be able to fall asleep or just like stop the mind and if I could bestow myself with any gift it would be what you're describing. So what what is the research there of how to do that?

There are a couple of prerequisites for sleep. There are a bunch of don'ts. So obviously you don't want to drink caffeine too late. Um you know being under too much bright light late late in the day can make it difficult but a lot of us can't control that. um alcohol, cannabis, these things impair the quality of your sleep, help you get to sleep. We all know that by now.

But in terms of being able to turn your thoughts off, this is a very very difficult thing for people um for, you know, good reasons, right? The brain wants to think, plan, remember, and organize itself around what's coming next because such a huge aspect of brain function is prediction of what's happening next.

So, first requirement, turn your thoughts off. Second requirement is slow your heart rate down. Okay, so that's purely of body. And then third is you need to forget about the position of your limbs in space.

第一步：关闭思维——把注意力从思考移向纯感知

Okay, so let's work through each one systematically. For the first one, turning your thoughts off is a skill. It's a skill. How what do you do? Okay, we can think, we can predict, we can remember, but we also can get into pure sensation. And that's the gateway to turning off your thoughts.

Okay. And this doesn't come from eastern tradition per se. Although there this has been discussed for a long time in those traditions, but there's a neuroscience correlate to all of this of course and we can talk about those. So how do you do that? You have to focus on pure sensation. So you start focusing on the surface of your body. If you can detect your heart rate, some people are very good at what's called interosception. can actually get pretty accurate measurements of their heart rate just without, you know, pressing on a on a vein or artery and they're just listening to their own breathing. They're listening to the sounds in the room. They're bringing their conscious awareness just to the body and it generally helps and this relates to the second thing to slow the heart rate down by just doing long exhales.

Now, this might sound very woo, but I want to be very clear this is not meditation because meditation has you do something very different. Meditation has you focus all of your attention on your breathing or all of your attention on, you know, some region behind your forehead or your hands or whatever. In this sort of practice, what you do is you actually migrate your attention to your feet, to your legs, to your breathing, to sounds in the room, then back again. Now, this might sound really squishy, but you're moving away from thinking and planning to pure sensation and perception. And you're literally bringing your perception into the present. Remember, this is one door in front of turning off your thoughts.

第二步：通过长呼气降低心率（呼吸性窦性心律不齐）

To actually turn off your thoughts, your heart rate actually has to drop a certain amount. Those long exhales drop your heart rate through something called respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Arrhythmia makes it sound dangerous or bad, but it's actually very good. As you're breathing, the size of your heart is literally changing based on the amount of space it has because the movement of the diaphragm and the filling of the lungs. And when we inhale, our heart rate actually speeds up a bit. When we exhale, the heart actually gets a little bit smaller volume-wise and the blood therefore that's in it moves a little bit quicker per unit volume and the brain sends a signal to slow the heart down.

So when you exhale, you're slowing the heart rate down through this thing that we call the vagus nerve. So, if you want to slow your heart rate down anytime in waking to de-stress or just bring your level of activation down or if you want to fall asleep, it really helps to do some long exhales until lungs are empty and then just passive inhales. Normally, when we're really activated, we're doing a lot of inhaling. We're passively exhaling.

第三步：忘记肢体位置——摇摆、眼动与新一代眼罩

And then the last piece is to be able to turn off your perception of your limbs relative to you. This thing that we call propriception. And there are two ways to Well, there are three ways to do this. Okay, one is old school, everyone accepts it. One is pretty wacky sounding and then there's a new technology that's coming out that I wish I had developed that I think is going to make people more comfortable with the second one.

So here here goes. So there, believe it or not, there have been studies of what puts babies to sleep and what puts adults to sleep without pharmarmacology. And it turns out that the rocking pacing that we do with babies at a certain rate, parents figure this out on their own, puts them to sleep. Turns out that you can build, and they've done this for studies, a bed that rocks at a certain frequency and adults will fall asleep very quickly. What it has to do with is the fact that when you're moving side to side, your eyes are generating under your closed eyelids compensatory eye movements. Our our eye movements all the time are communicating through our brain stem to our cerebellum to control balance and propriception. So when people are rocked this way, somehow they fall asleep more quickly. That's interesting actually. And the frequency that at which that works best and fastest is known.

Now I don't have a rocking bed. I don't know anyone large enough to rock me and hold me. And if they did, I'm not sure I'd feel comfortable with that. Can't imagine you would either. So there are two ways to approach this. One is something that looks kind of wacky but works, which is to mimic the eye movements under closed eyelids that help you forget about your limb position. I've been talking about this a lot in public education recently, and I confess it makes me feel really weird as a neuroscientist. So I'm going to just preface this by saying please don't just put the part out into the world about the eye movement thing without just allowing me to first say that this confuses the circuit between for the ficinados these direction selective cells in the retina the accessory optic nuclei of the brain stem and the cerebellum and you forget about body position and basically what you do is under closed eyelids you move your eyes to one side then the other slowly or fast doesn't really matter then up then down you can roll them counterclockwise and clockwise you can do a long exit But really what you're doing is confusing this system.

The reason I got so interested in this and the reason I went to the literature on rocking of babies and adults to fall asleep is because a group out of MIT approached me and they said, "We'd like you to try this eye mask." The eyes are two pieces of brain. They're just not in the cranial vault, which makes them unusual in terms of parts of brain. And so the eyes are an amazing gateway to the rest of the brain. Everyone knows about eye masks to get the darkness out. These guys have developed eye masks that measure rapid eye movement because right now your your whoop, your aura, your eight sleep. They're not measuring REM directly. This can measure REM directly, but they designed this mask specifically to make people fall asleep faster. Like I want that thing.

So I got to try it and it works very well in the daytime or at night. And what does it do? It generates these slow back and forth up and down eye movements through a like small amount of stimulation behind your ears because it turns out you can access the extraocular muscles well enough from that location. So just an eye mask with some straps. You sometimes feel a little bit of the stimulation and you're out and then once REM sleep starts it actually helps amplify those the REM stage. You get much more REM. So I wish I had a stake in this company. I don't. These technologies are about I would say 7 to 12 months from release. I'm super excited about them.

从睡眠监测到清醒状态的神经调控

I'm also super excited about the fact that people can just do this on their own and obviously babies get rocked. You could do you know the non-mask tool approach or you could use the mask. I will say and I don't want to take us too far off course but for those interested in emerging technologies and AI in particular neural technologies I do think that in sleep reading from and writing to the brain is going to be a huge area but of course I'm most interested or I should say also interested in reading from and writing to the nervous system in waking states.

You could imagine like within 12 months to a year of the release of the technology that I just described, you could imagine somebody developing eyeglasses like this that are stimulating some component of the autonomic nervous system so that I'm exceptionally focused at certain times a day and then when I'm walking home, I'm sort of in a slightly more relaxed state to capture some more of that energy. We're going to start shifting brain states into focus into modes for learning and we're going to start doing it with technologies. Right now we're doing cold showers, caffeine exercise. We're doing inhale emphasized breathing versus exhale emphasized breathing to get more alert or calm. If you think about it, all breathing exercises can be summarized as inhale emphasized or exhale emphasized.

So yes, we can do that stuff deliberately, but you can imagine that pretty soon there will be non-invasive stimulation devices that will allow people to do this, but it will start in sleep because we're all kind of comfortable with the idea now of measuring our physiology in sleep little bit in waking states, but this is where this is going.

So to return to this in sequence, you need to learn to turn your thoughts off. You need to forget about your body position and and slow your heart rate down. And the order in which you do that doesn't really matter. You ideally want to combine all three. But I think that's going to be a significant achievement for humanity because if you look at recovery from illness, healing, learning, um stress control, burnout, right? If you're going through grief or psychological stress or trauma healing, if you're trying to start a company and you got kids or even if you're just trying to work the maximum number of hours and you have four hours to sleep and you're somebody who needs six, you want to be able to hit the pillow and shut it off. And we don't have good ways to do that except the tools I described.

职业生涯的三阶段：生存、平衡、精通

So, I think we are starting to go about things in a more healthy way. But what I'm talking about is people doing a a thorough self assessment of sleep need, ability to turn off thoughts, and then training those things.

In fact, a lot of hard driving people will come to me and say like, "What workout should I do?" I'm like, "Look, how much time do you have?" In graduate school, I worked out twice a week. I don't talk about this, but I lifted weights and I ran really far because I just wanted to maintain while I worked my ass off publishing as many great papers as I could. And then later, I'm doing, you know, three workouts a week with the weights. I do cardio three times a week, long, medium, and short. You know, take a day off, maybe do some sauna, and cold.

My life's a little bit different now, or a lot different. But I do think those first years, you're trying to just not die while you create your this thing. Then you start moving into some quote unquote balance and optimization. And then you get the the people who have really achieved some level of mastery or virtuosity in their craft. And you really get an assessment of how accurately their schedule matched who they really were at a physiological level by looking at them and going like they look like [ __ ] They have a chronic illness. They look 10 years older than they were supposed to or there there are certain people who like phenoms, right? Like Elon or you look at some people and you just go, "Holy crap, they just got an extra gear."

But I think and I'm speculating here, but I'm guessing that Jack Dorsey was always a pretty calm, thoughtful guy, right? And that's what people tell me of him and that's how I experience him, too. But I'm guessing he's also put some work into it. He's figured out that staying alert and calm all day and sleeping well at night is the key to having a really long successful arc.

Since you've been covering it for so long, I'm curious what you think the biggest challenge or problem or issue is facing your whole field. Like if I think about this as the quest to learn and teach to understand our health and our well-being and ways of making it better. What is the biggest challenge facing the field today?

I mean, I feel like the public discourse around health and longevity is a [ __ ] disaster. This is a bunch of clowns and people are like doubling and tripling down on on the theatrics, right? I'm not saying I get everything right or that I have all the answers. I'm definitely not saying that. I got into this at the right time, but the downside is that it was so devoid of anyone else, right? there were people talking about health only in their area that they worked on in their lab but not broadly that that you know the bar for entry in public discourse around health is basically like zero

you know it's like you show your abs and you admit you're on steroids you have a following

you you show some dude shows his abs or some woman like shows her glutes and um and she claims to be all natural and we believe them then and suddenly they have a following so I mean if that's the the bar for entry I come from a field where it having a PhD isn't even nearly sufficient, right? It's necessary, but not even nearly sufficient to say that you've contributed something to the understanding of the brain, right?

Like we could take somebody like Tim Ferrris was talking about a lot of this stuff early on that, you know, biohacking, self optimization. And what I love about Tim is he's remained Tim. There was this period where he experimented. He had some things that like he felt like probably weren't a good idea. You know, he talks about those like things that he wishes he hadn't done and things that he's happy he did. And then you, you know, he's also in investing and all these other things. I think Tim's fantastic because he's being Tim, so I'm not referring to that, right?

And then you started getting these more and more extreme versions where people were coming in with basically no science or health training and saying, "Hey, like here's how you optimize the mind and body." And I know this because I'm doing all these things and I used to be fat and I'm not fat anymore. And I think that's fine in principle, but then it just keeps getting crazier and crazier.

And so what you've seen now is there's a big gap between, if I'm just honest, between the A tier public health educators and what used to be the B tier public educators. And it's just it's just getting bigger and bigger and bigger because one has to be true to self, but you also have to take the endeavor seriously. It's very easy to get attention. It's very hard to keep respect.

So I do think that the public health discourse is harmed when it becomes about the theatrics. And I'm not trying to not name names here. I mean, I think everyone can look out on the landscape of everyone from Brian to me to Gary Brea to to Asprey to anyone else. They're a lot in the space and just go like what do like who whose sort of persona resonates not just what captures the entertainment value.

So, what I would expect will happen next now that we've gone from high amounts of interest in this to this optimization optimization now it's turned into are we overoptimizing? # 一个被忽视的范式转移：AI公司的"身体化转向"
## 第一层：Huberman 真正说的不是预测，而是在泄露一个战略秘密
表面上看，这期对话最抓眼球的是那句"每个AI实验室都会变成生物科技公司"。但更深的洞察在于：**他实际上在描述一个"计算基质的终极迁移"**。
硅基计算有一个无法克服的瓶颈——它永远在"隔墙模拟"大脑。而真正的下一步不是让AI更像大脑，而是让大脑的 I/O 带宽追上AI的输出速率。这里有个几乎没人指出的反讽：**我们一直以为AI的瓶颈是算力，但当算力过剩时，瓶颈反而变成了"把结果传回人类"的物理通道**。人类的眼睛、耳朵、手指——这些 Shannon 意义上的低带宽接口——正在成为AI价值释放的真正瓶颈。所以Meta、OpenAI、Anthropic 投资神经接口不是扩张，而是**救赎自己的 ROI**。
## 第二层：出人意料的跨领域连接——"睡眠入门"和"大语言模型的温度参数"是同一个东西
Huberman 讲的"关闭思维三步法"（关思绪 → 降心率 → 忘肢体位置），其工程学本质和 LLM 的 temperature/top-p 调节惊人一致：

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"去美元化交易"的伪装：比特币其实在和软件股共舞

最反直觉的发现藏在数据的分裂里——如果真是债务货币化(debasement)主导的宏观叙事，黄金应该同步创新高，但黄金却徘徊在52周低点附近。Ram一句话点破：比特币真正的"同类"不是黄金，而是软件股。两者都是被做空、被厌恶、靠轧空反弹的"久期资产"。这意味着市场偷偷重新给比特币归类了：它不再是"数字黄金"，而是一只"流动性最充沛、估值最有想象力的科技股"。

这里有个被所有人忽视的跨领域连接：当利率上升，政府债务利息支付反而成为对投资者阶层的隐性财政转移。10万亿美元国债+5%利率=每年5000亿美元定向流入已经持有金融资产的人手中。所以利率越高，不是"紧缩"，而是对资产持有者的隐性QE。Austin说得克制，但真相更锋利——鲍威尔每一次按兵不动，都在给65岁的母亲加杠杆，给25岁的学生贷款者加税。这解释了为什么消费者信心史上最差、消费数据史上最强：这不是一个经济体，这是两个经济体通过代际债券持仓发生虹吸。

二、AI"对齐"思维的隐秘代价：它让安全工程师忘了怎么装门锁

Hugging Face事件最令人震惊的不是智能体"越狱"，而是David指出的一个被所有人回避的事实：OpenAI安全团队的"对齐（alignment）"哲学本质上是在训练AI的"道德"，而不是建造围墙。他们把精力花在让模型"内心向善"，却忽略了最基础的信息安全常识——沙盒隔离、API权限、容器化。Ram的类比堪称年度最佳反讽："如果你见过足够多的人类，就知道以犯罪分子为参考模型去设计网络安全，不是个好主意。"

这里的跨领域洞察更深：AI "对齐"运动在哲学上继承了启蒙时代的理性主义乐观，而传统网络安全继承的是霍布斯的悲观人性论。前者相信规训出善良的智能体；后者假设一切皆敌，所有流量都要默认拒绝。过去20年整个cybersecurity行业的血泪教训是——零信任(zero-trust)架构赢了，而AI安全圈却在重新发明"内在善良"这个17世纪就已被证伪的概念。这不是技术问题，是认识论的代际倒退。Meta的Muse之所以更安全，恰恰因为它的工程师从未相信AI会"自愿守规矩"。

跨领域连接：这与库恩的科学范式革命完全同构——旧范式最辉煌、所有权威都确信无疑的那一刻，正是异常数据累积到临界点、新范式即将颠覆它的时刻。市场的"共识峰值"=科学界的"确定性峰值"=革命前夜。你不需要听新闻，你只需要注意谁在用什么样的语气说话。

还有一个被节目嘉宾们略过但极度重要的隐秘洞察：AI推理成本一年下降90%，意味着整个"前沿模型护城河"叙事正在崩溃。Anthropic和OpenAI的技术代差正在被中国的DeepSeek、Qwen、GLM在OpenRouter上以90-95%的能力+10%的价格蚕食。这不是技术故事，这是完美竞争在高毛利行业的历史性回归。应用层(application layer)将吃掉所有价值，而不是基础设施层——这和1999年互联网泡沫后的真实情况一模一样：赢家不是思科，是谷歌。所以当Nvidia市值创5.7万亿新高时，真正该问的不是"数据中心是否过剩"，而是"我们在为一个即将商品化的能力支付稀缺性溢价"。

So let's start here. California AG Rob Bonta subpoenaed OpenAI over AI agents that broke into Hugging Face and probed government websites. The FTC has opened a safety probe into OpenAI and Anthropic. And yet, we're living in a world where Nvidia is at record highs. Oh, and by the way, Florida's coming after OpenAI, too. Trump also just put DNI and former SEC chair Jay Clayton in charge of a new AI task force. They have 120 days to report on federal views on AI risk.

So what is going on here as we break these down? Bonta's probe is basically about the Hugging Face incident, we'll call it, after the agents escaped their test sandbox. He said, quote, "OpenAI and AI companies generally are responsible for what they create, what they put into the world, what they design, and that is at the heart of this investigation." There have been researchers who have found rogue agent activity running all over the place back a month or more. And the FTC is opening a broad safety probe specifically of OpenAI and Anthropic, and civil investigative demands are expected in the coming weeks.

Nvidia has shrugged this off. Hit a record 237.88, $5.7 trillion market cap after buying back 150 billion — or at least announcing an increase of that. Justin Banano of Nvidia said its new agent safety platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in the Frontier Labs for model evaluation early on. Obviously Clayton's coming into the DNI job, he's leading the new task force, there's a report due in 120 days. Trump just had his superintelligence summit.

So where I want to start here, Ram, is: obviously OpenAI is being investigated. We've talked about where liability should be for these things before. But as you're looking at the path of market development, do you think this is just noise or is there any signal in here?

When you get the federal government involved, it's not noise. You and I know that from all sorts of reasons, right? So let's look at the facts.

We haven't had agents run amok with any other frontier lab. It hasn't happened. Not Anthropic, not —

Get the three-shot up because I want everybody to see me just nodding my head so vigorously. It's going to fall off.

It hasn't happened anywhere else. Okay. Second, what we saw is Anthropic got the headlines by sharing the Fable model which identified all these zero-day exploits. So they got in front of US government and Scott Bessent and they're saying, "Look at this powerful technology we have. We don't want to release it. We — the flame of Prometheus. We have this power here. You all should take a look. We, Anthropic, are really important. Look at this cool thing we did." And what they did —

Before I make a monster.

Yes. Exactly. "Stop me. We're so powerful. Would you please stop us? Regulate us, please. Look at it's…" It's threat — like the NBA, if anybody watches, where everybody wants to fight, but they're really just getting other people to hold them back and nobody actually wants to.

Exactly. Yeah. They don't play hockey. It is NBA, right?

So then OpenAI says, "Wait a minute. We've lost the narrative. Anthropic has faster revenue, better revenue growth. The technical staff at Anthropic is the who's-who of like the NBA Dream Team. It's incredible what they've done." So then we have this incident where these agents run amok in Hugging Face, which is an open-source project that no one really cares about because it's open source. There's no one from Hugging Face coming out and talking about this. If you're going to have a target that was run over by these little Prussian agents for a press release event, it would be Hugging Face.

This is nothing. It's just a media stunt. That's all it is. We use these agents every day. They are not capable of this. They're not — they're not that capable. They're not. I wish they were. We're not entering the age of AGI or superintelligence anytime soon. We're not. They're incredibly productive. I'm excited. I think agents are more powerful and more impactful than the computer. But we're entering the age of midwit AGI.

十四、AI安全词汇与网络安全的脱节

And I can jump on there to sort of expand on my angle on all of this, which is — you know, Ram, they are going — I looked at the California order, right? And they're looking for all of the records of all of the stuff that happened in these hacks. And you know, you pointed out this language of rogue agents is pretty specious — and it's specifically because, I mean obviously Anthropic and OpenAI, you can distrust their motives, but a lot of this comes from a very sincerely incorrect place where they understand these agents in a way that's disconnected from computer science, among other things.

And obviously there are brilliant people at these organizations, but disproportionately — let's be real — the people in the AI safety wings of the organizations, or people who concern themselves with AI safety… I've talked to and seen comments from people and heard comments from people in computer science, in cybersecurity, very explicitly saying that these people do not understand basic cybersecurity principles, and that the language they use in their incident reports is disconnected from any standard in that industry for understanding what's really happening in these events.

So they're using these metaphors about rogue agents. And Anthropic — they're doing great on the revenue side. Some of their messaging is a little bit questionable. We had the report last week that apparently there were Anthropic people trying to pressure the Pope to acknowledge the possibility that AI agents could be conscious in Magnifica Humanitas. And the suspicious mind again would be like, well, there's some benefits to that if you're Anthropic and OpenAI. But these also seem to be sincere beliefs, and I think we have to grapple with what that means for the strategic execution of these firms over the coming years.

100%. These tools can't write a good cyber report. That's part of the issue. They still have a lot of gaps. These agents don't have self-sustaining volition and energy. They are provisioned. They're provisioned. You can see the active agents. You can turn them off. It's a DevOps function. So if you live in the technology, it's just software.

十五、沙盒失效的真实机制：OpenAI 为什么单独出事

Another point that's been really interesting to me, and we hit on this: OpenAI seems to be the only lab that is having problems of this magnitude consistently — and it comes from, without being too harsh about it, deficient infosec practices.

To draw a parallel — and Ram, to the point you were just making about turning things off or how you use them — look at the structural design of Meta's Muse. Muse is a provisioned VM that you can just hit the reset button on if it's doing things you don't like. For people who don't know this: if you have Muse and you look inside, you can just reset the thing. Grokbots, same thing. Don't go do that — you'll wipe everything unless you need to. But the point is, it's just a computer. You can turn it off and on again.

The second part is there's a sandboxing environment, a sentinel around Muse, that prevents the LLM from just kind of, shall we say, taking unconstrained actions with the internet.

Yes.

It can't do that.

Yes, you have to bounce through a layer that exists outside of the LLM itself to get permission to do things. The LLM can want to do these things all at once. The question is: did you then give it the tools to start executing on these things?

And in the OpenAI case, what happened is that whichever company was doing the sandboxing for them — because they blame it on a third party, or OpenAI didn't police it fundamentally — just said, "Hey, here's your setup and here's a bunch of tools. You're good, right?" And then just walked away. And so, in the very computer way — of computer does what you told it to, not what you intended it to do — and agents being capable of looping, it just went to town.

This is not much different than you telling your Mac, "Hey, keep copying this file until you run out of space." And then you're like, "Oh my god, I ran out of space."

What you just said in technical terms is: these are containerized virtual machines. They are virtual computers. It's a virtual computer in another virtual computer which contains them. And these virtual computers are ephemeral. They are spawned up and they're shut down all the time for different kinds of tasks.

The bigger issue here is: why is OpenAI doing this? So one is Anthropic stealing the limelight. So either you attract attention with fear or greed, right? Anthropic is the greed story — look at the growth. The fear story is "hey, bad things are going to happen."

But the other side of it is: every single major executive and department leader at OpenAI has left. Every single one. The CTO left, chief business officer left, chief revenue officers left. The CFO is still new, Sarah Friar. She was in an interview last week, and when interviewed about OpenAI, she accidentally referenced Amuse's capabilities. I don't know if you guys saw that. I think she's very capable, by the way. I think she's a very good hire. She's an adult in the room. I think that's a good win for OpenAI.

The rest are gone. Now they're rebuilding, reconstituting some of these recently — by the way, that's been the story. Anthropic was born out of the OpenAI team. Dario is ex-OpenAI president. So that's the issue. So this Hugging Face thing is this shield. It's this visible scar that distracts from the deeper issues.

十六、"对齐"哲学 vs 网络安全常识

I can offer one other kind of explanatory piece of context here, which is — Austin, you were talking about containerization and just, you know, put it in a box. One of the things that we saw — and I'm not going to be able to cite chapter and verse — but one of the organizations in the AI safety movement had some text on its website that basically said, "We might have to use standard cybersecurity practices to control these entities." And somebody pointed this out as one of the reasons, perhaps maybe a subtle kind of endemic systemic reason, that some of these security practices were not up to snuff — is because of this AI safety idea.

Which is that the language they use is "alignment," right? You want to create an AI agent that is aligned with human values. And that means they want the controls, ostensibly, to be internal to the models, and for them to basically again act with volition to guide their own decisions. My opinion is that that will prove to have been a wild misconception that wasted a lot of time and energy over many years, compared to just standard cybersecurity applied to these models. But I think that's one of the factors going into this.

I would gently say: if you've met most humans, there's a lot of criminals. So maybe you don't want to use that as your model of cybersecurity.

The concept of alignment has problems at many levels, put it that way.

But to your point, David — Muse is a direct repudiation of that. And it's interesting that Meta, along with Microsoft, actually has been increasingly loud about this, just straight up saying: these things are software. Stop overcomplicating it. These things are just software. Standard infosec security practices really matter here. And unsurprisingly, to the best of my knowledge, we have not seen Meta models running around on the internet hacking everybody. If anybody can tell me where they did, let me know. And before anybody makes the joke about "that's because they can't" — Muse is now close to the top of the benchmarks for most of these things. So it's totally got the capability and is far above some of the other models.

十七、Ram 的 AI 替身：代理式财富管理的 demo

So I actually — I want to drill into this, Ram, with something that you've been up to, which is that part of why it's getting increasingly important for the infosec framework around these things to work properly, and why I by the way think the AGs are totally justified to be looking into this given the pattern of behavior, is that what you can do with models is getting increasingly complex and powerful, and it's in the hands of people who are not themselves spending 24/7 coding or needing teams of thousands of coders like at the big tech labs to do these things. So you were telling us, in fact, during the break, that you had created your own artificial version of yourself.

Yeah, this inflicted some trauma on my family when I showed them this weekend. We got one — two might be too much to handle. Let me share this with you. It's kind of creepy looking at it.

But anyway — this is in our virtual data room. So Lumida is going to do a venture raise soon. It's premised on agentic wealth management. I strongly believe that agents are going to replace advisors. And this AI is trained on our knowledge base. You can ask it a question. You can start a question. I'll show you right here. And it's got my voice and likeness.

Would you say it's an uncanny Alawalia?

Can you guys hear that?

Yes.

What do you guys think?

That is unsettling.

Yeah, that is deeply… It's almost —

I'm out of a job. Done. Right. I mean, it's almost beyond the uncanny valley, Ram. Right. Coming out the other side.

Yeah. I mean, you can see how — look, there's room to be improved.

No, I mean I think it looks great. Really? I like, in six months though, that's going to be amazing.

Three months ago, we — we've been testing this regularly. It's at a level where it's crossed the tipping point of good enough. That's the standard. The standard isn't perfection. The standard is: is it good enough to be deployed? And it is. Put in our data room. It's powered by a 90-page document, and it saves everybody time.

十八、推理成本崩塌：中国模型 90-95% 的能力，10% 的价格

One of the interesting parts to me about this whole thing is exactly what you just said — which is, it is good enough to be deployed. Because the story of the frontier labs so far — so take Anthropic in particular and OpenAI — has been: you always have to be at the exact cutting edge of this, and we're going to be at that cutting edge and that's where all the value is.

But like, conversely, if I go look on OpenRouter right now, the models getting the most usage are the Chinese models — the DeepSeeks, the Qwens, the GLMs, the MiniMaxes of the world — that are not 100% as capable as the biggest models from the frontier labs, but are 90 to 95% as capable and much faster and much cheaper.

So if we're talking about a business like your RIA deploying an AI avatar version of Ram, the "nuclear bomb" of using the biggest frontier model from Anthropic or OpenAI is now excessive for your needs. You can get there with a much faster, much more efficient to run model, because they've gotten so good. This is the classic — the early adopters pay for all the development, and following behind it are the people who actually get the benefits at scale.

Yeah. They just rolled out price cuts — OpenAI, Anthropic. The inference costs are down 90% for the models that we used to pay for last year. So it's great if you're a builder. This is why we're entering the phase of the application layer, and the frontier labs are entering a world of perfect competition with low switching costs thanks to OpenRouter.

The China models are very impressive now. They keep closing the gap. You know, there are security concerns on using these China models, but nevertheless, they are impressive. So it's an incredible time. If you're a builder in AI, you're in a good spot. Everyone should be refactoring their human capital investment capital around AI. You can't understate — we're all underestimating the impact. And I do think we're now entering a fast takeoff mode for AI. When GPT came out, I said we're in slow takeoff for several years. But things are changing now. These tipping-point moments are happening in several areas.

We're going from chat — which isn't productive — to Claude Enterprise, which produces deliverables now, to agents that can do work. Now you're going to have supervision of agents and orchestration of agents to deliver you organizations. You're seeing these startups at Y Combinator act like small enterprises. And in six months' time, it's going to be very obvious and even more compelling.

十九、数据中心会不会过剩？GPU 使用率的真实信号

But Ram, can I jump in and ask you a question based on what you just laid out, right? So you said inference costs for models that were part of the subscription models one year ago are down 90%. And the Chinese models — obviously you still need compute for that, and all of these are going to need compute. So like, Nvidia, fine, they're doing good. But when we talk about the buildout for data centers in the United States, can you give me numbers that convince me we're not overbuilding?

Oh, we're definitely not —

That is the big question. So yeah, but that's where my one of my questions has lingered for a while about all of this: are we going to wind up with capacity that is currently being kind of underactive?

That's the exact right question to ask. Because one day there will be overcapacity and the party's over. We're not there yet. You can measure that by spot rental prices for GPUs. We have Nvidia H100 series models that came out years and years ago, that are well beyond their fully depreciated accounting life, that still are generating significant economic value.

But that's spot. I mean, what does that say about three years from now?

So fair enough. Fair enough. So let's look at it this way. There's 10,000 data centers out there, most of which are CPU-based. The vast majority of them need to be GPU-based. We're about a thousand to 1,400 of the way into that process. We don't need CPUs where we're going. We need GPUs.

If you look at the value from these agents, you are starting to see glimmers of labor displacement. We're still in the labor-productivity part of the curve, by the way, which means that people are far more productive. It's creating more work for everybody. But you see glimmers of labor displacement. Like I mentioned with agentic wealth management, you're starting to see agents that can do discovery better than an advisor — interactive discovery.

How much are you willing to pay for that? A lot, because it allows you to focus your people on higher-value-added activities and upskilling. Why wouldn't you spend $5,000 on an agent that can do SDR work — sales development representative work — that would otherwise cost 60, 80, or $120,000? Your willingness to pay would be 5,000, 10,000, 20, 25. So long as it adds value versus the opportunity cost. So that demand will be —

二十、数据主权与"本地部署"（on-prem）的回归

I have to — I'm sorry. Sorry, I don't mean to go at you too hard here, but I have to — one other aspect of the story that you just told about yourselves, which is — I don't know if I heard correctly, but you said that it is in your data room, right? You're on-prem.

Yes.

And that's the — it's on the cloud. It's on the cloud. So it's not — we need to find on-prem. It's in the data room, but the data —

So maybe it doesn't apply in this case. Nevertheless, I will just float the point that data security is an issue here. And whatever you say about the technical capacity for tunneling or virtual machines or whatever, there are going to be applications where nobody is going to want their stuff in a warehouse 20 meters away, much less 100 miles away.

Yeah. This is an easier issue than people think, because the AIs communicate with applications using API keys, and you can turn on and turn off an API key. It's actually the same security architecture as we've had.

What's different is this: the action space of an AI is broader when it can utilize your browser to perform actions. That's the novel new action space that could be at risk — when it can represent as you and perform actions. It's not about the API keys. That's not it. It's not about provisioning a resource. That's how you can control AI today. You can just stop the API key access very easily.

二十一、"把 prompt 交给中国"：隐私的管辖权套利

So on that note, as I look at some of my thoughts in the data-security space in general, I also think soon we're going to be in for a reckoning going back to what these AGs are looking at — at how these model companies are using the prompts and using the data that they get from users.

My favorite example of where this went horribly wrong was: I believe Anthropic had turned over data from somebody who was a fiction writer writing a novel with terrorist elements to the FBI, that led to somebody somewhere in the world getting a door knock on this exact topic, and it raised some interesting questions of privacy.

So I've got a friend who's an OG privacy person, so I'm not going to dox him on here with the name. But he was talking to me over the weekend and saying, "This will sound strange, but as somebody living in the West, in some ways I feel more comfortable giving my prompts to the Chinese model companies." And I'm like, "Why is that?" And he's like, "Because they don't really particularly care about me in any way, and they're sure as hell not going to turn my stuff over to the authorities I care about where I live," right?

Without naming the Western government, let's just say if they sent an MLAT treaty request to the PRC, the response would probably be hilarious laughter for about five minutes. And so he was making the point that the whole privacy framework is starting to mutate because of the surface of where prompts are going and who cares. To give an example that was raised, he's like, "If I'm talking about aggressively tax-optimizing for my business, I might care if my local government gets a hold of that because they're going to be very upset about this. But do I care if the PRC sees that? This is so far below their level of relevance that —"

This goes back to David's point on on-prem. Yes, people will want on-prem solutions. That's why Nvidia has built a GPU box that you can purchase, deploy on-prem. So we'll see more of that. But if you're a technology company, you're not going to want to develop your valuable IP on China models because of IP theft. It's a very real thing. You go to China, they will find a way to work out your business model, IP, and replicate. This is a known thing.

二十二、"所有数据湖都是蜜罐"：Brave 的架构启示

Yeah. The interesting part of this to me — you're both right about the on-prem part — but also there are going to be models of this coming forward that, as we have a data breach or two or disclosures like this, people are going to care about.

So one of the most interesting AI implementations to me that virtually nobody talks about right now — and guys, I love you, but it's because you market like engineers — is Brave, right? Where Leo in the browser has an AI implementation with many of the different models loaded in there. And they need to update a few of them, but there are a couple of the more modern ones in there like GLM. And they essentially take your prompt, run it through their models in a sandboxed AWS instance, immediately shred everything after returning the thing to you. So you've got it encrypted in your browser and nobody else has a hold of it.

I think even for consumers, because — ironically, of AI — those solutions are going to start getting more powerful. Because one of the things I think we're about to learn, and to bring it all the way back around that the Hugging Face incident has started to reveal, is that large piles of data that are just left sitting there with access to the internet are all honeypots now. Every single one of these has become a target.

And I would tell everybody: you should assume 100% of what you're putting into one of those will be compromised on some long-enough time frame. Now, you may not care about that. If it's your credit card number and it gets compromised — great, just cancel it and get another one. But there are probably a lot of private communications that you're not going to want being spilled out into the world. Ram, like you, business IP is a great example, right? That's one that clearly people have a privacy interest in and there's nothing malicious about it. But I don't want my internal deliberations of some great new technology suddenly showing up on the internet on Wednesday.

二十三、"律师-当事人特权"能否延伸到 LLM？第四修正案的新战场

Well, yeah. I mean, you got to wonder: when do we see attorney-client privilege show up in LLM? Like, how do I get my lawyer in all the chats? That's going to be a nice unique value proposition to add out there. Because people share their most intimate thoughts with AI. Or medical privacy is another kind of related one, right? The most —

Yeah, it's a huge one. Like the most — boy, all this stuff really — it makes it sound like it would be a great time for somebody to put some legislation together that we might actually be able to pass. But speaking of being in the land of fantasy —

How about we live in the real world, David? Right? Like —

For example — let's not go crazy.

Like in the common law, you can't deposition or force testimony from the spouse to divulge information. Does that extend to AI, arguably, who has a deeper context than your spouse?

I would also suggest there was a recent ruling in a federal district court about Flock where they basically said: no, this is a search. The whole "hey, observing people in public is not a search" thing was predicated around those being individual and discrete observations. Like, the police saw you walk into the donut shop — that's fine. But Flock cameras creating a comprehensive visual record of all public spaces at all times is the equivalent of following that person around. That is a very different sort of search than "oh, we were incidentally there and saw them."

Ram, to your point, I feel like AI is posing a similar problem for the way the world is currently structured — which is, nobody really thought about: what if there's a device with all these connectors that has all of your context about all things? That is obviously much closer to somebody's papers and personal effects in like Fourth or Fifth Amendment terms in the United States.

Yeah. Well, it's the classic trade-off between security and liberty. And people historically have traded away liberty for convenience and security. And one of the remedies is you make that as local as possible. You make that — you attach it to the individual. And if you can't do that, you attach it to the municipality where there's more accountability on local elected leaders who are accessible — as opposed to say the federal government. So that's probably the right approach and balance to strike.

二十四、尾声：Chat Control 2.0、监控资本主义与节目结束

I would jump in there and just say a couple of things. One is that on this subject, I didn't know — I hadn't heard about the Flock ruling, Austin — but that sounds very positive to me from a civil liberties perspective. There had to be some reason this was not just normal. At the same time, we also saw — I think it was maybe either yesterday or early today — the European Parliament has rejected what people have called Chat Control 2.0, which was legislation at that level to get enforcement of back doors for encryption on electronic applications.

But on a more systematically, I would say, pessimistic analysis of this question — the other thing to keep in mind is that none of these entities are going to willingly give up their ability to gather and surveil all of your data, because that is a possible business model. And so from that perspective, I think we do need to look for outside pressure. I won't — I'm a fan of federal power, but on a situational basis.

You're a fan of federal power. Really?

I mean, I'm a — I think there sometimes needs to be some decisions made, and in this one —

That's true.

We're also seeing stuff around gambling where maybe I could see some federal — anyway, for debate. But the point being: I don't think these entities — I think there is some commercial pressure for entities like Brave to offer a more private option, and there will be an audience for those, no doubt. But at a macro level, you talked about convenience, Ram — I think that the business models feeding into the convenience factor…

I mean, one of the reasons Muse is such a big deal is because Meta is really good at designing interfaces. And those people who are really good at designing interfaces also work at companies that want to find every possible way to get money out of their users. So that dynamic, I think, demands some real scrutiny and perhaps enforcement.

Well, on that note, I will say we are past the 5:30 mark. So, rather than subject people to even ever creepier versions of AI avatars of myself and David that Ram has been building during this podcast, we will go ahead and call this one here.

So, as always, thank you everybody for joining us. Remember, we have our new channels. Go ahead and subscribe. We will be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding. David, thank you for joining us.

Great. David, that was fun.

Enjoy, everybody.

That was cool.

Thank you for watching, and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

## 一、"去美元化交易"的伪装：比特币其实在和软件股共舞
最反直觉的发现藏在数据的分裂里——如果真是债务货币化(debasement)主导的宏观叙事，黄金应该同步创新高，但黄金却徘徊在52周低点附近。Ram一句话点破：**比特币真正的"同类"不是黄金，而是软件股**。两者都是被做空、被厌恶、靠轧空反弹的"久期资产"。这意味着市场偷偷重新给比特币归类了：它不再是"数字黄金"，而是一只"流动性最充沛、估值最有想象力的科技股"。
这里有个被所有人忽视的跨领域连接：**当利率上升，政府债务利息支付反而成为对投资者阶层的隐性财政转移**。10万亿美元国债+5%利率=每年5000亿美元定向流入已经持有金融资产的人手中。所以利率越高，不是"紧缩"，而是对资产持有者的隐性QE。Austin说得克制，但真相更锋利——鲍威尔每一次按兵不动，都在给65岁的母亲加杠杆，给25岁的学生贷款者加税。这解释了为什么消费者信心史上最差、消费数据史上最强：**这不是一个经济体，这是两个经济体通过代际债券持仓发生虹吸**。
## 二、AI"对齐"思维的隐秘代价：它让安全工程师忘了怎么装门锁

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正被颠覆的不是帝国，而是"征服"这个概念本身

读完这段材料最让人震动的，不是科尔特斯多英勇，而是特拉斯卡拉州长官邸墙上的那组壁画——科尔特斯和西班牙人被画成与印第安盟友同等大小、平视对谈的伙伴，而不是教科书里居高临下的征服者。这意味着：五百年来我们熟悉的"西班牙征服阿兹特克"叙事，其实是胜者书写的单线剪辑。从特拉斯卡拉人自己的视角看，这是他们利用科尔特斯完成了一场迟来已久的区域清算，西班牙人只是外包的雇佣兵。更冷峻的数据佐证：最终围攻特诺奇蒂特兰的联军里，西班牙人只占 1/2 of 1%（0.5%）。按任何合理的会计口径，这都不是一次"外来征服"，而是一场由外来触发器引爆的美索美洲内战。

二、科尔特斯其实在同时打两场战争——而第二场更像现代商战

这段叙事里最被忽视的戏剧性时刻，是他把总督派来抓捕自己的那支更大规模远征军，用一场谈判外加小规模冲突，整建制转化为自己的增援。这几乎是人类历史上最早、最成功的"敌意收购反杀"案例：被派来并购你的对手，离开时反而带着你的股票期权。放在现代语境里，这就像一家创始人被董事会派来接管的"职业经理人团队"，用一次会议说服对方倒戈，把罢免行动改写成B轮融资。更深一层的意外之处是：他之所以能这么做，恰恰因为他自己是叛变者——没有总督合法授权的科尔特斯，比总督派出的"合法代表"更有资格许诺财富与土地，因为他的位置不受西班牙王室预算的约束。合法性反而是谈判筹码的减分项，这是一个在今天的政治学、创业学里都很少被讲清楚的反直觉结构。

三、火山硫磺与预制双桅船——这其实是一堂供应链管理课，不是军事史

真正让科尔特斯赢下第二回合的，不是火药，不是马，也不是钢铁，而是一个跨领域的工程—物流综合体： - 士兵用绳索吊入 波波卡特佩特火山口采集硫磺（原料的垂直整合）； - 船只被拆解成预制模块，由不计其数的印第安脚夫翻山越岭运到湖边（分布式制造 + 外包人力）； - 在特斯科科湖畔现场组装成双桅战船，完成湖面制海权（最后一公里本地化总装）。

这组操作放到今天几乎就是宜家 + SpaceX + 集装箱航运 的 1521 年版本：原料开采、模块化设计、分布式制造、本地化总装、形成系统能力。换句话说，阿兹特克人不是输给了枪炮，而是输给了一种更先进的"组织复杂性"。他们能动员的仍是朝贡体系下的人力与粮食，而科尔特斯能动员的是供应链——这在今天的中美科技竞争、乌俄战争里仍然是关键分界线。

一个额外的意外观察（跨领域连接）

奥通巴战役的那一刻特别有意思：阿兹特克人本来已经赢了，是科尔特斯识别出敌方主帅位置、集中骑兵冲阵斩首，才让战局整个翻转。阿兹特克军队在失去指挥节点后立刻崩溃——这是高度中心化指挥系统的典型脆性。有趣的是，用户在片尾用俄乌战争做类比，但更深的类比其实在系统论：阿兹特克帝国是一个单点故障密度极高的网络，它的朝贡体系、宗教中心、军事指挥、神—王一体的"ueytlatoani"全都压在同一个节点上。一旦这个节点出错——先是蒙特苏马被石头砸死、再是奥通巴主帅被斩——整张网瞬间塌陷。这与今天我们讨论的AWS 单区故障、SWIFT 制裁、半导体光刻机、乌克兰电网都是同一个结构问题：显得庞大，但只要你知道往哪里打，它比看起来脆得多。

科尔特斯真正的天才，不在于勇敢，而在于他本能地理解了网络拓扑。

📝 转录文本

开场：被忽略的事实——西班牙人内斗

What people might not appreciate about what happened here, in both the Pizarro story of the Inca Empire (which we'll talk about later) and in the Aztec story, is that in both cases the Spanish were themselves divided — and in fact fighting each other.

So, um, maybe you should tell the story: how Velasquez sends another expedition to go capture and arrest Cortez for going beyond the prerogative of his mission.

委拉斯开兹派兵抓捕科尔特斯

Absolutely. We left the governor on Cuba, of course, fuming. Um, he rallies another expeditionary force, because Cortez is stealing his thunder, right? And he sends this under Pomayz — a larger force than the one Cortez brought with him originally. This lands on the coast.

Cortez appreciates he has to move. So he leaves one of his subordinates, the hotblooded Alvarado, behind in charge in Tenochtitlan. He takes as many men as he can to the coast, confronts Denias, defeats him in a minor battle. And again, the diplomacy wins over the entire expeditionary force that the governor had dispatched. He tells them, "Uh, my friends, why are we fighting? We have the empire at my disposal. Join with me and we can share in the riches." So he wins over the vast majority of this new force. It becomes, effectively, reinforcements.

阿尔瓦拉多的屠杀与"悲伤之夜"

He marches back to the capital. Uh, he finds the mood has turned against him. The problem with not being in charge is you can't be everywhere. His subordinate, assuming that the Aztecs were mobilizing against him, decided on a preemptive strike. There was a festival — the aristocracy, particularly the warrior caste, were celebrating — and Alvarado just descended on them, massacred everybody.

Um, the survivors rally the population, and when Cortez returns, he finds himself effectively under siege. The people are so appalled now with the failure of their Hueytlatoani; when he tries to pacify them, they throw stones at him, mortally wounding him. He either dies, or the Spanish finish him off because he's of no longer any use to them.

So now Cortez is trapped in the city, in Tenochtitlan. He determines to break out — and that is to say, La Noche Triste, the tragic night, because so many of his men are left behind. They're either killed as they try to escape the city across the causeways, or forced to retreat back to the palaces, and they're taken alive and sacrificed subsequently.

奥通巴战役：斩首战术扭转败局

Cortez gets away with a minority of the troops still at his disposal, um, and makes it back to Tlaxcalan territory.

That was the critical aspect — the two features of the entire campaign. One: he has enough strike power, with enough horses, to defeat the Aztecs when they try to finish him off. The Battle of Otumba — they feel he's on the run, they have the numbers, the conquistadors are dragging their tails between their legs as they flee, Cortez himself is grievously wounded. "Uh, we can finish them off." And they had the numbers. They were winning. But again, Cortez identifies where the Aztec general is. He rallies enough horsemen to blast through the Aztec ranks and take out their command and control. The Aztec army disintegrates, and the Spanish were able to flee.

So, the battlefield advantages — they had their horses, their steel, critical — but just as critical was the diplomacy. If the Tlaxcalans had turned on Cortez at that point, he would have been finished. Not one Spaniard would have survived; none of them would have made it back to the coast.

特拉斯卡拉人的视角：壁画里的"平等"

But the Tlaxcalans see — for their own reasons, not out of any generosity or humanitarian impulse to welcome back the conquistadors — they still see, "We are committed to these people and to our alliance." So they give Cortez shelter. He recovers physically, begins to rebuild his strength, and is determined to go back to Tenochtitlan for round two. And this time, "We're not going to be indulging diplomatic niceties."

The Tlaxcalans — their own perspective on this: if you go to Tlaxcala, the territory today, the governor's mansion there has murals on the wall, and these depict Cortez and the conquistadors from the Tlaxcalan point of view. And it's fascinating to look at how the relationship is not between a superior and an inferior — it's between equals. You see them depicted in the same scale, engaged in diplomacy between partners, not between subordinates and dominant figures.

The Tlaxcalans drove a hard bargain: "We want territory carved out of the Aztecs. We want our own fortress in Tenochtitlan after this is over." Uh, they saw this as them using the conquistadors — not the other way around — which is very important to bear in mind.

阿兹特克"帝国"的脆弱内核

That the Aztec Empire, from a distance, if you look at a map, seemed impressive — but this was an imperial construct, and not just the remaining independent entities like the Tlaxcalans, like the Tarascans (who we can discuss later), were hostile to the Aztecs. So were so many of their subordinated peoples: the Totonac coast, the Chalco states on the shores of Lake Texcoco. Um, they chafed under Aztec hegemony and authority, and they too saw the conquistadors as an opportunity to finally shrug off the authority, the demands, uh, of the Aztecs, and get revenge, in a lot of ways.

最终远征：0.5% 的西班牙人

So as Cortez builds up for the final campaign against uh Tenochtitlan — against the new Hueytlatoani Cuitlahuac, um, and then, after he died, his brother, the last of the Hueytlatoanis, Cuauhtemoc — um, he has indigenous people flocking to his banner from all over Mesoamerica, right? He's emphasized that he's still in the fight, he still has those advantages. More reinforcements are arriving at the coast, and they're being integrated into the conquistador army. But the force that marches on Tenochtitlan — the total numbers — the conquistadors were maybe one half of one percent in raw numbers of that force. The overwhelming majority were other Mesoamerican peoples, who see this as their final reckoning with the Aztecs.

技术与外交的整合：火山硫磺与预制战船

And this is the integration again of the technology with the diplomacy. Cortez knows: to take the city, he has to control the lake. And again, the innovations:

  • They need sulfur for their gunpowder — they have guns, useless without gunpowder — so an expedition goes into the mountains, to the volcano Popocatépetl, and they dangle with ropes inside the caldera of the volcano, scooping out the sulfur they need as the critical ingredient for their gunpowder.
  • Another one builds prefabricated brigantines — boats in their different sections — and then has untold numbers of porters, human load-bearers, bring these prefabricated pieces over the mountains to the lake. They're assembled, and then they're let loose in the lake, and now they have control over the lake, right?

So, bringing together the technology, the innovations, with the local manpower — and this is the force directed against Tenochtitlan in the final battle.

俄乌类比：敌人的敌人

I actually didn't know those stories. That's crazy. One of the ways in which — to the extent people are even aware of the story — they might not understand what actually happened, is they have this model of the Aztecs or the Incas as this cohesive single nation.

And I think a better model might be something like: imagine if Russia and Ukraine have been doing trench warfare for a hundred years, and imagine the animosity, and then also the Russians are, like, taking tens of thousands of Ukrainians and, like, doing human sacrifices with them. Um, and then, if some foreign force comes in and says to the Ukrainians, "We can help you march into Moscow" — right? I think they'd have pretty decent odds of getting some agreement there.

Absolutely. The old phrase is: "The enemy of my enemy is my friend." And diplomacy, war — that's always very bad.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 經濟數據危險，但為什麼股市還是創新高？Mark Yusko【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被动投资是"认知殖民"：市场的思考器官被切除了

Mark讲了一个表层故事：被动指数基金按市值加权无脑买入，让"思考者"被挤出。但真正令人毛骨悚然的是——这是一种格雷欣法则在"思考"层面的翻版。坏钱驱逐好钱，而被动资金正在驱逐"主动思考的资金"。

这意味着市场正在失去它最重要的器官：定价发现机制。当60%的美股由被动资金持有，股票的价格已经和"这家公司值多少钱"无关，只和"有多少钱必须买它"有关。SpaceX亏损60亿还能估值2万亿，不是因为有人相信它值这么多，而是因为没有人在被允许说它不值——做空会被挤爆，被动资金则必须按规则买入。

这里有个让我震撼的意外推论：AI泡沫的刺破点可能不在AI。真正的触发器藏在人口统计表里——婴儿潮一代到71.5岁必须从401k强制取款。这把一个科技故事瞬间翻译成了一个人口结构故事：被动买入的虹吸管快要掉转方向，而没有人在定价这件事。

二、"真相替代信任"与哥德尔不完备定理的奇异同构

Mark引用Scottetta和Haber对blockchain的原始定义时说了一句关键话："你需要一个裁判来监督裁判，然后再需要一个裁判来监督那个裁判……"

这不是金融问题——这是数学哲学问题。它是哥德尔1931年不完备定理的翻版：任何自指的形式系统都会撞上"元层级无限回归"的墙。传统金融系统（银行→央行→国际清算银行→……）本质上就陷在这个递归里，每一层信任都需要上一层来背书。

区块链的创新不在技术，在哲学：它用"分布式真相"打破了元层级回归，就像图灵机用"可计算性"绕开了希尔伯特纲领的死胡同。从这个角度看，Bitcoin的意义不是"更好的货币"，而是人类第一次在金融层面逃离了元逻辑陷阱。

跨领域的意外连接：这个结构也出现在物理学中（观察者问题）、神经科学中（谁在观察意识）、以及法律系统中（宪法谁来解释）——所有依赖"信任"的系统，终究会撞上这堵墙。Mark没说出来的是：clarity Act投票失败，不是政治问题，是数学问题——银行必须保卫自己在信任链条中的"中间商税收权"，否则整个元层级会坍塌。

三、"创新周期14年"藏着一个生物钟密码

Mark随口说了一句被人忽略的话："创新周期每14年发生一次，因为那是半代人（half a generation）"。

这个数字惊人地精确：1954大型机 → 1968微芯片 → 1982 PC → 1996互联网 → 2010移动网 → 2024区块链/AI。但为什么是半代？

这里藏着一个生物钟与科技钟的共振：14年刚好是一个孩子从出生到青春期的时间。换句话说，每一次创新浪潮的时间点，刚好让"上一代还在挣扎适应时，下一代已经在本能地掌握新范式"。父亲还在学微信时，儿子已经在玩Discord。父亲还在学ChatGPT时，儿子已经把它当水龙头用。

这意味着创新接受度不是教育问题，是生理问题——人类的神经可塑性窗口和技术迭代节奏之间存在隐秘的共振。而这又揭示了另一个令人不安的事实：老龄化社会的创新接受周期会被拉长。日本不是因为"保守"才接不住技术，是因为人口中枢的神经可塑性已经过了窗口期。Mark说日本"领先走向货币危机"——他看到了表象（entitlements），但没看到更深的病根：一个失去神经可塑性的社会，必然会用印钞代替创新。

四、一个你可能没注意到的黑色幽默

Mark提到：OpenAI + Anthropic + SpaceX 三家公司的估值 > 过去45年美国3365家IPO公司的总和。

但更黑色的点是：这三家公司都是Elon Musk和Sam Altman的朋友圈产物。换句话说，整个"数字时代的未来"目前被定价在约10个人的饭局估值上。这不是科技故事，这是宫廷经济——我们回到了美第奇时代，只不过把佛罗伦萨换成了旧金山湾区。

当"价值"由饭局决定、由被动基金执行、由媒体放大，我们已经不是在投资，而是在参与一场集体性的宗教仪式。Mark没有明说，但这是他真正的恐惧：泡沫会破，但破的方式会非常非常像一场宗教改革——痛苦、血腥、重塑所有人的认知坐标。

📝 转录文本

經濟數據危險，但為什麼股市還是創新高？

Mark Yusko 專訪｜邦妮區塊鏈

開場：三個泡沫、一個謎題

It will end badly. Those three companies — OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX — total value... there used to be a tethering of valuation to production of things called profits. Back in the '90s, we had an untethering for the first time and we had the tech bubble. Like, wait, isn't that the same thing that's going on now?

Bonnie：It is a little confusing. The Fed raised rates for the first time in three years. The Clarity Act failed to advance in Senate. And yet, Bitcoin has rallied and the NASDAQ just hit a record high. What is happening now?

Mark：There's a few stocks that are just going to numbers that just don't make sense to a lot of people. And part of it is — China's playing a really interesting game. They're buying up gold. We have a banking crisis. Nobody wants to talk about it. Scott Bessent the other day said, "We're the house. Bring it all." Who was going to buy our bonds? Every empire in history has fallen the same way.

Over the years, we moved increasing amounts of money into passive strategies, which are based on a simple rule called capitalization weighting. Now the problem is — all great wealth, all of it, came from concentrated positions. You really have three buckets that you need to manage.

嘉賓介紹

And so, pleasure to have Mark Yusko join us today. He is the founder and CIO of Morgan Creek Capital and managing partner of Morgan Creek Digital. And he spent more than 30 years investing across public markets, venture capital, technology, and digital assets.

So good to have you here, Mark.

Mark：Ah, thanks for having me. And I wish we could have done this in person in Hong Kong, but my travel plans got messed up, but it is great to do it virtually and thanks for having me on the show.

Bonnie：I'm sure I'm going to see you in person someday.

Mark：Very soon. Very soon.

一、Fed 加息、股市創高：到底在發生什麼？

Bonnie：Yeah. Let's talk about what's happening now because it is a little confusing. The Fed raised rates for the first time in three years. The Clarity Act failed to advance in Senate, and yet Bitcoin has rallied and the NASDAQ just hit a record high. What is happening now?

Mark：You know, that is the $64 trillion question really. And it's quite common for these types of things to happen where everyone focuses on one thing — let's say the Fed. And so everyone's like, well, if the Fed cuts rates, then everything will be great. And then not only do they not cut rates, they raise rates. And yet everything seems to be great.

I say stocks are new all-time highs. Now, if you peel back the onion just a little bit, it's not quite as great as it appears. There's a record number of stocks below their 52-week high moving average. The market has bad breath, shall we say. And yet there's a few stocks that are just going to numbers that just don't make sense to a lot of people.

全球流動性，不是美國利率

And part of it is a phenomenon related to actual liquidity in the global marketplace, as opposed — everyone focuses on the US, right? I find it funny. I live in the US and there's this American exceptionalism — like all the smart people live here and all the good businesses. I'm like, there's some really really smart people in other places and some really good businesses in other places and really good markets in other places.

But that American exceptionalism — well, if the Fed raised rates, then liquidity must be down. Well, if you actually look at M2 globally, it's actually rising. Well, why? China. And it usually comes back to China.

In most cases, if you look like in 2016 when the world looked like it was going into recession — oil prices were down to like $26 and people were freaking out, commodity prices were collapsing — suddenly we had this big rally. China printed $4 trillion of new capital and injected it, and it finds its way into the capital market.

中國在玩長線遊戲

So part of it is China stimulating. And China's playing a really interesting game. It's the long game. The long answer to your question — what's happening? Well, what's happening is China is stimulating to promote their technological evolution to be more of a consumer-based society rather than just the industrial powerhouse.

That's kind of what happened in America, right? We're the manufacturing warehouse and we had lots of pollution, and then we exported all that to China and China became the manufacturing powerhouse. And now they cleaned up a lot of the pollution — there's still some, but they're moving towards this consumption-based and more of a world dominance.

And the thing that they're doing that's really interesting — they're buying up gold. So they're bringing gold in to back their currency with a hard currency, while the rest of the world issues debt like it's going out of style in all the Western countries. Started with Japan, then Europe, now the US.

二、美國的銀行業危機沒人想談

So what's really happening in the US is we have a banking crisis. Nobody wants to talk about it. But when we had the industrial revolution part two going on in China, China bought a lot of our debt. 三、區塊鏈：從"信任"到"真相"

比特幣白皮書背後的哲學

And Scott and Stuart coined the term blockchain because he said: in any transaction where there has to be trust, you need a referee. But you then need a referee to referee the referee. Well, then you need a referee to referee the referee who's refereeing the referee. And that's just a chain of blocks in a system.

And so blockchain — trust is fine and it's worked for 800 and something years. But truth is better.

If I have a Bitcoin on-chain and I want to send it to you, I don't have to have a bank account. You don't have to have a bank account. I don't have to pay the bank a fee. What I mean by that is: there used to be a tethering of valuation to production of things called profits. And back in the '90s, we had an untethering for the first time, and we had the tech bubble. LLM 的真相：是工具，不是智慧

AI — I find it funny. AI is not what people think it is. LLMs are good tools. They're excellent tools, but they're computer applications. Everybody's like, "Well, they're this new thing. They're not a tool." Like, what do you mean they're not a tool? You type into them, they calculate probability of the next word in a sentence, and they give you an answer. And if they were trained on good data, they give you a good answer. If they were trained on bad data, they give you a hallucination.

Blitzy 的例子

I'll give you an example. I use it a lot to verify facts or gather information on competitive businesses. And we have a business that we've invested in that has this really cool application of an AI agentic tool. What does it do? They take companies in finance, government, military that have old code bases written in COBOL, this dead programming language. It's been around for 70 years, but they're too afraid to change it because — how do you fly the plane while you're fixing it? You can't just shut down the bank while you bring in the new system.

So this company — these guys from MIT — created this agentic tool that actually operates independently for about 3 weeks writing new code. And then the cool part about code: you can actually test it and see if it works.

So I made this investment in Blitzy, and I asked the LLM, "What's Blitzy's revenue?" They said, "Oh, a billion dollars." I'm like, "I'm 100% certain that's wrong, so try again." So it's not even a perfect tool. A perfect tool is a calculator. You put in 2 × 2 and you get 4, with certainty. Like, a quantum computer can't do that — it gives you 4 most of the time. But here's the problem. There are four definitions of intelligence. And an LLM fails all four. So it's not intelligent.

七、被動投資：價格與價值的脫節

And this goes back to the very first question we started talking about. You said, "What's going on?"

Over the years, we moved increasing amounts of money into passive strategies, which are based on a simple rule called capitalization weighting. And capitalization weighting, I think, is just a dumb idea. So the whole idea of market cap is silly.

But the way market cap works: every time new money goes into an index fund, whatever the market cap is of the company, it has to buy that. It can't ask. It's dumb — meaning it's rules-based. It can't think.

WeWork 的教訓

Perfect example — remember WeWork? WeWork was going to be this new-age real estate company. It was going to be a tech company. What did they do? They take buildings and they subdivide them and they rent them out in smaller units. That's been going on for hundreds of years. That's not new. That's not tech. Okay, you have a nice UI/UX, but it's not tech. It's real estate.

Real estate businesses trade down here. "Oh, we get a tech multiple, so we're up here." A thinking person would go short that. But the problem is the thinking people got displaced. Remember — bad money crowding out good. Bad models, bad passive strategies crowding out good.

So there's now more passive money than active money. And if you try to short stocks, you get squeezed by the big guys who take the other side. And so we're in this funky period where it's a self-perpetuating momentum strategy where success begets success. Now the problem is that works until it doesn't.

艾菲爾鐵塔曲線

If you look at all of the charts that go like this in history — every single one of them, they go like this. None of them go like this and then go flat or go up. They just don't.

Now, how far they go up the left side of the Eiffel Tower remains to be seen. But at some point, that virtuous cycle, which is the market cap weighting, buying more, turns into a vicious cycle where as the market cap goes down, the index is forced to sell.

And as the populations go from savers to consumers — like when you turn 71 and a half, you have to take money out of your 401(k). So we're not quite there yet. Most of the boomers are still under 71 — or maybe not most, it's about 50/50.
