九、人生的三個桶：Lifestyle、Get Rich、Stay Rich

I'll leave you with this. So if you think about your life, you really have three buckets that you need to manage. You can think about it side by side. I like to think of it as — this bucket drips into the big bucket in the middle, and then there's this hole on this side and drips into the bucket at the bottom.

Bucket 1：Lifestyle Bucket（10–15%）

So the bottom bucket is your lifestyle. It's your spending. 10 to 15% to live. And the hole in the bottom can be small or big depending on how much you spend.

Bucket 2：Get Rich Bucket（10–15%）

Up in the right hand corner, you got the get-rich bucket. That's the 10 to 15% to do the brother-in-law's condo deal or the friends venture deal or whatever. I would say you're going to lose all that, so keep it small. Now, you're not going to lose it all, but that's the get-rich bit.

Bucket 3：Stay Rich Bucket（70%）

But in the middle, that 70% is your stay rich bucket. So either your get-rich bucket or your income flows into your stay-rich bucket. And your stay-rich bucket should be diversified.

Because the interesting thing about investing — all great wealth, all of it, came from concentrated positions. Concentrated stock position, concentrated real estate position, business ownership. But all small fortunes come from concentration.

How to create a small fortune? Have a large fortune and stay concentrated.

Because there are cycles. Over 30 years, 85% of the companies in the S&P disappear. So over a long period of time, natural selection takes over. So don't ride forever. You got to change. You got to go with innovation.

十、比特幣是不是例外？

So this is what I was going to say. In that savings bucket, you have three time horizons.

5 年內：流動性

In the next five years, you want to immunize those liabilities. Maybe you got to save up for a car. You got to save up for kids' college. You got a big vacation you want to take. You want to buy a house. In that five years, you need liquid. It could be bonds, it could be Stretch, it could be converts — anything where you're getting an income that's guaranteed by something for those five years. Do that.

5–20 年：股權風險

Then in that 5 to 20 year range, you got to take equity risk. Equity risk can be private equity, common stock equity, real estate equity, any type of equity.

And equity — think about investing, there's four ways you make money. All of them require you to take risk. If you take no risk, you get the risk-free rate, hence the name. That equals about 4% long-term, which roughly equals inflation. So if you leave your money in cash, you basically stay even. Now, lately, you've lost because of currency devaluation, but that's another story.

  • Cash / risk-free rate — you make no money
  • Credit risk — buy a bond, make 2%, 3%, 4%; something like Stretch, maybe you make 8% above risk-free
  • Equity risk — 7% above risk-free, 10–11% long-term — because equities are a contingent claim; you only get paid if the bond holders get paid back

Oracle — great example. Oracle bonds are collapsing, their yields are exploding because people are concerned that they don't have enough money to pay the bonds back. Well, if they can't pay the bonds back, the equity should be worth a lot less, and the stock just keeps going down. So equities have risk, but when they work out, they're fantastic.

20+ 年：黃金與比特幣

For that period over 30 years where your biggest enemy is currency devaluation, you have to own gold and Bitcoin. You have to, because it's the only thing — and collectible cars, art, fine wine, some real estate, anything that's scarce. But I'm going to argue gold and Bitcoin at the core. And if you want to have some Pokémon cards and some cars, fine. But those scarce assets are the only thing that will protect you from the long-term ravages of inflation.

And Elon said, "My company is worth $1.75 trillion." Like, based on what? And then Anthropic came out and said their TAM was $30 trillion for them. Annual? You realize the GDP of the United States is $31 trillion?

Jensen Huang 的數學問題

So your company — and look, Jensen said something similar. Jensen Huang, smart guy, way more important than me, he's richer than me, great representative of the country you're living in. He said, "Well, one 1-gigawatt data center can generate $600 billion of revenue with my chips."

But wait, Jensen — the total profits of the S&P 500 companies, 500 companies, was $2.1 trillion. So you're saying one data center — and there's like 184 gigawatts trying to get built — one is going to generate $600 billion? That's 30% of the total profits of the S&P. That's just not going to happen.

I mean, I'm not going to spend 30% of my profits on Frontier Models. I'm just not. I spend zero dollars until such time as someone gives me something that I want to spend money on.

十二、下一個大機會：亞洲資本流動

Bonnie：One last question before we end this conversation — it's been great by the way. Would you say the next big opportunity would be in maybe Chinese stocks or Asian markets?

Mark：I think global capital flows matter, and they matter in places like Japan, and they matter in places like China. Everyone's been focused on US — all the money's been flowing into US companies. I think that will shift. Will it shift tomorrow or next quarter or the next quarter? I don't really know.

Howard Marks 的智慧

But the thing about buying value — Howard Marks, everyone loves Howard, and he just wrote his latest letter, and he says: you don't get to buy at the bottom. You have to buy on the way down, because it never stays at the bottom very long. When it finally decides to turn...

You saw this with Bitcoin, right? It was $58-60k for a while. Very few people bought it. And then — bang, it's $86k, and they're like, "How did that happen?" Well, that's entertainment. You had to buy it on the way down, because once it decides to bounce, it's violent.

Mrs. Watanabe 現象

I think what will happen — slowly but surely — you saw this in Japan. There's the infamous Mrs. Watanabe, right? The woman controls the purse strings, and she would eventually become an investor, and she would build.

So I think the same thing will happen in China. They'll eventually have the Charles Schwab-ification, and it's already happened. There's lots of day traders in China, but I think what'll happen is the average middle class family will start to graduate to having things like 401(k)s and savings and retirement plans and savings accounts and equities, as opposed to trading accounts.

結語

Bonnie：Mark, that has been wonderful. I hope you come back soon. I find this very insightful. Thank you for the conversation.

## 一、被动投资是"认知殖民"：市场的思考器官被切除了
Mark讲了一个表层故事：被动指数基金按市值加权无脑买入，让"思考者"被挤出。但真正令人毛骨悚然的是——**这是一种格雷欣法则在"思考"层面的翻版**。坏钱驱逐好钱，而被动资金正在驱逐"主动思考的资金"。
这意味着市场正在失去它最重要的器官：**定价发现机制**。当60%的美股由被动资金持有，股票的价格已经和"这家公司值多少钱"无关，只和"有多少钱必须买它"有关。SpaceX亏损60亿还能估值2万亿，不是因为有人相信它值这么多，而是因为**没有人在被允许说它不值**——做空会被挤爆，被动资金则必须按规则买入。
这里有个让我震撼的意外推论：**AI泡沫的刺破点可能不在AI**。真正的触发器藏在人口统计表里——婴儿潮一代到71.5岁必须从401k强制取款。这把一个科技故事瞬间翻译成了一个**人口结构故事**：被动买入的虹吸管快要掉转方向，而没有人在定价这件事。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：这份榜单的"沉寂"恰恰是爆发的前兆

Olivia 轻描淡写地提到"这次只有 11 个新面孔，是历届最少"——大多数人读到这里会以为市场在固化。但真正的信号恰恰相反：消费者 AI 正处于"品类坍缩"的临界点。

想想看：Perplexity 当年用了多少年才做到 10 亿美金 ARR 广告？而 OpenAI 几个月就到了。当新进入者减少、却伴随顶部玩家指数级膨胀时，这不是行业放缓，而是从"工具竞赛"切换到"注意力沉淀"——就像 2010 年移动互联网的 App 爆发期之后，到了 2013 年新 App 大幅减少，但 Instagram、Snapchat、Uber 的用户量却在那两年真正起飞。AI 的 2013 时刻正在发生。

二、一个藏在数据深处的悖论：越私密的 AI，越难形成网络效应

这是整期最被低估的洞察，但 Olivia 一句带过了：

"这个软件比历史上任何产品都更了解我们……可你真的想把这种亲密性引入和他人的互动中吗？"

把这个问题放到跨领域看，你会发现一个惊人的对称：AI 助手正在变成"数字版的心理治疗师"。心理咨询之所以从不发展成社交网络，恰恰因为其价值建立在单向、私密、无评判之上。治疗师不会把你介绍给另一个来访者，否则治疗关系立刻瓦解。

这意味着：消费 AI 的"社交化"可能根本不是未来，而是一个范畴错误。真正的多人价值不会来自"把 AI 介绍给朋友"，而会来自代理与代理之间的交互——你的 Muse 和我的 Instinct 代表我们各自谈判、协作、交易。这才是 agent 时代真正的"网络效应"：不是人际网络，而是代理人际网络（agent-to-agent network）。这件事还没人系统做出来。

三、"4.5% 用户贡献 85% 订阅收入"揭示的更深结构性真相

数据层面大家都注意到了"头部用户 1% 月花 \$93"——但真正值得警觉的是 Olivia 自己说的一句反直觉主张："我其实不希望这 4.5% 的付费比例继续扩大。"

一个消费 AI 投资人为什么不希望付费用户变多？因为她看到了一个被忽略的历史模式：消费互联网史上，所有真正的巨型公司（Google、Meta、Amazon、Uber）都不是靠订阅起家的。订阅是一个"工具型产品"的收入模式，而巨头都是靠交易费和广告，建立在"用户即产品"的反转之上。

这里有一个跨领域连接非常锋利：AI 行业目前的订阅主导，像极了 1998-2001 年的互联网付费墙时代——那时候 Salon.com、Encyclopedia Britannica Online 都靠订阅，所有人都觉得"内容值得付费"。真正改写格局的是 Google 用 AdWords 把搜索免费化，把成本藏到广告商口袋里。

所以 Eugenia Kuyda 那句"人们不是在寻找节省时间，而是在寻找消磨时间的方式"击中了全局：AI 的下一个巨头，不会出现在"效率榜单"里，而会出现在今天还看不到的"娱乐 / 陪伴 / 发现"榜单里。Suno、AI 微剧的爆发只是序曲。

四、彩蛋级洞察：Anthropic 的"克制"是一种被低估的护城河

Claude 付费订阅超过了 Gemini——尽管 Gemini 有 Google 整个分发引擎在背后。所有人都在归因于产品力。但看看这组数据：Anthropic 7.5% 的订阅者在 \$100+/月的 Max 计划上，Chat GPT 和 Gemini 这个比例只有 1%。

这不是"没有广告的选择"——这是一种阶级化定价的隐秘策略。Anthropic 在悄悄做的事情，是消费 AI 领域的"爱马仕化"：不追规模追密度，不追 DAU 追 ARPU。这在历史上有且只有一个成功模板——Bloomberg 终端。Bloomberg 从不打广告，用户也从不抱怨 \$24,000/年的订阅，因为它卖的不是信息，是身份。

Claude 正在成为"开发者和重度思考者的 Bloomberg Terminal"。如果这个判断正确，那么关于"AI 必须大众化才能赢"的叙事，可能完全错了。

📝 转录文本

The Current State of Consumer AI — a16z 播客实录

开场：个人代理，是这一轮最有意思的新趋势

Josh Elman： The most interesting big new trend is in personal agents.

We're in this world where we're so excited by what ChatGPT did with turning things into conversation, and now these agents we can get in our messaging apps to turn them into more conversation. There's this incredible paradigm.

Olivia Moore： About half of Americans report using AI. Around 4% of US consumers are paying a subscription to an AI product. The top 1% user is spending $93 per month personally on their personal credit cards on AI.

The reality is people are now building software. They're building these really rich products. They might be using their agents to write some of that code, but when they're delivering this whole experience to a user, it is much more than just a shim on the model.

Josh Elman： The run rate that OpenAI has reached through advertising — what does that tell us? That would previously take a company years and years and years to get to even after launching an ads product. What I'm fascinated to see in terms of the evolution of the ads product is…

主持人介绍

Elena Burger： Welcome to the a16z podcast. I'm Elena Burger, and I'm joined by Olivia Moore, who's the author of our ongoing Top 100 Consumer AI Apps report, and Josh Elman on our consumer team.

Today we're digging into the seventh edition of this report: - 谁在为 AI 付费？ - 为什么各大助手正走向不同方向？ - 以及，个人代理能否把日常琐事变成下一个大型消费业务？

Team, thanks so much for joining.

Olivia & Josh： Thanks so much for having us.

第七版报告的几个关键发现

Elena： Olivia, let's just get right into it. I would love to hear your top takeaways from this report.

Olivia： Yeah, so this is the seventh time we've done this list.

The very first time we only ranked all global websites that were AI-native by just traffic — like hits on the website. That worked then, because the way almost everyone was using AI was like a prompt-box product in a browser. We've had to evolve that a lot over the last few years as AI expands.

So this list is our most expansive yet. We added revenue data for the first time. We worked with the Yipit data to get specifically consumer card-spend data — so not accounting for enterprises or SMBs — and we ranked products by what consumers are actually paying for.

流量在趋稳，但消费数据揭示了另一张地图

I think, for me, the biggest takeaways from this report:

On a traffic basis, it looks like a lot of these products are kind of settling. We only had 11 new products across the web and mobile list combined, which is the least we've had in any of the prior editions of the series.

But the spend data really introduced a lot of new variables, because of those 50 that ranked for spend, 29 of them were not on either traffic list. And that also connects into the other big conclusion of the report — which is just how much of a power-user game consumer AI is right now.

幂律游戏：从企业端蔓延到消费端

Elena： That's something that's funny. We also recently released our State of Markets, and something that Sarah Wang actually commented directly on is — she said: hey, there's such a power-law game happening now. It's happening at the enterprise level, and it's happening at the consumer level.

So one thing that's probably notable is: yeah, we have the fewest number of newcomers on this list, and it seems like the space is ossifying — but I think the past few months things have actually been picking up a little bit more. And I think the most interesting big new trend is in personal agents. So what are you seeing? What are the big shifts that are happening?

OpenClaw 的落幕与新一代消费代理的崛起

Olivia： Yeah, it's funny. The last report we did ended right before the cutoff of when OpenClaw traffic would come in. We had done kind of a retro before we published, and we had found that it would have been very high up in the rankings.

This time, actually, OpenClaw is nowhere in the rankings because the traffic has completely declined. I think the team was acquired by OpenAI — they're probably working on the agent-assistant products there. But it's also been overtaken by some of the other attempts at prosumer agents:

  • Grockbot
  • Town (has some fantastic agents)
  • Dots now by OpenAI (which is new)

But also on the consumer side, we're finally seeing things that I would feel comfortable giving to a family member and telling them that they can safely use. Most of those, because this consumer-assistant trend has literally been the last three weeks to a month, didn't appear on the ranks yet. But we did pull the data to see what's happening with them — and it's been very, very fast growth, and yet still not quite reaching the mainstream user.

从"工具"到"替我办事"：OpenClaw 的开创性意义

Josh： We're in this really interesting era that did really change at the end of last year, beginning of this year with OpenClaw — that AI went from something we were using as a tool to enhance our productivity, maybe search for us faster, to something that would actually get things done for us.

OpenClaw was an incredible pioneer here. I know they're still doing a lot of work through their open-source foundation to continue to advance that. But it really turned a lot of heads on: wait, what can these products actually be?

We were seeing people buying Mac minis. We were seeing people run all their own data with their own local OpenClaw. There was a huge run on that. It was really inspiring to feel this new energy of what is possible.

Like most trends — the spark happens, it takes a while for those first products to get built, it takes a while for the momentum to then start getting those released in the market for users to see them. In some ways, this report is showing: that's what we're talking a lot about on our podcast in Silicon Valley, but this does a great job representing what's happening in the broader world. AI really is showing up everywhere. Even if there's not a lot of new entrants, all the entrants are all getting so much bigger.

Muse 与 Instinct：真正走向大众的消费 AI 助手？

Olivia： When we talk about pure consumer assistants, the biggest developments have been Muse and Instinct, I would say — although there's many other fantastic products that we list in the report. Poke was a very early pioneer here. Tommo has a very big audience and is doing incredibly well.

  • Instinct had announced like 100,000 users, growing 10% day over day. They had announced like 40% of users connected a credit card in the first three weeks, and they were spending over $1,000 on average in their first month.
  • Muse is interesting because, in many ways, a very successful launch — especially within the tech community. I think the number was like 500,000 downloads and 250,000 active users in the first 12 days or so.

But if you look at it versus Threads — another somewhat recent big splashy Meta launch — it still pales in comparison in terms of appeal to the average person who doesn't work in tech.

If you look at the downloads: Muse is still only US and Canada. So we grabbed the Threads US-and-Canada downloads only. In the first 22 days or so, Threads had about 16 million downloads, and Muse is still sitting around 5 million over that same time period.

分发策略的差异

Elena： Is the distribution mechanism different? I remember with Threads, it was already tied to your Instagram account, and there was this very natural distribution. Are they trying a similar strategy with Muse, or is it a different strategy?

Olivia： From my point of view, it's not as aggressive, for sure. Part of that is because there's a much higher cost to serve these users, so they don't want it to get too big too fast.

Josh： I also think Threads very much had a critical-mass effect — if they didn't get a lot of people on it communicating quickly, you don't actually get to that leverage of a new network starting to form.

Whereas Muse is still such a personal tool that they're pushing it, and it's very exciting to see this early adoption and people having these experiences. If you were using OpenClaw in January, you were having incredible experiences. Using Grockbot when that first launched earlier this summer / spring, you were having these incredible experiences. And now we're seeing — our moms, our families, people who don't just live on the "what's next in AI" cycle — I think that's what's really exciting about this consumer trend.

I assume when we do this again next time, we're going to see massive adoption. But it hasn't needed to push as hard to have that early network effect. I also think about what's going to make these things stick around for a long time — it is going to be things like network effects and marketplaces and all the businesses you can interact with those agents. That's going to be really transformative too.

平台生态与网络效应：Agent 时代的新护城河

Olivia： This is one of the things we talk about a lot when it comes to consumer agents and assistants — they are getting kind of the compounding effects of building out a platform, at least in terms of the ecosystem of other apps that are available and more easily usable by the agent.

We've seen that cut both ways: - Amazon is like: we're not going to allow Muse to browse and purchase products on our site. - But also, Muse has already hundreds of other partnerships — e.g., being able to buy things on Shopify.

人际网络效应仍是未解之谜

I still don't feel like any of the assistant products have unlocked person-to-person network effects. Part of this for me is: this software knows us more intimately than any other product in the past — based on email, but also I find myself telling extremely personal things to my AI.

So there's this natural tension: the more useful the product is to you as the consumer, the more it knows about you — and then do you really want to introduce that into other contexts with other people? It's the same thing as many people having a separate ChatGPT work account and personal account, and no one has quite cracked that yet.

隐私、安全与信任，是增长的真正瓶颈

Josh： As we talk about consumers and AI, privacy, safety, security are becoming more and more important.

There's the overall trends of trust in AI — this belief that AI is good for the world — that is in some ways affecting adoption and the excitement around these products. But on a very personal level: if you don't trust the thing that you're giving your most intimate access to — your email, your life, your credit card — and it might do rogue things that you wouldn't expect, or share things with other people you wouldn't expect — that's going to be the biggest impingement on these things really growing as massive consumer apps.

We're in a fascinating time where we're all learning these new norms. As people, we're actually very good at it: we're good at knowing what information we're comfortable sharing, what information if somebody gives it to us we're trusted to be able to pass on or should be protecting. And we're all of a sudden expecting software to do this too. It's a very interesting new set of things we're learning.

内外两股力量：平台的开放 vs. 用户的意愿

Elena： You both just brought up two interesting facets of this.

  • There's an endogenous force: all of the platforms and how they allow agents to interact with them.
  • And a more exogenous force: how comfortable am I using this, how I feel about the agent.

(Maybe I mixed up endogenous and exogenous — one is on the outside, one is on the inside: what the platforms are doing, and how you feel about it.)

Which do you think is going to get resolved sooner, and whose responsibility is resolving those questions?

用户舒适度，比平台能力演进更慢

Olivia： I think what the platforms are capable of is improving faster than true consumer willingness to use them — which we've seen throughout AI so far.

It's interesting because a lot of people are seeing these numbers that founders of these assistant products are posting — that it costs like hundreds or thousands of dollars a month to serve a user. How is that possible? I was stumped as well.

But I've been working with David Pollon, who runs assistant benchmark — who's fantastic (there's a recent podcast with him). What he's done: - Created a website tracking over 170 agents (I checked it last night; it's probably 200-something this morning). - Users use them and rank them on success on different tasks. - He also hosts group chats and communities of early adopters — a group of 1,500+ users.

He pulled some cool data for us: what are they doing with agents, what are they talking about doing with agents? And the vast majority — the number one use case — was still coding and technical automation, even for these consumer-assistant products like Muse and Instinct.

So under that framing, it's like: of course it costs that much. When we talk to some agent or assistant products that are aimed towards the more mainstream consumer, they're seeing costs in the tens of dollars, not the thousands of dollars a month.

So I think that is maybe a representation of the fact that we have a very long way to go in terms of consumers getting comfortable with these products.

普通人缺的是"模仿样本"

Josh： People who've been coding and have been working with AI — I mean, it's been such an incredible enhancer, and that shows up in a lot of the data on the Top 100.

But when you just hand this to somebody new, it feels like a blank box: what should I do with this? Maybe there's examples of getting a reservation or booking a flight. But if you're not actively seeking a reservation or booking a flight, it's hard to figure out how to personalize it.

So much of what we do as people is: we learn from others, we get these great ideas, we try the things people tell us. So much of how social media has worked is: people put things on social media, and other people see that and try the same thing, and then it spawns these effects. People make a little riff on it, and those riffs become cascading snowballs.

With AI, because so much of it's so personal, we haven't seen any of that flourish yet outside of areas like coding and productivity. All of the creative work — "I created this incredible video" / "How'd you do that?" / "I used AI." Those tools have been growing and are here. But it's so interesting that we have to figure out how to mainstream this.

消费 AI 的"收入几何学"：少数人撑起整片市场

Olivia： If you look at broad usage data now — about half of Americans report using AI, and about 25% of Americans think they are interacting with AI probably close to a daily basis.

But the spending data is much more concentrated: - Our Yipit panel shows sub-5% — around 4.5% — of US consumers are paying a subscription to an AI product. - Some sources say as low as 2 or 2.5%, or maybe a little higher. - It is expanding — doubled from a year ago.

But even within that top 4.5% of people who spend: - The top 10% of them are more than half of the revenue. - The top 1% are 20% of the revenue. - The bottom 50% are only ~16%.

So the top 10% of users are driving this market.

把收入拆到"每个人"身上

This was the other interesting thing about revenue data — we could look at it on an almost person-by-person basis. Who are these people spending on AI?

The top 1% user is spending $93 per month personally on their personal credit cards on AI.

Elena： Wow.

Olivia： And the median is spending $25. All of this is within the only 4.5% who are spending at all.

It was also helpful because we could see what products they're actually spending on. Unsurprisingly, it was mostly developer tools, productivity tools, creative tools — things used to build, make, sell: n8n, Granola, Higgsfield, Manus. All over-represented amongst the top spenders.

一代新的"创造者"正在诞生

Josh： In a way, this is actually really cool. Even though these numbers aren't everybody yet, we're enabling this whole new generation of makers — people who are not just using this for work, but using their personal credit cards to code things they never coded before, make art, make videos, make content, and really have this power of making.

If you're spending $900 a month on a set of AI tools, you're really using that to hopefully make things faster, better, have more ideas in your head coming to life than ever before. When I was looking at the categories between creativity and coding — that's actually hopefully really powerful.

开发者心态 vs. 普通人心态：杠杆视角的鸿沟

Elena： I think this is a point that's really important. Developers and coders are people naturally attuned to asking: how do I get leverage over this thing? How do I build a product that gives me leverage over my time? AI obviously supercharges that.

But it's a specific kind of mindset, a specific worldview. Part of my understanding of these numbers is: it's still a worldview reflected only among a smaller group of people. The question might be — how do you expand that worldview? How do you help people understand: here are all the ways you can get leverage over your time and life?

Eugenia Kuyda 的那句话

Olivia： We talked about this in the report — areas where we have not yet seen AI-native startups pop up.

Eugenia, who's one of our portfolio CEOs — she runs a company called Wabby, which is fantastic — has this great quote. I'm probably going to butcher it, but it's something like:

"Most people aren't looking to save time. They're looking for ways to spend their time."

This is why social media, entertainment, Netflix, TikTok, YouTube are the most-used consumer products we have. Much of what we've seen in AI thus far is: how do I do this thing a little bit faster, easier, more impressively. And that's not an incredibly compelling daily or hourly active value proposition for most people.

从"省时间"到"把脑中想法变现实"

Josh： Saving time is still very much a hyper-productivity, work-or-creativity focused group. But I'm also seeing the next wave of people who used to be coders — people who want to make videos but never quite mastered Pro Tools and Adobe Premiere — all of a sudden able to sign up for these things and take the ideas in their heads and make them happen.

I look at these numbers as: we're still so early. The fact that we're even here, that 1% of people are spending $900 a month — I see these as harbingers of what's to come as more people feel empowered to create. It's not about saving time. It's about the joy of actually willing this thing into reality.

There were all these jokes of people in the peak phase of using OpenClaw for the first time — their agents, they'd walk around with their computers and laptops open, they'd say: "I'm not sleeping. I'm coding and I'm making things more than I ever have."

为什么 Olivia 不希望"付费人群"继续扩大

Olivia： I actually don't necessarily want to see that 4.5% of people paying for AI products directly expand — which is maybe controversial because I invest in consumer AI products and I'm a consumer AI maximalist.

The reason I say that:

Substantially all of the consumer AI revenue thus far has come from direct subscriptions.

On this list, we looked and it was like 85% of our web list monetized via subscriptions. Another 62% monetized via credits or token / extra-usage payments. Only like 13% had ads or other options where you are the product instead of paying for the product.

If you look back at the history of the consumer internet, that's a pretty unnatural inversion. Almost all the really big consumer-tech companies we have now make the vast majority of their revenue from ads or transaction fees, not subscriptions. Because most people don't have the funds — or don't want to spend their funds — on software.

If you look at the top 20 consumer subscription products globally: ChatGPT is already on there, which is crazy in like 3.5 years of growth. Almost all the others are media companies or big platforms like Amazon or Uber, where you have very frequent purchase behavior.

So I'm a big believer that we need to move — we have transcended the need for everyone to buy a subscription to AI, and we need to see these other business models come back.

为什么以前的"烧钱—后变现"不管用了

Josh： We're still at the early days of inference costs coming down. Still early days of people finding ways to run lower-cost models to build great products. As they do that, a lot of the other business models that have always been on the internet — transaction fees, ads — will finally start working. We need that to happen.

That's where we're still in the sort of: "well, if it's going to cost me a lot to serve, at least let me just charge money so that people pay for it," which became the early default.

Olivia： You can probably speak to this from seeing many prior eras of the consumer internet, but it used to be — at least for me as a consumer investor — if a company was making money in the first five years, it was: whoa, what's happening?

The rule was: let's build density of users, and because they cost near zero to serve, we can wait and make money via ads or start charging for transactions once we have liquidity and density. That just isn't the case given how high COGS are.

Josh： This cost thing is a really interesting challenge, and companies get afraid of growing too fast. If they grow too fast and they don't have meters on how they're charging for it, you can actually have out-of-control spend that's very hard to manage.

It's created this very different shape of what we see in the top apps right now. But again — we're all still so early. So much to build and learn: bring cost down, bring value up, introduce advertising and other ways to spend money. And if we subscribe to services we love and that's what we get continual value from — that's amazing too.

广告的回归：OpenAI 的 \$1B 跑率意味着什么

Elena： I think this is a great transition to talk about ads.

Your consumer top-100 report had a really interesting fact in there: the run rate OpenAI has reached through advertising. They're at a billion dollars now in annualized run rate on advertising. What does that tell us?

Olivia： The number was from August, so there's probably a chance it's reasonably higher a month or so later. They have been very slowly rolling out ads with a network of partners, and they're already at ~$1B annualized run rate.

That would previously take a company years and years and years to get to, even after launching an ads product.

Two interesting things:

  1. Real density. The last reported number a few days ago was 1.2 billion weekly active users — a real density.
  2. Deeper personalization. Hypothetically they should be able to charge more and have higher conversion rates, because they know so much more about you as a user. ChatGPT has launched things like "Log in with ChatGPT." I think a wallet is coming. You could imagine it becomes a much more compelling value prop for advertisers — and that just juices the ad business even more. But we'll see. Very early days.

AI 广告必须被"deftly"引入

Josh： There have been some really funny conversations about ads and AI. If you are talking to this incredibly personal thing, and then it's like: "let me tell you about health, let me introduce you to this crazy product that can help you lose weight fast" — that's not building trust with AI.

How do we as an ecosystem — these products are so different, so much more personal than ever before, giving you custom-tailored answers based on what it knows about you — introducing ads has to be done very deftly.

I've actually been really impressed with the OpenAI rollout of ads. When I've seen an ad, it's very clearly labeled, and actually feels like a natural part of the conversation I'm having.

One of the other shifts: people are starting to rely on ChatGPT for a lot more queries. It used to be: look up a fact, tell me the history of this, help me with my homework. Now people are going to it for real advice, shopping, trying to figure out where they want to go or what they want to do. Those are great opportunities — when you're in discovery mode, ads are often a great answer to help solve that.

More commercial queries and commercial intent create that opportunity. But again — it has to be done very deftly, not this weird interruptive thing where ads just get shoved into the conversation.

一个真实的 AI 广告体验

Elena： I'd be super curious how the unit economics on ads work. Presumably it's a lower-cost query compared to coding or image-gen. For OpenAI, what kinds of margins are they seeing on ads — super interesting question.

Josh, what kind of ads do you see? I don't get any ads — I guess I'm pro-enterprise.

Josh： I was doing a bunch of travel research recently and was going to be in New York for a few days. I started seeing ads for a couple of things going on in New York I might have wanted to do. I found that really useful.

I've started using it more for commercial shopping. I was looking for a special keychain that would have really easy separation for a valet key, and I was having trouble finding this on Google. I finally was like: "let me just go ask ChatGPT." I went back and forth, describing what I wanted, and it started giving me really good examples.

At the end, I said: "Great, and I'd also love one that's made in America." It actually found this incredible option from a factory in Detroit that often makes a lot of other metalwork and other stuff — that had this really cool key for me. If I had never had that chance to really go back and forth — no ads were presented in that conversation, but it was entirely open for ads that would have helped me find stuff — eventually I went to this website. I'd never heard of that company before. Great experience.

定向能力可能超过 Meta，并带动垂直领域

Olivia： So interesting. I feel like we may see — as they lean into it — OpenAI being able to do crazy good targeting. Even better than Meta, which previously was best-in-class, because they knew so much about you — but now you're having this live conversation.

I do think it'll help ChatGPT, but also support a lot of these more focused — almost verticalized, to use the enterprise term — consumer AI products.

Another company that has seen early success in ads is OpenEvidence, an AI product for doctors. It already has 50–60% density of all US physicians on the product. When you have that kind of density of a really valuable, targeted audience, you can advertise really effectively. There will be and should be more of those.

大模型三巨头：ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini 的差异化

Elena： Is it worth taking a step back and talking about OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini — companies and labs that have been on the list pretty much since the beginning? Are we seeing any kind of evolution in the way people are paying for these products? What can we surmise about the different kinds of users of all three?

Olivia： From the very first time we did this report, the main conclusion was: ChatGPT is the dominant global product by both usage and revenue on the consumer side. That continues to be true.

Everything below ChatGPT has seen more movements and shakeups.

  • ChatGPT is now ahead of Claude ~6x on the web.
  • Ahead of Gemini ~2x on the web.

Given a lot of usage is concentrated in power users who are paying, the revenue numbers could be even more useful here.

Claude 的意外赶超

Probably one of the biggest surprises in this report: we got a panel of US spenders, and Claude has actually passed Gemini in terms of number of paid subscribers — which is kind of crazy given Gemini has a much bigger install base and user base overall, and the natural distribution mechanism of something like Google.

That's a big accomplishment for Anthropic. It's come on the wave of a bunch of very successful product launches over the last few months — like Claude Design. It's also come from a lot more press, starting with the "Department of War" stuff all the way back in February.

商业模式差异：Anthropic 的"无广告"路线

The other main difference in how these products are monetizing — and ChatGPT still is far in the lead by monetization. They have around three times more paid consumer subscribers in the US than both Gemini and Claude.

But Anthropic has said very famously: no ads. So they're much more aggressive about subscription: - Around 7.5% of their subscribers are on the $100+/month Max plan. - That's like 1% for both ChatGPT and Gemini.

Those users naturally look different and are doing different things on the product, even in that paid user base.

创意工具：音频、图像、视频的三条分叉

Elena： Should we talk about creative tools? One thing that's interesting: all the big labs have gotten really good at creative tools. One thing Anthropic kind of famously abstained from — but then somehow achieved anyway — was creating an image model or video model. But now people are making images and videos because coding is so good at creating images and videos.

Interesting that they didn't build the diffusion model, yet they're still capable of doing image gen. But about the pure creative tools — the companies that have verticalized in that category — what are we seeing?

音频：labs 不碰的领域，Suno 和 ElevenLabs 独大

Olivia： Creative tools is very interestingly distributed in terms of who is succeeding where.

There are a few modalities where the labs have not focused energy and attention, for many reasons.

A lot of those are around audio — text to speech, music. ElevenLabs and Suno are now very reliably near the top of our traffic list, and also ranked very highly in our spend list.

The labs have so many things to do — building coding agents, building AGI. Does it make sense at this point to deal with all of the IP headaches Suno has had to go through and launch a competing music model? I don't know. In the meantime, Suno has been able to run away with a really strong lead.

为什么专业化工具仍然赢

Josh： I'm a big believer that the labs are going to do what they're going to do, keep growing, and are great baselines for everything. But in so many markets, you're seeing really specialized products — really focused, knowing their audience, that can build really custom things.

  • Suno — if you want to make music just for fun or something you're really producing, it's an incredible tool and speaks to you from the moment you start using it.
  • ElevenLabs — if you need voice and audio within the product you're making, it has a way of working and interacting that feels completely different.
  • Video tools, design tools even like Figma — designed to use deeply for the thing you're trying to express. They speak to designers, not to people who want to just skip that step.

We're going to see so much more value from these really bespoke interfaces — where the software layer of all the things you can do, the things you save, the way you interact with it become where the value sits. Not just the models.

图像：labs 吞掉了大众流量，但专业用户仍留在 Midjourney

Olivia： This is the second category of creative tools — images and video — that looks different from audio.

On images: OpenAI has really leaned into images quite successfully — Images 2.0 is very good for both creation and editing. And of course Google with the various iterations of Nano Banana and Veo.

They have candidly taken away a lot of the high-level consumer traffic that was previously going to standalone image generators. Midjourney was fairly high on our first-ever rankings; it has fallen off the traffic rankings completely. But on empower-users — if you look at the revenue rankings, Midjourney is back.

Power users still want the model that they feel has taste, has an aesthetic sense, that they can tune in a really specific way.

视频：野西部，中国公司有数据优势

That brings us to video — kind of a wild frontier right now. Chinese companies that can train on any data have a real advantage. Video is just so complex to generate — the visual, the sound, synced and looking a specific way. The more data you have to train, the better. They've been successful there thus far.

Agent 友好型创意工具的新机会

More broadly in creative tools — I'd be curious if either of you have experienced this: I've recently been asking Astra and other really powerful models to generate or edit creative for me, and it does a very good job and will tool-call to elsewhere on the internet.

I think creative tools that are agent-friendly and agent-accessible are going to increasingly see really compelling tailwinds.

把 Agent 当作创意编排器

Elena： It's actually crazy what you can do if you just empower an agent and say: "yeah, install whatever you want to install." I actually had Astra and 5.5 go head-to-head and animating some stuff for me — it just knew exactly what to do.

Josh： What I love about this: this is the tinkerers, the people at the edge, figuring out these capabilities. We're going to build products over the next year that are going to show up on these lists, because they're going to take all of this complexity of what you can do and package it up in a way that makes it really easy to use.

You think of this gap of "all AI vs. consumer AI" — it's exactly this movement of packaging these up and building great product experiences that really turns it into these things that sustain.

Olivia： It has to start with the tinkerers, and then they post on X, and then six months later we get a real product and startup out of it — or 12 different startups all competing.

跳出 Web：生产力类产品的全面兴起

Elena： Outside of the web window there have been a big proliferation of mature products: Granola, Whisper Flow, Superhuman. And obviously the ones that exist in chat and messaging — Instinct.

What are you seeing when it comes to distribution, and the kinds of products and users they're approaching?

"大扩张"：消费产品正快速变成企业产品

Olivia： Two interesting threads.

I wrote this piece maybe six or nine months ago called The Great Expansion — basically: why are consumer companies becoming enterprise companies so quickly? Things like Krea, Replit, ElevenLabs, Gamma.

Previously, Canva took six-plus years to have real team and enterprise revenue. What's happening is that they're very successful and growing via PLG — Whisper Flow and Granola are great examples. Because they are work-productivity related, they get pulled into enterprises, and then the founders are like: "oh, we got to add privacy and security and a team plan." Very effective, very low-cost distribution. Works really well for these tools that can be used personally but are work-adjacent.

Incumbent 的两难

Whisper Flow, Granola, Superhuman are another good example of a trend we've seen: incumbents being unwilling or unable to cannibalize their existing interfaces.

Classic example: Google. We haven't really seen them reinvent Docs or Gmail or Calendar for the AI age. I think it's even happening with OpenAI and Anthropic — they have been much less successful in anything that is not a launch within their existing ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or Claude Code interfaces.

Many of them have attempted to incubate killers for these many startups, but it is difficult from a product perspective to innovate beyond that — especially when they have so many other things on their plates.

产品与模型协同进化的"水涨船高"

Josh： All that's true. And we now, as we get used to some interfaces, we're still in such a period of incredible reinvention.

A lot of the reason we've seen so much growth over the past year, year and a half, is: the models got so much better. The people who had been spending time creating these incredible interfaces that were easy to use, natural, easy to share and get a team on — Whisper Flow and Granola were so easy to get started with — then would say: oh my gosh, now they've gotten so much better as the models have gotten better. The product's utility gets so much better too.

You build something great, but it may not do everything you want because the model capabilities weren't quite there. Then the models get better, and your product gets to explode in demand and utility. This rising tide lifts everything.

To think that we only have one or two companies that can build that experience layer — I think is what this sort of report debunks. Those are certainly some of the top companies, in these very general use cases. But the reason so many other things are growing: there's so many interfaces that get to be reinvented, and the rising tide lifts everything.

The infra value may still go to the model providers, or go to the other things serving inference — a whole different conversation. But what consumers are adopting are things that work for them, are easy to use, and bring into their lives.

大玩家与初创公司的生态位

Olivia： To continue to make the case for startups:

OpenAI and Anthropic in many ways are startups — but they have been so successful that they have become big companies with thousands of people. There are just so many extra considerations — a larger ship is harder to steer or turn around.

One of the companies on our revenue list this time is Plaude — an AI note-taker device that started in China in the east, and now has come to the US. You buy the device, and you can also buy a subscription.

OpenAI can and will do a hardware device, but as we've seen with them, everything takes longer when you're a big company. You have to integrate with maybe other existing products. There's more checks and balances it has to go through.

So I do think the big labs will continue to be very successful — there's a lot more for them to do — and startups will continue to find quite big windows of opportunity.

核心难题：模型变强时，你的产品是增强还是被吞噬？

Elena： It also sounds like the question for startups is: how do you build a product that — as Josh said — gets better as models get better, but doesn't get cannibalized as models get better? Which is an interesting sweet spot to exist in.

Josh： Part of the reason I was so excited to join Andreessen Horowitz a couple of months ago was this belief: the value really now is moving back to the software layer.

Now that we have these incredible models at our capabilities and we can access them, you can build really rich products that leverage the models. There are new innovations — like Jeb from Typesafe — that allow even developers to build things in new ways. We haven't even seen all the incredible new ideas that can be done when you have access to a model like that: fast, easy to integrate, gives you very structured answers back.

The creativity is back to the experience: the network you can build, the ways you can serve a lot of people and bring them together, using the models to be something powerful — but the context and the community really become the asset.

Almost every category has a chance to be reinvented. Some big companies will be able to make the leap and become the relevant company for their sector in the AI era. But not all of them will. That's where startups come in — to beat them to that punch and really be the best new possible experience.

Town 的例子：Playbook 作为新护城河

Olivia： To that point: I think a lot about compounding personal value — and hopefully eventually compounding multiplayer value that becomes like a lock-in to some of these startup products.

Example: Town — more on the prosumer end of the agent assistant. It can connect into all your systems — Slack, email, Google Drive — understand the context of you and your org, and then do things for you. I use it to write a lot of my emails, helped with a lot of this report.

It's easy for people to dismiss things like this as: "oh, it's just a harness" — which is now the slightly less derogatory term for wrapper, I guess. But Town has built these playbooks of who I am, what I sound like, that no other product has — and that I cannot easily take and migrate over to something that comes along tomorrow.

The difference between an email that is 99.9% sounds like me, and even an email that's 85% sounds like me, is the difference between spending 10 seconds to fix it and 10+ minutes. We'll see more products like Town — doing a really good job of collecting context and acting on that context to build playbooks around you — continue to be successful.

Josh： I try to avoid using words like "harness" and "wrapper," because the reality is: people are now building software. They're building these really rich products. They might be using their agents to write some of that code, but when they're delivering this whole experience to a user, it is much more than just a shim on the model, or a harness that brings some context to the model.

It's a really rich product and experience that happens to use a model as part of what makes them able to deliver that. That's really the excitement of where it's going. Many of these already are doing that. The next wave — they are all going to be these companies that have built so much more value. The model is just one piece.

未被 AI 征服的领域：下一轮消费 AI 的空白地图

Elena： Olivia, I think you referenced this chart that you made — maybe we can bring it up. All of the white space that still exists for all the product categories that exist in Web 2 and the pre-AI age. Maybe you can just talk through some of these categories — where are the big opportunities?

Olivia： The vast majority of pure consumers are basically using AI still as a replacement for search products, things like Google.

Maybe especially as you get into education use cases — kids are using it to write essays, or more expansively, homework help. Or people in the workplace to write emails.

But if you look at this chart, almost all of the areas where we've seen startups succeed thus far have been in and around that theme of getting things done: productivity, photo and video design and editing, search and answers.

还未被填满的类别

So many categories are wide open — many of them are what I'd call network categories where you need a multiplayer product.

  • Dating — we haven't seen it. There are certainly startups there I hope and believe will make future additions, but no one on the list doing dating now.
  • Recruiting — similar networks to dating in trying to make matches.
  • Social AI — we really haven't seen anything take off. Most of social AI is people posting AI-generated content on existing social platforms.

Then there are categories that look more like marketplaces: shopping, home buying, retail. We'll have to see if those end up living in agents like Instinct or Muse, or living as standalone products — or the next ones (there will be many) — or a mix of both. Perhaps your agent is calling the AI-native marketplace.

Categories like gaming and entertainment — the models just have not been good enough to produce content that the average person likes to watch (maybe with the exception of AI micro-dramas, which are blowing up). But I think that is coming soon too.

从"对话"到"视觉与故事"：下一个范式

Josh： We're in this world where we're so excited by what ChatGPT did with turning things into conversation — and now these agents we can get in our messaging apps to turn them into more conversation. Incredible paradigm.

But when you're shopping, you want to visually see options and explore, and have things customized for you, and be able to say: "I really like that, but I wish it had some piping on the collar" — and actually have AI help you both realize that, and maybe even get it made for you. Shopping has so much invention there.

Entertainment — we've barely started scratching the surface of the ability to tell better stories, to empower people to be better storytellers, which then creates these incredible networks of people consuming stories. TikTok was this incredible place where people came together and just created little videos — you see people around the world you're now watching. But there's still so much captured in people's heads that if only they could express their ideas even better. AI is going to help that, and we're going to have incredible new networks.

We are just at the cusp of all these categories. We've needed the models to get better so you could start to dabble in some of these ideas. As that happens over the coming years with new model capabilities, I still think the value is going to end up in this software layer in the process.

结语：Save Time vs. Spend Time

Olivia： This gets back to what we were talking about — products that help people save time versus spend time.

Almost everything we've seen in consumer AI is save-time. The spend-time — those end up often actually being amongst the biggest companies, if not the biggest ones. So we need that to exist. Many, many builders, I'm sure, are tinkering away on that right now.

Josh： Absolutely.

Elena： Absolutely. I think that's a great note to end on. Thank you both so much for joining, and absolutely make sure to check out the top 100 consumer AI apps, seventh edition.

Olivia & Josh： Thank you. Thanks for having us. We will see you for edition 8.

Elena： Yes. Yes.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的发现：这份榜单的"沉寂"恰恰是爆发的前兆
Olivia 轻描淡写地提到"这次只有 11 个新面孔，是历届最少"——大多数人读到这里会以为市场在固化。但真正的信号恰恰相反：**消费者 AI 正处于"品类坍缩"的临界点**。
想想看：Perplexity 当年用了多少年才做到 10 亿美金 ARR 广告？而 OpenAI 几个月就到了。当新进入者减少、却伴随顶部玩家指数级膨胀时，这不是行业放缓，而是**从"工具竞赛"切换到"注意力沉淀"**——就像 2010 年移动互联网的 App 爆发期之后，到了 2013 年新 App 大幅减少，但 Instagram、Snapchat、Uber 的用户量却在那两年真正起飞。**AI 的 2013 时刻正在发生**。
## 二、一个藏在数据深处的悖论：越私密的 AI，越难形成网络效应
这是整期最被低估的洞察，但 Olivia 一句带过了： > "这个软件比历史上任何产品都更了解我们……可你真的想把这种亲密性引入和他人的互动中吗？"
把这个问题放到跨领域看，你会发现一个惊人的对称：**AI 助手正在变成"数字版的心理治疗师"

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽视的"时间悖论"：恐慌本身正在制造反弹燃料

小陶的分析里藏着一个被他自己低估的洞见——当市场把加息概率从75%砸到18%，而美债收益率却仍在单边上行时，这不是"定价错误"，而是一种罕见的"流动性真空"。通常利率预期下行应该带动债券买盘，但现在债市"没有买家"。这意味着恐慌已经脱离基本面逻辑，进入了纯粹的仓位出清阶段。换句话说，真正的买点往往不是在"坏消息出尽"时，而是在"好消息也无人响应"时——现在就处于后者的边缘。这与2018年Q4、2022年10月的底部结构惊人相似：都是在利率-股市脱钩的最后一周见底。

跨领域连接：这场"AI泡沫辩论"其实是一场会计学 vs 认识论的战争

小陶把泡沫拆成"估值泡沫"和"盈利泡沫"，这个框架看似财务分析，实则暗合科学哲学里的波普尔证伪原则——估值泡沫是可量化、可证伪的（PE就在那里），而盈利泡沫是不可证伪直到它爆炸的（你永远无法证明"未来EPS没有水分"，只能等它被打脸）。这就解释了一个诡异现象：为什么所有AI空头的论据都是"故事"（电力瓶颈、折旧周期、循环交易），而所有AI多头的论据都是"数字"（capex指引、hyperscaler收入）？因为空头在打一场认识论战争，多头在打一场会计学战争——两边根本不在同一个语言体系里对话。而历史告诉我们：在数据被证伪之前，数字永远赢。这也是为什么2000年泡沫顶部是EPS拐头那一刻，而不是估值见顶那一刻。

最意外的观察：Meta卖算力给Anthropic才是整个视频里最被低估的"宏观信号"

小陶一笔带过的这个细节，其实是整个AI周期中最关键的结构性验证。它揭示了一个反直觉事实：AI产业链已经进入"二级市场"阶段——算力不再只是终端消耗品，而是成了可以套利、可以转租、可以证券化的"类金融资产"。这意味着什么？意味着AI算力正在经历和1990年代电信光纤、2000年代页岩油井位、2010年代云服务器一模一样的路径：从"自用资产"→"可交易资产"→"金融衍生品"。按照这个节奏推演，下一步会出现"算力期货"或"GPU租赁REIT"——而当那一刻到来时，才是真正的周期顶部。现在远未到。

更有趣的跨界联想：Anthropic愿意用2-3倍溢价买Meta的算力，这个价差本身就是一个隐含波动率指标——它测量的不是股价，而是"AI推理需求的紧迫度"。这是一个藏在产业链里的、比VIX更前瞻的恐慌/贪婪指数。如果你能持续追踪这个溢价率，你就有了比任何宏观数据都早的AI周期温度计。

第四部分：刻舟求剑 — 当下和2000年科技泡沫的对比

The second part is what I shared with you guys last weekend. I picked some that I think you might be interested in. I talked for more than two hours, so I can't share them all in this video. So I picked some that I think you might be interested in.

I compared this picture with the entire technology bubble of the year 2000.

两种泡沫的区分

When we talk about bubbles, we actually have to distinguish between two types of bubbles. One is called solid bubble (估值泡沫), and the other is called basic bubble (盈利泡沫). The basic bubble can be reflected in the previous EPS, and the solid bubble can be reflected in the previous PE.

So when we talk about bubbles, we must distinguish between the bubbles. It's not easy to say whether the technology bubble of the year 2000 will repeat now. Instead, we need to separate these two bubbles to see if there are solid bubbles or basic bubbles.

回顾2000年泡沫

Let's review the trend of technology bubbles in the year 00. The blue line is the previous-line market share price of S&P.

Let me share with you the key point here. If we look at the time of the entire technology bubble, forward PE is not that expensive. It's 22 times the highest, which is about 25 times the first point. Before the technology bubble broke, the first point was 22 times. So the interval is about 22 to 25 times. In fact, it is not much higher than it is now. Now, until Friday, the standard is about 19 times. But in the beginning of this year, in the beginning of 2026, it was 23 to 24 times.

Then the line in orange is the index. The line in orange is almost at the height before the bubble broke before August 31, 2000. At that time, the point of the index was 1518. The lowest point of this wave bubble is 776, which is almost a backflip.

关键的时间差：EPS拐点才是真正信号

But we can actually see a time difference here. What is the time difference? When the red line fell, on August 31, 2000, the pre-strike market profit rate of SPX500 on the blue line began to decline before that.

The same is the picture in front. The blue line is still the pre-strike market profit rate, but I changed the number of SPX to a pre-strike EPS or a pre-strike profit. We can see the profit of the previous position. Here I have a 66. 66 is the highest point of the previous position EPS.

If I put the highest point of the previous position EPS and the previous chart, the index, together, we will find that when the chart starts to fall or the bubble breaks, it is actually the starting point of EPS starting to fall. Then in the entire process of the fall in the index, we saw a drop in PE, a drop in the previous market market rate, and a drop in the previous EPS. In the entire process of the fall, we saw a double kill of Davis. But at the beginning of the fall, there was actually a problem on the basic side. When the problem of the previous EPS began to fall, the index began to fall.

对照现在的情况

So if we put the timeline to the current situation, like the picture in front, the blue line is the pre-strike yield, and the red line is the pre-strike EPS. We can see that from 2024 to now, the pre-strike EPS is all the way up. We haven't seen any EPS turning point. The blue line is indeed at a relatively low level, about 19 times. 19 times is relatively close to this year's low point, and not so far from March 2025. In the past year, we saw that the EPS of the previous stand was constantly rising, and there were no signs of a turning point. Then the PE of the previous stand or the market rate of the previous stand has been declining, from 23 times in the beginning of the year to 19 times now.

Now that we know the current situation, if we bring this situation back to the 2000 technology bubble, we can argue that is it possible that the pre-season or the preparation for the pre-season is falling now? In the pre-season preparation, we saw the PE, in the red circle, we saw the blue line, the pre-season adaptability dropped. At the same time, the orange line, the pre-season EPS, rose.

So if we have to go to the 刻舟求剑, we can assume that this year to now, the trend of the WTO is very similar to the time when the bubble of technology broke down. PE fell, and then EPS rose.

第一个结论：没有估值泡沫

So now I think we can basically make a observation or conclusion. What is the observation and conclusion? There is no solid bubble in the entire SPX 500. Because the solid is now at a relatively low position. Whether it is compared to this year's horizontal trend, this year's March or the March of 2025, they are not in a very high position. Or if we compare it with the technology bubble in 2000, it is now 19 times the level. The highest point was 25 times, which is not a very high position. Even when it fell from the beginning, it was also about 22 to 23 times. So the US stock is not there.

第五部分：盈利泡沫 — 逐一检验大科技

What's left is profit. I have talked to some foreign KOLs. They also think that the US stock is a profit bubble. That is, they think that the E in EPS is problematic. So on this basis, we need to disassemble which companies can affect the basic face of the standard of the standard of wealth.

When we talk about the basic face of the standard, we must not leave the big technology. Simply put, we need to answer the question of whether there is a bubble in the index.

I have already divided it for everyone. We are going to divide the solid bubble and the profit bubble. We have talked about the solid bubble. The remaining question we need to answer is whether there is a bubble in the profit. To answer whether there is a bubble in the profit, we need to answer the question of whether there is a bubble in the profit of big technology or the profit of semiconductor. If the semiconductor and the big technology profit have bubbles, then the capital of the capital is the bubble. We are completely repeating the trend of the 2000 technology bubble. And we are now walking in this decline.

逐一审视每家公司

So does the profit of big technology have bubbles? At this time, we are going to take a look at every big technology company. We want to see if Microsoft has bubbles. Does Google have bubbles? Including other 100,000, there are no bubbles in the end. Every company is basically different. This is why I will share all the financial reports of the big tech in every quarter. The most important thing is not the past quarter, but the future.

What I can confirm now is that we are about to enter the third quarter financial report. What I can confirm now is that there is no way that any financial report of any big tech will be bombed in the third quarter. All major tech talents are basically related to hyperscale. For example, Microsoft, Amazon, GCP, Google, these three companies, their profit will only rise, not only rise, but also accelerate, only rise, not slow down. And my expectation is that they will continue to adjust their guidance for the future. This is my confidence in these three big tech companies, these three hyperscalers. This confidence also comes from their financial meeting, including their previous investment.

To a certain extent, if we think that their previous investment can be returned, or we believe that their investment has been returned, then we should assume that their profits will accelerate.

老黄的罕见前瞻

And the assumption that profits will accelerate, if we listen to the financial meeting, should be a name tag. The largest silver in the semiconductor industry, the old yellow rare to put 2027 in the year 2027, 2028, the next year's future revenue expectation, all handed over to the market 70% or 80% of the revenue increase. In the past, the old yellow would give a quarter to two quarters, this time it directly gave a quarter of revenue to a quarter of a year.

So from my personal perspective, to answer whether there is bubble in big technology or whether there is bubble in semiconductor, I will start from the perspective of each company. So far, I have not seen any signal of the profit of big technology or semiconductor, the future profit. We can't talk about the past. Where is the bubble in the future profit? Until the future, I have seen some private signals from big technology or semiconductor companies' financial reports. Then I may have this worry.

为什么要看这么多公司？交叉验证

And why do I have to look at so many companies' financial reports? So many companies' financial reports, we can do a mutual verification between each other. If a company has a problem, it does not mean that the entire industry has a problem.

So, for example, a while ago, Meta started to sell garlic (算力), does it mean that the whole AI is slowing down? At that time, there was such a storyline in the market. But at that time, I told everyone that it was exactly the opposite. Because Meta's garlic is sold to who? Sold to Anthropic. Because Anthropic's drop is very good, so Anthropic is willing to buy garlic at this price of two to three times, and Meta is also willing to sell it. So the fact that Meta sells hash power does not mean that AI is slowing down. It just means that AI is in a very good place to be in this situation.

So if these big technologies or semiconductors have bubbles in their profits, I believe that we can see this signal from one or two companies' reports. And we can verify each other.

总结

So finally, let's make a summary. We take a trend in the current market and the bubble of 2001 technology to make a comparison.

First answer the first question. Is there a bubble in the current US stock market?

The bubble is divided into two parts, the solid bubble and the basic bubble. - The solid bubble: has no bubble. - The basic bubble: is a question of seeing people and seeing knowledge.

To answer the basic bubble, we must answer whether there is no bubble in big technology and whether there is no bubble in semiconductors. For the time being, from all the companies and the press conference, I did not see any company's future profits have a risk there. So I can't get this conclusion. I will not expect the next orange line to go up. Now the ratio is going up. Now the ratio is going up. This line will appear in the trend of the technology bubble in 2000.

But if we just go to 刻舟 to see, it is true that the trend of the current trend this year and the technology bubble in 2000 is very similar before the break-up. EPS increases up and down, and the valuation drops down.

That's it for today. See you next time.

item.description:
## 一个被忽视的"时间悖论"：恐慌本身正在制造反弹燃料
小陶的分析里藏着一个被他自己低估的洞见——**当市场把加息概率从75%砸到18%，而美债收益率却仍在单边上行时，这不是"定价错误"，而是一种罕见的"流动性真空"**。通常利率预期下行应该带动债券买盘，但现在债市"没有买家"。这意味着恐慌已经脱离基本面逻辑，进入了纯粹的仓位出清阶段。换句话说，**真正的买点往往不是在"坏消息出尽"时，而是在"好消息也无人响应"时**——现在就处于后者的边缘。这与2018年Q4、2022年10月的底部结构惊人相似：都是在利率-股市脱钩的最后一周见底。
## 跨领域连接：这场"AI泡沫辩论"其实是一场**会计学 vs 认识论**的战争
小陶把泡沫拆成"估值泡沫"和"盈利泡沫"，这个框架看似财务分析，实则暗合科学哲学里的**波普尔证伪原则**——估值泡沫是可量化、可证伪的（PE就在那里），而盈利泡沫是**不可证伪直到它爆炸**的（你永远无法证明"未来EPS没有水分"，只能等它被打脸）。这就解释了一个诡异现象：**为什么所有AI空头的论据都是"故事"（电力瓶颈、折旧周期、循环交易），而所有AI多头的

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Cortés took the Aztec Empire by taking its emperor hostage - Si Sheppard
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"认知协议漏洞"：这不是征服，这是一次"社会工程攻击"

大多数历史叙事把科尔特斯描述为军事天才或冷血征服者，但 Sheppard 隐藏的洞见更锋利：科尔特斯没有真正的授权。他对所有人宣称自己代表"伟大的查理五世神圣罗马皇帝"，但查理五世根本不知道他是谁。他是在凭空"表演"主权——用一个尚不存在于当地认知体系中的身份框架，强行写入对方的世界模型。

这与计算机安全里的 缓冲区溢出攻击在结构上惊人相似：攻击者注入一段系统从未设想过的指令，而系统因为"缺乏对应的异常处理分支"而直接执行它。蒙特祖玛的"心理崩塌"并不是胆怯——而是他的操作系统没有处理"外来陌生人直接夺权"这个输入的协议栈。活活烧死官员这一刑罚之所以能让整个宫廷在"冷静的沉默中"旁观，是因为那同样是一种 Aztec 认知体系里不存在类别的暴力。科尔特斯真正的武器不是火枪，是范畴外事件。

二、"把 CEO 带走就等于把公司带走"——一个跨千年的治理结构漏洞

Sheppard 对蒙特祖玛的翻案极具颠覆性：允许科尔特斯进城不是错，错在自己留在城里。这指向一个被反复验证却从未被真正解决的治理原理：

中心化系统的脆弱性，与它的效率成正比。

同样的逻辑贯穿了： - 恶意收购：敌意并购方只需控制 CEO 和董事会，不必接管每一家分公司。 - 病毒生物学：HIV 不杀死每一个细胞，它劫持 T 细胞的"指挥节点"。 - 政变政治学：从罗马禁卫军到现代"斩首行动"，都是攻击"决策节点"而非"组织肌肉"。 - 区块链设计哲学：中本聪的全部设计就是对蒙特祖玛错误的一个千年回应——让系统失去"可被劫持的皇帝"。

有趣的是：蒙特祖玛的弟弟 Quitlahuac 其实预言了结局——"若让此人入你家门，他将夺走你的家。"这句话几乎可以直接写进现代风险投资的尽职调查手册。

三、翻译者 Doña Marina：历史真正的"API 层"

最被低估的角色不是科尔特斯，不是蒙特祖玛——是那位夹在两个世界之间的女翻译 La Malinche。两个帝国的"接口"由她一个人实现。

这揭示一个被反复忽略的系统性真相：

在任何两个异质系统碰撞的瞬间，权力并不在系统本身，而在"翻译层"。

同样的模式出现在： - AI 时代的 Prompt Engineer——人类意图与大模型内部表征之间的接口持有者。 - 跨国并购中的本地律师——他们事实上塑造条款的最终语义。 - 外交史上的沙皇翻译、郑和的通译、冷战中的 Kissinger——所有重大转折点都挂在一个会双语的人身上。

科尔特斯之所以能"即兴发挥"（Sheppard 说的 "winging it"），正是因为 Doña Marina 替他把每一次胡诌都翻译成了对方文化里有分量的话。她不是传话筒，她是把一种本不该成立的叙事在实时翻译中赋予合法性的协作者。换句话说：帝国的倒塌，发生在翻译的那半秒里。

一个意外的收尾观察：整段故事里科尔特斯真正展示过的"硬实力"极少——没有大规模战役、没有攻城器械、没有压倒性兵力。他赢的是叙事速度。他在对方更新世界模型之前，不断注入新的事实（我是大帝使者、你被保护性拘留、这是我的刑罚、这是我的船）。蒙特祖玛每次都要花时间"重新加载认知"，而加载速度永远赶不上注入速度——这正是今天信息战、Meme 战争、金融闪电战的原型。五百年前就有人实验成功了。

📝 转录文本

一、两个世界的相遇

And there's this dramatic moment when Cortez passes through the causeways out into the city and encounters Moctezuma II, the Huey Tlatoani as he was called, the great speaker, the emperor of the Aztec Empire. And these two worlds come together at that moment.

The interface between them was Cortez's interpreter mistress Doña Marina, Malinche as she became known, who is translating from one side to the other. So the dialogue that occurs then is one of those great tipping points in history.

二、蒙特祖玛的视角与双重博弈

What was the perspective of Moctezuma II? He was aware Cortez was coming. This is his empire. He has envoys and emissaries and scouts and spies everywhere, and they're reporting back to him that something has washed up on the shores of our empire and it is determined to meet with us.

He initially bargains with Cortez, urging him to leave. He provides him with precious gifts — which of course just inflames Cortez even more. And just once he's got hold of Aztec gold, he's just determined to go all the way to the center.

So he continues playing this double game. His advisers, his council urge him not to allow Cortez to proceed to the capital. His own brother Cuitláhuac tells him: "If you allow this man inside your house, he will take your house away from you." But Moctezuma proceeds — and for that he's been condemned by generations of historians.

三、被误解的"错误"：为何让科尔特斯进城反而是最优解

Right? This was a mistake to bring the conquistadors into the heart of the empire itself. I actually think that was his best option, whether he was aware of it or not. Because it was better for him to have Cortez as his guest within Tenochtitlan than it was to have Cortez this random element at loose within his empire, talking to the subject peoples, inflaming them possibly against central authority.

He felt perhaps Cortez was what he said he was: an envoy from a great emperor on the far side of the vast ocean. Cortez, again with the mind games, had no warrant to say he was a diplomat or ambassador for anybody. He kept telling anyone who'd listened, "I speak for the mighty Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor." Of course, Charles V had no idea who Cortez was. Cortez again is just winging it — the incredible improvisation here.

四、转折点：沿海冲突成为借口

And for a moment, the stasis — the great turning point comes when word arrives from the coast that one of the Aztec regional military officers, on his own initiative, has taken action against the conquistadors left behind on the coast, the ones with the Totonacs, and some of them have been killed.

Cortez seizes this as his pretext. He marches into the palace of Moctezuma II, the Aztec Huey Tlatoani, tells him that for his own safety he was now being taken under the protective custody of the Spanish, and he should come with him — or else there will be violence.

五、世界观的崩塌

And this is the moment when Moctezuma's entire worldview just collapses. Right? Nobody had spoken to him like this before. His psychology just disintegrates at that point, and he meekly allows himself to be led away. He tells his people: "Don't resist. I don't want bloodshed. I will pass with these strangers."

And then once Cortez has rounded up the officers at the coast responsible for turning on his men there, he has them in front of the emperor and the entire court burned alive — which is a form of punishment totally unknown to the Aztecs. And they watch this in grim silence.

六、通过皇帝统治帝国：斯德哥尔摩综合征

So once Cortez has seized the emperor himself — once he has Moctezuma — he already has the empire. He governs through what is increasingly becoming his puppet. And Moctezuma seems to have fallen almost under the spell of Cortez — the classic Stockholm syndrome.

He gives him a grand tour of the city. Cortez, again a subtle flex on his power, has brigantines — small sailing boats — built, and he takes Moctezuma with him on a sailing cruise on Lake Texcoco. And the emperor is astonished at this new technology of using the wind to sail on the water.

七、真正的错误：留在首都

Having the emperor was the key. So the emperor's mistake wasn't inviting Cortez into the city — he was making himself vulnerable by staying there also, in an adjacent palace.

If he had gone to some further location, made some excuse — a pilgrimage or an expedition of some kind — and had ruled through subordinates, Cortez would have been baffled. He couldn't go chasing after the emperor; that would be obviously too provocative. But without the emperor there, Cortez would have had his options extremely limited. And I don't know what he would have done in that circumstance.

But because Moctezuma stayed in his capital, he made himself the target. Once he was taken, this was the key to controlling the entire empire at that point.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.
