item.description:
## 一、征服从来不是军事事件，而是一次「可复制的算法」首次运行
最被忽略的事实：皮萨罗不是天才，他是**第一个被 Cortés 口头传授了「剧本」的学徒**。征服印加不是一次历史偶然，而是一次 OS 的二次部署——同一套"直接摘掉社会金字塔的塔尖、让下面的科层继续运转"的协议，被从墨西哥搬到了安第斯山。
这里真正惊人的，不是 168 对 10 万，而是人类历史上**第一次出现了"殖民算法"的 fork-and-reuse**。Cortés 是 v1.0，Pizarro 是 v1.1，之后菲律宾、印度、非洲全是不断迭代的后续版本。它比火药更可怕——火药只能杀人，剧本可以**自我复制**。你会在后来的东印度公司、硅谷"PayPal 黑帮"甚至现代 PE 的"玩法手册"里看到完全同构的模式：第一个走通的人把一次性经验压缩成可传授的步骤，于是奇迹变成流水线。
## 二、阿塔瓦尔帕的"胜利"才是他真正的死刑
反直觉的观察：**阿塔瓦尔帕刚刚打赢内战这件事，不是他的优势，而是他的死因**。
他是印加世界里的"分布内最优解"——所有的直觉、战术、威信判断，都是在"前哥伦布战争"的训练集上

item.title: [Latent Space] Which GPU Clouds Are Actually Good? | ClusterMAX 3.0
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：ClusterMAX 本质上不是"排行榜"，而是一个行业强制升级机制

表面上，ClusterMAX 是在给 GPU 云打分。但如果你观察它的二阶效应，会发现它扮演的角色更像美国劳工部的 OSHA 安全检查——它不是在评价现状，而是在用公开羞辱重塑行业基线。

证据链很有趣： - 第一代门槛"super low"，第二代第三代"harder and harder" - 结果是"趋势是降级"——这不是评分系统的失败，这是设计意图 - Jordan 甚至开发了免费 CLI 工具 cmax，让客户能自己检查供应商 - 发文后几小时 Ilya 跟进 tweet——这是一种精心编排的声誉共振

跨领域连接：这与 Moody's / S&P 评级机构的早期历史惊人相似。1909 年 John Moody 开始给铁路债券评级时，他做的不是"反映市场"，而是强行给市场创造了一套可比较的语言。SemiAnalysis 正在对 GPU 云做同样的事——而且他们比评级机构更聪明：明确拒绝 sell-side 收入，把全部商业模式建立在 buy-side 的 TCO 模型订阅上。这是一种罕见的结构性诚信（structural integrity through business model），而非道德性诚信。

二、一个被所有人忽略的隐藏模式：Nvidia 正在用"防御性收购"模仿冷战时期的 CIA 安插工作

Pullside 70 亿、HuggingFace 收购——所有人都在讨论"人才"或"技术"。但 Jordan 提到的那段最犀利：

"them doing this is going to incentivize other people to invest a bunch of money into them... they actually didn't spend any money because now they've created a new customer, a new cloud"

把它翻译成系统性语言：Nvidia 的收购不是在收购公司，而是在给资金循环加装一个单向阀。$7B 现金 → 10B 融资 → 75% 杠杆 → $40B → 1 GW 数据中心 → 全部回购 Nvidia GPU。

这个闭环的最隐藏特征是：Nvidia 把"收购支出"变成了"客户创造工具"。会计科目是 Operating Expense，但经济实质是 Customer Acquisition Capex。

跨领域连接：这与美国标准石油时代 Rockefeller 的"借贷换客户"结构同构，但更精巧——Rockefeller 还要承担借贷违约风险，Nvidia 不用，因为它卖出的 GPU 本身就是抵押品。更有趣的是这与日本 Keiretsu 的交叉持股也有相似性，但 Nvidia 做得更隐蔽——没有股权纠缠，只有现金流闭环。

三、你应该为之惊讶的时间信号："推理赚钱"重构了整个算力市场的玩家资格

转录中最被低估的一句话：

"Base10 was running at 10% gross margins... now 60% gross margins on open models using VLM"

6-9 个月，推理毛利率从 10% 跳到 60%。这个数字背后发生了一场悄然的权力转移：

  • 过去：GPU 稀缺 → 分配给能"烧钱训练"的人（AI 实验室）
  • 现在：GPU 稀缺 → 分配给能"立即赚钱"的人（Inference provider）
  • 结果：NeoLab 的入场券从"800 万美元"降到"几节点就能赚钱"——但同时它们必须和一个赚钱机器竞争同一张卡

这创造了一个经济学上极其罕见的现象——我称之为"流动性诅咒"：一个资产的流动性越强、变现越快，它对长周期研究者反而越不友好。因为长周期研究者的现金流无法以周为单位竞标。

跨领域连接：这正是15-16 世纪西班牙"白银诅咒"的翻版——美洲白银流入让西班牙变得"富有"，但同时让所有需要长期投资的制造业无法与短期贸易利润竞争，最终西班牙去工业化。今天 Google 内部研究员"被卖掉"的那种抑郁感，和 16 世纪塞维利亚手工业者看着银船出港的心情，是同一种结构性无力。

而真正隐藏的洞见是：ClusterMAX 的排名之所以有价值，不仅因为它测试了技术，更因为它锁定了一个即将不存在的市场的快照——managed cluster 这个品类本身，可能在 24 个月内被"直接吃 token 的无状态推理"和"自建 GW 级裸金属"从两头挤压掉中间。所以 ClusterMAX 3.0 可能是最后一次这种形态的榜单，而 Jordan 已经在悄悄为 Endpoint X 做准备——他们在给自己的产品预埋寿终安排。

📝 转录文本

开场与个人背景

Swyx: Hi Jordan，恭喜 ClusterMAX 发布。能先简单介绍一下你的个人背景，以及你是如何走到构建 ClusterMAX 这一步的吗？

Jordan: 当然。我去年六月加入 SemiAnalysis，在技术团队任职，过去一年我们成长了很多。个人背景方面，我在 Hewlett Packard Enterprise 工作了 10 年，设计了很多这些 NeoCloud 在购买的硬件系统——这是在 ChatGPT 发布之前，以及 2022-2023 年大批 NeoCloud 涌入市场的那波热潮期间。

我是 SemiAnalysis 的忠实读者，每一个字都读，也在场外的一些群聊里认识一些成员。当 Dan 和团队发布 ClusterMAX 1 的时候，我看到自己的很多观点被呈现了出来。而在 SemiAnalysis 找工作最好的方式，就是找到 SemiAnalysis 正在做的某件事然后批评它，接着 Dylan 就会雇你来修复它——这就是发生在我身上的事。

Swyx: 那你一定要告诉我们，当时你对 ClusterMAX 1 的批评是什么？

Jordan: 我自己做了版本 2，所以我可以来讲这些批评。

从 ClusterMAX 1 到 3：方法论的演进

Swyx: 从版本一到版本二，有什么变化？让我们来聊聊有什么新东西。

Jordan: ClusterMAX 1 的问题是漏掉了很多供应商——总共测了 24 个，但其中有很多大型供应商本应被测试却没测，团队当时太小没时间。此外，当时重点在 Slurm 上，但对我来说 Kubernetes 同样重要，必须测试。

在评价标准上我们没有太多改变，但一路从 ClusterMAX 1 到现在，排名页面看起来已经非常不同——名字少了很多。我们当时发布 market view 时大约追踪了 120 个供应商，其中 111 个 emerging NeoClouds。

这次我们没有完整发布 market view，而是把它放在了 NeoCloud 模型的付费墙后面——我们追踪了所有这些供应商，很多是公开的，很多即将 IPO，我们为整个行业建立了金融模型。到 3.0 版本，我们追踪的供应商总数已经达到 323 个。今天早上我邮箱里就有人联系我说他们有 3,000 个 GPU 想让我们测试……这是一个巨大的演进。

关键的变化是：ClusterMAX 1 的所有测试都是手动的——那是 Claude Code 之前、Codex 还没认真起来的时代。我们用了一年半开发出一整套 repo，包含行业标准 benchmark、自定义 benchmark、可靠性和烤机测试。现在它非常自动化，我们可以让编码 agent 启动它、运行它，并在我们不介入的情况下自主修复一堆问题。覆盖的广度和深度都大幅提升。

什么是 ClusterMAX？什么是 NeoCloud？

Swyx: 介绍一下，ClusterMAX 是什么？NeoCloud 评级和排名是什么？你们到底在测试什么？

Jordan: 网站上描述了 10 个评价标准。我们对 NeoCloud 的定义是：任何出租/销售算力访问权限的公司。"Neo"（新）这个前缀意味着在 ChatGPT 之前就存在的 Hyperscaler 和 Legacy Cloud——AWS、Google、Oracle、Azure，以及一些老派的 Rackspace、DigitalOcean、甚至 Cloudflare AI。任何运行大型数据中心并出租访问权的，就是 Cloud；NeoClouds 是新来的那批。

我们说所有人都在变成 NeoCloud，因为 NeoCloud 的差异化在于专注于 AI——他们为 AI 工作负载部署 GPU 和其他加速器：训练、推理、以及越来越多的 RL。

我们测试的是：谁会给你最好的性能、安全性、可靠性，以及易用性、价格、可用性。我们做的是综合评估而非单一 benchmark。

ChatGPT 刚出来的时候，很多人联系 SemiAnalysis 说："我在五个供应商之间做选择，怎么想？" 他们在用同样的问题反复烦扰 Dylan。他们说："嘿，我刚融了 2000 万美元，准备把其中 1.05 亿给某个供应商——这是我的整个种子轮，这是关键决定。"

与其让 Dylan 和团队每次个性化地回答这个问题，不如写一篇文章给出粗颗粒度的初步想法——快速 tier list 排名、podium——然后你可以聘请我们做更详细的内容：咨询、尽调，针对你的具体需求深入挖掘。

安全性：触目惊心的现状

Swyx: 10 个标准里让我最先想到的，是你们引用 Ilya Sutskever 说的——所有 NeoCloud 的网络安全都糟糕透顶。NeoCloud 安全的现状是怎样的？

Jordan: 你说了——糟糕。嗯，取决于我们在说谁……

Swyx: 我也先跟刚加入的 Dylan 打个招呼。Dylan，NeoCloud 网络安全的现状如何？

Dylan: 对不起我迟到了。安全真的很糟。即使从第一代 ClusterMAX 开始就有重大安全问题。人们没有正确实施网络安全控制，所以我们能看到别人的作业、别人的数据、别人的存储等等。第一代时我们升级报告给了相关公司以及 Nvidia，当然把那家公司评为"underperform"，强烈建议大家不要使用。

第二代 ClusterMAX 我们看到类似情况。我觉得很多人因为我们的曝光而变好了。但在第三代，Jordan 和他的团队测试时又看到了相当严重的安全问题。所以我们发了一篇名为《Most NeoClouds Suck at Security》的 newsletter。然后几个小时后，Ilya 发推说大多数 NeoCloud 安全很烂——他们显然是非常注重安全的公司，有很多来自前网络安全界的人，我想他们对不少云做过自己的工作。

而且情况有多糟？有一个案例里，我们能看到某国国家情报的东西——他们有多个国家安全机构和军事情报类的东西在那个 NeoCloud 上运行。天啊，我们只是来测试集群的，就能看到这些东西。想象一下如果我们是恶意的——我相信那个集群上确实有恶意或可能恶意的人。谢天谢地他们后来修复了。但不应该是我们来发现某人安全好不好，不过行业确实需要这个服务。这是我们标准里的一大块。

Jordan: 技术层面，我们的检查非常简单：你的软件版本是最新的吗？驱动是最新的吗？配置正确吗？这些是相对简单的检查，但当人们运行 2-3 年前的软件版本，并且有大量公开记录的 CVE 时——你不需要前沿模型就能创建 PoC exploit，你只需要知道去哪儿看。

所以作为这篇文章的一部分，我们发布了一个免费 CLI：人们可以安装 cmax，用它检查集群上的软件版本，终端输出里会有链接告诉你去哪里升级，试图帮助大家保持软件更新。

Dylan: 另一件事是网络密钥。Infiniband 和 Ethernet 都有各种——至少 Infiniband 这边有 M-key、P-key 这些东西。它们是否正确配置和部署？大多数 NeoCloud 有多糟糕——真的很糟糕。

代际升级：被降级的"趋势"

Swyx: 从一代到二代到三代，有什么有趣的大跳跃、重大改进吗？

Dylan: 我们在 ClusterMAX 上的门槛——第一代超低，每一代我们都抬高难度。所以趋势是人们被降级。当然也有少数人被升级。Google 做得很好，在各代 ClusterMAX 里都在上升——他们从 bronze 升到 silver 再到 gold。而很多云在各代中被降级，因为他们停滞了：改进了一点点但不够多，我们一直在抬高门槛，教所有人——这些是你应该做的事情以变得更好。

Jordan: 这次的门槛是"最新最好"——你有没有在 2026 年部署 GB300 NVL72？这是极受欢迎的芯片，所有 Frontier Lab 都想买，所有 NeoCloud 都想买。来找我们的典型客户是："我融了 1 亿美元，想花在算力上"——他们想要 GB300 NVL72 集群。

而一些原本在 gold 的供应商不提供 GB300 NVL72。为什么？因为你得应对一大堆不同的东西：新网络、NVL72 意味着 rack 内的 scaleup domain、要上 ARM CPU、Blackwell GPU、800Gig 网络、强制直接液冷。从物理数据中心到如何部署操作系统再到如何管理驱动和网络，几乎一切都不同。

当人们说"哦我们只是做了战略业务决策不做 GB"——那 Vera Rubin 明年来的时候呢？你信谁？所以趋势是：如果人们部署 10,000 台 GB300、我们测试集群能工作、我们和支持团队沟通、我们给反馈他们一小时而非两周内修复——他们在排名中上升。其他人如果不部署最新最好的 GPU，或者部署了但完全坏了、修复要很久、或者我们发现安全问题、或者客户反馈巨大的可靠性问题（可靠性可能是顶级客户最在意的第一标准）——他们在排名中下降。

算力市场：史上最紧张

Swyx: 假设你是一个 NeoLab 刚融了几千万美元想开始租——市场状况和一两年前相比如何？变好还是变差？

Dylan: 祝你好运。

Jordan: 糟多了，兄弟。

Dylan: 现在是有史以来最难搞到算力的时候。Anthropic 和 OpenAI 一直在购买越来越小的集群规模。但同时所有推理供应商也越来越赚钱。6-9 个月前 Base10 可能跑 10% 毛利率，但现在 Base10、Fireworks、Together 和许多公司，甚至像 Morph 这样的小公司，在开源模型上用 VLM 或 SGLang 加一点优化就能跑 60% 毛利率，表现出色。还有 Inact、Radix、Arc 这些。

所以任何能拿到 GPU 的人都能立即赚钱。而我是一个 NeoLab 想训练有趣的新模型，我却在和"现在就能赚钱的人"竞争，而不是像以前主要和亏钱的 OpenAI、亏钱的 Anthropic、亏钱的实验室竞争——几乎没人靠 GPU 赚钱。现在人人能赚钱。所以要搞到任何算力都非常非常困难。

Swyx: 实验室现在下探到什么规模和主要供应商竞争？

Dylan: 他们以前只从一个供应商拿 8K GPU。现在稳步下降，我们甚至看到实验室只租 1,000 个 GPU。1,000 个 GPU 更接近 NeoLab 想要的规模，所以市场被挤压了很多。

再看 Base10、Fireworks、Together 这些推理供应商——他们能接受 4 个节点，像 Modal。这些家伙 4 个节点就够。他们的编排很难——Modal 对此谈了很多，他们跨 20 个云做编排。所以如果 Modal 能靠一家公司的 4 个节点大赚一笔，那所有人要搞到任何算力都很有挑战性。

Jordan: 真的很糟。甚至个人——你现在不能 spot 租单节点了，整个 stack 都完了。

实验室格局：OpenAI 与 Anthropic 领跑

Swyx: 实验室的状况怎样？你怎么划分 OpenAI、Anthropic、Google 这些大玩家？谁拥有最多算力？

Dylan: 显然是 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 领跑——无论从大规模裸金属 Hyperscaler 租赁来看——OpenAI 是 CoreWeave 业务的驱动者，也是 Microsoft 的驱动者，他们也在和其他 Hyperscaler 探索，和 Oracle 做了巨大的自建项目。Anthropic 则有和 AWS 的大合作 Project Rainier，和 Google Cloud 的大量 TPU，和 CoreWeave 签了东西，和其他家也签了。

所以他们是大驱动者。你看 ARR，必须有东西驱动它，这就落到算力端。

Jordan: 另一方面——很多供应商比如 Crusoe 有极好的裸金属，但那不是我们在 ClusterMAX 测试的东西。我们不测试裸金属——它是标准的一部分，但很多标准是关于托管集群：managed Slurm、managed Kubernetes 这些。这是人们想要的 GPU 之上的另一层服务。

初版 ClusterMAX 的一大部分叫《如何租一个 GPU》——我们也在教人们该做什么来租 GPU。在我们看来，大多数小客户不在乎节点是否裸金属；超大客户想要裸金属因为他们要放自己的 Slurm/Kubernetes fork；但中小客户想要托管的 Slurm、托管的 Kubernetes，并且想要云在节点失败时帮他们热插拔。ClusterMAX 聚焦于此。

像 Crusoe 这样的公司会租裸金属，和企业有巨大合同，在数据中心表现很好，在推理 API 上也开始起步，但在托管服务上他们表现不佳。而 ClusterMAX 瞄准的正是托管服务层——否则太复杂，人们想租的领域太多：有人要裸金属，有人要托管服务，有人要 token out，是一系列选项。

甚至 Google 也在从别人那租算力——他们和 CoreWeave 签了协议，和 SpaceX 签了协议。相当大量算力，他们签了超过 1000 亿美元的算力合同。Nebius 也和实验室有协议。但这些家伙只做裸金属。

OpenAI 和 Anthropic 绝对是购买份额的狮子的那一份。Google 在这点上明显落后——OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的算力加起来已经比 Google 多一点。到年底，它们两家各自用于 R&D 的算力都将超过 DeepMind。所以 Google 总体上目前还有更多算力，但很多卖给了其他地方、分配给其他产品。但 DeepMind 的 R&D 算力对比 OpenAI/Anthropic 的 R&D 算力——这两个实验室现在有更多算力，因为它们达到了那个规模。

所以"Google 有最多算力所以会赢"的说法实际上不再成立了。他们还有成本优势因为自己造 TPU，但最终 DeepMind 的算力少于 OpenAI/Anthropic。

Swyx: AIE 上对我最大的洞察之一是，我遇到的一些 DeepMind 研究员非常沮丧，因为他们说"我们的领导一直在把我们想要的算力卖给别人"。

Dylan: 想象一下作为 XAI……

Swyx: 对啊，我以为 SpaceX 是 NeoCloud 吗？什么鬼？为什么我们标它 unavailable？

Jordan: 他们在清单上，一旦我们能测试他们就上升。他们会是竞争者。SpaceX 和 Google 的交易，以及和 Anthropic 的交易都超级有意思，因为它触及 Dylan 说的——实验室正在机会主义地考虑成为 NeoCloud。Meta 也在考虑同样的事情，Mistral 和 Poolside 也在清单上。

这些公司具备建数据中心和管理的技能，有机会通过租给别人或推理服务变现算力时就想追求，但只到某个水平，并始终保留选择权——一旦负担得起就把算力拉回去用于研究或"英雄 run"。他们想用能负担得起的最大算力做研究，所有多余的都机会主义地赚钱为研究提供资金。

SpaceX 和 Google 的合同比如有双向 90 天取消权——SpaceX 研究开始见效就能把算力拉回来；Google 在那个算力上停止从某个推理端点赚钱也可以拉回来。这是非常有趣的结构——两方都在小型对峙，看谁先眨眼、谁更相信 AGI。

Dylan: 对 SpaceX 来说另一方面是，如果你是 XAI 员工被 SpaceX 买了然后 SpaceX 卖掉了所有算力，至少你不沮丧，因为 Elon 在建更多，你会有访问权，他这么做是为了帮我们在财务上更可持续、为 IPO。而 Google 这边——我为什么卖算力？我已经是非常赚钱的公司。为什么不能直接用算力建模型并以更高的毛利卖这些模型，而不是给 Anthropic 或 OpenAI 或其他公司？SSI 也是 Google 的客户。

Google 的两难：资助自己的对手

Swyx: 你怎么看 Google 资助那些离开去做 NeoLab 的人、然后他们回头在 GCP 上花钱——比如 Dave Silver、Jeff Dean 独立出来，拿 Google Ventures 的资金然后花在 GCP 上？

Dylan: 如果你只看 GCP 作为独立公司，Thomas Kurian 持续推高收入、运营利润、运营收入，这是绝佳举措。但对 Google 整体来说真的很蠢——你不应该激励你最好的研究员离开。你不应该以每 MW 20-30M 卖掉本来可以用来跑模型赚每 MW 50M 的算力。

如果 Discovery Loop 有大突破，你觉得 Google 能把他们留在轨道内，还是 Jeff Dean 带着那个突破去做某件事，Google 作为投资者和云服务商却无法分享任何上行？

你去看 Anthropic——Google 确实投了 Anthropic。如果 Google 没投，Anthropic 今天会存在吗？因为 Google 是非常早的信仰者。Opus 3、Sonnet 3 和 3.5 我觉得都是在 Google 基础设施上训练的。他们后来才带进 Amazon——Amazon 也很棒，但至少 Amazon 不做训练并销售模型的业务。但 Google 做。

所以 Google 是不是扶植了自己最大的竞争者和对手？现在 Anthropic 不仅从 Amazon 和 Google 租，还从十多个云租。Anthropic 还在建自己的数据中心、租自己的数据中心、开始填满它们、和 Fluidstack 合作在自己数据中心部署 TPU。Google 还在拿收入，但——我以前从你这租，现在我从你这买 TPU，这对你是更低的毛利；未来我自己建自己的芯片，我什么都不用你了。所以 Anthropic 的情况已经很清楚了。

Jeff Dean 如果在 Discovery Loop 做出惊人的事，为什么他要被绑在 Google？他能用任何云。切换云最终不是不可能——AI 时代前人们谈的"数据重力"等等在 AI 时代相关性少得多，因为 AI 可以帮你迁移一切。GPU 不只是 GPU，但 GPU 作为可替代资产在云之间基本可行，如果你技术好。

Swyx: 所以你觉得 Google 完蛋了？

Dylan: 我觉得你们比我更专家。Google 是一堆不同东西的大型集团。Google 最大的优势是数据优势。但有组织挑战，现在有新领导——愿上帝保佑 Koray，他有世界上最难的工作要修这个。但他是非常非常能干的人。他们知道需要重置。

对我来说 Demis 基本上退出领导职位是完全的黑天鹅——我从来没想过有可能。也许我不认识他本人，可能他真的"我只是很在乎 Isomorphic"。但他创立了 DeepMind，他是 DeepMind 的精神领袖。这可能是第一次真正的前沿实验室领导层完全过渡。

Swyx: Sam 离开过两天……

Dylan: 但他从没真正离开过任何人的心。

Swyx: 这是 Tim Cook 式的……

Dylan: Ilya 离开 OpenAI——不是领袖。是的，很多人分裂。总之，这是我的粗略观点，可能没比你们更辣。

Poolside 与 HuggingFace：防御性收购

Swyx: 你们提过 Poolside，从没写过他们因为没那么大。但他们被 Nvidia 以 120 亿收购了员工。怎么回事？

Jordan: 很酷啊，因为 Nvidia 为所有这些研究员付钱让他们能让 Nemotron 变得更好。

Dylan: 不，这是防御性的。Poolside 从一开始就——所有 NeoCloud 都有点烂，所以他们开始建很多自己的基础设施，越来越擅长建，然后试图部署自己的集群，和 CoreWeave 有合作，但他们一直慢慢向 stack 下移。可能是第一个甚至在 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 之前就试图运行自己基础设施的 AI 实验室。

Swyx: 这很疯狂，作为副业——人们必须这么做吗？这是全职工作？这对他们几乎是副业。

Dylan: 现在是他们的全职工作了，因为他们把研究员卖给了 Nvidia 做 Nemotron。Nvidia 显然想让 Nemotron 好得多。我觉得他们对很多开源玩家失去了希望——Reflection 还在努力，Thinking Machines 开源了一些，但 Nvidia 对美国开源有点失去希望，他们觉得只能自己做。所以买了一堆员工。

我以为是 70 亿，不是 120 亿……

Swyx: 我们文章里有细节，120 亿。

Dylan: 我采取更大的数字。

Swyx: 许可和员工 50 亿，数字是 60 亿。

Dylan: 总是取更大的数字。但归根结底，Nvidia 可以说实际上我们只付了 1/4 价格，因为这些钱都要回去买 GPU。所以他们到底付了 70 亿、60 亿买员工加 10 亿投资——还是实际上只付了 15 亿因为其中 70 亿要回去买 GPU？

而且他们这么做会激励其他人投资更多到他们身上。所以雇所有这些人实际上是正面的事，他们实际上没花任何钱，因为他们创造了新客户、新云，将建大规模集群。想象他们现在有 70 亿现金，再融几十亿，假设账上有 100 亿现金，能拿 75% LTV 的贷款——25% 首付，75% 贷款。现在他们有 400 亿。能建 1 GW。又一个 GW 级 NeoCloud。他们刚创造了一个真正的新竞争者。

Swyx: 我们文章下面有。如果这是 playbook，更多人应该这么做。

Dylan: 做什么？做和 Nvidia 的这种交易？因为 Nvidia 会把你变成王，就因为他们想要更多云。

Jordan: 不是每个人都发布美国第二好的开源模型。花多年建它。我们在略过 Poolside 确实建了有趣的东西这件事。对我来说，这个和 HuggingFace 都是 Nvidia 的防御性收购，Nvidia 不希望竞争对手抢走真正有东西、有势头的实验室——那种真正有训练模型和运行集群所需真实经验的，而不是加密矿工，那些"嘿我找到个场地有电有钱"的人没有执行能力。而证明自己能训练世界第二好美国开源模型的人（Poolside 做到了）——他们可以。

HuggingFace 收购

Swyx: 你提到了 HuggingFace。你们怎么看 HuggingFace 收购？

Jordan: 我觉得很相似，是防御性的。我不觉得 Nvidia 希望其他公司进来拥有生态系统中关键的东西并产生影响力。

Dylan: 有个 Galaxy Brain 的解读——现在 HuggingFace 可以起诉 OpenAI 黑他们。现在 Nvidia 可以……有锁死吗？我不觉得。但我觉得 HuggingFace 显然是遥遥领先的……

Swyx: 在什么意义上领先？

Dylan: 作为开源仓库。我团队有些人开始为 ModelScope 提交 PR 以让生态系统互通。但归根结底——如果你想，有办法在 Amazon Trainium 上部署 HuggingFace 模型，一键就能部署。那个会消失吗？以后只有 GPU 了吗？还是会发生某种封闭？我们看吧。但我也喜欢价格是用 emoji 代码表示的，太酷了。

Jordan: 团队很棒。看，我们略过了 HuggingFace 和 Poolside 两个组织里都有不可思议的人才这一事实。很多人会说这是 Nvidia 收购的动机。我说是防御性的，因为看 Nvidia 的业务——他们每季度产生近 500 亿自由现金流，一年 2000 亿。Nvidia 有企业战略团队拿这笔钱的一部分决定怎么部署——投资、收购。用 10% 自由现金流收购 HuggingFace 和 Poolside，这些是你队伍里不费脑的好资产。

至少不让它们为你的竞争对手工作。假设 HuggingFace 保持独立并遵守收购的法律字面意思，继续支持所有其他芯片。如果被别人收购，就会主动对抗 Nvidia 的利益。我觉得这不是他们想要的。所以你会看到更多这类情况。如果公司长大一点，建起 100-200 个难以置信的人的团队，Nvidia 想把他们纳入以确保他们留在 Nvidia 生态系统，而不是去和别人一起竞争。

Swyx: 不是贬低 Poolside 做的任何事。我们是粉丝。他们被收购前一个月上过我们的播客。有兴趣的听众可以听 Model Factory 的工作、训练基础模型的方法——他们建立这一切的方式非常好。

Jordan: 回到 ClusterMAX——所有 NeoCloud 应该如何证明自己（像第 4 条标准）：请自己训练一个前沿模型，然后证明一切能工作。

Swyx: 我不觉得每个人都应该有训练前沿模型的技能……

Jordan: 但有很多开放配方和东西。

Dylan: 我们需要 Mosaic。让我们谈谈到那一步需要什么。如果你要训练……

Swyx: 我觉得 Poolside 和 HuggingFace 过去可能都考虑过类似价格的收购选项。

Dylan: 具体来说，Nvidia 年初试图买 HuggingFace，万一有人不知道。Nvidia 处在一种收购狂潮中——有过关于 Thinking Machines 和一堆 Nvidia 收购的传闻。

Jordan: 创始人在很多这些建了东西的人中都有"想变现时就变现"的选项。什么时候决定变现？Poolside 可能看出去想："好，我建了 10,000 GPU 集群能让 Logona 出来。但如果要竞争，我需要 100,000 GPU、400,000 GPU 的研究集群。我怎么跟上明年的开放前沿？"保持下去很难。钱来了，"好吧，就套现和其他人一起建吧"。

但技术面值得指出的是——Poolside 关于基础设施的论文很好。我和团队聊过，如果你要训练前沿模型，你需要集群健康检查，需要高可靠性，不能有模型训练时不进步、不断失败的情况。他们有令人难以置信的基础设施。所以这种人才能把它作为服务提供给他人显然是正确的。只有有限的人有这经验——我们进入 silver 和 bronze 层级时，大多数 silver 层和整个 bronze 层的人不训练前沿模型。很多推理，一点 RL，很多研究，但坦白说除了 Azure 我都不会信任他们能建 100,000 GPU 集群。但建呢？已经证明能做到的有五家公司。

面对批评：ClusterMAX 的边界

Swyx: 让我们直接面对批评。这是非常有价值的清单，人们确实根据它做采购决策。大多数人的批评是什么？

Dylan: 有很多批评。首先这测试的是托管集群——这不代表一家公司在其他方面不好。Crusoe 在托管集群上被降级，但他们是世界上最好的数据中心建造者之一——如果不是最好的。他们管道里的 contracted gigawatts 几乎最多，正在很多场地快速建设。但这不是对他们数据中心建造能力的批评，只是对他们托管集群产品的批评。他们还是最好的之一，但被降级了。同样，Together 有很好的推理端点，和托管服务无关。

所以有很多关于这测试什么的困惑——这是针对托管集群，不是数据中心建设、裸金属集群、推理端点，虽然推理端点越来越是模糊的线，因为所有人都在做。

另一大批评——"是不是收钱做的？"不，我们任何排名都不收钱，那是违法的。我自己在 Crusoe 有个人投资。我在 Fluidstack 有个人投资。这两家公司都不在前五。因为我不是来当有偏见的。Jordan 会说他有完全的自由做任何事。他甚至不知道所有我们有合同的公司。

如果我看世界前 20 家公司，有 5 家不是我们的客户。像 Eli Lilly 和 Saudi Aramco 这类——他们是比 CoreWeave 或 Nebius 可能永远更大的客户，因为他们是预算大得多的公司。AWS 是比 CoreWeave 或 Nebius 更大的客户。但这与排名无关。基础设施供应链里每个人都买我们东西。但不代表我们会偏颇排名。

如果我们收钱排名却不披露，那是违法的。但其次，这没道理——我们对行业的价值是我们说实话、说我们相信的。如果不这么做，没人会在乎我们说什么，我们就是对着虚空喊。所以我们的声誉比快钱重要得多。

Swyx: 换个说法：你们是 buy-side 服务，人们指控你们从 sell-side 收钱，他们不理解 buy-side 的收入可能是 sell-side 的 1000 倍。

两种常见批评

Jordan: 我听到两个清晰的批评——写得不够详细，应该发布更多数据；或者"这是 30,000 字我读不完"。所以很难平衡。

Dylan: 你在评价 NeoCloud。

Jordan: 对前者，我们有一个研究产品叫 Cloud TCO Model，任何人都可以来授权，年费。我们每周写笔记关于行业趋势。我们有 dashboard，底部有去识别化的截图，所有数据都在那。所有性能数据都在。你让我们全年每周为你做研究，而不仅仅是每年或每半年一次发布。所以这是给想要更多细节的人。

Dylan: 还有一类批评——通常是某人持有某个股票而我们排得差或好。但我们对公司表现好坏在股市的看法与 Jordan 和他团队无关。我们确实为所有这些公司估算远期收入，你可以授权我们的数据看你认为那意味着怎么交易，但我们从不推荐交易。

但有过这样的情况——比如我们觉得 Nebius 比 CoreWeave 更好。原因是尽管 CoreWeave 还是比 Nebius 更好的云，Nebius 的合同是短期的，GPU 价格飙升时 Nebius 更能抓住上行。这是我们在研究中发布的，由不同团队，不是 Jordan 和做 ClusterMAX 的技术员工。

或者 Iris Energy 有巨大数据中心即将上线，我们觉得会被租掉，发报告时同时说你永远不应该用 Iris Energy 的托管服务。他们把那个数据中心作为裸金属卖给 Microsoft。所以机构研究端为可能买股票的人准备的，和 ClusterMAX 真正为 Periodic Labs 或 Applied Compute 这类公司准备的（他们公开说他们喜欢 ClusterMAX），是完全不同的东西。

甚至 OpenAI 都说他们喜欢 ClusterMAX，我们有他们的引言。我们有各种买家说他们很欣赏方法论和我们在为所有云抬高门槛。所以如果你根据 ClusterMAX 买股票，完全错了，与股票表现无关。

Swyx: 100% 兄弟。这严格是给买家，帮人买算力，不是给人 YOLO 全部储蓄挑股票。

Dylan: 在某个极限上会相关。某个运营云很糟但有 1 GW 数据中心正在建、且真的可信的 GW 级数据中心——他们可以是 ClusterMAX 排名最差的，还能赚很多钱。重要吗？按当前股价，很多名字便宜，很多名字贵……

Swyx: 我理解。基本面 vs 一个产品对整体基本面的贡献。它贡献于整体估值和方向。我以前是对冲基金的，我懂。只是说你们是领域专家，人们重视那元素的评级。

Dylan: 可能需要未来的另一个免责声明"这不是对他们当前股价估值的背书"。

Jordan: 做个二维图表可能很有趣——这里是 ClusterMAX 排名，这里是相同分析的股票排名——差异会是有趣的研究。值得一提的是后续还有很多：个体名字和 logo 这里的业务比我们在排名的托管集群大得多，所以我们将在 newsletter 上处理推理端点、裸金属、RL 基础设施、沙箱——所有这些。因为很多人联系我们帮助决定端点供应商、托管 RL 训练供应商、沙箱供应商——那是和托管集群不同的问题。

Swyx: 所以解决方案是更多 Max、更多 benchmark？你有多少？InferenceMax？

Dylan: 当你去杂货店饿着的时候，就是这样。我们想做一切。看吧，希望能执行。

Jordan: 说清楚——InferenceMax 今天的名字是因为它针对推理性能，但它是关于芯片的，关于比较芯片和系统。我们将发布叫 EndpointX 的东西，测试无服务器推理端点供应商。类似方法论——超越性能，看成本、可靠性、安全性、监控基础设施。所有这些都归入推理端点，不是说某人在 batch=1 的构造测试上命中更高目标就一定是你扩展推理需求的正确伙伴。

Dylan: 有性能更好的供应商——原始性能更好、优化工程师更好——但 API 不稳定、更粗糙。各种原因可能对终端客户没那么好，即使 token/秒/用户更多、成本更低。

多元芯片：Nvidia 以外的宇宙

Swyx: 你们怎么覆盖非 Nvidia 宇宙？Ryzen……

Jordan: 你清单里有一些，像 TensorWave 是 AMD 云。

Dylan: 这是另一个我明确有投资的——我们还是排得差。很多这种偏见——是的我可能投资我会跟他们聊试图帮他们，但归根结底排名就是排名。Prime Intellect 我在第一代 ClusterMAX 投资的——我们还是把他们列为 underperform。

所以我们确实想扩展到更远。但归根结底 Fluidstack 不会把 TPU 租给我们，因为他们把一切都租给 Anthropic。

Swyx: 也许？我们看吧。希望。

Dylan: 他们标 unavailable 挺不可原谅的。

Jordan: 不，这是合理的。看，它对我们是 unavailable 所以我们不能租。你除非真的真的超酷否则也租不到——因为他们什么都卖。SpaceX 不会租给我们，不会租给你，不会租给随机公司。他们租给大客户……

Swyx: Dylan，我觉得你需要……这是我第一次给你这个反馈，但我觉得你需要在自信心上下功夫。我们能搞到的。我觉得我们能和这些家伙搞到。

Dylan: 随时间推移……

Jordan: 今天很多这些供应商——即使 Fluidstack 和现在 SpaceX AI 的人——看到读文章的价值，看到获得外部意见的价值，即使他们不一定公开提供他们提供给我们的服务。他们享受第三方技术意见——公司外的、诚实的、给他们真实反馈。我们在这里为所有这些事提供帮助。

多元芯片的未来

Jordan: 回答关于多元芯片的问题——明年会巨大，Rubin 一代 Nvidia 会把 LPU 从 Groq 引入，LPX 系统。所以即使只测 Nvidia 我们也要测多元芯片。AMD 显然有自己的东西。Cerebras 正在成为 NeoCloud 为 OpenAI，建自己的数据中心，从只做推理端点转到真正为其他人管理芯片集群。我们看到 SambaNova 上市。很多芯片初创公司——Positron、Etched、Mad X——很多人在推出这类东西。

有传言——Fluidstack 显然有 GCP 以外的 TPU，那里还有更多东西要来。Trainium——AWS 能产大量芯片，也许未来不会全部自建，他们有和 Cerebras 的异构 Trainium 公告。所以明年这方面会多得多，我们必须应对多元芯片作为领先 NeoCloud 综合产品的一部分。他们未来需要能支持异构计算。

Swyx: 这都主要聚焦推理吧？因为……

Dylan: Anthropic 比如主要用 TPU 做训练。所以那种情况下相反，他们大部分推理在 Trainium 和 GPU 上，大部分训练在 TPU——Fable 5 比如预训练在 TPU，后训练和推理主要是训练和 GPU。所以多元芯片——大多数情况下其他芯片产品是给推理，但有些情况人们用于训练。

Jordan: 关键是推理 vs 训练现在不是硬分割了，RL 中做研究和实际后训练模型时有很多前向传递。所以……

Dylan: 实际上大部分工作负载是前向传递，所以你可能把它经典地叫推理，即使它是强化学习的前向传递。

Jordan: 对 RL 中的前向传递用更便宜、能高吞吐的芯片有一堆好处。但用两种不同芯片有一堆数值正确性挑战——即使只是两代不同的 Nvidia GPU，B200 vs B300，不同内存大小、不同 batch size。所有这些效应。所以我绝对期待训练和推理会有异构芯片。预训练可能同质集群，人们可能不会在 400,000 GPU 规模上冒那险，但我们看吧。

Dylan: 但 RL 现在和预训练工作负载一样大甚至更大。所以这实际上意味着你需要新形式的 disaggregation——同一数据中心有不同种类计算来回传输。

Jordan: 甚至不必是同一数据中心。人们跨许多站点做 RL——这个数据中心做 token 生成，那个数据中心做 token 生成，用不同类型芯片实际上没问题。只是非常复杂的基础设施问题——你会不同地分片模型，不同时间进行权重更新，所有这些……

Dylan: Async……

Swyx: 听这个的人现在都"天啊不请不要"。你要跨数据中心异构芯片 RL on-the-fly 更新——天啊请不要。你在对抗光速。你怎么传所有这些数据？

Jordan: 关于分离式去中心化 RL 有些有趣的架构工作。MIMO 2.6 刚出来，是关于他们如何超级扩展 RL 的好开放论文。

中国芯片：追赶的曲线

Swyx: 你提到很多定制芯片。华为、中国芯片有什么？你们看吗？

Dylan: 我们在追踪。华为芯片在快很多的速度上变好。有一段时间，被美国政府禁后，他们花了几年重置——Ascend 910B 和 C——但现在他们相当快速地推出了 940、950 和 960。我们在试图获取并沿所有维度测试——租以测性能，看规格和制造能力。也在试图获取以便在我们俄勒冈的逆向工程实验室做逆向工程分析。我们在所有这些维度上努力。

Swyx: 可用性如何？有集群吗？实验室没有 Nvidia 没问题吗？早期信号？

Dylan: 总体上？人们是……我是说实验室在用 Anthropic 四个不同的……

Swyx: 不，我是说中国实验室用自己的芯片。

Dylan: 对，我觉得 GLM 明确说他们有 50,000 个非 Nvidia 芯片——中国制造的 AI 加速器，用于他们最新模型的推理。扩展到其他公司——Cambricon、Iluvatar、Enflame 和许多其他——有一批不同公司，他们都在推上曲线。显然他们落后 Nvidia，华为肯定是其中最好的。然后 BU 把芯片业务分拆成完全独立的公司。所以中国芯片生态系统有很多发展，特别是推理——随着前沿模型甚至现在开源模型越来越擅长写 kernel，移植越来越容易。

所以你会有更多多样性和异构性，这就是 Nvidia 转向超快节奏、试图每年发布新芯片和新系统的原因——他们知道必须以光速尽可能快跑，否则会被追上。因为 CUDA 护城河正在迅速被腐蚀。

Jordan: 但这只是量的问题。这些芯片今天确实能工作，但他们没法生产足够多来真正服务所有国内需求。

Dylan: 如果你做 H100 等效或 GB200 等效——Nvidia 在造数百万数百万芯片，Google 在造数百万数百万芯片，Amazon 在造数百万数百万芯片，AMD 在造数百万芯片。但你看中国公司，真正只有华为的毛芯片数超过百万，而且华为芯片是落后的，所以必须打折扣。其他人还在数十万单位，扩大生产非常困难，特别是考虑出口管制。中国明年和后年会快速爬升产量。到 2028 年甚至会生产数千万芯片。但需要时间。

Swyx: 我们不要忘记他们是第一个有国家计划围绕这所有东西的。他们动起来的时候，是我们在人类历史上从没见过的真实规模。

收尾

好了，这里有很多东西要讨论。恭喜 ClusterMAX 和你们所做的一切。实际上我觉得我们成功涉及了今年到目前为止的很多主要话题，很棒。等有空赶上看看你们在俄勒冈建的硬件实验室——我真的想去看看。我们应该做某种旅行。

Jordan: 是，飞过来。我们带你参观。

Dylan: 任何时候你要去给我们个提醒，我们来参观。

Jordan: Dylan 会带你坐他的橙色 Jeep。

Swyx: 我想去 Abilene。让我们就做所有这些事。你们显然也去过。总之，你们要走了。很高兴赶上。恭喜一切。还有我觉得有更多工作要做。Jordan 给我们预览了你在做的事情。EndpointX 听起来有趣。市场真的在细分，这就是我觉得你们早期识别出来并为所有人抬高标准的东西。所以代表大家——谢谢你做这个。

Jordan: 谢谢你，兄弟。

Dylan: 谢谢。

Swyx: 和你们聊很好。再见。

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：ClusterMAX 本质上不是"排行榜"，而是一个**行业强制升级机制**
表面上，ClusterMAX 是在给 GPU 云打分。但如果你观察它的二阶效应，会发现它扮演的角色更像**美国劳工部的 OSHA 安全检查**——它不是在评价现状，而是在**用公开羞辱重塑行业基线**。
证据链很有趣： - 第一代门槛"super low"，第二代第三代"harder and harder" - 结果是"趋势是降级"——这不是评分系统的失败，这是**设计意图** - Jordan 甚至开发了免费 CLI 工具 `cmax`，让客户能自己检查供应商 - 发文后几小时 Ilya 跟进 tweet——这是一种**精心编排的声誉共振**
跨领域连接：这与 **Moody's / S&P 评级机构的早期历史**惊人相似。1909 年 John Moody 开始给铁路债券评级时，他做的不是"反映市场"，而是**强行给市场创造了一套可比较的语言**。SemiAnalysis 正在对 GPU 云做同样的事——而且他们比评级机构更聪明：**明确拒绝 sell-side 收入，把全

item.title: [a16z] Why Building an AI Agent Is Easier Than Deploying One
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、系统记录的"暗物质"：真正的工作发生在不可见处

视频中一个被轻描淡写却极具破坏性的事实是：ERP 系统里显示的"8K 一吨铝"，背后是 30 场利益相关者会议、500 封邮件、20 张 Excel 表、3 周 3D 建模。真正的工作有 80% 发生在系统之外——而过去 20 年整个企业软件行业，本质上都在优化那不到 20% 的"可见残渣"。

这让我想到物理学的暗物质概念：宇宙中可观测物质只占 5%，但过去几百年人类所有的工具都在打磨这 5%。Leo 之所以能颠覆存量巨头（incumbents），不是因为它做了更好的记账系统，而是它第一次把工具伸向了那不可观测的 95%。这是一个认知范式的切换——从"记录工作"到"承载工作"。

跨领域连接：这与法律科技高度同构。合同签订只是终点，但 90% 的工作是无数邮件、备忘录、电话会议——这些从未进入 Case Management System。Vlad 的框架暗示：任何"系统记录仅是冰山一角"的行业，都存在同样的 AI 原生颠覆机会（医疗诊断、投行并购、保险理赔、研发管线……）。

二、反直觉洞察：70% 的准确率 ≠ 70% 的自动化（而可能是 -20%）

这是整期访谈最反直觉的一句话，但几乎没有被展开。Vlad 说："如果你能达到 70% 的性能，这不意味着 70% 的自动化——因为那 30% 的错误会污染 100% 的信任，于是人类必须复核 100% 的输出。结果：你可能比不用 AI 时产生了更多的工作。"

这揭示了一个被普遍忽视的 AI 价值不连续曲线：从 70% 到 95% 不是增加 25%，而是从"负价值"跳到"正价值"的相变。这不是线性函数，而是像冰到水的相变——在临界温度之前，再多的热量也不会让它变成液体。

跨领域连接：这与自动驾驶的 L2→L4 困境、与放射科 AI 读片的采用曲线、与早期无人机自主飞行完全同构。所有"必须被信任才能释放价值"的技术，都存在这种相变门槛。而这也解释了为什么 Vlad 那句话很关键："incumbents 不是在 hold back，而是 being held back"——他们的组织结构（两个 VP，两个 P&L）让他们永远跨不过这个相变点，因为跨过去意味着让一个 VP 死掉。

三、最意外的一个预言：procurement 将变成"交易双方的共同基础设施"

视频中有一个几乎被埋没的瞬间：Vlad 说"未来买方和卖方都会有 agent"，然后他意识到——如果 5000 项任务中有 4999 项双方激励一致，只有"价格"是零和的，那么 Leo 的真正野心不是服务采购部，而是成为买卖双方之间的协同层（coordination layer）。

这是整期访谈最大胆也最隐秘的预言：采购软件（一个历史上典型的"单边 SaaS"）正在变异为类似于交易所、清算所、SWIFT 网络的多边基础设施。

跨领域连接：这与博弈论中的"科斯定理（Coase theorem）"深度相关——科斯说过，交易成本降到足够低时，产权归属不重要，市场会自动达到最优。但过去企业间协作的交易成本极高（Vlad 举的例子：一封被漏掉的邮件 = 1 亿美元损失），所以企业必须垂直整合。当多边 AI agent 把企业间协调成本压到接近零，整个"企业的边界"（科斯的核心问题）都会重新定义——这不是采购软件的升级，而是对公司这种组织形态本身的重新定义。

另一个让我震惊的 Easter egg：Vlad 顺带提了一句"agent 应该参考 Polymarket 的赔率来判断供应链中断的概率"。预测市场作为 AI agent 的输入信号——这是我第一次听到有人把投机金融工具当作企业决策的实时感官。如果这个思路成立，Polymarket 这类平台的真正客户，可能根本不是赌徒，而是未来 Leo 这样的 agent。

四、一个被低估的 moat 模型：Sema 的"你无法预测护城河"

Sema 有一句很"反创业指南"的话："所有最棒的生意，早期都不是在规划护城河，他们只是在赢得客户信任，然后卖更多的东西。" 这颠覆了 MBA 式的护城河分析框架（五力模型、网络效应矩阵等）。

真正的护城河是涌现的，不是设计的。这与进化生物学的观察一致：没有一个物种是"规划出"自己的生态位的，而是在生存中偶然锁定了资源依赖关系。Leo 现在能垂直整合 legal/finance/engineering，不是三年前的 PPT 规划，而是在服务客户过程中被动涌现的——客户的依赖加深了，才有了后视镜中看起来像"战略"的东西。

📝 转录文本

Why Building an AI Agent Is Easier Than Deploying One

频道：a16z | 嘉宾：Sema Amble (a16z Partner), Vlad Kyle (Co-founder & CEO, Leo)

开场：几个预示性片段

"If you want to build an aircraft, you need to procure thousands of suppliers. Someone sends a confirmation of like, hey, sorry, this part is going to arrive 2 weeks later. And if they missed this email, hundreds of millions of damage."

"Procurement historically may have been more in a box, and now it's touching legal, it's touching finance. It's touching a bunch of different software systems and people. The opportunity for the AI native startup is to say, we're going to own that entire end-to-end arc."

"No company and no enterprise starts with fully autonomous negotiation agents from day one. Why? Because they don't trust us and they don't trust the technology from day one. And by having this human-in-the-loop approach, we have feeding our agent with all the feedback and all the learnings — and then they suddenly trust us for like 10k negotiations, 20k negotiations, 100k negotiations."

"When you think about what a durable vertical AI company looks like, what are the qualities that you look for? It's really really hard to forecast your moat going forward. If you look back at all the best businesses at the early stages, they were…"

一、引入：Incumbents vs. AI-native Startups

Elena（主持人）: Welcome back to the A16Z podcast. I'm Elena Burgerer. And today I'm joined by Sema Amble, a partner at A16Z, and Vlad Kyle, a co-founder and CEO of Leo, which builds AI agents for enterprise procurement.

Sema, you recently wrote a piece called The incumbents are coming, and it asked a question facing almost every AI application company. If an established software vendor already has the customer and the data and the model can work across its tools, where does a startup have an advantage? And we have Vlad here, and Vlad can really help us understand where a startup has an advantage. So I think a good place to start is the cases for and against the incumbents. If a company can connect a capable AI agent to the software it already uses, where does another application actually have a use case and an advantage there?

Sema: Yeah, let me back up and frame it up a little bit. Historically we thought about: there's the incumbent, and then there's the startup, and they're fighting — you know, it's a fight between distribution and innovation, to take my partner Alex Rampel's phrase.

However, now there's like this third piece which you're pointing at — which is, the incumbent can layer on one of the models on top, and then there's a much more formidable competitor in the market. So why do you need an AI-native startup if you've got Clodeforce, which is taking Clode plus Salesforce and putting the two together? And then you've already got all your data and your customers — sorry, your employees are all used to using the product. So why another product?

I absolutely still think there's obviously still a case for the AI-native startup, and it really centers around the fact that the legacy incumbent is limited to their system of record, and they're not completing the end-to-end job.

一个具体例子：客户支持

Say you're a customer, and they call and say they got charged after they got canceled. Resolving that cancellation history isn't just the customer going into the chat and saying "hey, I got overcharged." The response has to hit billing, it has to look at all the chat history, it has to look at the contract. That's not one system of record — that's the knowledge around that customer and everything it touched. That's something that one system of record wouldn't touch.

However, the opportunity for the AI-native startup is to say: we're going to own that entire end-to-end arc. That could be in legal — owning everything from brief all the way through trial. Or in procurement. It's really this concept of owning the end-to-end work.

二、采购的真实样貌：被遮蔽的 80%

Elena: Vlad, do you want to talk about where that does show up in procurement — where an existing incumbent plus a model is just insufficient, and what have you seen with the companies that you work with?

Vlad: Sure. When we think about procurement, I would assume that most people think about prices, right? What is the end price that we negotiated on? And surprisingly, the record looks always very very simple — it's just 8K, that's the result, for example.

It's the same for sales, right? Even if I come to Sema and tell her "hey, we now partnered up with another enterprise, look at the signature here for this contract," it looks very easy — but Sema doesn't see all the work behind it. There probably like 30 stakeholder meetings happened, 500 emails, 20 Excel sheets.

That's the same for the counterpart: procurement. You see in the ERP system, 8K for aluminum. But you don't see that maybe the supplier did a pushback and asked for 10K. You don't see that a cost engineer had run 3 weeks of Excel sheets and 3D modeling to find out the prices of the part and everything else. Most of the work in procurement actually happens outside of this ERP or any system of record.

三、四种 Agent：从 retrieval 到 principal

Elena: In the workflow that you described, an agent can do a huge number of things, and different kinds of agents can do a large number of things. A year ago, I think a lot of the incumbents were releasing chatbots, and that was kind of the extent of what you would see. But Sema, in this piece that you wrote, you lay out four different kinds of agents: retrieval agents, process agents, policy agents, and principal agents. Can you walk us through all of them and explain what changes in the kind of judgment that's necessary across all of them?

Sema: A year ago, I made this meme — the "slap on a chatbot" strategy — which was essentially all the incumbents effectively had a chatbot that sat on top of the system of record, which you could chat with to retrieve information, maybe do some light analytics. That was in the first bucket of what the retrieval agent is.

Let me walk you through an example using customer support, because it's easier to understand.

  • Retrieval agent: There's a service outage and you call in to say "I want to get compensated." The retrieval assistant can pull up the contract term, verify there was an outage, synthesize the information back to you.
  • Process agent: Pulls through an approval of credit — based on the policy handbook, it was out from these dates, therefore you're entitled to money, and it applies the bill. No judgment involved.
  • Policy agent: Not just applying the process, but saying: "In this situation, it was out for 20 minutes — that's enough to be considered a significant outage." Applying judgment because there isn't a strict definition.
  • Principal agent: Weighing — "should we offer more compensation because that was a pretty terrible outage, and we want to preserve the relationship, and it's worth doing more beyond even what a process or policy would call for."

The importance of these four things is that most incumbents started out in bucket one. Now they're marketing that they're moving towards process and policy. But if you look at what they've launched — workflow agents that help you get a document signed or input information from a transcription — they're very much still limited to retrieval and a little bit of process. They've not gotten into more judgment.

为什么存量巨头被卡住了

Elena: Do you want to say why some of the incumbents are holding back?

Sema: They're holding back, but they are held back. I'm sure they want to be full force. There are probably two pieces:

  1. Distribution advantage: They have the customer trust, which enables them to sell more products. Take Salesforce — when Agentforce launched, it was very easy for customers to say "yeah, I'm going to sign up," especially if it was offered at almost no extra cost.
  2. Internal incentive issues: If you start getting into more complicated agents, it's an internal conflict with an existing product that's offering workflow versus resolving the work. Those are different buyers. If you're solving a customer support issue end-to-end versus providing a workflow for a human agent — two VPs, different orgs, different products, and they will never figure out the right set of incentives.

四、Leo 在哪一层？外部信任的建立

Elena: Vlad, where across this spectrum of retrieval / process / policy / principal does Leo sit?

Vlad: We span across all of those categories, and it really depends on the complexity and the risk our agents take. Sometimes we already have use cases where we run fully autonomously; sometimes we have the human in the loop. It really depends on the budget approval, how complex and how risky this is.

Coming back to what Sema said about trust for the incumbents — you talked about internal trust. I think there's also an external trust thing. How do you convince someone to go from "an agent that retrieves information" to "an agent that does something completely autonomously"? Obviously there's a product component, but mainly it's a people component. They need to trust you.

We as a startup have to earn the trust. Incumbents already have the trust — but this also means they can destroy the trust if they ship something too early.

一次意外的发现：exception handling 才是 80%

Interestingly, those process agents actually became kind of a side quest for us. When we looked at the invoice process — retrieve information, match it across other documents, push to SAP or Oracle — we figured out: that's 100% of the software market today. But it's only 20% of the actual job. 80% of the problem is: what if the invoice is fraudulent? What if there's a mismatch? What if we don't take the happy path?

So we shifted very fast to the next step — agents doing exception handling. We got lucky being always slightly ahead of the curve. Three years ago, retrieving a document was "crazy impressive." We pitched it, found it was a real use case, and shipped it weeks later. We're doing this now for process agents, fully autonomous agents, and long-running agents.

Sema：双重信任

Sema: An interesting point on trust is this internal versus external trust. You need your customer to buy the procurement software and trust to use it for their internal processes. But one of the really interesting things when we first met Vlad was that they're also doing the negotiation. So you have to trust that the Leo agent is going to then interface with a third party — that's another piece of trust.

五、采购的全景：谁都卷进来了

Elena: Can you paint the picture of what's involved in procurement — who your customers are, what legacy systems they're used to?

Vlad: When you think about procurement, you might think about purchasing — just buying something, like in B2C. But actually it's a very intense process that runs the economy. It includes multiple stakeholders: legal, cost engineering, procurement, finance — all of them have to work on these decisions.

How we convinced them: we were always a little bit ahead of the curve. We started a few weeks before the ChatGPT breakthrough. We'd already heard all of the problems, then we heard the hype, and we were able to pitch these enterprises quickly.

There's also the product perspective — we have a lot of evals in place. No company and no enterprise starts with fully autonomous negotiation agents from day one. Why? Because they don't trust us and they don't trust the technology from day one. So you have a very easy approach of having a human in the loop — and this is extremely helpful because we may have the "perfect procurement negotiator" overall, but we don't know exactly how a specific Fortune 10 enterprise operates. By having this human-in-the-loop approach, we're feeding our agent with all the feedback and learnings — and then they suddenly trust us for 10k negotiations, 20k negotiations, 100k negotiations.

Then you have other agents that are more long-running. For multi-million-dollar negotiations where you analyze complex 3D models and technical drawings, we on purpose always have experts in the loop. An agent runs for multiple hours, then we ask for feedback from the cost engineer, and it does the next piece of work.

Human-in-the-loop 具体长什么样

Elena: Where do you put the human in the loop on the negotiation side?

Vlad: It depends on the level of negotiation.

  • Low-stakes negotiations enterprises never did before: They didn't care about anything below 50k because they didn't have capacity. (Hack for other startups: send an enterprise an invoice for 40k — they probably won't negotiate… unless they have Leo agents.) Risk of a bad negotiation agent here? Nearly zero. Better than nothing.
  • Business-relationship-sensitive: Maybe not big spend, but you need the relationship — podcast or marketing services, someone who already knows how a16z operates. Here procurement people care about tone of voice. Mostly autonomous, but with HITL.
  • Strategic multi-million-dollar negotiations: Multiple steps — contract design (legal), collection design (finance), cost structure (cost engineering), commercials (procurement). These are not back-office people. They're highly trained specialists feeding Leo's long-running agents with insights.

Sema: That's another example of how procurement historically may have been more in a box, and now it's touching legal, it's touching finance, touching a bunch of software systems and both specialists and generalists.

六、垂直案例：造飞机需要什么？

Elena: Can we map this onto a specific vertical? I'm a drone manufacturer, I manufacture humanoid robotics — how many parts, how many factories, how many suppliers?

Vlad: When we as Leo talk about procurement of purchases, we don't talk about laptops and pencils. That's solved — we solved that three years ago, that's easy. We talk about: you want to build an aircraft, or robots, or drones, or — we're doing a podcast about the AI hype, but even AI needs to be built, right? Data centers.

Building means procuring. If you build an aircraft, you need to procure thousands of suppliers, build a factory. Really small frictions can have crazy impact. If one specific part arrives 2 weeks later, this can be hundreds of millions of dollars of damage and postpone the project.

One part is: you need to figure out what you need, with what suppliers you work, what's the best supplier for this part. Then once decided, there's all the operational back-office stuff — someone sends a confirmation "hey, sorry, this part is going to arrive 2 weeks later." That's one of 500 emails in Outlook or Gmail. If they miss this email, hundreds of millions of damage. The only thing stored in the system of record is then just the date. Our agents are not only retrieving the information — they're making the decisions. Does this have an impact? What kind of impact, and how can we resolve this?

物理世界的介入边界

Elena: When you're so deeply embedded in the physical world, what kinds of physical world problems can you intervene with? Some things seem unsolvable — a shipment falls off the ship, or the strait is closed.

Vlad: It's about probability. You can't change damage on a ship — but you can predict it. You can predict how reliable a supplier is. If you have one supplier where 20% of goods are missing, and another where 1% of goods are missing, but the first is 10x cheaper — for this use case, maybe it's fine to pay 10x the amount because you have higher probability it actually arrives.

The powerful thing is you have context not only within one enterprise, but outside: news, bets on Polymarket ("okay, those disruptions are going to happen"), information on the supplier side, seller side, demand side. Combining all of those contexts — I wouldn't say there's a limitation in the long run.

What we're building at Leo is much bigger than just procurement within a company — it's inter-company, how enterprises are doing business with each other, buyer and supplier side.

七、Leo 作为多 agent 系统

Elena: You describe Leo as a multi-agent system. What are the different agents doing?

Vlad: Leo's agents span across all four categories Sema mentioned. But the other thing is: to do a job end-to-end, those agents need to share information with each other in a very specific order. The human-level task involves 8 people, 8 stakeholders, maybe 3 departments and 5 different software tools. Only with a multi-agent system can you do a job end-to-end.

When we started out, we had a retrieval/co-pilot. Then a single agent. But we discovered: you can't solve a negotiation without a contract agent, or without an agent looking at the news.

具体例子：Boeing 采购一颗螺栓

Elena: If Boeing needs to procure a bolt — what exactly is that process, and where does Leo step in?

Vlad: This is one of the purchases we can run fully autonomously, because of the multi-agent system.

  1. Demand: Someone has a demand. Even this is complicated — you're a construction worker, you open your laptop only every second week, and you're required to work with SAP. We make it easy: take a photo, upload a quote, upload an Excel sheet. That's everything you should know about procurement. No one outside the procurement department cares about categories, GL accounts, framework contracts.
  2. Our agents take off: Check inventory → ask another plant "can we source these bolts internally?" → if no, talk to the sourcing agent → do we have internal suppliers or external? → another agent drafts the RFQ → sends it out over email → bunch of emails arrive, some nonsense, some PDFs, some Excel sheets → retrieve information.
  3. Next step: Based on price benchmarking, is there opportunity to negotiate? Agents decide the next step — strategic negotiation with HITL, autonomous negotiation, auctions, e-auctions — calling the specific agent.
  4. End-to-end: Confirming the order, shipment tracking, invoices. All fully autonomous, capturing context.

Direct vs. Indirect Procurement

Elena: What's direct procurement?

Vlad: Everything above is indirect — the main goal is automation. "What are you doing a thousand times a day that you actually want to do zero times a day?" Run fully autonomous agents, capture savings along the way. Indirect = MRO parts, building a factory, bolts, laptops, pencils, marketing services, podcast studio.

Direct procurement = when you build an airplane. Suppliers you actually need to build the airplane / drone / robot. Not 50,000 suppliers — 100 to 2,000 maximum. Extremely strategically important. One supplier might represent $1 billion of spend. You don't want to run an autonomous negotiation here — you want 3 months of preparation, engineers analyzing: "What's the index for aluminum? For oil? How did the price change?" Check the quality of the part. This is where it gets really exciting deploying agents.

Elena: For something like that, the expert engineers are more "front of house" and the agent is "back of house"?

Vlad: Obviously more back of house. 90% of the work is preparation. The end result in your system of record is "instead of $1B, I paid $900M." But there's 3 months of preparation and 10 people working full-time.

We also have use cases helping in real time. Imagine we're negotiating now — I have real-time insights popping up on my screen: "The index for oil increased by 10%, that's why we need to increase prices by 10%." And immediately a popup: "True, oil increased by 10%, but the product has only 30% oil contained — you shouldn't increase the price by 10%, maybe only by 4%."

八、模型、Harness 与 Fine-tuning

Elena: Companies like Harvey and Decagon are really fine-tuning models now. What underlying models do you use, and how do you approach fine-tuning or harnessing?

Vlad: We use multiple models from all providers — we really see this as a commodity. Good for general business purpose: reading, creating a PDF, creating an Excel sheet.

For some use cases, you can get extremely far with foundation model + harness — maybe 100% of the job. But other use cases: best foundation model, best harness, still only 80%.

需要 fine-tune 的两个用例

  • Should-cost modeling (cost engineers analyzing drawings to determine what a part should cost): there's an opportunity we've already started fine-tuning for.
  • Price benchmarking: In a perfect world you'd drag-and-drop a quote and get the perfect price. But this info isn't publicly available — it's all proprietary data within or across enterprises. General-purpose models can't train on that.

Maybe not just training an LLM — more like what we see with models like Jeff (?), where you train on text data but the output is an outcome, just the perfect price. You can't do this with harness, because if I give you a quote from BCG and a quote from McKinsey, they could do the exact same work but at a 10x different price — a procurement manager has a gut feeling, "this quote makes sense." If you ask them to write down the rules, they can't — it's gut feeling and instinct.

Good analogy: content creation. I don't know how much I should pay someone for creating a video — but there's a gut feeling. We see opportunity training an agent not as a classic LLM but outcome-based: price benchmarking, should-cost modeling.

九、什么样的垂直 AI 公司能长久？

Elena: Sema, we've talked about labs moving into industry-specific work. When you think about what a durable vertical AI company looks like, what qualities do you look for?

Sema: One is around owning the end-to-end work, building up a data asset, doing something that hasn't been done before.

I think when you talk a lot about moats — it's really really hard to forecast your moat going forward. If you look back at all the best businesses at the early stages, they were just thinking: "I'm winning customer trust, I'm selling more to them, there's a lot of opportunity." Versus "I'm going to do these six steps and then get to the seventh step and then we'll have a moat."

A big part is: you're locking in the customer, there are more dependencies, they find it valuable, you're doing more of the work. Old CRM company was a log for all the deals. New sales AI agent is actually owning a lot of the sales prep process and the outbound process, fielding inbound, doing a bunch of the work. The overall customer is dependent on that product, and that's a really important signal of getting to the moat. Everything about stickiness and network effects is downstream of that initial customer use and value.

为什么客户不自己 DIY？

Elena: Vlad, have you had conversations with customers who ask "why can't I just plug into a model and do this myself"?

Vlad: 100%, and it's a very fair question. Even internally at Leo — our first use case 3 years ago was retrieving a quote and getting the information into SAP. Technical, but tremendous business value. It's now a case study: if you apply to work at Leo, we give you 8 hours to build it. A product that was one of our first use cases can now be built by engineers within 8 hours.

So the obvious question is: couldn't a procurement department also build everything in 2 months? Answer: yes, but you'll only reach 70% of the performance. And 70% of performance doesn't mean 70% automation — it depends on the task. You might have 70% performance but still need to do 100% of the work, because 70% is not that much. All the people still have to check the data. Maybe you even created more work than before.

Sema: Two things to layer on:

  1. Overall, it's good if there's more adoption of base models or GPT products — it means people are more willing to trust vertical-specific products as well. The familiarity, comfort, excitement about AI tools is generally good for the market.
  2. I was chatting with the management team of a Fortune 500 company 2–3 weeks ago. They had tried to build out their own cash collection product. After 3–4 months, they found there wasn't enough context — poor quality context, recordings, screen grabs. They tried to pull it all into one system but it wasn't good enough. Then: "We've got now two different ERPs, and we were about to acquire another one. Who's going to update all the mappings? Test it out? Does it work? And exception handling — you now need to map that onto a totally different system."

They realized the internal build didn't make sense. Enterprise companies generally realize that there's their core competency and then there's building internal tools — and they should focus on the first camp.

Vlad: Exactly. They can get to 80%, but those last 20% really matter. You can only get into production with them. That's why you need this harness — integrations, memory, workflows — and sometimes you need vertical data. Pareto principle: those 20% make 80% of the effort.

十、买卖双方都用 Agent 之后会发生什么？

Elena: Vlad, are you seeing suppliers start to use agents or AI? What happens when both buyers and suppliers are fully AI-enabled?

Vlad: We 100% believe in the future there will be agents on both sides. Surprisingly, when we look at the supplier side (which also equals the seller side) — historically sales was always ahead of procurement. But for suppliers to Fortune 500 companies, this is actually not true. They're advanced in things like video recordings, tools like Granola — but not really having agents deployed to automate the work.

The cool thing: procurement is unsexy, but it's one process, and procurement is the counterpart. In industrial companies, procurement has bigger power over the supplier. As an automotive supplier, you dictate what tools your suppliers use, what the quality has to be, how they have to respond to an RFQ. So the opportunity: if we serve procurement and they can dictate what a supplier uses — why not push them to Leo agents too, owning both sides of the transaction?

Sema: It could extend to legal work. Two adversarial parties — two law firms with clients with different interests — but both benefit from knowing: here's the latest draft, here's where we are with open issues, here's what's been agreed upon. Even just tracking that doesn't really exist right now — it's being created by humans. The coordination effort could be done by an agent.

Elena: It's super cool to think about how both sides are evolving in tandem — one side might go a little bit faster, but over time potentially people are on the same platform, and it's way better coordinated for everyone.

Vlad: 100%. The obvious question: if both parties have negotiation agents, isn't price a zero-sum point? But price is the outcome of 5,000 different other tasks, and on those 5,000 tasks they have the same incentive. Sales wants as little friction as possible. Buyers want fast time to market. If you're building a data center or an aircraft, you want it built as fast as possible — you don't want it 6 months late because it took so long to analyze supplier responses. On those 5,000 other tasks, the incentive is exactly the same. That's why Leo can deploy agents on both sides.

十一、定制化的新经济学

Elena: There used to be this logic that you shouldn't customize your software too much to one end user. But something about LLMs and AI in general — it might increasingly be possible to customize without slowing yourself down. Is that something you're seeing?

Sema: There's a lot of forward-deployed work happening right now, partly because the state of customer data and understanding customer N is a lot harder than understanding N+1. We're in the early stages of deployment overall — that's why there are still a lot of humans as part of the product.

That's harder for incumbents — they're not set up to have their product feedback cycle work this way. They have implementation teams, but it's an afterthought versus something that feeds into the product side.

The beauty of AI: it learns over time. With learning loops and the right eval process, you can do more and more complicated jobs. Part of that is automating the deployment itself. Many of our companies are doing that at a rapid clip — more customization is handled in an automated way, and the customer can turn the knobs via software. Versus the old world: "I needed to bring in Accenture to do your SAP customization." Now it's forward-deployed teams, and ultimately it will be completely software-driven.

Vlad: That's why 85% of Leo's people are engineers. The rest mostly have engineering backgrounds. We don't want to be a consulting company — we want the best agents in indirect, direct, finance. But enterprises have different nuances in their processes.

How we work: build the product so it reduces customization, with a lot of self-service. The job of our FDEs (forward-deployed engineers) is making it self-service while internally automating their own job. Their KPI is literally: your job is to automate yourself. Once you automate yourself, you go to the next task. I think it's an approach Google does too.

十二、现场故事：Bots and Buyers Summit

Elena: There was recently a very big system-of-record event — and we're not talking about Dreamforce, we're talking about the Bots and Buyers Summit that Leo hosted in New York. Just wanted to hear stories from the ground.

Vlad: It was the third time we did this event. Now we did it in New York, just a few blocks from our office — over 100 procurement leaders arrived. We make sure we only invite high-caliber people — C-level, VPs.

Two reasons it's amazing:

  1. The last 26–27 years of procurement: a lot of tools emerged — 500 procurement tools on LinkedIn landscapes. If you talk to procurement people, it's very painful. I challenge someone to find a person who loves working with procurement. People hate working with procurement — requesters, suppliers, and even procurement people themselves. 1,000 tools made the process more efficient — but never changed how people actually work. It's crazy: they work in emails, Microsoft Teams, Excel sheets, PowerPoints. Zero AI-enabled.
  2. Cross-department perspective: We're not showing "look at this crazy invoice feature." We're showing: someone needs something, and in the end you have it on your table — spanning indirect, direct, logistics, finance. We put it into the physical world — AI agents are very abstract, so we build booths (we also have this in our offices in New York) where you walk through and experience the agents hands-on. That's what people love. The next event will have around 700 people.

Elena: Procurement people gone wild. Where's next?

Vlad: Munich. We do them in Europe (Munich) and New York all the time.

为什么会有人为采购激动？

Elena: What do you think it takes to get people excited about procurement? I remember talking to a guy out of procurement 7–8 years ago — "I hate talking about this product, I use this legacy system of record, I'm on Coupa, I don't want to buy anything else, don't want to talk about it." Most disgruntled customer call I've ever done.

Vlad: The reason I like procurement: it's highly emotional. If you talk to the people, they're really frustrated. B2B SaaS, okay, but highly emotional. Combine that with boring and niche — the last revolution they saw was 20 years ago, maybe a nicer UI 10 years ago. So it's easy to amaze them.

Boring + highly emotional + crazy business impact. It feels unnecessary, but has crazy P&L impact — and impact on the whole economy: how data centers, aircrafts, cars, drones are built. Also: to get 1% margin increase, you need 10% more revenue. If you manage 1% savings, that equals 10% more sales.

Combine all three and you have a trillion-dollar business opportunity. That's my opinion for procurement — but there are probably other things that are emotional, boring, and have crazy business impact.

Elena: Well, Vlad, thank you so much for joining us. This was a ton of fun.

item.description:
## 一、系统记录的"暗物质"：真正的工作发生在不可见处
视频中一个被轻描淡写却极具破坏性的事实是：ERP 系统里显示的"8K 一吨铝"，背后是 30 场利益相关者会议、500 封邮件、20 张 Excel 表、3 周 3D 建模。**真正的工作有 80% 发生在系统之外**——而过去 20 年整个企业软件行业，本质上都在优化那不到 20% 的"可见残渣"。
这让我想到物理学的暗物质概念：宇宙中可观测物质只占 5%，但过去几百年人类所有的工具都在打磨这 5%。**Leo 之所以能颠覆存量巨头（incumbents），不是因为它做了更好的记账系统，而是它第一次把工具伸向了那不可观测的 95%**。这是一个认知范式的切换——从"记录工作"到"承载工作"。
跨领域连接：这与法律科技高度同构。合同签订只是终点，但 90% 的工作是无数邮件、备忘录、电话会议——这些从未进入 Case Management System。Vlad 的框架暗示：**任何"系统记录仅是冰山一角"的行业，都存在同样的 AI 原生颠覆机会**（医疗诊断、投行并购、保险理赔、研发管线……）。
---

item.title: [YC Root Access] Building AI Agents for Everyone
