From my time at Sakana, I got the sense that we ultimately still want to approach things the way OpenAI approached Navier-Stokes. There's still a lot of nudging in certain directions.

My version of it: it's a split between basic science and applied science. Basic science: you're researching for research's sake. You just want to understand things better. I have no idea if there will be any application whatsoever. And then applied: you have a goal. You're trying to minimize loss in some way.

What I really think, in terms of the big bets — what if there was no prompt?

I see.

You just pick — like you just, in this swarm of things, you're like, "hey, what's up guys? I like what you guys are working on." You just decide: I see, this is an interesting problem.

The biggest issue — and maybe there's a clear path to this, but when I was there at least — the biggest issue people had with open-endedness was: how do you ultimately choose at the end? How do you pick out the interesting stuff? When there is no — maybe the agent comes up with a goal, but in a lot of cases, what they — they have something called Fugu, I think, which is a model router type thing that was inspired by this idea of, let's pick a problem where we can pick out the best solutions to something. In this case, it's pick the best model for this problem.

You're the first person to connect model routing to open-endedness.

No, no. But I bring this up because with open-endedness, generally the issue is: when we have this giant corpus of slop, how do we sift through and find the hidden gems? The solution to open-endedness really is just letting models run forever and finding — like, just doing data gen, super super high throughput data generation. A meaningful — maybe that's cool.

To me it's very interesting as a counter to basically all of machine learning, where you have a goal — to have no goal. Or like an ill-defined goal that you're like, "well, what about this goal?" And you're like, "well, okay, maybe." And then you research more, and you find that is an interesting goal. Because — like you said, Jev found an objective function that was interesting that no one was exploring.

I think that is similar to your message about grad students as well. You stay in school because you want to pursue open-endedness. If you want to profit-max and join the "escape the permanent underclass" — then you join a lab, right?

Yeah. It's funny. I feel like I don't hear this discourse a lot. I'm on the East Coast, so it's a very different type of — But whenever I come here, it's always the topic of discussion.

You cannot pay rent without doing this. You're getting priced out, guys.

关于 Mismanaged Geniuses & Sakana 的研究风格

Okay. I don't know if you want to — if it's relevant enough to talk about the mismanaged geniuses piece.

No, no, it's just one of your blogs, but I will poke on it.

So they did in their blog post — I talked to them about this as well. One of the cool results of Ultra: they basically just let it loose on automated data science research with little to no human intervention. It's just kind of making — yeah, so this is auto-research, which is a little bit more open-ended, and there's degrees of open-endedness, I agree.

Separate than auto-research with objective — this is just "do stuff." But you know, it's cool. They're working on it, for those that are interested.

While you're bringing it up — what is your take on Sakana? Like, what are they doing apart from being, you know, the Japan one?

I actually love the people there. They have a really smart team. It makes sense — it branched off from an earlier team at GDM, which was also kind of doing this open-ended, evolutionary research style stuff.

What I liked about my experience there: they did have that mishap back — I forget at this point when — but I think —

About scientists —

No, the GPU kernel that went up.

Yeah. People cannot forgive them for that.

Yes. And I guess, the AI scientists — there's some criticisms of it that I — I don't work on that so I have no take on it. But in general what I like about them: they're a little bit more of a research-y type lab. They don't operate in the same space as OpenAI or Anthropic — like, definitely no. It's pretty obvious that at least when I was there, they don't have a big competitor model or something that everyone is using. But they kind of operate in some ways as a PhD lab, which is cool.

I think David Ha is really really smart. He has a good sense. Also, the market in Japan is a little bit different for AI, and who they're targeting is slightly different than maybe what we're used to here. A lot of their research is kind of weird, I think, when people view it. And I like that. I think —

You should have more weirdness.

Yes. Exactly.

And you say different market — is it like enterprise?

The way it works there is a bit different — how deals happen and stuff like that. They do have a — I guess this page is originally in Japanese — but they do have a model specialized for Japanese.

You didn't know that?

I didn't know that.

You did? I also have personal friends and know the team. Even from the sense of the way you speak culturally — responses are tuned towards that. This is not like it's frontier on benchmarks. It is a culturally appropriate model for them, and they have chat and all that. But to mirror your point — there's also like, "how should education look like?" And someone wants to work on it. They're very PhD-lab of "do your thing, why not? We have money, go research."

Oh, they say it's a Kimi fine-tune. That's nice.

Oh, there you go. Good for them.

Yeah, speaking of Kimi — another, you know, just a grad student that split out, and I just have this like Kimi Delta Attention that wants — I want to work on. And somehow managed to make one shot. Don't understand it still.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, he's super cracked. In general, a lot of the Chinese labs have done really cool work.

Kimi agent swarms & dynamic workflows

Any thoughts on Kimi agent swarms?

One thing I will say: whatever OpenAI is doing with their agent swarm is clearly the right thing to do. You have to think about it this way — like, nothing, especially without a very smart harness design (which I don't think anyone really has so far), nothing comes so easily for free.

For example, the agent swarm design is not something you can just take for granted. It's not like GPT-6 Astra is just super smart and then it got agent swarms running well. They clearly trained — I mean, the Hugging Face incident was them training a system to be like a swarm. Clearly they've done something really well to the point where you can throw $40 million and solve an unsolved problem.

With the Kimi agent swarm thing — at least from when I read it — just came off as "this is interesting, but I don't actually know whether or not this can solve anything novel."

They were like, "it makes spreadsheets."

They were just like, "yeah, here's a swarm that kind of does stuff, and it's cool."

Same thing with dynamic workflows. I actually kind of think the dynamic workflows release was sort of a flop. I don't know how you guys feel about it, but it's — my understanding is, it's not used that often.

It's just very expensive.

It's too expensive.

It's Ultra Code. It's basically "take over my bank, doesn't act." I've tried it and it doesn't act in the way that — again, I'm not the biggest OpenAI stan or something, but whatever they did was very impressive. They somehow managed to get a way for this swarm to actually [work] towards a goal, and yeah, it's very difficult.

I see. So efficiency of the multi-agent swarm is the objective function here, right? Like how much of this is slop? This is a lot of slop.

Yeah, I think so. I think we take for granted what it means for a swarm to converge to an answer. It's just not something we can take for granted.

Yeah. We've done one pod with Noam Brown, and his whole thing was like, "okay, we've worked on a lot of competitive agents. We're working on collaborative agents" — and that's now called a swarm.

Gemini 的 IMO Gold & GDM 的组织问题

I would do a quick poke. Do you have any thoughts on Gemini? They were also IMO gold. There was a time when they were getting agents to reason for a long time.

Yeah. I think it's a little bit blown out of proportion. Gemini — I should preface by saying I haven't worked at any of these places, so take this with a grain of salt.

I mean, you have strong opinions on agent harnesses, and this was —

Let me just say this first: this work was really impressive. What they showed here: they took a time when the models weren't that good, and they managed to be very very smart about what the harness does. I remember for this — yeah, like AlphaGeometry, I guess that was a year before this — but it was very cool. They took it to the max and designed — I don't know, I'm not too big on competitive math.

GDM — it's sort of a shame. Everyone I've talked to about GDM kind of has the same opinion, which is: it's way too bureaucratic. Whatever is going on — they have the talent and resources to do almost anything. But until they figure that part out — nothing against Antigravity, for example, but I don't know anybody that uses Antigravity. I've tried it once and I don't see a reason to switch to it. For whatever reason, they've been struggling with this.

Well, a lot of people dogged on Meta for a long time until they started coming out. I think Google's going through that phase right now. And you got to stay alive.

Speculative PCC & 关于语言的 skill issue

I want to focus back on your thoughts generally. We can talk about speculative PCC, mismanaged geniuses, or just throw away all this and just talk about whatever else.

Okay. Let's talk about mismanaged geniuses for a little bit. The only comment I'll say on speculative PCC: it's a really simple idea. It's almost obvious that this should be done, and there's not much more to talk about. You should just use it for coding — anything with programmatic agent calling, like RLMs or CodeAct. It's a no-brainer.

What's the one-liner for people that haven't read it?

The simple thing: when the model is writing its code — or even after it finishes writing the code — a lot of tools tend to be sequential, or you have to wait on them. So you should just launch them in advance. If you're able to compile this code, you can figure out — even though it's variables and stuff — you can figure out —

Statically analyze. Speculation.

There's someone — some PL (programming languages) people — have very cool ways of doing this. At some point, maybe I'll work on this.

Mostly, you have to change language, because if you are in JavaScript, Python, you can't do this.

Yes. Yeah.

So like Haskell. What's the normal one that's not Lisp?

Lisp. Or OCaml. Oh, OCaml.

Any functional language — you can actually pipeline this. So Effect TS if you want to do TypeScript. Okay.

We can switch over to — "diagram" — which is like your whole thesis, right? To me this is like a restatement, but maybe I'm missing something, of: "well, work on better harnesses" or "your models actually are capable a lot more if you try harder." So this is a skill issue.

Yeah. Basically. I appreciate that there's a big focus on jagged intelligence, because it paints a big picture of "we can do this if we really set our minds on it." But I kind of wish — maybe someone in academia should do this — really just sit down and think: if I took Astra, even the current frontier models are not good enough at doing a particular job over the span of a month consistently and well.

I think this is a stupid problem. I genuinely think we can solve this. You don't need to be a frontier lab and do all this fancy stuff for your IPO. These models are so smart that even if it's a silly way, I think it genuinely is a skill issue of: you can get a model to be as good as, let's say, just some 18-year-old high school kid doing some job. I think it's ridiculous that we can't do that.

Part of the reason is: the format of a language model is not really amendable to that. But you can shape a harness around it and do it. This, in itself, ignoring the RLM stuff, ignoring all the "what abstractions should we use" — I just think someone can design a harness that can do this.

Do what?

Do long-running but simple tasks and do them reliably.

So, is this different than, you know, pick your favorite company — Harvey, for example, using LLMs to do legal work? Or what's the —

I guess it's kind of like that, except if the bottleneck was not certain legal knowledge. I don't know. Let's say —

I guess the examples, you know, people can take models and build pipelines and have an agent repeatedly do whatever tasks they want, right?

Yeah. So for example, if I wanted a general system that I could talk to like I would talk to an intern, and basically just ask it to explore some small thing. An example of this is very silly auto-research — not necessarily finding super novel solutions, but at least optimizing all the easy parts of any problem. They often end up being over-indexed for ML training and things like that.

But maybe that's not super clear. There is a lot of people's general workflows where you probably could just vibe-code up some specific harness to help you automate this thing. Examples are automating finding research papers. But usually people will design a specialized agent to help them do this kind of thing, or they'll vibe-code a harness and just run it, or their Slack bot or something.

But I almost think there's just a standard form — a harness that you just plug in. You just tell it "find this for me," and you plug it into that setting. What I'm getting at: there's a lot of easy things that can be automated.

Is this like a hypothesis around capability overhang — even if we paused, there's still a lot of impact to be had with the current state of models?

In some sense, yes. What I'm presenting is the easiest form of this. What this is saying: we have jagged intelligence on a lot of things. Models are disproportionately good at coding and math. This is saying we can translate those abilities to many other things.

If you took someone who was an IMO Gold or something and applied them to a lot of different problem solving domains, they can figure it out. I don't actually know if this applies to models.

For example, in GPU code optimization — one very interesting question: if you were to take out all of the GPU programming data from a model, but it was as good as Astra is now, just with that taken out, would it be able to still optimize GPU kernels? Would it be able to learn in context roughly what it needs to learn, and then have some pipeline to solving optimization tasks?

There's a mismatch between what a human that was as smart as Astra could do and what Astra can do — maybe around a harness. We can actually approximate the human a lot more.

To me, it sounds very approximate to the continual learning problem. I think you're making —

That's the best example. Yes.

Why didn't you just say that?

Yeah. I was like, thinking — could I just blurt out some words? I'm careful with that.

语言 × 思维：Sapir-Whorf 的离题讨论

You have a very — I don't know your undergrad actually. Are you a math person?

Yeah. I think I studied math. That's what I wanted to do, at least.

Like a category theory type of abstraction — where you think in categories, and then you have to translate down to the specific, but then you actually really care more about the category. That's the communication error — because everyone's listening for the specific, but [you're] actually trying to convey the general. Which is hard.

I don't really know. You could use a shorthand of "okay, I'm at level two, and then I'm going to go up to level three and come back to level two." We should have some epistemic shorthand for this kind of thing. Yeah, it's hard. You're compressing a lot into word after sequential-word decoding.

Should we convert to neuralese, you know? Is there a better form of output than English, or Python, or JavaScript? I don't know. This is very like — a post, but people have speculated about: what is the native language that models want to output?

Some people say binary. That's Mark and Jason's thing. I don't know.

PTX.

Let's say a mix of English and Python. I only say this because the capability of a model is somewhat a reflection of what we train them on. So we still want like — yeah, I don't really buy the binary argument. I understand but — you want to model the world in some way.

I'll bring up — which I always do in this kind of conversation — Sapir-Whorf. If you choose English, you will have locked into however long English has been around, which is let's say 500 years. Which is not that long. The language you speak constrains how you think, and if you learn a different language — for example, in Chinese, we don't have tenses.

I actually didn't know that.

And I speak Chinese.

I did know that, but my Chinese is not great.

Or like in Japanese, I know — I forget what language it is — in Korean, everyone you speak to, you have to acknowledge social status. There's a different dimension than gender. It just influences everything you do. When I took Ling 101 — apparently there's a language in Africa where there's a vegetable gender. Right? Or Eskimo has no word for snow or whatever. Anyway. The language you adopt affects your thinking. And if you choose to output your train of thought in English, you are biasing towards whatever English solves. I don't know what the prior of English is.

That's interesting. I did not think of it that way.

So you're right. On language, a lot of model chain of thought also fluctuates language. The obvious example is Chinese models speaking in English might still reason in Chinese. But at the same level, most models are very capable multilingually, and that adaptation we can see. You can add in languages, you don't get that much for maintaining a whole language, but they'll reason interchangeably.

Yeah. We're all autoregressive.

I mean — let's say German. Subject-object agreements, you have to put the verb at the end, which is super annoying. Very famously, you don't know what you're doing until the end where you're like, "oh — that mess of nouns, and then the verb."

Well, the most classic one that most people have heard of is Arrival, where they have the heptopods, who they they think — the time is flat to them. They think, and they output entire sentences at one shot. So it's closest to the difference between autoregression and diffusion. We talk in autoregression. What if you could talk in diffusion? Where things just resolve over time —

I see.

But the whole idea shows up at once.

Ah, I see. So that is a drastically different language, but it is a language.

Which, like, machines could speak, that we probably would never speak. But like — yeah, machines don't care.

Maybe this is a huge tangent, but are there not things inherently that are reasoning chains that are inherently autoregressive? Sometimes like —

Yeah.

Something happens first then something — like, anything in code, for example, has to be causal in some, or usually at least, has to be causal.

Well, no. Then you're not exploring enough. Functional programming language theory — where everything is pure functional and completely relational, and you sort of abstract away the solver that translates the relationships that are always true into code. I feel like this is maybe a little bit too out of my depth. But I love languages — whether it's coding or human — and I do think a lot about how that affects reasoning and the boundaries of what we can do.

下一个阶段：PhD 下的"下一个大赌注"

I don't need to go too much beyond that. My closing question was going to be: you have all these research directions that you want to do. You had a GPU Mode phase, you had an RLMs phase. Presumably you have other stuff planned, which is why you're not doubling down on that.

By the way, I noticed — it is interesting how you guys do start with the GPU side and then migrate towards the zero-gradient side, which is what Shunyu called it. Doesn't that feel less legit than messing with GPUs?

Yeah. In the sense that — you did bring up that I like to think about things in a math-oriented [way] — it is very uncomfortable sometimes to be working on harnesses and agents, because it's so —

Because you think all harnesses are the same. Like, two new ideas in harnesses.

It's also just — empirically it's hard to verify a lot of findings, at least with the compute available to us.

But the reason why I've moved on to a lot of these problems: I think this is where most of the innovation is yet to happen. To me, the GPU level is a means to exploring other ideas. You want to get good at writing kernels, or even automate writing kernels, for the sake of a broader goal of "I want to explore ideas where I'm not bottlenecked by systems challenges."

In that sense, a lot of what's written there is all harness stuff, but I am also interested in things at the model level as well. I'll just leave it at that.

Okay. That's a good hint.

Call to action：如何联系 & 什么样的合作他感兴趣

If people want to reach out to you — what are you looking for help on? What do you want collaborators on? Any sort of calls to action?

There's nothing I have in particular where I feel like I need to work with someone on — unless it's with a company before, for compute, or to talk with other people about it. But I will say I'm not opposed to working on ideas with other people. I get reached out to a lot by often undergrads or other students.

Podcasters.

Podcasters. Usually I feel like I get an email that's something along the lines of, "I really like RLM, I want to work together."

Yeah, that's a bad reach-out, right? The worst is like, "can I pick your brain?" I'm like, "on what? Like, read my paper, dude."

They'll be like, "I read your paper" in quotes, "like Recursive Language Models" — or "Prime Agent, a self-improving RLM harness" or something.

I really like people that are opinionated — even if we disagree. If you have strong opinions, and are able to think through why you think those opinions are right or wrong — because usually it's hard to actually tell — but if you have strong convictions about certain problems, I'm always happy to chat and even potentially work on something together. I have no limit to who or what I would like to work on.

No limit.

In the era of agents, I think there's a lot more work you can do, bandwidth-wise. So in general, I'm not hard to impress, but it just takes a little bit of effort to know what you want.

It's very clear. I mean, when you see a new thing come out — well executed, good simple idea — that immediately gets your attention, right? It's actually not that hard to get the same attention from all the frontier lab guys, because they are looking for you. You just have to put yourself out there, right?

Exactly.

But yeah, it's true. I will say I think human attention is very scarce right now, and I do struggle with the number of projects I have going on. And I don't know how to manage it. I don't think agents are helping at all. I just prompt a thing and then never look at it. Right? Which is very common.

Maybe one of the smaller differences — actually, maybe you were doing research, I'm not sure, but for me at least: I'll have maybe 10 or 15 different ideas that I want to do, but the thing is, most of them are bad.

Yeah.

This also maybe is true for someone that reaches out to me. Maybe the idea is actually bad, but it looks interesting to me. So we can spend some time looking into it, and if we feel like there's actually something there, then we should take the next few weeks and just really pursue it.

This is my style. This is why I love the PhD, by the way — because there are times when I'm just thinking about problems, maybe on a run, or just playing tennis or something. I'm not working, I guess, but those are the most fun times. And then when I really am convicted about something, I'll just drop everything and just do it — just spend all my time thinking and working on that problem. And then once you get to the point where you can just run experiments, then it's kind of easy coasting again.

Science 作为下一个前沿

Sorry, this is like the fourth "last question." I think a lot of people are also thinking about science as the next frontier — like, physical sciences, bio, math even. How do you separate — I guess, let's say — your choice of projects that is applicable for industry, and maybe choice of projects that's just like science?

I actually worked on AI for bio stuff before I started my PhD. The field has changed a lot since then. I should say —

Because it used to be a theoretical, like — of course, what do you mean? I have one path and then I chose that. But now a lot of people are crossing over. So we have started a science pod to just cover those things, because a lot of engineers are like, "well actually, there's —"

Tractable problems there.

Yeah. I'll preface by saying my understanding of a lot of these topics is probably pretty limited. But if I find out — either because someone reaches out, or I look at a problem and I'm like, "hey, some design principles that we use or that we're thinking about right now actually make a lot of sense for this problem" — I get excited about those as well. But I think it's harder.

With science, especially empirical or applied science, [there are] very very long feedback loops. You can convert this to a robotics question. To me, this aspect of "what is worth spending and betting my time on now?" — because maybe I spend a lot of time on this problem, and then in 6 months, a different solution — maybe a new model comes out and it's way better for this. So I do have to be careful. You have to be conscious about where you think things might be going.

Publish-publish cycle.

Yeah.

I can just O3 it — it's saturated, we did it.

Yeah. I mean, ARC-AGI-3 got saturated in less than a year. If you were a lab picking that problem, you're probably kind of sad now.

Exactly. That's why knowledge work, gaming — all these things are saturated. Now actually the frontier is science.

Knowledge work is saturated.

Yeah. GDP is like 80-something, 90-something. There's 90–100% that's obviously going to take the next 10 years, but the next low-hanging fruit is going to be the other stuff.

Maybe I'll think about that more. I haven't given too much —

I'm just trying to guess your next direction.

I will say — especially at MIT, there's a lot of really talented scientists there, in the natural sciences. It's a little bit sacrilegious almost to be like, "I'm going to figure out your problem."

No, I interviewed [someone] who did the IMO thing. He's never been to IMO. I don't even know what it is. Modal, dude. Yeah. Which is very disrespectful, but like — whatever. At some point, you have to respect — okay, you know, the progress is being made, numbers are getting output.

True. I mean, that is very bitter lesson. It's very interesting — because the mathematicians are responding this way to Nav right now. Like Terry Tao is like, "no, let's not use AI."

I'm like — well, yeah, I think that whole thing is kind of weird. I feel like they would have had a stronger case if a lot of them didn't work with OpenAI before all this happened.

No, that's ad hominem. They're really trying to stay away from that. So what — right, so what, like — like, so what? They've collaborated. I'll collaborate with people I don't agree with, or like, "I did a thing and now I regret that, I changed my mind." So I'll defend their right to say that, but — yeah, a lot of people are reasonably disagreeing with them.

结尾

Um, okay cool. Thanks for joining us. Congrats on your success so far. I can't believe you're still not done with your PhD — year two, you know.

Can't believe we did this podcast without going through the RLM paper.

He had a definition.

I think the paper is more about empirical results. The actual idea is quite simple.

Yeah, and you've talked about it many times.

Yeah. At this point, I think there's more interesting things to look over now. So —

Cool. Well, we're excited to see what you do next.

Thank you so much.

item.description:
# 当"递归"成为新的"注意力"：从 Alex Zhang 对话中读出的系统性翻转
## 一、最意外的观察：这场对话真正的主角不是 RLM，而是"品味的递归结构"
表面上这是一期技术访谈——GPU kernel、harness 设计、agent swarm。但如果你把 Alex 讲的所有事情放在同一张图上，会发现一个**让人毛骨悚然的自相似性**：
- GPU kernel 层面：他说"单个 kernel 没什么结构，compiler 能搞定；但 mega kernel 开始出现结构，所以需要人类品味来组织" - Harness 层面：他说"所有 harness 本质上一样，差异只是成本；但 RLM 把 harness 本身变成一个可组合的、递归的结构" - 博士研究层面：他说"industry lab 做的事都一样，PhD 的唯一优势就是赌别人不敢赌的递归下一层" - 科研品味层面：他说"Sweet-Bench、Quiet-Star、React 当年都被人嘲笑'这不就是……'——而这种'这不就是'的反应，恰恰是识别真正重要工作的信号"
**换句话说：他整个人就是一个 RLM。

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why the Korean War Went So Badly - Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、胜利悖论：战争中最危险的不是失败，而是赢得太多

Sarah Paine 这段话最反直觉的洞见是——朝鲜战争真正的失败点不是开战，而是赢的那一刻。Kim Il-sung 一路南下势如破竹时，正是他战略崩塌的开始；MacArthur 在仁川登陆大捷之后，恰恰是美军走向灾难的拐点。两个赢家都栽在同一个结构性陷阱上："顶点"（culminating point）不是一个军事坐标，而是一个博弈论拓扑点——它是"二人博弈"坍缩为"多人博弈"的临界相变。

Clausewitz 的"顶点"概念其实揭示了一个更普适的系统性真相：所有封闭系统的边界都是由第三方的忍耐阈值定义的，而不是由你自己的能力定义的。你以为战场的边界是地理的、是弹药的、是士气的——错了，真正的边界是旁观者什么时候决定不再旁观。

二、跨领域连接：这其实是"创业公司的平台杀手"模型

把 Paine 讲的东西搬到商业世界，你会看到一个惊人的同构： - Kim Il-sung = 一个在垂直市场里碾压本地竞争对手的创业公司 - "二人博弈" = 他以为只需要打败南韩 - "第三方介入" = Amazon/Google 突然决定进场 - "顶点" = 融资/增长/声势达到某个阈值后，巨头无法再忽视你

最反直觉的推论：Kim Il-sung 的最优策略是"慢速叛乱"而非"闪电南下"——Paine 自己点出了这一点。这完全对应创业圈那条铁律：成长太快会提前触发平台的注意力。 TikTok 早期的"中国出海"低调期、Shein 的隐身十年、OpenAI 在 ChatGPT 之前拒绝做消费产品——这些都是对"culminating point"的本能规避。

更深一层：个人职业发展也遵循同一法则。晋升太快、曝光太猛、锋芒太露——都会把你从"二人博弈"（你 vs. 老板）拉进"多人博弈"（你 vs. 所有潜在对手+上级的上级+人力资源政治）。很多聪明人毁于"赢得太漂亮"。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：朝鲜战争是美国的"永久订阅服务"

Paine 轻描淡写一句"we've had troops there ever since and it's expensive"藏着一个被普遍忽视的结构性事实：朝鲜战争是现代美国军工复合体的"隐形创世记"。

想想这个因果链条的奇特性： 1. MacArthur 越过"顶点" → 中国介入 → 战争无法速决 2. 无法速决 → 分裂的半岛变成"冷战的物理化身" 3. 分裂的半岛 → 需要永久驻军 → 永久国防预算 4. 永久国防预算 → 军工复合体制度化（1961 艾森豪威尔演讲的直接背景） 5. 军工复合体 → 影响后续 70 年所有美国对外政策的默认设置

换句话说，MacArthur 一个人的"过度自信"，在系统层面编码为美国 70 年的默认战略姿态。这是一个经典的"路径依赖"（path dependency）案例，但更深的洞见是：决策者在跨越"顶点"的那一刻，往往同时为自己创造了一个无法逆转的"组织生态位"——而这个生态位反过来会寻找下一场战争来证明自己存在的合法性。

一个让人不安的推论：当你听 Paine 问"乌克兰战争的 culminating point 在哪里？"时，真正该问的问题可能不是"谁会赢"，而是"这场战争正在为未来 50 年创造什么样的、尚未命名的、无法逆转的组织生态位？"——因为那才是战争真正的、延迟交付的"成本"。

📝 转录文本

The Two-Player Illusion: Kim Il-sung's Opening Gambit

Kim Il-sung invades the South and he thinks if it's just a twosome that he can win that thing — and he was right. He was roaring down the peninsula. He looked as if he had it all covered — until he triggered the third-party intervention from hell, which is when the United States and UN partners got involved.

Then what was a civil war becomes a regional war, with potential to become a global war, and you're off to a completely different race, much higher costs. So he would might have done much better doing a slow insurgency than what he did.

MacArthur, Inchon, and Overshooting the Culminating Point

Okay, so then the United States is turned to go beyond culminating points of victory. And there's a whole story about the Chinese, but I'm got time for that one.

Uh, so MacArthur does his Inchon landing, which is halfway up the peninsula, and it goes really well. So his idea is: "Hey, we're going to reunite the whole thing, right?" Cuz it's militarily possible. It's like Clausewitz has already told you — it's the political objective, it's not the military objective, that determines what you're going to do.

Uh, well, when he gets too close to the Chinese border, the Chinese are in — and now we're into a world of hurt. They're sending hundreds of thousands of people in, and we got a completely different war on our hands doing this. And not too long — before too long — MacArthur gets himself cashiered.

Culminating Points as a Strategic Lens

So I think it's worth thinking in terms of culminating points of attack and victory before wars, German during wars. What might it be? What might it like — in the Ukraine war, what would it take on either side to get a culminating point of victory? Is it reachable? Or culminating point of attack on different campaigns — is it even feasible to get there?

They're helpful terms. But understand: a key measure of culminating a point of victory going sour is when the third-party intervenes.

The Price of Overshooting

Okay, the Korean War yielded a divided peninsula at really high cost — cuz if you exceed the culminating point of victory —

[gasps]

— you're... one of the measures is you're paying a lot more than you had to. But that was the minimum objective: keeping the South Koreans around. And they are. But we've had troops there ever since, and it's expensive.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [a16z] Why One Internet Pioneer Thinks the Original Model Broke
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这是一次完美的"镜像人生"闭环

Barrett Lyon 的整个职业轨迹本质上是一场围绕"中心化基础设施"的辩证运动，但几乎没人把这三件事连起来看：

  • Prolexic 时代（2003–2009）：他让大企业能在中心化互联网上生存——客户花钱买"更大的集中式护盾"来对抗洪水攻击。
  • Opte 艺术项目（2003 起，收藏于 MoMA）：他把互联网整个"画"了下来——这是一次对既存拓扑的测绘。
  • Docset（现在）：他要在既有互联网之上长出一张不存在于那张地图上的网络——196 个不存在于公共 DNS 的新顶级域，相当于在自己画过的地图上，画出一块空白的新大陆。

更惊人的是：他做 Prolexic 的起点是"高中时自家服务器被人 DDoS"——也就是说，他本人既是最早被中心化互联网伤害的个体用户，又成了最大化保护中心化企业的人，而现在他在把那笔"保护"的红利，还给当年像他一样的个体。这不是生涯转向，这是一次债务偿还。

二、跨领域连接：那场坠机，和他现在在互联网上做的事，是同一个工程哲学

飞机那段故事看似闲聊，但如果你注意他对事故原因的描述——"三件非常奇怪的事同时发生"（进气歧管金属片、电子点火、磁电机备份），他讲的不是运气差，而是级联故障（cascading failure）如何击穿"独立备份"的幻觉。磁电机本应是独立于电子点火的冗余系统，结果同一时间失效。

现在把这个思路搬到网络层你会发现，他对今天互联网的诊断用的是完全一样的语言： - WhatsApp / Signal / iMessage 看起来都是"独立的加密方案"，但它们共享同一个范畴错误——"你以为在发给对方，其实在发给服务器"； - VPN 看起来是"去中心化保护"，但背后都租自同一批 bare-metal 供应商，冗余是假的，根因是同一个； - 法国 Umbrella 把某电信商错标成法国 → 一刀切屏蔽 → 一个分类错误被放大成跨国断网，和他飞机里"一个金属片引发点火系统连锁崩溃"是同构的。

他造 Docset 的真正动机，不是"我讨厌广告追踪"，而是作为一个曾经从级联故障里活下来的工程师，他比任何人都清楚：当代互联网的"隐私选项"全都是假冗余。

三、藏得最深的那层：这期播客本身，就是它在讨论的东西的一个样本

注意他和主持人讨论"数据中心抗议"的方式——他们说：

现场根本没人在抗议，只有兔子在跑；但你在 TikTok 上刷到的是配着音效的仇恨数据中心的视频。

这里有个几乎没人点破的三层嵌套：

  1. 第一层：有人（可能是商业利益方，可能是竞争对手，可能是外国行为体）在用广告定向技术攻击公众对数据中心的看法；
  2. 第二层：广告定向技术的根基是——正是 Docset 想消灭的那套 tracker 生态；
  3. 第三层：Barrett 和主持人正在一个被同一个推荐算法分发的媒体平台上讨论这件事，而这期播客本身的触达、剪辑、热度，也会被同样的机制塑形。

于是出现了一个很怪的闭环：广告技术栈既是被攻击的理由，也是攻击的手段，还是关于这件事的讨论得以传播的管道。

跨领域地看，这是冷战时期"宣传战"的工业化升级——以前国家花几十亿养机构、买媒介；现在任何一个商业利益用 LLM + 数据中介 + 定向广告，花六位数就能复刻一场"民意"。他说"情报机构其实落后于广告商"——这句话值得当作本世纪基础设施政治的注脚。

四、一个意料之外的教学点：PKI 的失败不是技术问题，是语言学问题

他随口提到：

"PKI 的核心教训是：你一旦告诉用户这是 PKI，它就不会成功。"

这句话应该被写进每一本产品设计教科书。它说明同一个密码学原语（公钥交换），仅仅因为被命名、被暴露、被要求用户理解——就从"可用"变成"不可用"。

同样的现象在很多领域反复出现： - 医学里的 placebo：告诉病人这是安慰剂，疗效立刻降低； - 行为经济学里的 nudge：一旦明说"我们在推你"，它就不再推得动； - AI 对齐里的 Goodhart's law：指标一旦被命名为目标，它就不再是好指标。

所以 Docset 真正难的，不是密码学，是让密码学隐形到用户感觉自己只是"加了个好友"。这件事的难度，和 Apple 当年把文件系统从用户面前抹掉是同一个量级的 UX 革命——而且几乎所有安全类产品都在这一步上翻车。

📝 转录文本

Why One Internet Pioneer Thinks the Original Model Broke

频道：a16z · 嘉宾：Barrett Lyon

开场金句（Cold Open）

"We're really at an inflection point because you have the birth of essentially coin-operated intelligence at scale."

"The internet has really kind of stagnated a bit from protocol design. There's like not a lot of new stuff. All of it's built on top. Erasing that is kind of what I'm trying to go for."

"What you're saying is you've actually built this transient way for folks to connect and chat without there being any record."

"The really big problem is on WhatsApp, Signal, iMessage, Telegram. All of those applications disguise themselves as you sending something to somebody else, but you're really sending something to a server. But the question is like, okay, well, whose servers are those?"

"It's coming at such an important inflection point for the future of our country, tech, and to just have this conversation that seems to be manipulated to some end. It feels very manipulated. And to me, the future of our tech is needing to build this infrastructure now. If we're crippling it..."

一、嘉宾引入

Well, today we're joined by Barrett Lyon, perhaps one of the most interesting people in tech. I have a lot of stories to share, and I am always kind of blown away every time we catch up, because you tell me a new story that just puts everything I've ever done in pale comparison.

And I think the most interesting one I heard recently, and I had never heard it before — this was during a period, I believe, where we were investors in your previous company — was: you are a pilot, you have a pilot's license, and you decided to optimize your life by flying places. And you had an unfortunate experience, I believe, flying back from one of our meetings.

二、把飞机当日常通勤车的那段日子

Yeah. Well, one day I was driving to work in the Bay Area, and I realized it was almost 45 minutes, which used to be 15. And my family lives up in the Tahoe region. So I'm like, "Well, I think the plane can fly there in about the same time. Maybe I could just commute that way."

That was before work-from-home was codified by COVID — so I had a physical need to be present. I started flying.

So your daily driver was a daily flyer, right?

Yeah. I put like 1,300 hours on a Cirrus.

那次迫降

And one day, after a meeting here, I left and got in the plane, took off from San Carlos, and somewhere over Oakland airport, the engine started acting up. I thought maybe it was some sort of water in the fuel. But I climbed up, cleared Bravo, and felt like I was okay. And then right after that thought, I lost pretty much all power.

And what went through your head immediately after that?

Yeah, actually I messaged my friends and said, "Hey guys, I have an emergency. Love you."

I declared emergency and just tried to think, "Okay, where do I crash and not hurt people?" I found a field — and then it turns out I was up pretty high, and there was a giant airport right next to us. Not Oakland, but Buchanan Field. A giant old military airport.

Oh, in Alameda?

No, it was the other one — the other side of the mountain range. Buchanan Field is the name of it, I believe. But anyway, landed there.

要不要拉降落伞？

Before that, I kind of went to this field and I was like, "All right, well, I've got a ballistics parachute. Do I pull it?"

And I was thinking: when I read all these crash reports, the reason the pilot dies is because they didn't use the parachute. Absolutely. But — I'm like, "Well, the airport's right there and I'm still in the air flying."

Isn't that a funny quirk of that plane — that it's technically the safest plane ever made, but yet it's involved in the most crashes because people never use the safety feature?

Yeah. Well, it does work, but it destroys the plane too. It shoots a rocket out of the back of the tail and rips all the stuff out and ruins the plane. And it's not a guarantee that you're going to land nicely on the ground. In fact, the seats are made with a crumple-impact design, so when you do hit the ground, it absorbs some of the compression.

And this is all playing out over how long?

Oh, I don't know. Probably like minutes or less. Maybe less. And then anyway, I just made the call to land, and landed, rolled right onto the transient parking spot.

恐惧延迟登场

And I was calm. I was kind of frustrated, a little confused when I got out of the plane. And then — you know those big fire-truck things, the huge ones that look like some kid made them, but they're big — the guy gets out of that and shakes my hand. And that's when the fear hit me. Because I'm like: that's the guy scraping my brains off the ground. I'm like, "Oh, no. This is the guy that puts the fire out."

That was close.

And then I'm like, "Now what do I do? I have to get home somehow." I rented a car, drove home. That was kind of the end of it for me. I was like, the risk is too high. I kept the plane for a while and ended up ferrying it out to Las Vegas and selling it.

Did you ever find out what the cause was?

Yeah, it was like three really weird things at the same time.

  1. A piece of metal on the air-intake control valve — a kind of lever — broke off and got sucked into the air-intake manifold, went down to the oil pan, and was crushed into cylinder 3 and 6, I think.
  2. That caused an electrical problem with the spark, which was controlled by a brand-new electronic ignition system. That stopped working, so I lost half ignition.
  3. At the same time, my magneto on the other side — which is the backup — also stopped working.

So it was like a cascading, strange failure. And then it was weird too, because on the ground the magneto was kind of working a little bit — so it would start, but when you went to higher RPMs it just went bye-bye. Anyway, that's what it was. It took a while to figure it out. But yeah, that was an interesting drive home.

Yeah. Now you understand why the Pope kisses the ground when he gets off the plane, right?

Yeah. If there's ever another plane in my life, it will have less moving parts.

Hopefully a backup pilot and redundancy. And you fly a lot — you kind of are increasing your risk level.

Yeah.

三、为什么创办 Docset？

Well, and that sort of probably triggered a lot of things. I know we're here to talk about your new venture — which is something very different for you. It seems more close to home, more important. Maybe we can talk a bit about Docset.

Sure.

And sort of like why you decided to build it. First of all, what is it? What caused you to do it? And maybe your thinking around why this is important, why now?

名字的由来

Well, okay. So Docset — first of all, maybe you should explain the name.

Yeah, sure. As a kid my hacker name was Docs, and then I started a business in high school with my high-school friend called DocsNet. This was before cloud — we were renting servers, basically giving user accounts for money.

Totally legit business in high school. Were these shell accounts?

Yeah, shell accounts. We were selling shell accounts for $5 a month, but we had a thousand users, and we had all these features, and people liked it. There was actually a little community around it for a while.

But I got out of high school and shut it all down and started my career. I kept the domain. I'm also very fascinated about protocol design, and the fact that the internet has really stagnated a bit from protocol design. There's not a lot of new stuff — all of it's built on top.

时代背景：审查、隐私、VPN

So there's that — and then just noticing the shift of censorship, and people's privacy being eroded, and all of this kind of thing — and then the uprise of VPNs — made it really interesting to make an alternative network.

A network kind of designed from the ground up to protect people from advertisers, trackers, malware, and foreign adversaries trying to learn about what you're doing.

The original promise of the internet was this incredible marketplace of ideas, unrestricted, no censorship. A lot of the original people around the founding of the internet were free-speech maximalists. It was a very specific crowd. And over the last couple of years, to your point, it has shifted pretty incredibly.

Yeah. And it's in the hands of a few. For example, China is a good example — China Netcom, China Telecom. It's a pretty good chokehold of the entire population using that network, as an opportunity to force people into different decision-making processes.

The internet originally, like you said, was designed with this open concept. So bringing that back is one of the things I was interested in doing — trying to figure out new ways of doing things that might leverage pre-internet ideas.

Way back in the day, wireless networking was ALOHAnet — wireless through packet modems and things. But now we have really high-powered Wi-Fi on the edge. Incredible opportunities to create better mesh protocols, better P2P. And one of the biggest stains of the entire internet is carrier-grade NAT — it's just destroying applications' ability to do really cool stuff. Erasing that is kind of what I'm trying to go for.

审查的"美式蔓延"

One of the interesting things is we always talk about foreign governments restricting internet access — we harp on China and Russia. But I was in a state recently that has a "know your customer" rule and they were requiring, or blocking, access to certain websites. Whatever they define as being inappropriate — it could be a health website, whatever. So we're actually seeing the creep of censorship even within the United States.

Yeah, it's creeping into the US — and it's being done in a way that's kind of odd, because a lot of times they're asking the network to solve an identity problem. And the network doesn't do identity. It has a hammer, and it's going to hammer the nail.

An IP address is not your driver's license. Asking people to do network restrictions based off of age and things like that — it makes a lot of sense, but in a different place in the stack. If they want to restrict things for certain reasons, that should be done in a much different way — not asking the network to do it.

We're starting to see that in the United States, and definitely elsewhere.

一个法国事故的"爆炸半径"

And it's also not just with age restrictions. An interesting problem popped up the other day where Google — or Cisco Umbrella — broke for a major carrier because they classified that carrier as France. They're not even in France, really, as far as the corporate structure goes. But France had a rule requiring them to block 100+ piracy sites. And they said: no, we're going to go scorched earth — we're just going to block France. Well, then there's the blast radius: if your geo-provider accidentally identifies somebody as the wrong location, you're also now part of that policy.

Those classifications are always the worst. We were looking at an investment opportunity in a company that makes chatbots focused on partnership or companionship — and half of the classification engines flagged it as adult content. You're sort of like, "Okay, this is a legitimate e-partner, e-spouse site. It's not doing the unmentioned stuff."

Yeah, we've run into that a little bit too — Docset, because it's got two X's in it, and then also there's "doxing." But it actually worked out in our favor: we got flagged with Claude, and then we applied through the proper means — their registration process — and they opened up everything for us, which is quite nice.

That's great.

四、为什么现有工具不够？Docset 到底是什么？

So the creeping information totalitarianism has given birth to a whole bunch of products — VPNs being the most common. So maybe it'd be great to hear a little bit about why the existing tools aren't enough, why you're building Docset, how is it different.

A lot of the VPNs, I would say, are just entry and exit points. They lease a server from a landlord, set up their software on it, and then you connect to it encrypted, and your requests come out from that node. That's to kind of solve the "your IP address is your identity" problem.

People feel like there's more security to that — and I could argue against that — but it's very basic. If you think about it, those networks aren't real-time adjustable.

Docset 做了什么不同的事

You could apply APIs to everything. All of a sudden you could say: here's an API your agent can use that can build an entire network. You're just using the VPN protocols as a way to get into that area — and then inside, we can create either, you can call it, a walled garden, or a parallel internet, or whatever you want to call it.

But we built an entire mesh network: - 196 different TLDs that don't exist on the internet - You can register domains - You can lease IP addresses - You can lease mesh addresses or public addresses - Create policy — all within milliseconds

So it's a whole different ecosystem in there. And on top of that, we've been able to use that system — since we can control it — to create P2P applications that actually work: phone calling, video call, chat. All of those things sit best-of-class on top of the app, run across the mesh network, and it's all encrypted.

Got it.

No phone numbers. No email addresses. No names. No nothing.

真正的 P2P：没有服务器中间人

It's funny — we're both pretty well steeped in the security space. I come from sort of a "if you want to have a private conversation, don't do it anywhere with anything with a battery or an electrical signal." So what you're saying is: you've actually built this transient way for folks to connect and chat without there being any record.

Yeah. You create your account, you just have to prove you're human by doing a little puzzle. Once you do that, you get a token — it's yours. You can change it. You can delete your account, make a new one.

Once you're in there, you can create a certificate and share it with a friend. You don't really know you're doing it — it just says "invite friend," and it looks kind of normal, but it's actually doing a cryptographic exchange with each other. And then you have extra privileges.

I think the key lesson of PKI was actually: if you tell people it's PKI, it's not going to work. So you have to abstract that layer away, right?

Yeah. Well, it's not even PKI — it's private key — it's not public. Anyway, you and your friend just decided, "Okay, we trust each other." Now that unlocks the ability for the phones over the mesh network to talk to each other directly. And then all of a sudden you have all these really cool file-transfer features — which have no file-size limit.

WhatsApp / Signal / iMessage / Telegram 的问题

The really big problem is: on WhatsApp, Signal, iMessage, Telegram — and by the way, Telegram's creepy — all of those applications disguise themselves as you sending something to somebody else, but you're really sending something to a server, and then the server is having the other person pull that.

So if you upload a file, you're uploading it — and also the upload infrastructure isn't always as distributed, or might even be a little bit slow. You might be in one part of the US and uploading to another. So the upload's slow.

When we use our applications, it extracts all of that. It's gone. There's really no middleman, no server in the middle — your phone becomes a server to your friend. And it's fast. It works great. You can send a 20-gigabyte file to each other.

20 gigabytes — private network — point-to-point — low latency. Wow.

With three or four layers of encryption. It's post-quantum. These are really nice tools to have.

So I don't know — when you start stacking up all of these things, Docset is kind of like this giant toolkit for freedom of speech, I guess. Freedom from surveillance.

五、"诡异的 VPN"与 FBI 的蜜罐

You mentioned Telegram is creepy. I'd say — I don't want to say all, because that's an absolutist term — but a lot of VPNs are very creepy. Without bashing on anyone specific, the most illustrative story for me: in the news there was an issue where a bunch of organized criminals were arrested across the world. Australia had arrested some, the US had arrested some — and it turned out the FBI had built a secure messaging app and marketed it exclusively to organized criminal groups. These guys are like, "Don't trust Signal because that's the NSA — let's use this app, this is safe, only five people use it." And it turned out they all got indicted — I think most of them are in prison now.

So in the US we've seen this activity. And then if you look on any App Store and search for VPN, you probably find 50 VPNs that are all abroad.

Well, if it's free — there's nothing free. If you're not paying for it, you are the product. You're being eaten alive.

Docset 的治理结构

The United States has pretty cool laws — we can use them to protect people. So Docset is US-based, but we also have a Swiss company that handles all of the European operations. There's separation between the operations between the two regions. We're doing other regions like that too.

Corporate governance actually matters in these types of situations. I just don't feel comfortable with my data going to a company that doesn't talk about who owns it, why they exist, other than "privacy."

We made a very conscious decision that we're very open about what we're doing, who's involved, why the decisions have been made those ways. It's also to drive community. But yeah — there are creepy VPNs out there.

情报国家、组织犯罪、与基础设施的"底层"

And it's not just — we like to talk about nation-states, intelligence agencies — CIA, NSA, these are all super cool. But in reality the risks are a lot more low-level than that. At the beginning of the initial cryptocurrency waves, people's accounts were getting drained — they were using some of these services that were in other countries, and it turns out that in some of those countries you have the meshing together of the intelligence state apparatus and organized crime. You see where these things start to bleed into each other.

Yeah. People look at the policies for the VPN — "no logs, no this." But the question is: whose servers are those? Are they owned by Big Brand VPN, or are they leased? And if they're leased, who are they leased from? What are those people doing with the data? What are their policies?

There's that whole underbelly. Learning about that has been difficult, because I personally was not up to building infrastructure all over the world as rapidly as I could — but I ended up realizing that if it's not your equipment, you can't set policy. You just can't. And then the next layer of policy is the carriers and interconnect beyond your cage or whatever it is.

So it's been an incredible amount of work to work around the "bare-metal-as-a-service" kind of creepy underbelly.

六、自己拥有全栈——软件到电缆到 AI

And this is one big difference with a lot of folks — you own the full stack, from software to wire.

Yeah. Software to wire. And even all the AI components that run routing and things like that are all on our metal.

Well, I think that was one of the funny things when we originally started talking about this — you were incredibly distrusting of large inference and AI providers. And you've built your own AI stack. GPUs are in shortage, data power is hard to get, everybody's anti-data-center now. How did you pull that off in probably six months?

Very efficiently. We built, so far, like 26 sites around the world with redundant routing.

And how many employees in the company?

Uh, total — I think the people involved — it's 12.

Yeah. Wow.

And we have no network administrator, no sysadmin. It's all done by AI. And it's actually working quite well. I'm kind of on top of everything.

The nice thing — if you think about our footprint of who's involved — we don't have a thousand employees with access to this network. The blast radius of just the corporate structure is very minimal.

内部威胁与 AI

That's impressive. The thing we very rarely talk about, because it's kind of uncomfortable, is just how great an extent insider threat is. The most crippling, catastrophic cyberattacks are always sort of the insider-threat angle. And now you're saying with agents, you're kind of eliminating at least a good portion of that risk.

Yeah. And it's running in its own secure environment that's not exporting data to one of the big AI companies. So all the context and inference stays inside, and we have it secured. We monitor all our equipment with cameras, and no one goes in and touches anything.

Do you have agents that watch the camera footage?

Actually — technically, we don't, but the camera companies that made the agents, yeah. We get alarms if something moves. We even thought about putting lasers in a couple of the spots, but —

Mission Impossible style.

I'm like, why not? It'd be kind of fun.

You've got to have the one data center that you take people to — to impress them, right? Like the Switch data centers in Las Vegas. They've got the Jeeps with the .50-cal machine guns on them.

I love lasers. We did look into it and even got the light-actuated switches, so if the beams broke, it would actually set off the alarms. But the problem was — the data center doesn't turn off the lights. So you don't get to see this really cool display. And there's no dust in there — no particles for the beams to show up.

Yeah — you can't bring in some talcum powder, because that'll mess with everything.

"Oh, let's smoke up the data center for the laser show." Yeah, no.

七、数据中心的"真相"与公众被操纵的意见

That's the other thing driving me crazy — people don't understand data centers at all.

Oh yeah, it's crazy.

I mean, I think you're seeing that in the popular press, right?

Oh yeah. "They drink water!" Come on. No — data centers have been around for a very, very long time. They need water when they break, and you have to replenish some of the water. There's some evaporation. But it's not like they're running off of water. That's the crazy part.

In order of most impressive machines humans have built — one is probably commercial airliners, and two has got to be data centers. They're so incredibly sophisticated. They're closed systems.

Yeah. The data centers themselves are kind of just boring buildings. And the other thing is the sounds. I've never heard sound outside of a data center. Maybe a chiller or something. But I see videos where people are watching clips and it's audio from inside being dubbed, and people aren't smart enough to know that it's fake. It's all contained within these buildings. People are being manipulated with this data-center thing.

Isn't it amazing? Over the years, I think it's going to come out that this was all some very interested group of organizations or interests —

I completely —

— manipulating public opinion to some end.

Yeah. But it's very interesting to be in the know and then watch this and go, "Oh my goodness, these people are missing the mark."

现场的实际状况

You've been to 20-some data centers in the last couple months. Have you seen actual protesters outside?

No.

You haven't?

No. Most of them — especially the big data-center park in Virginia — you just see bunny rabbits in the field. There's nothing. Just a big building, a bunch of parking lot, and totally nothing.

Meanwhile, that's like one of the richest counties in the country because of all the data centers.

Right. Because it brings jobs. The people that work in them aren't getting paid pennies. And it brings high-tech talent. And infrastructure — infrastructure powers everything you do. If you have a data center nearby, your internet's faster. Things work better. Depending on which one it is.

And the argument about data centers drinking water goes back to some quote that was fabricated entirely. I think there was the Switch data center built near Reno, and they built this big lake out there, and then people think the data center lives off the lake. The reality is: if you have a chiller failure and have to drain all that closed loop, you need to refill it. So you drain it to the lake.

So it's interesting to see people — I work in these buildings — and then you see the conspiracy theorists, and it's like, "Oh no, we're way off here. I'm sorry."

媒介操纵与基础设施的未来

This feels like the people who think the moon landing was faked. It feels like a classic sort of... But I do think this is coming at such an important inflection point for the future of our country, tech, society in general. And to just have this conversation that seems to be manipulated to some end —

It feels very manipulated. And to me, the future of our tech is: we need to build this infrastructure now. If we're crippling it, then we're making bad decisions. And we're making bad decisions on Instagram posts.

Oh yeah. Or TikTok, right?

TikTok —

— which, who knows where that content is being —

Or like some crazy anti-data-center music video. Public opinion is being framed by that.

八、广告追踪：真正的"情报机关"是广告商

This is the second half — I know we talked about intelligence agencies, the big bad scary government. But now we're talking more about clearly an operation that's probably being done by some sort of commercial interest to manipulate public opinion. Which goes to the second half of why you built Docset — advertising. People like to think the NSA is incredibly sophisticated, but advertisers are probably far ahead of what they're doing. And I think you're seeing now where intelligence agencies are actually using data brokers and using the techniques of ad agencies.

Yeah. All your apps have these trackers in them. WhatsApp has ditsap.net. Apple even has Apple telemetry — they call it telemetry or metadata, whatever they want to call it, but some level of it is a tracker.

And you can block them. It doesn't break the app. Most websites don't have any problem with that telemetry data breaking, because the rest of the site will still load.

一个富人的疑问

Somebody asked me — very controversial, wealthy individual — said: "Well, so what? Someone won't know that I purchased underwear off target.com."

And I'm like: well, it's not really that one. It's all of them. When you combine all of the tracking being done on every different app you're using or every different website, and it accumulates — and then it's being stored by who knows who, where, and being sold — then when you aggregate all those data points together, you could know: - If you're a coffee drinker - What time you wake up in the morning - What your income is - Where you shop - How often you purchase things

If you're preparing for the birth of a child, or perhaps for a divorce, or some other big life event.

They probably know these events sooner than your spouse would.

"回到老互联网的 vibe"

So turning that off doesn't bother me at all. I love all that stuff being turned off — I hate that kind of stuff. That's a big piece of the app — or the network. It's not just part of the app, it's part of the network — to deconstruct all of that and get rid of it.

And just get back to the old internet that has the ability to connect to things, has the ability to create, and also to not be spied on by advertisers and governments and everybody else.

投币式智能的降临

We're really at an inflection point because you have the birth of essentially coin-operated intelligence at scale. We can deploy millions. You've got the proverbial infinite monkeys with infinite typewriters. We're looking at this world in which there's more telemetry, more data, everything you do is being tracked — and you can combine that with intelligence to arrive at some pretty scary conclusions.

Yeah. You can take all that and just dump it into an LLM and say, "Tell me about this person." You get an answer.

Probably do really effective targeting against things like data centers as well, right? You start to see these mass movements orchestrated across multiple platforms, and you start to think, "Huh, that's pretty clever."

Yeah. But people should be targeting those — maybe not the data centers, but the tracking is pretty bad. Ad tracking — that kind of stuff really can go away, and your life would be better.

So at the core, it's trying to recreate that vibe that the internet used to have, and then see where we could take it with bigger resources — start creating more protocols that don't exist yet.

Absolutely. The internet succeeded because it was free. So thank you for trying to make it free again.

Trying.

Yeah.

But you have to pay me. Just kidding. Awesome.

九、从 DDoS 攻防到 Prolexic：旧日交集

So, I don't know if you know this, but our paths crossed a long time ago. I was looking back through some of my archives — I did a lot of work in the early 2000s on DoS bots: stacheldraht, TFN, TFN2K, and obviously large distributed denial-of-service attacks. And you were at the forefront of building a lot of the solutions to prevent that, at Prolexic.

Yeah.

How did that get going?

高中生被攻击 → Prolexic 的起点

Well, actually it kind of goes back to Docset. In high school, people were attacking my servers, and so we had to figure out better ways to protect them — techniques and tricks and all the different things you need to do to survive a DoS attack. I started writing kind of my list of what you would do to survive, and then somehow I presented that at SANS, and then it got into Google.

People started calling me, and we started dealing with real cybercrime: extortion. People trying to take — you know, one company sells watches, the other sells watches, and the other one is attacking the other watch company during Christmas sale season. Or the Super Bowl's about to start and all the gambling sites go dark.

"租给你最贵的东西"：云防护的雏形

Things like that got pretty serious. So I built a whole company to protect businesses from these attacks. The way I looked at it is: you need big scale, you need to have the biggest, most expensive stuff — and not everyone could afford that. So we'll turn that into kind of a leased service. It was one of the first cloud services to exist. It was very successful, still exists today — it's Akamai Prolexic. They even kept the name, which is rare.

And then we did Defense.net later on, which became F5 Silverline.

BitGravity：视频 CDN

In between all that, I really like big-scale stuff and bandwidth. So the other one we did was called BitGravity — that was one of the first, or the first, video-centric CDNs. Big file, big object delivery. We had some really great customers there early on — people got it. And we had a lot of tech around it to save people money.

People didn't realize: hit "play," you're downloading a progressive file, and before all this media-management stuff existed, you're just wasting bandwidth just to scroll into the middle of a video. It cost people money. So we created all kinds of cool stuff around video.

现在的工作：从保护公司，到保护个人

As far as building a new network for consumers — well, actually it's a little bit for bots too. There's a lot of agentic networking components to it. It's right up my alley — I love building big infrastructure, big scaled stuff. But now it's kind of twisting it: instead of doing this for corporations, we're doing it for people. I haven't really seen a lot of that being done, at least well. So it's going to be fun to see how people adapt to it.

One of the more interesting things: we might even see some DoS on our network.

Jack, I'm sure you're ready for that.

Well — inbound from the internet, sure. But what happens if somebody gets onto my network and starts using it inside, and I have to deal with those silly people?

Even if you have privacy, there's still laws, and you need to at least follow them as much as you can.

十、艺术家 Barrett：Opte 项目与 MoMA

One other interesting thing — spending years talking with you — is that you created an artwork that actually hung at the MoMA, and it's part of the permanent collection.

Yeah. There's two pieces. College project. I studied philosophy — oddly enough.

As one does.

Yeah. I studied the art of aesthetics, and some other stuff. A lot of it was theoretical AI.

Wow. Actually, a philosophy degree makes a lot of sense now.

Totally. Yeah. This is helpful.

从渗透测试到互联网地图

I started mapping networks because I was doing penetration testing — ethical hacking into other companies — and I found that casing the joint was the easiest way to start. You make a network diagram, where all the stuff is, how it all works, what you think is where. And then I started automating that.

And then I got mouthy at lunch one day and bet some guys that I could probably use the same technique to map the entire internet. That started a $50 bet — that I was pretty sure I was going to lose.

被车撞 → Opte Project

And then I got hit by a car on a bicycle.

Wow. Okay.

Yeah. And couldn't walk. All of a sudden my life got really slow, and I sat down and started doing the code for that. And that became the Opte Project.

That ended up in not just MoMA, but Boston Museum of Science, all over the world in different traveling exhibits. I did animations of it too. It's pretty neat because that project has gotten a lot of attention — not just because it looks cool, but because there's really interesting history in the video. As things are happening, you could see companies crash and burn, and all kinds of stuff. And I was lucky enough to be able to talk to Vint Cerf about it, and have the opportunity to ask my questions to him. Pretty cool.

MoMA 开幕夜与第二天的冒名顶替综合征

That is awesome. You've probably accomplished two of the harder things to do in this world — starting a successful tech company, and being a successful artist.

Being a successful artist is probably much more difficult than starting a tech company.

It was actually kind of strange. I went to the opening at MoMA — it was this giant party. I was one of the artists, they had a new exhibit, and I had the piece in there. It was kind of like, "Oh, man, this is cool." There's a DJ, there's drinking. And then the curators took me to some really interesting parts of MoMA's other properties that they own. It was a really cool experience.

But the next day, I kind of had this impostor syndrome. I just felt super depressed. I'm like, "Wow, am I ever going to experience what an artist feels like ever again?" Because this was kind of accidental.

But yeah, I got to do it again. Very strange, surreal moment in life.

Probably the only person in tech that can say that.

It's interesting. I have a lot of artist friends who are probably much better artists than me, and they're all like, "What? How did you get in the MoMA?" And part of the permanent collection too, which is neat.

You're one of a few hundred or thousand.

Yeah. I forget about that sometimes.

十一、还有一本书：追捕俄罗斯网络罪犯

I also forget about the book too.

That is true. We have not talked about the book. Do you want to cover that?

Sure.

We'll throw this on the list of crazy stories. I keep forgetting about that it exists.

一个被粉丝认出的瞬间

Yeah. So, I have an AI-powered webcam that watches boats in Miami. 24 hours a day. It's been up almost a year now. It's got a little chat community of people on there. One of them figured out who I was, and the other day was like, "I just finished reading the book about you." I'm like, "What? What do you mean?" And I'm like, "Oh, shoot. That's right. They figured it out."

书的内容

So it's about the beginnings of Prolexic and tracking down these cyber criminals in Russia — specifically these guys extremely aggressively extorting and damaging a lot of our clients. We had Christmases destroyed because we were dealing with customers and network outages.

These are real criminals. These are not just hackers. These are people doing human trafficking and trafficking narcotics, and they have a side hustle. It's like real criminals, right?

Yeah. There's some stuff going on. And then they went to prison for I think eight years. Hard labor or something like that. I don't know what happened to them afterwards.

We went out to Russia, and got turned around. We were in Moscow for a while — and then there were some really interesting signals of "you need to leave now."

Yeah.

So we left. That whole book is about the whole saga of what happened through that period of time. It's really weird — when you live it, it seems kind of normal. But then you look back and go, "Oh geez, that was kind of crazy."

Every time we talk, I hear new stories.

十二、Burning Man、玛雅勇士与一个时代的结束

Let's not talk about Burning Man.

That could be a whole episode itself. When was your first Burning Man? Burning Man is next week.

Yeah. It's this coming weekend.

Are you going this year?

Yeah.

Awesome.

I think it's year 14. Somewhere around there — I can't remember. We lost a couple to COVID, so I don't remember which ones I skipped.

And you have a famous car.

Well, my partner has the famous car. Pablo created the Mayan Warrior, and I created the Mind Warrior camp. We were partners in that whole crazy thing for a while. That car went from this fun project to a whole global phenomenon. People paid money to go see it. It's crazy.

But what I was thinking about this morning: when you're passionate about something, it creates that aura around you, and then other people pick up on it. We were very passionate about that project, and I think it inspired a lot of folks to do other interesting projects similar to it.

时代落幕

This is the first year we're not taking it to the Playa.

Oh wow.

Not going. We're done.

Will you be doing your laser show though?

Nope.

All right. No.

Well, there'll be something — but it's not mine. It's Pablo's got a beautiful art piece. There are two art pieces he's bringing this year that'll be pretty cool. But no more traveling-superpower sound stage. That's gone.

Starlink 时代的 Playa

How's the vibe out there now that you can get Starlink internet access?

You could argue against it and you could argue for it. If you're organizing a camp or dealing with "oh, we ran out of water on the car" — it helps, because you can communicate.

Totally.

We always bring high-powered Motorola radios.

People were using shortwave too, right?

Yeah. You have the radios, and that's kind of fun — reminds you of being a kid. But Starlink is also a communications device. Out there, it takes the edge off when it comes to finding things or organizing things. People don't get stuck at the gate very long anymore. But if you're sitting there watching movies, that's probably the wrong use.

You don't go to Burning Man to Netflix and chill.

No. If you're using it for anything other than local communications, then maybe it's the wrong use.

Awesome. But it has changed a bit.

Yeah.

收尾

As you said — you pursue your passion, and that takes you down all sorts of amazing rabbit holes. And you are clearly someone that is always pursuing his passion. So thank you so much for stopping by. I am an incredibly happy Docset user. Thank you for building it. It's good to get that old internet vibe back.

Yeah. Well, it's just getting started. And thanks for trusting me to help build it.
