item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：这是一次完美的"镜像人生"闭环
Barrett Lyon 的整个职业轨迹本质上是**一场围绕"中心化基础设施"的辩证运动**，但几乎没人把这三件事连起来看：
- **Prolexic 时代（2003–2009）**：他让大企业能在中心化互联网上生存——客户花钱买"更大的集中式护盾"来对抗洪水攻击。 - **Opte 艺术项目（2003 起，收藏于 MoMA）**：他把互联网整个"画"了下来——这是一次对**既存拓扑的测绘**。 - **Docset（现在）**：他要在既有互联网之上长出一张**不存在于那张地图上的网络**——196 个不存在于公共 DNS 的新顶级域，相当于**在自己画过的地图上，画出一块空白的新大陆**。
更惊人的是：他做 Prolexic 的起点是"高中时自家服务器被人 DDoS"——也就是说，他本人既是**最早被中心化互联网伤害的个体用户**，又成了**最大化保护中心化企业的人**，而现在他在把那笔"保护"的红利，还给当年像他一样的个体。这不是生涯转向，这是一次**债务偿还**。
## 二、跨领域连接：那场坠机，和他现在在互联网上

item.title: [YC Root Access] Better AI Starts With Better Verification
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Hallucinate 的真正商业模式不是"训练 AI"，而是"重建会计学"

表面上，Jerry 和 Wyatt 在做 RL 环境。但如果你把访谈逐字拆解，会发现他们反复回到同一个词：verification（验证）。他们选择金融作为切入点时说了一句关键的话——"finance is somewhat verifiable"。

这句话比它听起来重要得多。它暗示了一个被整个行业忽略的事实：金融之所以能被 AI 快速吃掉，并不是因为它"数字化程度高"，而是因为过去 500 年里，金融业已经演化出了全世界最完善的"验证基础设施"——会计准则、审计师、监管机构、GAAP、LBO 模型的标准结构。换句话说，金融业无意间已经为 AI 建好了 reward function 的脚手架。

这反过来预测了一个冷门结论：哪个行业演化出最强的"外部可验证性"机制，哪个行业就会最先被自动化。因此真正率先沦陷的不是"规则简单"的行业，而是"规则复杂但有裁判"的行业——医学（诊断可验证）、法律（判例可对照）、合规（规则明文化）。而创意、战略、品味这些没有裁判的工作，反而会在短期内变得更加人类独有。这与大众直觉完全相反——人们以为 AI 先取代重复性工作，实际上它先取代的是"有标准答案的高价值脑力工作"。

二、"模拟公司"愿景中隐藏的乌洛波洛斯（Ouroboros）

Jerry 预测未来 Hallucinate 会出售"simulated companies, simulated industries, simulated governments"。这个愿景听起来像科幻，但它内部藏着一个诡异的递归：

企业将付费购买"自己的模拟版本"，用来训练将替代自己员工的 AI。

这是劳动经济学中前所未有的拓扑结构。类比过去的技术革命——蒸汽机不需要工人去模拟自己才能被替代。但 LLM 时代，被替代者必须亲手铸造替代自己的模具。这与纳瓦霍织工在最后一代前故意织错一根线以留住灵魂的传说形成了诡异镜像：当每一个工作流都被完整数字化模拟，人类作为"过程持有者"的身份就彻底消散了。

跨领域联想：这与生物学中的"端粒"异曲同工——端粒每复制一次就缩短一次。每一次 RL 环境扩容 2 倍（他们的"Moore's law"），人类知识工作的"端粒"就缩短一截。6-8 个月的倍增周期意味着：从单文档任务到"模拟整个投行"可能只需要三到四个倍增代。

三、"软性 reward hacking"揭示的是人类组织病理学

访谈中最被低估的洞察，是 Wyatt 描述的"soft reward hacking"——agent 跳过中间步骤直接给出答案，不展示工作过程。他拿投行分析师作类比："analyst needs to prove out, whereas the agent maybe just goes right to the answer"。

但这里有个惊人的反转：人类分析师之所以要"show work"，并不是因为他们真的在推理，而是因为组织无法验证他们的大脑。中间步骤是一种可见性的仪式，一种让 principal-agent 问题变得可管理的表演。McKinsey 的 PPT、律所的 memo、学术论文的 methodology section，本质上都是为了被验证而存在的 performance，而不是认知必要环节。

于是悖论出现了：我们正在训练 AI 模仿一种只有在"验证能力弱于执行能力"时才需要的行为。等 AI 能被更廉价、更精确地直接验证输出时（而不是通过中间步骤间接验证），全人类知识工作中大约 40% 的"中间产物"将被证明是组织病理学的化石——它们是过去我们无法窥视彼此大脑时的妥协。

跨领域连接：这正是人类学家 David Graeber 在《狗屁工作》(Bullshit Jobs) 中无法解释的核心机制——他看到了狗屁工作，却没有理论来预测什么会消解它。Hallucinate 这类公司正在无意间构建这个理论的实证：凡是只能通过"show work"而非"verify output"来管理的工作，在高质量验证器出现后都会蒸发。

四、名字即预言：为什么叫 Hallucinate？

最后一个彩蛋：这家公司叫 Hallucinate，但他们做的事情是消除幻觉的根源。这不是巧合——这是一种对冲式命名（apotropaic naming），和古希腊人把复仇女神称作"Eumenides"（仁慈者）同构。你为你最恐惧之物命名，以便驯化它。整个 AI 行业的下一阶段，可能就藏在这个名字的双关里：真正的 AGI 之路，不是让模型更聪明，而是让"幻觉"在被产出之前就被环境捕获。

📝 转录文本

Opening

[music]

John: I want to welcome Jerry and Wyatt of Hallucinate, who went through the Summer '25 YC batch, now building one of the fastest growing companies in the last year. You recently announced your $30 million Series A led by Oak HC/FT. Congratulations guys.

Jerry: Thank you so much, John.

John: Really happy to talk to you and learn more about all the cool stuff that you guys are doing.

What Hallucinate Does

John: So let's first talk about — what is Hallucinate? What do you guys do?

Jerry: At Hallucinate, what we do is we build frontier RL environments and benchmarks to push what models can do in non-coding knowledge work domains, starting with financial services.

A very simple way to visualize our impact on the stack is: if you've ever used a foundation model or product to not write code, but do things like generate spreadsheets, generate PowerPoints, help do due diligence on your deal, or help you make investments — a lot of those gains in financial and economic reasoning and literacy have come from the benchmarks and environments we've built and scaled with the leading frontier labs here in the United States.

In the last year, like you said, our team of less than 10 people has scaled to over mid-eight figures in run rate. And we currently work with four of the top five closed-source US labs here today. So it's been a crazy few years.

Wyatt: Pretty crazy 12 months since then, yeah.

Origin Story: From Capital One Labs to Cornell to YC

John: How did you guys get together and work on this? What gave you the insight? Because as I recall, this wasn't actually your first idea — this was not the idea that you were originally working on.

Jerry: Yeah, so Wyatt and I met at Cornell. We've known each other for almost eight years. We've lived together for almost seven and a half years. Pretty insane period of growth together.

When we first started Hallucinate 2 and 1/2 years ago, our original problem space was Evals — Evals and benchmarking, which for many of those listening now, is a very well-known problem space today. But the idea initially started because I was working at Capital One Labs, and while at Capital One Labs, we were training one of the first AI agents for finance. The constant problem we kept running into was: how do we verify, how do we test, how do we benchmark quality and efficiency?

So we started Hallucinate originally to solve this problem in Evals. And while we were working on Evals and really partnering with some of the leading enterprises and startups on this problem, we ended up working specifically on computer-use and browser-use Evals. We've worked with a few browser agent companies from YC — Skyvern and Browser Use — on this specific problem.

The Pivot: From Evals to Environments

Jerry: The way we realized there is this huge need for environments was because, in order to eval and benchmark a web agent or a browser agent in late 2024, early 2025, on say flight booking, what we realized we needed to do was build a simulated environment for, say, Google Flights or a shopping website or a checkout website.

And then we realized: this work is incredibly hard, but building this environment was also incredibly valuable. Our hypothesis was not just for Evals, but actually for post-training. This is when we saw some of the early scaling laws around RL and DeepSeek and reasoning models as well.

So we basically made a pivot and said, "Hey, let's take this competency we've built in Evals around building verification frameworks and environments, and let's try to apply that to building very high-quality post-training environments for model builders — i.e., the labs." We made that pivot early 2025 and have basically been scaling that thesis ever since.

John: Right. And this is sort of around the time when computer use and the first Sonnet 3.5 browser-use model had already been permeated into a lot of the solutions for automating knowledge work.

Why Finance, Not Coding

Jerry: Exactly. When we first started building environments, we were focused on computer- and browser-use environments. But as we started working on environments continuously, the reason we eventually moved into this specialized vertical — knowledge work and finance — is: we realized that everyone in the space was working on coding or computer use, but it was very obvious to us that if we extrapolated where the models were going and where adoption would be, we had strong conviction that these enterprise knowledge-work, non-coding use cases would actually accrue more value in the long term.

Put simply, more people in the world work non-coding jobs than coding jobs. But models were still far behind in these categories, and our hypothesis was that fundamentally there's a lack of training environments, data, and benchmarks for these domains. So we really took that initial competency and eventually specialized into the verticals that we work on today.

What Is an RL Environment, Really?

John: Now, for people that are completely not familiar, I just want to level-set. Help us understand what really goes into an RL environment — and how that's different than just pure data that's used for a lot of the other training methods.

Wyatt: Yeah. An RL environment is actually pretty simple. You give the agent an objective — some prompt, a problem statement. You have some environment that it runs in — it could be a computer, it could be the browser, it could be the terminal. And then you have some ability to evaluate the work that the agent has done.

If you're going to do an eval, then you just take that and that's the score for the eval. If you're going to do post-training, that becomes the input to the reward function in the post-training pipeline.

The core loop of that is not that complicated. But what makes it complicated, especially for us in the world of knowledge work, is a lot of the verification is less clear than in something like coding — where you might just be able to run unit tests — or even in some of the stuff we've seen in math, where the Lean compiles. Knowledge work: it's harder to verify those. It's a little bit less clear.

A Concrete Example: Building an LBO Model

John: So for people who don't know, can you tell us an example of an RL environment and a model doing the learning loop with an RL environment?

Wyatt: Yeah. Take an Excel modeling task like building an LBO model. You might give an agent a prompt for it to finish a half-constructed model. You give it that initialized spreadsheet with maybe some pieces missing or broken, and then possibly some supporting context to fill in the pieces — or references that the agent needs to make in order to find the right information.

The agent is then going to solve that task. It's going to try to create the correct output model. And then as part of verification, you're able to take that model that the agent created and compare it to the ground truth — basically a golden Excel model. You can do things like: compare, did it get the correct formulas in the right cells? Did it derive the information from the right sources? Did it format things the way that the formatting checklist specifies? These are all things that real bankers care about.

When you put those things together, that's where you get that holistic score of: this agent solved this task this effectively.

The Quality–Volume Tradeoff

John: If we look at the construct of both an environment, a set of tasks, and evals — what is the most difficult part about creating something that is of high quality? Because I suspect you can easily get into this sort of volume because of the scaling laws — obviously volume is one of the factors — but really to create something of high quality is actually quite difficult, I suspect.

Wyatt: Yeah, the tradeoff of quality and volume is kind of the core thing to overcome in environment building. The quality of your environment is directly determining the quality of the model that's post-trained on that environment. So having high-quality environments is the most important thing you can do if you're building environments. Better to have fewer that are better than a lot more that are poor quality.

When it comes to thinking about quality, verification is definitely the most important part of that. We've seen this recently — lots of misalignment articles that have been coming out. Typically, the result is that there's some lack of quality in verification: is this task being verified the right way? Can the agent get credit for work that it didn't do and doesn't deserve? Or vice versa — is the agent actually solving the task and not getting credit it should get?

Either of those situations, you're going to end up with a model that's learning the wrong stuff, because that verifier is directly teaching the model. If the verifier is not aligned with the intention of the task and what a successful output looks like, then you're going to get models that are learning the wrong things.

Reward Hacking — Hard and Soft Versions

John: As you look at how you're constructing the verifier in these models, how are you thinking about reward hacking and the various ways in which you can asymptote in the amount of learning that the model ultimately does?

Wyatt: There are a few ways. When you use the word "reward hacking" — obviously there's the Hugging Face issue: actually breaking out of the sandbox, finding the answer key, knowing the answer before it needs to solve the problem.

But there's other, maybe softer versions of it, where the agent does something — maybe it takes a shortcut, it doesn't show its work. In real life, if you wanted to give some task to an analyst at an investment bank, that analyst needs to prove out the model — whereas the agent maybe just goes right to the answer. You don't want to give the agent credit in that case, because it didn't solve the task the right way.

Understanding the different ways that reward hacking can manifest itself is very important. It's also really important to have the quality assurance and oversight on task creation — not just pumping out tasks and training models on them, but making sure with subject-matter experts that these tasks are aligned, that the scores the verifiers are producing are aligned with what an expert would give.

That's where the scale-and-quality tradeoff comes up — but quality assurance is a huge part of producing good tasks. You can't really skip that.

What's Next: Expanding Beyond Finance

John: As you look forward to how to continuously achieve that at greater scale, what does that look like? What's coming up next for you guys?

Jerry: There are a few super exciting areas we want to continue growing. A big reason why we chose finance as our starting vertical in knowledge work is: one, finance is the world's largest knowledge-work service industry — on a headcount basis, it's one of the highest value. It's somewhat verifiable, which has a lot of nice properties for RL. And there are so many different subgroups within finance — investment banking, private equity, equities research, etc.

But most importantly, we had this belief that really being excellent at building finance environments and teaching financial reasoning would generalize to a lot of other knowledge-work domains — such as consulting, accounting, FP&A, even insurance. A lot of these knowledge-work workflows come from the same capability curriculum that we can help climb on as an industry.

What we're expanding into as a company — and with all this funding we've acquired — is growing into these adjacent knowledge-work domains. We've already seen a lot of our skill sets and quality research translate into many of these other categories that our customers are super excited about.

The "Moore's Law of RL Environments"

John: So as models get smarter, how do you imagine that the environments you build continue to evolve over time?

Jerry: It's a really good question. Internally at the company, we've noticed — we've been doing this for almost 18 months — something that we internally call the Moore's law of RL environments: every 6 to 8 months, the complexity, scope, or size of the environments that we train on roughly doubles. This roughly corresponds with the intelligence of the models.

Another way you could think about it: if we want to keep pushing the frontier of what models can do, we as an industry need to roughly double or increase the complexity of the environments we can build and scale for model training.

If you extrapolate this out, our belief at Hallucinate is: today we're building environments of PowerPoints or Excel or email writing and a few of these apps together. In 6 to 8 months, we'll be building environments of multiple agents operating in a team, doing large chunks of work. In the future, what we are actually going to be building and delivering are simulated companies — simulated industries, simulated governments — that teach agents not just how to do work, but how to be autonomous operators and co-workers in our economy and our society.

These large digital simulations of real-world work are going to be extremely hard to build, but they're really going to be necessary to continue pushing the frontier of models in the future. And whether it's labs or enterprises, we believe they'll rent and purchase time in our environments. That's our vision of where the space is going.

Alignment and Safety as an Industry-Wide Problem

John: There's been a lot of dialogue about alignment and safety of these models. How do you guys think about that as the underlying infrastructure to actually make the models a lot smarter?

Jerry: Alignment is a huge issue. But the really interesting thing for those interested in working on alignment is: if you really look at the reports, alignment and safety issues that emerged were really a product of poor-quality data — and specifically poor-quality RL environments.

If you look at the Hugging Face paper, a lot of the behaviors that allowed it to escape were poorly built sandboxes, a lack of robust verification on process techniques, etc. So I think alignment and safety is an industry-wide problem. I don't think it's just for a lab safety team or an independent evaluation group. Really, it's an industry-wide problem — specifically for data and environment companies like us.

Having robust quality and mitigation of issues all the way down the stack, with companies like us working on the frontier, is some of the highest-impact ways for us as a whole industry to ensure that what we build is truly safe and aligned for everyday use.

Hiring

John: If someone wanted to work on that with you guys — are you guys hiring? How should they be thinking about joining you to do that?

Jerry: Yeah, definitely. There are so many problems to solve. Building an environment is very much like a supply chain: you need to layer on research and engineering, data, people, and then the whole process and financing around it. On the upside, we're hiring for great generalist operators that can work both in product and ops senses.

Wyatt: What you touched on with these simulations — I think we are moving more into the world where engineering is the fundamental bottleneck. Something we're really excited about: we've been building out the research team at Hallucinate, so we're looking for people who know really in-depth post-training and benchmarks/evaluations from the research side.

Also, platform and infra — some of the infra challenges around hosting the simulations are just thorny problems. And generally, we've seen people who can come in and use tools, use AI tooling to solve problems, be really successful — and it doesn't really matter their background, doesn't really matter previous roles. The future of work is changing a little bit, and it's driven by people who can have agency and solve problems. That's really what we're looking for.

Closing

John: Fantastic. Well, congratulations to you both on the amazing progress and on the recent fundraise. Thanks for joining us today.

Jerry: Thank you so much, Sean.

[music]

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Hallucinate 的真正商业模式不是"训练 AI"，而是"重建会计学"
表面上，Jerry 和 Wyatt 在做 RL 环境。但如果你把访谈逐字拆解，会发现他们反复回到同一个词：**verification（验证）**。他们选择金融作为切入点时说了一句关键的话——"finance is somewhat verifiable"。
这句话比它听起来重要得多。它暗示了一个被整个行业忽略的事实：**金融之所以能被 AI 快速吃掉，并不是因为它"数字化程度高"，而是因为过去 500 年里，金融业已经演化出了全世界最完善的"验证基础设施"——会计准则、审计师、监管机构、GAAP、LBO 模型的标准结构**。换句话说，金融业无意间已经为 AI 建好了 reward function 的脚手架。
这反过来预测了一个冷门结论：**哪个行业演化出最强的"外部可验证性"机制，哪个行业就会最先被自动化**。因此真正率先沦陷的不是"规则简单"的行业，而是"规则复杂但有裁判"的行业——医学（诊断可验证）、法律（判例可对照）、合规（规则明文化）。而创意、战略、品味这些**没有

item.title: [Odds on Open] Ex-Lehman Trader: AI Won't Give You Edge
item.dc:creator: Odds on Open
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：AI 不是边缘，但顶级机构疯狂烧 compute 的原因，恰恰证明了这一点

Yoshi 抛出了一个表面矛盾：既然 AI 不能带来 edge，为什么 Jane Street、Citadel、Jump 还在数据中心上砸天文数字？他的答案可以浓缩成一句隐藏公式——他们买的不是 edge，而是"把 edge 执行到位"的边际改良成本。普通人以为顶级量化在用算力换认知；真相是，他们已经是执行上的职业拳手，compute 对他们而言只是更好的护齿，不是更好的拳头。这里有一个让人不寒而栗的推论：AI 对普通人是幻觉，对专业选手是复利。工具的平权假象，实际上在加速两极分化——不是因为穷人拿不到工具，而是因为富人（在"自律"这个意义上富有的人）早已拥有把工具转化为成果的操作系统。

二、跨领域连接：从昭和"渡边夫人"到硅谷 YC 对冲基金——边缘人群永远是市场的最大玩家

这段访谈里最被低估的一句话是：日本主妇因为"无聊"，用高杠杆交易美元日元，曾经推动过整个外汇市场。请把这个事实叠加到他后半段讲的——YC 过去 18 个月涌现大量"AI hedge fund"申请者，Robinhood 的 solopreneur 浪潮，以及 LLC 一键注册把个人瞬间"机构化"的现实。你会发现一条跨越 40 年的隐秘规律：每当一个被主流体系边缘化的群体同时获得（闲暇 + 资本 + 杠杆通道），他们就会短暂成为市场的边际定价者。昭和主妇、2021 年的 WSB 散户、今天 YC 的单人对冲基金——这不是三件事，是同一个结构的三次迭代。而更深的意味是：Alpaca 本质上是在为"下一代渡边夫人"修建基础设施——只不过这次穿着连帽衫、住在拉各斯或河内。

三、他真正的护城河，是 12 岁那次失败——以及一个"反职业"的生存哲学

最让人意外的洞察藏在他回答"你为什么会想得这么不一样"的那一刻。他的全部商业直觉——"不要和任何人竞争"、"做基础设施像空气和水"、"永远想 objective 而不是 process"——不是来自雷曼，不是来自 YC，而是来自 12 岁时考砸日本初中入学考试那一瞬间的"人生已毁"。被告知"赢不了"的那个孩子，把整个人生重构成了一场"永远走捷径"的游戏——不是偷懒，而是拒绝任何人告诉他正道是什么。这里有一个鲜少被说破的事实：失败者的世界观一旦被 YC 这种精英筛选器盖上戳，会变成最可怕的商业武器——因为它既保留了反叛性，又获得了合法性。

跨领域钩子：这几乎是 Steve Jobs 大学辍学去学 Calligraphy 的日本版翻拍。真正差异化的创业者，几乎都在青春期的某个节点经历了"被主流系统宣判失败"——然后把余生花在证明这个系统的坐标系本身是错的。

四、一个隐藏的、你没问他但他回答了的问题：AI 时代，稀缺性正在从"思考"转向"坚持"

当他说"having an edge is only step one; execution is a completely different skillset"——他其实在描述一个正在发生的宏观范式迁移：在信息时代，稀缺的是注意力；在 AI 时代，稀缺的是跟随力（follow-through）。LLM 把"找到 edge"这件事的边际成本压到接近零，这意味着未来对冲基金之间比拼的不再是谁更聪明，而是谁的手不抖。这反而让"交易"这件事回到了它最古老的本质——一种关于人性驯服的技艺。他把它比作拳击"反人类本能的身体姿态"，这是整段访谈里最精炼的隐喻：量化交易正在变成一种身体修炼。

五、一个让人想完就想关掉播客去思考三小时的问题

节目最后他反问主持人："你为什么觉得你的技能必须 defensible？" 这句话值得被单独裱起来。因为它暴露了一个几乎所有知识工作者都没意识到的认知陷阱——我们默认人生的目的是"保住某种技能"，而不是"活着并感到对劲"。他给出的终极 shortcut 是：如果 AI 把一切表层技能剥光，剩下的那个"你还愿意做的东西"，就是你真正的职业。这个答案看似鸡汤，但放在他 Okinawa 甘蔗农场实习的背景里就变得锋利无比——他 20 年来一直在用"如果一切崩塌我还能种地吃饭"作为心理底仓。这是全场最硬的风险管理模型，比任何 Value-at-Risk 公式都更深。

📝 转录文本

AI 不会给你 Edge：前雷曼交易员访谈

开场：核心观点与争议

I think that AI and agents will not give you edge. Technology continue to evolve but executing that requires execution by human.

If that's the case, why are all the trading firms spending exorbitant amounts of money on compute?

Because they're already pros of executing those things, you know, creating the intelligence and the agents and the rules and finding edges. That's the reason why they are able to grow.

Are you seeing an explosion in the number of people who are systematically trading today?

The number of the monthly active developers, it's been growing from 20,000 to 80,000 plus in six months. That's what I love about capital markets. Capital markets in my opinion is like street fighting, right? I'm partnered by risk. I started at the Lehman Brothers. You know, nothing is going to last forever.

Yoshi, thank you so much for coming on the pod. Thanks for having me here, man.

一、零售量化今天还有 Edge 吗？

Is there edge for a retail quant today?

Yes, when you create one. It depends on if you can create one or not. So I don't think it really matters if you're retail trader or pro traders. It really depends on like when you create it, you have an edge. If you cannot create it, you don't have an edge.

You're seeing this from a very differentiated angle. Um, you know, your API is used by a lot of these guys. What sort of edges do you tend to see them exploiting?

So the reason why I said that you have an edge when you have an edge and when you create one — the whole point that I wanted to try to explain is that even retail traders could have an edge when you do it enough or when you really find it. So, you know, our platform is offering programmable access, API access, and then there are people who create their edge, who find their edge, and they keep making money. So there are people like that. I don't know if they are considered to be pro or retail. I don't know the categorization, but it is true that some people do find edges using our platform.

二、AI 如何改变 Edge 的创造过程？

The reason why I find this so interesting is because I think as a society the cultural trends that exist today are pushing everyone in almost this direction — to trade more, to access financial freedom, and in some cases even punt their way to the top. Right? I mean, that is what I think everyone is seeing. You look at perp exchanges and they are absolutely booming. I had learned with a founder of one of the top perp exchanges and their product is just ripping.

And so my question for you is: if you were in those shoes today — and I know you have some background in that — what processes would you implement in order to build a systematic framework for making money in the markets?

If I were the actual participant side and trader side — I mean that's where this AI and agents conversation kicks in. Because of the AI and LLM, it really hugely reduces the resources and time, even if you're an individual trying to explore where the edges are. Any process of trying to create an edge, it's just trial and error. It's an R&D. And without an AI, it of course takes much longer time, right? It's all about coding, it's all about the optimization and then constant fine-tuning based on the trend of the market changes.

So how we can do that kind of process and automating to fine-tune it — it becomes much more resource-intensive in terms of what you do. That means that you can do more trial and errors. So the process to get to finding an edge, I think it got shortened up because of this AI/LLM.

So if I were doing this today, so that's how I would approach it. It's not going to be okay if I use AI and agents I can find an edge. It's really more for me to make the whole process much shorter so I can do more trial and error so I can get better edges. So that's how I would frame it.

三、Edge 的民主化，还是精英化？

And do you think that that shortening of the time horizon for iterating on certain processes — do you think that that democratizes opportunity within the markets, or do you think that concentrates it in the hands of people who are absolute experts in those iterative loops?

In my opinion, I think we also have to think about that having an edge doesn't mean that you're going to be successful. Having an edge is a first step, and the second step is actually execute and follow through based on your edge. And that's a completely different skill set.

Human behaviors don't change, right? We have always greed, always fear. And because of that reason, some people will never be successful — even if you have amazing edges — because you will never be able to execute the edges if you are so fearful of actually executing it.

And I think that's the interesting part of this trading, or anything that we do in life. We may happen to be in the exact same situation, in the same weapons or same features, but outcomes will be all different based on you or based on me or based on anyone. And I think that happens in this trading environment too — even though you have an edge.

四、成功零售量化交易员的共同行为模式

You touched on the behavioral dynamics just there. In speaking to your users, in understanding your users — which retail traders, retail systematic quantitative traders — what sort of behaviors do they tend to have that you see come up often?

What I see that tend to be more successful is that they're repetitive — basically having agent actually executing — and then when the market dynamics changes, they actually completely stop trading and take a pause and improve it or fine-tune it for the new market dynamics and come back. And that's a pattern that I see for those people who actually have edges and in addition to that being able to execute in the right way. So that's a pattern that I see with regards to these successful retail quanters.

How do they approach the problem of the markets from a wealth creation perspective? Do they tend to see it as a cash flow business — that the models are making money on their money and they spend that — or is it a compounding game where they're really trying to build wealth in the process?

I think of course it really depends on the people — how people started. Probably it's all different. Like, some people just had spare money and spare time, and you're able to code (at this point you don't have to be able to code), but create these rules and start trying. And most of the time you're just playing around, right? As a hobby — let's see how it works, let's actually execute what you're thinking into the real world. This is the easiest way to verify what you think actually makes money. Things happen in a very short feedback loop: when you do bad things, you lose money, and when you do it right, you make money.

So I think that happens. But at the end of the day, it's very difficult to see that because all of the people who come into this situation have different motivations. So some people may find and become very confident that it continues to work well, so they may put more money into it. Some people continue to be very very tight and then have their own rules that they're not going to risk any more dollar amount than certain amounts. I think again this is based on each individual's amount of fear and greed.

八、争议性观点：AI 不会给你 Edge

Real quick, before we tap into what are the ways you're building towards that future: on the hedge fund industry, do you think that your vantage point has led you to any differentiated or contrarian takes? What do you believe about the hedge fund industry — and I guess broadly quant trading, about competitive advantage, about the business of it — that most people would disagree with you on?

I think that AI and agents will not give you edge. A lot of people ask me, "okay, because agents and AI will figure out how to make money, what's the point of hedge funds? Everyone can now make money." That's what I completely disagree.

AI, agents, LLM — it's just technology. Technology continues to evolve, but executing that requires execution by human. Because the money belongs, at the end of the day, to you as a human. You have a tax; agents don't pay tax. You're the one who's liable for tax. Which means a human has to execute, and that element is underestimated so much about how much of it impacts the results of running strategies.

So I disagree about the AI and agents will give you an edge over how to make money.

This is going to be a hard question, but if that's the case, why are all the trading firms spending exorbitant amounts of money on compute, on data centers — Jane Street, the pod shops? It seems like they're just opening up their bank accounts and throwing cash at these things. What's the reason for that?

Because they're already pros of executing those things. Creating the intelligence and the agents and the rules and finding edges — that's what they'll continue to invest in. Because they have a tight rule and discipline. That's the reason why they are able to grow.

And just like regular amateurs — most of the regular humans — I don't think we are able to execute with discipline. That itself is a profession, in my opinion. It's like boxing. I think reading, you know, The Hard Thing About Hard Things — Ben Horowitz's book — being an entrepreneur or CEO, it's not a natural posture of the human. You have to kind of learn to take the posture of it. It's so unnatural as a human. And he was talking about boxing — how you do the form of boxing is so not natural as a human being, as an animal.

And I feel the same way, because executing that strategy or rules — by things that's not working, but statistically logically it should be working — can you continue to execute with discipline? Even the odds may be same as gambling. You believe in the statistics, logically it should work, but most of the life it doesn't. It may come back, but who knows. That's so unnatural.

So which means that that itself is, in my opinion, an extreme profession to be able to execute that way. So that's the reason why all those institutions you just said — they know how to do that as a profession. So now they have to continue to fight and improve their edges against their competitors.

So you would say that because they are operationally not perfect but excellent, they look for any little bit that can improve certain processes, and investing in frontier model infrastructure is what they're doing.

Yeah. And of course there are competitors doing the same thing. That's going to impact how the market works, and then they also have to understand how that's going to influence their own certain small edges, and then they're just going to have to do it against the new market movement as well. But again, it's all depends on this foundation — that expectation that you can actually execute based on that rule. I think most of us — I don't think we can. Even though we kind of know statistically it's going to work, execution is a very different game.

九、Alpaca 的使命：Financial Freedom for Everyone

I want to hear now about — we've talked a little bit about how you think the future of the hedge fund industry is going to look. What are the ways in which you're most excited to be building towards that future?

I think personally, I believe in — freedom is very important in many ways. I know it's such an abstract conversation, but our company's mission is open financial services to everyone on the planet. And I know it sounds kind of boring without thinking about it, but to me it's really important.

I grew up between Japan and the US. And based on where you are as a location, you have certain access to certain things, and you don't if you're not there. For example, when Robinhood launched their app — I feel like I keep bringing up Robinhood, but I love the app — launched in 2013 or '15. I was back in Japan. I was on the wait list but I couldn't even install the app because I was not an American resident at that time.

I know it's such a small thing. But when I think about my life — for example, even Spotify or Apple Music — you needed to have a credit card. The billing address was in the United States, and if you're not a resident there, you don't have that kind of credit card. So you can't use Spotify or Apple Music. That itself is so not freedom. It's so not fair.

So for us, I want us to remove the unfairness based on the location, based on where you're from, what kind of person you are, status, anything. As long as infrastructures are there, if you can use it, it's going to give really fair access and opportunities for everyone.

So going back to your question — that's really important to us. Making sure all the infrastructure is not really exclusive. So we want to be completely opposite of that: to be usable. Of course big institutions can be using that too, but that has to be as low barrier as possible.

So that's what I'm personally excited about. Because solopreneurs can be real big hedge funds, but there has to be some starting point that the person doesn't have to come with a certain background of "okay, I worked at Citadel for 10 years."

Well, I try to be honest to my feeling, and that frustration — I think that's really motivation, my energy. And that's really all a feeling: "this is not fair." I think that really drove me always. And I just didn't want to be in the place where a lot of people are.

十四、"Shortcut" 的真正含义：回到 Objective

It seems that a lot of history's greatest entrepreneurs are always trying to find the points of highest leverage — shortcuts. What are the ways in which you are applying those principles to your business today?

I think shortcuts — some people think that that's a bad way of the word. But to me, it means thinking what is really truly fundamental. So "shortcut" actually means: what is really the objective of doing anything? Then if you try to start optimizing what you want to get as objective, you start realizing the conventional way of other people doing is just people are following because other people are doing, instead of thinking about the objective and the problem.

So if you start optimizing there, you just happen to be ended up doing the shortcut.

So I think about a lot: okay, what is the objective? What is the problem? And our angel investor Vlad — who is the co-founder/CTO of Revolut — he always tells me: "okay Yoshi, before you start talking about it, what is the problem? Don't just give me the conversation. What is the problem?" That really opened my eyes. Anything that we do or think about — not the process, "we have to do this" — no. What is the problem? What is the objective? Then everything becomes the shortest path. I think about that during the business.

I think that's a very powerful example and I want our platform Alpaca to somehow contribute to that. And I hope other infrastructure to be that way too, because that is really the manifesting of how I think things should be. Because you didn't choose to be born in certain country in certain environment. But I believe financial services — or at least capital markets — capital markets in my opinion is extremely fair place.

Like when you become independent from working at Citadel Securities or Citadel and then start trading by yourself, markets treat you fairly compared to you who graduated from — I don't know — worked at Citadel, or a person who has no experience, born in a third-world country, has no education, nothing. They treat you completely fairly.

And that's what I love about really capital markets. Then what makes it even more fair is that the toolsets and the accessibility becomes the same. Then we can actually see real fairness as well.

I feel like capital markets in my opinion is like extremely street fighting, right? It doesn't matter if you're wearing suit or if you're wearing — I don't know — just t-shirt. You just need to fight. And I think it's really fair fight. And that exact example that you said — achieving that by us would be like a dream. And I think that's an amazing future, in my opinion.

No, I agree. I think tall, short, fat, skinny — regardless of where you're from — you make money, you make money.

Exactly. You lose money, you lose money. I know. It's so result-driven and practical and pragmatic.

There's no excuse. You have to embrace it. When you fail, you fail. You have to embrace it because the numbers tell you you fail.

Oh yeah. If you're down in July, you're down in July.

Exactly, exactly.

二十、个人风险观与 AI 时代的职业选择

I want to ask a couple final questions about how you view — they're going to be quite general, but because you've been a trader, because you're building at the intersection of the buy side, the public markets, and you're building — I think it's, I can't really call you a startup now…

It is a startup.

…startup, right, big — how do you view, what is your mindset for personal risk taking? And I asked that question given that I think the AI models, the foundation models, are really commoditizing a lot of the skill sets that were formerly defensible. I'll give an example: software engineer. I would even argue high finance jobs, entry-level jobs especially. A lot of those skill sets, I would be short — even now, with what's priced in. I think those are not gone but declining in value. What do you think that implies for the way one should play their career today?

I would really go back to: why do we live? Like before going into career. "Career" itself is a word that stops us from thinking about things. When we use the word "career" — okay, for what? What's the objective? What is the problem we're trying to solve? Is that money? Or is that because you want to be looking good? Or because you want to get married? What is it, right?

With that thinking that I have — when I was in college, that's what I would have focused on even more. I did one internship in my whole student life — when I was in university, only one internship. That was a sugarcane and tobacco farm in Okinawa. That was my only internship that I did, because that was what I was most interested in. Because I wanted to understand what is it for me to live. Because if I didn't get a job, or if I didn't make money, if I couldn't make money, how do we live? Probably I need to eat, so I need to intern at the farms. That was my kind of logic that I had. [laughter] So that's what I did.

And I still think that way ultimately. If I can grow vegetables and hunt the animals and then cut them up and chop them up — I think that's enough, right? That's the ultimate answer, shortcut, when the objective is to live.

So I would definitely focus on that, especially because all those things are getting done by AI. All those things on the surface is getting ripped out by the AI. What is it that we left? I think we have to really think about why do we — what do we do.

二十一、如何在 AI 时代构建差异化？

How do you think about building defensibility around one's skill set today then? Given that the models have commoditized so much. And as an add-on on top of that: should one even think to build defensibility, or should one just try to build something that grows really fast to where it won't matter?

Are you talking about the trading aspect, or just the personal — I think that's very very easy. You just do whatever that you feel right. Like, what you think — it's not what you think, right — what you feel right.

I think about this a lot — doing Alpaca. Because doing two other businesses before this, I think three businesses, I completely burned out. And the reason why for that is I couldn't get my — how I feel: curiosity or excitement or gut feeling of frustration trying to solve it — to what I'm doing, to be matched.

As long as it's matched, you're going to continue to do it. You're going to continue putting 120% of what you do. And Elon Musk was saying the similar thing, right? If you read certain things for certain hours, you're going to be the expert. What's so difficult is to make yourself do it through. And the only way you can do it through without burning yourself down is be honest to how you feel.

I think that is the only way. And as long as that's the case, you're going to be specialist.

I was at this event called SIFMA event — industry event — yesterday, and I've been looking at all those high-profile names of legal or compliance or trading. They all have such different lives and profiles. And I was just looking at LinkedIn for every one of them. And they all have so many different backgrounds and somehow they ended up to be there. And I think they're doing certain things long enough, they become the expert regardless of how you get in there.

So doing that for a long time just gives you the edge simply. But in order to do that, most people can't do it if you are not honest to yourself, because you get tired of it and you just going to stop. So I think that is the most important thing — what you feel right. It may be super niche or it may not be for making money. But again, that's not the objective, right? The objective is to create your skill set. Then you focus on that. And I think the solution to do it is: what is that you feel honestly that you're interested and curious? Then you're going to keep doing it without even thinking.

二十二、最终问题：如何找到那个"对的东西"？

Final question. We've talked about how you think the hedge fund world's going to evolve, retail edge, building Alpaca, and then building skill set — and you know, even towards the end, just personal advice of "do what you genuinely enjoy and think is for you."

If you had to figure out what that is and you have no idea — right, especially today, there's so much noise — I'm not even asking give an answer, but how does one find the answer? Because I know plenty of people — and not even just young people, a lot of people who are older — who realize their skill set is not defensible. And there's a little bit they can do, but a lot of people are still have jobs because of goodwill. How does one figure out what that thing is where they can build true differentiation and scale it up?

Do you have to have a defensible skill set? What is the reason you need to have a skill set? Because if you feel right of doing what you do as a skill set — like, why would you care?

Yeah, I mean, that's how I think. Because if your skill set is accounting — I don't know, I'm just making it up — accounting. If you really truly enjoy — and also, I want to be careful because the word "enjoy" is also very misleading. "Enjoy" means like you are trying to enjoy, but then that itself will burn you down. You need to just feel: "oh, it's really just funny, right, doing this." That to me is very important.

But if you feel that way doing accounting, then yeah, probably that's automatically became your skill set. And at the same time you're going to keep doing that regardless of — I try to replace what you do. You probably continue to enjoy and then see what's happening to be so interested, and then you're going to do more things around it.

So having the skill set and then worrying about if that's going to be defensible or not itself then may not be even something that's really solving the problem of objective. Like, what is the objective of having a skill set? Is there — is that even the objective, to have a skill set? What is the objective anyway, right, for that?

二十三、拥抱风险、拥抱不确定性

I love it. [laughter] Makes sense. I mean, what I would say to that is — and keep in mind I'm still very young [laughter] — but I think the differentiation, the defensibility, helps you sleep at night. So that's what I would say. But thank you very much.

But that's virtual, man. That's really the worst, synthetic or like fake. Because — I don't know, because I'm paranoid, right? I'm paranoid about risk. I started at Lehman Brothers. Nothing is going to last forever. Which means everything's going to be different every day, next day. At the same time, because that's the de facto, you need to sweep through as well. You need to get used to the reality and embrace it first. That that's the case, without worrying about it. Because you start worrying about it and you make that into your routine, so you don't worry about it anymore. But anyway, [laughter]

Embrace risk, embrace uncertainty, and relax.

Yeah. And relax because that itself becomes the routine and then normal life. Then you're already relaxed because that's become your normal.

I love it. Now that I enjoy. Thank you very much, man, for coming on Odds on Open. This was an absolute pleasure.

Yeah, this was really amazing. And thank you very much for this.

Yoshi 抛出了一个表面矛盾：既然 AI 不能带来 edge，为什么 Jane Street、Citadel、Jump 还在数据中心上砸天文数字？他的答案可以浓缩成一句隐藏公式——**他们买的不是 edge，而是"把 edge 执行到位"的边际改良成本**。普通人以为顶级量化在用算力换认知；真相是，他们已经是执行上的职业拳手，compute 对他们而言只是更好的护齿，不是更好的拳头。这里有一个让人不寒而栗的推论：**AI 对普通人是幻觉，对专业选手是复利**。工具的平权假象，实际上在加速两极分化——不是因为穷人拿不到工具，而是因为富人（在"自律"这个意义上富有的人）早已拥有把工具转化为成果的操作系统。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、九月的"隐形撕裂"：指数平静下的板块地震

表面上标普仅下跌0.5%，纳指甚至上涨1.9%，这是一个"安然度过"的九月。但如果你撕开指数的表皮——银行-8.5%、国防-9.3%、REIT-7.4%、必需消费-5.2%——这是衰退级别的离散度，几乎达到2008年或2020年个别板块的回撤幅度。

真正值得警惕的洞察是：指数越平静，底层撕裂越可怕。这和CPI里"核心通胀温和"却掩盖了房租7%、商品通缩-2%的结构性分裂是同一种现象。市场的"平均值"正在说谎。半导体板块+11.3%的能量，几乎独自对冲了价值股的全面崩塌。这种"由少数标的扛指数"的结构，在物理学里叫临界态（critical state）——沙堆看似稳定，但只要一粒沙就能引发雪崩。换言之，九月不是"涨得很弱"，而是"跌得很有秩序"——而有秩序的下跌，恰恰是最脆弱的。

二、美光的"去周期化"：这是半导体版的SaaS转型

美光签26份SCA、锁定2030年35%营收，表面是财务工程，本质是商业模式的物种变异。这个动作的历史对标不是其他芯片股，而是： - 2000年代初软件行业从一次性License转向订阅制SaaS——同样是把波动的现金流强行平滑化； - 2015年后TSMC与苹果签长期产能预订协议——把代工从拍卖市场变成要客定制； - 甚至好莱坞片商预售海外发行权对冲票房风险。

出乎意料的观察是：市场定价美光，关键根本不在毛利率86%还是87%。毛利率是"证据"，不是"故事"。真正的重估来自前瞻市盈率从6.7倍→8倍→10倍的轨迹——那意味着市场相信"美光不再是周期股"。这是一个信念估值，不是财务估值。英伟达一年前走过同样的路：毛利率停滞，但PE维持，EPS继续推股价。美光现在就在这个"信念临界点"前面排队。

隐藏的反向风险：SCA占比如果超过70%，公司虽然摆脱周期，但也丧失了价格暴涨期的爆发力——变成"受监管的公用事业股"。这就是为什么管理层说"目标保持SCA占比50%左右"——他们在故意保留一部分野性。这是驯化与野性的张力管理，像动物园给圈养老虎留的狩猎训练。

三、"故事线"的递归悖论：批评叙事者本身也在叙事

视频中最深刻却被一笔带过的时刻，是作者说"22年市场的故事线——加息=科技股跌——被证伪了，很多时候故事线只是从结果出发合理化价格"。

但紧接着他立刻用另一套故事线——"进入九月前科技股setup很弱、Mac7 YTD很弱、所以九月反弹是合理的"——来解释九月的异常走势。

这是叙事递归（narrative recursion）：批评叙事的人，用叙事来批评叙事。塔勒布称之为"叙事谬误的二阶形式"。真正清醒的态度不是"寻找正确的故事"，而是承认——市场在每一个时刻都在生成多个互相矛盾的故事，而幸存下来的故事是被价格事后筛选的。

这里有一个让人不安的跨领域连接：这和进化论是同构的。基因不"知道"自己要适应环境，是环境事后杀死了不适应的基因。市场叙事也不是"预测"价格，而是价格事后杀死了被证伪的叙事。所以，当你听到"债券市场需要一个事件来见顶"——这不是预测，这是在为未来的任何一次见底，预先铺设一个可被追认的叙事骨架。

真正的操作启示：不要寻找"对的故事"，而要观察"哪些故事正在被市场批量生产"。当叙事高度集中（比如现在"债券无底、财政部必须出手"），说明仓位高度一致，反向机会就在那里。

📝 转录文本

九月血流成河回顾 · PCE数据解读 · 美光财报分析

开场：九月的血色与十月的加息悬念

一年里面最艰难的9月份已经在身后了，那今天就有这个机会，我们一起去回顾一下9月份资产价格的走势。其实除了几个个别的板块以外，整个9月份——美股也好，还是其他的一些资产也好——用一个词去形容的话：血流成河。其实下跌的幅度非常的大，特别是价值股板块，我认为这个跌幅几乎已经赶上熊市了，包括市场的参与度。

所以今天一开始我们先去回顾一下九月份资产价格的走势。然后周三的这个市场公布了最新的PCE数据，这一组PCE数据出来之后，十月份美联储加息的这个预期再次从周二的50%降到了37%至38%左右。那我个人认为十月份加息这个概率几乎是非常的低，为什么会非常的低，和大家一起稍后聊一下。

最后就是周三盘后发布财报的美光，那美光到底有没有走出这个周期行业？

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析员小涛。那在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞、加转发。我也不知道点了之后会不会让更多的人看到我们这期内容，但是点了再说嘛，大家说是不是。

一、九月资产价格全景回顾

好，我先回顾一下整个9月份资产价格的走势，会让我们可能感到非常的意外。

其实如果我们把芯片板块和前七大科技股放在一边的话，整个9月份——我前面说了——用一个词去形容的话：血流成河。

宏观指标： - 美元指数上涨了2.1% - 两年期和十年期美债收入分别上涨了55个基点和54个基点，非常大幅度的上涨 - TLT下跌了5.7% - 垃圾级别债券的利差上升了48个基点

但是在这种情况下，三大指数里边标普500没有出现下跌，或者说下跌的幅度仅仅只有0.5%。

通常来说，无论是美元指数的上涨也好，美债利率的这个上涨也好，包括油价的这个上涨——原油价格整个9月份也上涨了5.3%——这几个因素单拿一个因素出来，理论上来说都是利空美股。但是整个9月份美股却并没有出现非常大幅度的下跌，甚至纳指还上涨了1.9%，道指下跌了4.3%。

黄金随着美元指数的上涨、美债收入的一个上涨，也出现了比较大幅度的回调6.3%。罗素2000下跌了5.4%，IGB下跌了3.2%。

几乎所有的一些价格、资产价格都出现了下跌，除了纳指是出现上涨，标普500是没怎么下跌。为什么？是因为科技股上涨了5%，前七大科技股上涨了4.2%，半导体板块或者芯片板块上涨了11.3%。

二、半导体板块的反转叙事：故事线的失败

那么我在X上面，在9月份、9月初的时候，我在接受一家媒体采访的时候，我有非常明确地说到：我说6月份的时候，整个半导体板块是大家都在真的去抢，真的在讨论。也就正好三个月之前，也是美光发布财报的时候，当时大家真的去讨论——美光不是一家周期股。结果就美光的财报发布完之后，出现了一个sell the news，一路下跌、一路下跌，反弹、调整到现在这样的一个位置。

三个月过去了，在八月底的时候我说过：七月份大家争相恐后要进入半导体板块，而整个八月份半导体板块是无人问津。

结果整个9月份，即使在利率大幅度上涨的情况下、美元指数大幅度上涨的情况下，半导体板块非但没有出现下跌，还反弹了11.3%。

所以再次证明了一件事情：就是很多时候我们在聊的故事线，包括22年市场给我们的一个故事线——如果加息、如果利率上涨，科技股就应该下跌、半导体板块也应该下跌。但是在9月份，不好意思，我们并没有看到。

说明什么问题？说明故事线本身很多时候真的只是从结果去出发，试图去合理化价格的这个走势。

那我们9月份的走势怎么去解释？怎么去解释明明利率上涨，科技股却出现上涨，然后芯片股也出现上涨？感觉上好像不符合逻辑。

但其实我个人认为是合理的。为什么合理的？就是在进入9月份之前，整个半导体板块8月底是没人问津的。那前七大科技股是因为一些个别的消息，包括Meta的一个上涨，使得前七大科技股相对会强一些。那即使在Mag7里边，也有一些相对强的、一些相对弱的，但是整个Mag7进入9月份之前的一个setup是什么？setup就是Mag7 YTD走得相当的弱。

所以并不是美股这边对于利率不敏感，美股这边对于利率非常的敏感。

三、价值股板块的全面崩塌

我们来看一下价值股板块： - 非必需品消费一个月下跌6.6% - 必需品下跌5.2% - 银行板块一个月下跌8.5% - 公共事业6.6% - REIT下跌7.4% - 国防板块下跌9.3%

当一个板块本身下跌要将近10%，像银行板块下跌将近9%，这已经是非常大幅度的下跌了。

所以几乎我们如果现在去看美债收入，现在一定是在一个超买的一个区间，非常超买的一个区间。你看TLT的话，就是在一个非常超卖的一个区间。去看这些价值股ETF的话，也是在一个非常超卖的区间。

所以现在市场其实非常的极致。

但是我希望通过我们对于9月份资产价格的一个回顾，再次理解一个道理：就是进入一个事件之前、进入数据之前，整个市场的一个setup太重要了，市场的一个仓位和看法太重要。

然后另外一点，很多时候我们只能做一个模糊正确，甚至于这个模糊正确的一个时间跨度可能会长一些。

我什么意思？就是比如说在昨天视频下面，有一条留言——我记得非常的清晰——他说如果我们去看今天市场的一个走势，因为是九月底、9月30号的话，会有养老基金的这一个再平衡。那整个九月份债券市场非常的弱，所以他的一个期待是：他说确定性最高的反而是TMF，就是三倍做多ETF、三倍做多TLT的ETF。他认为因为养老基金这个再平衡，TLT在9月30、就周三那天一定会出现上涨，所以他认为确定性是最高的。

结果我们看到什么？的确我看了一下，在三点到四点的时候，是有债券市场这一块的一些买家进去，是有一些养老基金的一个再平衡资金进去，但是并没有成为整个市场里边的一个主流的一个力量。主流的一个力量还是做空美债这一块。所以美债最终的一个收盘，TLT在周三还是出现了0.6%的下跌。

所以我们在看待市场的时候，我认为不要去做很多的一些假设。就比如说九月份市场一定要下跌，所以进入九月份之前我要稍微小心一些，但最后九月份你看一下——即使在利率上涨的情况下，纳指仍然是上涨的，标普也几乎没有动，那整个9月份也安全地度过了，或者平安地度过了。

四、债券市场的恐慌度量：垃圾债利差与MOVE指数

然后我们来看一下这张图，就是我前面说到的垃圾级别债券的这个利差。其实过去一周上涨的幅度非常的大，那也使得整个9月份总体来说上升的幅度要将近50个基点，现在已经来到了3.09%。

这是一个利差，垃圾级别债券的一个利差，越高就代表整个市场越恐慌。在今年3月份的时候，这个利差去到了3.30至3.35左右，所以现在垃圾级别债券这个利差已经在一个相对比较高的位置。

同时，我昨天视频里面有和大家分享过债券市场MOVE Index。债券市场这一块的一个波动率，在昨天视频和大家更新的时候是106.6。那随着在周三债券市场的利率继续出现上升，然后TLT的价格继续出现下跌，我们看到这个波动率再次出现上升，去到了110.5。那110.5已经非常接近于今年3月份的这个水平了。

所以从很多个角度去看： - 无论是这些价值股ETF它的一个RSI现在是在一个非常超卖的一个位置 - 还是垃圾级别债券的这个利差现在是在一个相对比较高的这个位置，接近于今年3月份的这个位置 - 还是说债券市场这一块的个波动率MOVE Index，现在也是在一个相对比较高的这个位置 - 还是说整个市场的一个参与度——截止到周三的一个收盘，标普500 20均线、50均线、100日均线分别在23、21和31——都是在一个相对比较低的这个位置

虽然指数在一个高位，但是从各个角度、从量化的角度去看待这个市场，现在市场就是处在一个非常悲观的位置。

宏观和利率对于市场是有影响的，但主要是影响到了这些价值股板块，而科技板块、半导体板块相对比较的强势。那因为科技板块、半导体板块的强势把指数是拖在那边。

五、债券市场等待一个"事件"

那我个人的期待，我在今天X上我有说过，我对利率这一块的上涨我不是那么的担心。为什么？因为财政部可能比我更加强地担心利率这一块的上涨，我不认为财政部可以忍受。

但是当下的这个市场，在债券市场这一块好像是失去了这个信心——就是无论有任何的一些消息，债券市场利率几乎是每天都在上涨，所以让市场情绪面砸得非常的低。

那接下去，一旦有一些事件——就我说，市场见底，它是需要一个事件进去的。我说债券市场的价格见底、利率见顶、价格见底，它是需要短期来说、它是需要一个事件的。所以现在市场里边缺乏一个事件。

一旦有一个事件呢，这个事件可以比如说来自于周四——那周四早上我记得在11点的时候，财政部将会公布他们接下去短债这一块的一个融资体量。如果说财政部把短债这块的融资具体的一个融资体量往上抬的话，那对于市场来说有可能是一个解脱。

所以债券市场的一个利率什么时候见顶？我认为是要有一个事件进来的，不然的话市场确实当下信心非常的低迷。那这一个事件可以是由美国财政部所主导，那至于什么时间点去发生，我并不知道，但是我自己的一个预期仍然是在中期选举之前。美债利率如果持续保持在一个高位，对于中期选举是不利的。

六、PCE数据深度解读：方法论修正才是关键

讲到美债利率这一块，我视频一开始有聊过，在周三公布了PCE数据。

理论上来说，PCE数据其实对于什么影响是不大的，因为PPI数据、CPI数据有了之后，可以直接推出PCE数据。但是这一次的PCE数据呢，是BEA美国的劳工局把数据计算方法进行了一个修改。

那这个修改本身它是在期待之内的。那我在昨天我在X上面我就有说过，我说现在PCE同比、PCE核心PCE就是在3%。那实际上如果你去看市场预期的话是在3.3%左右。为什么我在昨天视频、X上面我就说是在3%？是因为我已经把今天周三要公布的这个调整给计算入内了，因为这个调整本身对于PCE的一个影响就是下修0.2至0.3左右。

所以如果根据昨天市场的一个预期，这一组数据公布完之后是在3.3的话，你往下下修0.3的话，那就是同比在3%。所以周三公布的这个数据，核心PCE同比增速就是在3%，然后核心的这个环比是在0.2%。

真正的重点：三个月环比数据

那这一组数据的一个重点，其实不是在一个环比增速也好、还是在一个同比增速也好，而是经过下修完以后，我们来看一下六月份、七月份、八月份的这三组环比数据。

我们是从右往左看，最右边这边0.26——我这边圈出来，红色框框里面圈出来0.26是今年的3月份。三月份、四月份、五月份那三个月其实环比增速是比较高的：0.26、0.28和0.31（核心哦，核心PCE的环比增速）。你假设是0.31的话，你把它年化完之后，起码要3.6%以上、3.6至4%了，这是一个非常高的一个年化之后的一个增速。

但是如果我们看过去三个月，六七八这三个月的话，环比增速0.13、0.13和0.25——这三组数据0.25相对会高一些，你把它年化完之后3%。但是0.13的这组数据，是低于2%的，你把它年化完之后是低于美联储的这个通胀目标2%。

所以经过这一次修正之后，我认为过去三个月的数据、6、7、8三个月的数据，其实是在美联储的一个预期范围之内的，或者是在他们喜欢的这个数据里边。

七、十月加息概率为何极低

那在这样的一个背景之下，包括我们去看核心CPI的环比增速，可能和核心PCE的环比增速过去3个月是类似的。那在这种情况下，我不认为十月份美联储有加息这个空间和数据支撑在那边。

那这时候大家可能会有一个疑问：那接下去在十月份加息之前，一周还是两周之后，我们还会再看到一组CPI数据。的确，那除非这一组CPI数据真的是非常非常的糟糕。但即使在非常糟糕的情况下，你把这一组CPI数据再和PPI数据结合在一起，即使9月份的PCE数据在0.3%，我们可能也没有办法做出一个结论——通胀的这个趋势在往一个更高的一个方向去走。

当然了，因为9月份出来之后，如果9月份是在0.3的话，那7、8、9变成了0.13、0.25、0.3，似乎是每一个月都比上个月稍微高一些。但是我的理解里边，凯文沃什有说到他看的是一个趋势，他不看重一组数据，所以一组数据是不会影响美联储的这个决定的。

那除非是连续三组数据，比如说今年的3月份、4月份、5月份，在这种情况下0.26、0.28、0.31非常明显地告诉你，通胀是在一个不可以接受的范围，那那时候加息是非常正确的这个决定。但是7、8、9、6、7、8这三个月加在一起，我实在没有办法得出这个结论——或者我认为这个数据是根本不支持美联储在10月份加息。

所以最终我们可能去看一下CPI的这个结果：如果CPI的这个结果加上PPI最终是在0.3以上的话，可能还会存在30%左右加息的一个概率。但如果PPI数据加CPI数据加在一起，推出的一个核心PCE是在0.25的话，我认为0.13、0.25和9月份的0.25三组数据加在一起，不支持10月份继续加息。

所以周三PCE数据的这个公布，意义并不在环比增速或者同比增速比市场预期要好，这些几乎都在市场期待之内的。意义是在修正完之后的6月份、7月份、8月份这三个月的数据完全不支持美联储10月份去继续加息。

八、美光财报深度解析：SCA战略与去周期化

OK，讲完宏观之后，我们来聊一下AI。那今天和AI相关的一个话题就是周三盘后发布财报的美光。

1）26份SCA协议：锁定2030年的35%营收

我们先来看一下财报会里边管理层所准备的这一段内容：

截止到目前，管理层说到我们已经签署了26份战略合作协议，叫做SCA。SCA它就是一个长期的订单。管理层说到，据我们估计，这些协议将占到我们截止2030年总收入的35%以上。那并且在这些订单里边，或者在这些协议里边，有3/4的这个协议拥有明确的定价框架，其中大部分设有包含价格的上限和下限的定价区间。

在上个季度财报里面，我就有聊到为什么美光要这么去做。它这么去做就是试图用这些长期的订单来确保未来自己的这个利润率。

之所以美光历史上它是一家价值股，是因为它那个利润率在糟糕的时候，它有可能非常的低，当利润率非常的低的时候，它有可能会出现亏损这种情况。那现在用SCA、用这些长期的协议去确保自己未来的这个毛利润，确保了未来自己的这个毛利润在一个相当高的这个位置，就能够确保自己起码在未来是盈利的。

所以SCA长期的这个协议合作就是为了去摆脱周期板块。

然后SCA里面其中的1/4，这未来的这个价格会根据市场的价格去进行定期的一个谈判。所以并不是所有的SCA全部设定了价格的一个上限和下限。那设定了价格的上限和下限，就是设定了自己的一个利润率或者毛利润的一个上限和下限。那剩下的不去设一个上限和下限，其实是好事、也不见得是一件坏事。为什么？如果价格持续在一个上涨的一个过程里边，你去保留一部分的订单，有一个灵活性在那边，那你反而因为价格的这个上涨会获益的——就不去提早的去设定或者框架住自己未来价格的一个上涨区间。

2）Q1指引：营收大幅超预期，毛利润引发短暂疑虑

那么回到他们CFO所给出的这个指引，并没有给全年的这个指引，只给了接下去下一个财年第一季度的这个指引。给的这个营收指引在61.5亿，市场的预期其实只有56.8亿，其实是大幅超出了市场预期8%。

毛利润这一块，因为我看了一下盘后——就盘后可能让空头和多头都失望了，盘后几乎是没有任何的波动，就是在上下0.1%这边浮动。看空的人可能认为利润率在第一季度并没有达到市场的预期——市场预期是在86.7%，管理层所给的这个指引是在86.3%。

但在财报会里面管理层有做出了这个解释：他说股权激励是导致Q1毛利润率稍微下降一点的这些原因。但是管理层期待Q1是整个全年2027财年毛利润最低的这个季度。随着——因为接下去的一个涨价——接下去三个季度毛利润会越来越高。

那有没有可能管理层是过于乐观了呢？其实不可能。为什么？是因为订单是在上年就下了，上年就下的这个订单价格已经确定了，成本也已经确定了，那就基本上能够保证他们在第二、第三和第四季度这个毛利润会比第一季度还要高。

3）毛利润是否见顶？

第一季度你看一下市场给，就公司管理层给的预期是86.3，上一个季度是整个这一轮周期以来最高的这个毛利润——87%。

那市场其实很有意思，市场的一个定价是：当你毛利润已经去到一个非常高的位置，接下去市场就会变得有些悲观、有些谨慎。为什么？因为你毛利润上涨的空间可能不大，接下去市场担心的就是——什么时候你毛利润可能出现一个拐点。那这就是进入这个季度之前市场的一个担心。

然后Q1的一个预期出来之后，哎，似乎好像确实比市场预期低了一些，但是管理层给了这一个解释了，就为什么Q1的这个毛利润会更低。假设管理层如果能够做到自己在Q1所给的这个指引——毛利润86.3——且接下去的三个季度还会比一季度还要高，那非常大的这种可能性，今年第二或者第三或者第四季度的毛利润会达到整个全年的一个新高，或者甚至于去破历史上的一个新高。

因为你第一季度就是86.3，上年的第四季度才87，你说86.3接下去的三个季度会比86.3还要高，那你说去破87的这个概率有多高？我认为相当的高。

所以美光的毛利润有没有见顶？那管理层的这个指引已经说得非常的明确了——其实是没有见顶，起码今年你会看到更高的这个毛利润。那从28年开始，这个毛利润可能会出现一定程度的一个放缓，但是即使放缓完之后，还是可以保持在我认为80%以上的一个毛利润。

4）财报会议其他重点：回购、紧缩、英伟达降规、SCA占比

那在财报会议里面还有几个重点：

第一个重点：巨额回购。 接下去管理层会把多余的这个现金进行回购。有点类似于——因为现在美光所手里所持有的这个现金已经比苹果还要高、比英伟达还要高，他们手里有非常多的一些现金。那你这个现金如果没有办法反馈到整个行业链、行业这个供应链里面去的话，那你只有用来回购或者回馈自己这个投资者。所以接下去他们会进行非常大体量的这个回购。

第二点：27、28年比26年更紧缩。 管理层说27年和28年比26年将会更加的一个紧缩，价格会继续上涨。那之所以能够做出这样的一个判断，是因为他们能够看到背后的这个需求，也能够知道整个行业包括自己的一个产能扩张的一个速度。只要需求是超过产能扩张的这个速度，那整个行业还是处在一个紧缩的一个阶段，那甚至比26年会更加的紧缩。

第三点：英伟达降规格的解释。 接下去一点也是可能市场担心的一个点，有两位分析师都问到了英伟达降规格的这个事件。那美光给出的一个解释就是：因为英伟达自己本身要保住这个出货，而HBM又非常的紧缩，所以英伟达必须要降规。但降规本身并不是不看好HBM，而是HBM本身非常的紧缩。

第四点：SCA占营收比例的目标。 最后一个问题也比较的重要，分析师有问到二季财年的营收75%已经被锁定了，其中也包括了SCA。那有没有可能当SCA全部谈妥之后，这一个季度SCA签了26个——上一个总共26个，然后上一个季度我记得是18个吧，所以每一个季度SCA在越来越多——所以分析师就有问到：有没有可能当你的SCA全部谈妥之后，未来向前看的这个营收70%都会被SCA所锁定？

那这个问题问的他的目的是什么？他的目的是希望管理层说——哎，如果说你未来的营收都可以被SCA所锁定的话，那你美光就是摆脱了一个周期板块了、就摆脱这个周期行业了。

管理层给了一个回答：未来的目标是SCA占营收差不多还是保持在50%左右。

5）综合判断：美光的"英伟达时刻"

那把这些财报会议内容全部综合在一起做一个总结的话： - 首先，27、28财年的营收确定性非常的高 - 第二点，毛利润起码还没有见顶、起码在27年不会见顶，甚至于27年的毛利润会越来越高。28年有可能会是毛利润见顶的一个时间点，但是即使见顶完之后，毛利润可能还是可以保持在80%以上 - 然后，SCA所签的这个订单或者签的这个协议本身，其实现在已经签到了2030年了，甚至于有两家公司已经签到了2031年

所以如果我们放短线去看，毛利润还没有见顶；但是我们放长线去看，毛利润一定会从现在的80%到87%稍微出现一些放缓。但是即使放缓完之后，还是可以保持在一个相对比较高的一个毛利润。

那只要能够保持在一个相对比较高的这个毛利润，通过SCA去锁定，那就能够让美光走出这一个周期板块。

那所以从这个角度去看，现在美光的前瞻市盈率在6.7倍，我个人认为不是非常地低估，但也绝对不高估，是处在一个比较合理的一个阶段。甚至如果未来市场情绪面稍微回去一些的话，美光前瞻那个市盈率去到8倍左右，就从现在可能还有20%左右的一个上涨空间，我也不会感到意外。

那即使我说过，对于美光这类的标的来说，即使它的一个PE不扩张，单凭它EPS增速这个扩张，对于价格的一个反馈已经非常的好了。

6）与英伟达的类比

所以美光这个季度财报，我认为是不错的。那美光有点类似于可能一两年前、一年前左右的一个英伟达吧。

就是当你的英伟达的毛利润一直在上升、上升、上升到一定一个阶段，你的毛利润不再进行上升的时候，接下去市场就开始担心你的毛利润什么时候见顶、什么时候会出现一个下调。但是如果能够持续execute，你的毛利润如果能够持续保持在一个高位——就像英伟达，毛利润保持在高位，保持在多少？一年多了，对吧，市场一直担心你75%、76%的毛利润能不能维持下去，那是英伟达证明给你看——我能够维持下去。

那你既然能够证明给市场看、你能够维持下去，即使市场给了你一个相对比较低的一个前瞻市盈率，没有关系，你通过EPS这个增速、股价仍然可以去破新高。

市场失去了这个想象空间——无非就是在毛利润这一块继续上涨的一个想象空间，因为不存在了。现在86%、87%，难道你还希望毛利润去到99%、95%吗？毛利润从86%、87%再去到99%、95%，其实已经没有意义了。因为从公司这个角度，没有必要再去持续非常激进的这个涨价，那不如把这一部分利润还给整个市场，让市场可以有一个更加健康的一个增速。

其实对于美光这类的企业来说是一件好事。

结尾：订阅活动

最后是今天的活动，来自于Seeking Alpha他们的一个量化选股策略。那这个量化选股策略现在有一个免费试用的一个区间，并且首年的订阅可以立马省50美金。同时，Seeking Alpha还有一个Combo的价格，这个Combo包括了Premium还有Alpha Picks，原价是798美金，现在是629美金，在639美金的基础上继续降了10刀，也就是更大的一个折扣价格。

大家如果感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里边找到Seeking Alpha订阅的这个链接。

那今天这期内容就到这边，下期见。

## 一、九月的"隐形撕裂"：指数平静下的板块地震
表面上标普仅下跌0.5%，纳指甚至上涨1.9%，这是一个"安然度过"的九月。但如果你撕开指数的表皮——银行-8.5%、国防-9.3%、REIT-7.4%、必需消费-5.2%——这是**衰退级别的离散度**，几乎达到2008年或2020年个别板块的回撤幅度。
真正值得警惕的洞察是：**指数越平静，底层撕裂越可怕**。这和CPI里"核心通胀温和"却掩盖了房租7%、商品通缩-2%的结构性分裂是同一种现象。市场的"平均值"正在说谎。半导体板块+11.3%的能量，几乎独自对冲了价值股的全面崩塌。这种"由少数标的扛指数"的结构，在物理学里叫**临界态（critical state）**——沙堆看似稳定，但只要一粒沙就能引发雪崩。换言之，九月不是"涨得很弱"，而是"跌得很有秩序"——而有秩序的下跌，恰恰是最脆弱的。
## 二、美光的"去周期化"：这是半导体版的SaaS转型
美光签26份SCA、锁定2030年35%营收，表面是财务工程，本质是**商业模式的物种变异**。这个动作的历史对标不是其他芯片股，而是： - 2000年代初**软件行业从

item.title: [YC Root Access] The Startup Industrial Base: Building for the Next 250 — Washington, D.C.
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察一：这场活动本身是一个"制度演化"的元事件

表面上，这是YC进军国防科技的宣言；但更深层的信号是——Silicon Valley正在完成一次"逆向殖民"。过去二十年是国防语言（DARPA、互联网、GPS）殖民了硅谷；今天硅谷的语言（batch、demo day、iteration、YC batch编号）反过来正在殖民五角大楼。你注意到没有？Emil Michael用"drone dominance"命名一个采购项目时，实际上在借用产品经理的思维模型——gauntlet、leaderboard、top three get money，这根本就是一个游戏化的A/B test。这不是国防部在"引入"创业公司，而是创业方法论正在重写国家安全的操作系统。

洞察二：一个被所有人回避的隐藏悖论——"可消耗性"与"美国工业文化"的根本冲突

Robert Thielen那句"MSL = Mass × Silicon / Loop duration"是全天最深刻的一句话，但没人接住它背后的悖论。美国的整个工业哲学建立在"精工细作、终身保修、六个西格玛"之上——从福特到波音到SpaceX，成功的密码都是"把每一个单元做到极致"。而未来战争要求的却是反向文化：可抛弃、可失败、可迭代。Perseus的Jason说"如果我们便宜30倍，需要打两发也没关系"——这句话在传统美国工程师文化里几乎是异端。

这里有一个跨领域的震撼连接：这与Netflix从DVD邮寄转向流媒体时的组织悖论惊人相似。当年Netflix必须同时维护两种彼此矛盾的文化——一种追求物流完美，一种追求算法冒险。最终Reed Hastings的解决方案是组织切分。今天美国国防工业面临同样的分叉：Palmer Luckey们（Anduril）和Lockheed们不是竞争对手，他们是两种物种，需要在同一生态位共存。而华盛顿至今没有认识到这一点。

洞察三：真正的"稀缺资源"不是资金也不是技术，而是"测试地点"——一个被严重低估的地缘信号

多位创始人反复提到同一个瓶颈：找不到地方测试。Congressman Pat Ryan开玩笑说"德州所有的国防科技公司都在同一个农场主的地里测试"。这个看似琐碎的运营问题，其实揭示了一个深刻的地缘政治现实：

美国已经把自己的国土"消费者化"了。每一寸土地都被划入FAA空域管制、环保法规、城市规划、私人产权。相反，中国和乌克兰之所以能"每两周迭代一次无人机"，不是因为他们的工程师更聪明，而是因为他们的物理测试自由度更高。

这里有一个出人意料的历史类比：18-19世纪英国工业革命领先，一个被忽视的原因是英国有大量的煤矿、运河和荒野作为"低监管试验场"。今天美国的"物理试验场稀缺"正在成为它的新版本的"土地问题"。而Sean Duffy谈到"阿拉斯加需要自主飞机"——这不是随口一说，阿拉斯加可能会成为美国的新硅谷，不是因为人才，而是因为它是唯一还能"合法犯错"的地方。

洞察四：一个跨领域连接——"月球砖"与"宋朝活字印刷"的隐秘同构

Skylar Chan讲Gru Space要在月球上造第一块砖时，我脑中浮现的不是SpaceX，而是毕昇发明活字印刷。为什么？因为二者共享同一个深层原则：当你无法把资源运到目的地时，你必须发明"最小原子单元的本地制造能力"。

活字印刷的革命不在于印刷本身，而在于把知识生产的原子化了——每一个字都可以本地组合、无限重排。月球砖的革命也不在于砖本身，而在于把"文明"原子化为可从月尘中提取的建筑单元。

这暗示了一个更大的模式：每一次人类文明的跨越性扩张，都是先解决"最小可制造单元"问题，再解决其他问题。宋朝的活字、印加的石块、SpaceX的Raptor发动机、月球砖——它们在概念层面是同一个东西。所以Gru Space真正在做的不是"太空建筑公司"，而是跨行星文明的语法书。

洞察五：最容易被忽视的"啊哈时刻"——DIU的Christopher Murphy说了一句改变游戏规则的话

他说："Don't expect anybody to want your thing more than you."（别指望任何人比你更想要你的东西。）

这句话看似创业鸡汤，但在国防语境下有颠覆性含义：它意味着美国国防采购的心理结构正在从"父权制"转向"市场制"。过去七十年，五角大楼扮演的是"慈父"角色——你带着方案来，我告诉你要不要。今天Murphy在说："你必须自己去争、去证明、去活下来。" 这是一场深刻的心理契约转变，其历史意义堪比日本明治维新时期武士阶层被要求"自谋出路"。

这场YC活动，本质上是美国国防产业从"贵族制"向"平民资本主义"转型的一次公开仪式。而大多数与会者甚至没有意识到自己正在参与一场制度更替。

📝 转录文本

The Startup Industrial Base: Building for the Next 250 — Washington, D.C.

开场引导

Ladies and gentlemen, please take your seats. Our program will begin in a few moments. Please take your seats at this time. Thank you. Please take your seats. Our program is about to begin. Please take your seats at this time. Thank you. Please take your seats. Our program is about to begin.

Ladies and gentlemen, please watch this presentation on the screen. Thank you.

一、Gary Tan 开场致辞（Y Combinator CEO）

Good morning everyone. Thanks for being here. My name is Gary Tan. I'm president and CEO of Y Combinator. It's great to have founders, government, industry all in one room this morning.

从软件到硬件：18年的转变

When I went through YC as a founder in 2008, I was building a blogging company. Software was the frontier and the big challenge was getting it into as many people's hands as possible. In 18 years since, software has left the screen — it can see, it can navigate, it can fly, it can run entire factories. We've got computer vision, autonomy, batteries, chips, advanced manufacturing, and most importantly, the engineers who know how to make it all work. Most of it was built for commercial reasons, but all of it can be pointed at defense.

YC funds startups at the very beginning, often when it's just a couple of founders and an idea. We've backed more than 5,000 companies since the beginning, including Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, OpenAI, and Coinbase.

为什么谈拦截器与弹药

So if you're wondering why I'm in Washington talking about interceptors and munitions, the honest answer is: we followed the founders and what they want to build. Over the last few years, more and more engineers have come to us convinced that keeping America safe is a problem worth spending their lives on, and we agree. They want to build hardware and they want to build it here in America. They want to get it into the hands of people who need it.

I want to be specific about who those people are. Right now, there are Americans deployed on ships, on bases, at the edge of a jammed network, and they're all depending on whatever equipment they were handed. They deserve the best this country can build, not just whatever happened to be on contract.

今天在场的创始人们

Some of the founders building that next generation of equipment are here with us today. They're working on hard problems that give the US a real strategic advantage with systems that don't cost a fortune per shot, permission or per unit.

  • One team is building navigation systems that let drones operate when GPS gets jammed.
  • Another is building interceptors that can take down cheap drones without costing more than the drone.
  • Others are using rockets to deliver cargo to contested areas or building aircraft that fly in the stratosphere and stay up there for weeks.

Then there's the supply chain. You can't have an independent defense industrial base if you rely on your adversary for critical parts, which is why one company here is making high performance magnets in America; another is securing the firmware inside the vehicles and aircraft we operate.

To the founders: you're asking people to rely on your work in situations where failure can cost lives. Reliability, security, manufacturing, support — all of it matters and it matters deeply. A great demo isn't the finish line. It's the beginning of the obligation.

创业工业基础（Startup Industrial Base）的呼吁

Institutions have an obligation to keep the bar high, but to make it possible to clear, so that when someone builds a product that works, there's a path to actually getting it used. That's why we're all here. And it's what we mean by the startup industrial base.

America should be able to draw on its entire capacity to invent and build. The industrial base should be open to a team of 20 people with a better answer. Small teams have a particular advantage: they can learn something on Monday and change what they're building on Tuesday. The person who heard the customer's problem can walk across the room to the person who can fix it. That matters when the threat keeps changing. Drones get jammed, comms go down, adversaries adapt. The people using our technology need to adapt too.

今日的核心问题

So here's the question I want us to work on today: What would it take for a 20-person company to become a dependable supplier to the American military?

The big defense companies play an essential role. So do the manufacturers, suppliers, and workers who've spent decades learning how to build things people trust with their lives. What we need is more ways for new companies to join them. More competition, more suppliers, more manufacturing capacity, more opportunities for a good product to earn a real customer.

So let's talk about faster awards, clearer requirements, and fixed price contracts where they make sense. Let's give founders a way to prove their technology under tough conditions and a credible path to orders when they do.

今日的三方请求

My ask today is practical:

  • If you're a founder, tell the people in this room exactly what's in your way, and be specific. What tests do you need? What kind of feedback from customers? What contract? What would let you deliver?
  • If you're in government or you're a buyer, bring a real problem. Tell these founders what success looks like and what it would take for you to feel confident enough to buy.
  • If you're at an established defense company, take a look around. A team you meet today could end up as a supplier or a partner who helps you solve a problem you've been stuck on for years.

We have people here who are willing to devote their lives to building for this country. Let's give them a fair chance to deliver. Thank you all for being here. Let's get to work.

二、Gaurab（Solugen）— 弹药供应链的重塑

Hello. Good to see everyone today. My name is Gaurab. I'm the co-founder of a company called Solugen. We're a winter 2017 YC batch, and we were a strange fit. We're this chemical company. We figured out this new technology to miniaturize chemical plants and we went through YC, which was effectively a software incubator at the time. But what we realized was: the same exact principles that you could apply in software could be applied to the chemicals industry, and you can move faster than anyone's been able to do it.

So today I'm going to tell you about a little work that we've been doing on the munitions supply chain with our chemistry and what we have to offer.

Holston 工厂的历史困境

In 2026, every missile, every munition, every platform is dependent on one plant in Tennessee called Holston. It broke ground 1942. The RDX pilot plant went up in 13 days, which is insane. Composition B from phone call to first shipment in three months. And in 1945, we had one and a half million pounds per day. 2020 — nine million pounds. So what we made in a year, we now take too long to make.

If you look at 1942, our munitions capacity was 300 million pounds for obvious reasons. 1976, 2016 — everything kind of went sideways. We had to put in $1.8 billion into Tennessee, but even after that, the maximum volume that we got out of it was 30 million. Now if you compare that to where China and Russia are, we're probably two orders of magnitude off, which is a problem.

四大供应链问题

Even with all the announced expansions, how do we do this safer? How do we do this faster? And how do we do this better? That's really the fundamental question we had. And we discovered four problems in the supply chain:

  1. There's just not enough munitions.
  2. These unmanned platforms are getting smaller, so you need higher energy density energetics.
  3. Stockpiles are visible from space.
  4. (Fourth issue also identified.)

Terraforge 与 Nitroforge 的分布式方案

We solve all four. We've put in $100 million of private capital to solve this problem, and the way we did it was by studying how it works today. Right now, a chemical plant is a regulatory nightmare. An energetics plant, a regulatory nightmare. Put those two together, and you've got the worst combination possible.

So what we ended up doing was disaggregating the two. We took the chemical plant, put it centrally, and we created distributed production units for payloads. That way you're not taking the risk of an energetics plant and a chemical plant at the same time, and it allows you to build much faster. We got permitted in three months because of this technology.

We've actually executed on this across the United States. Our home base is in Houston, Texas, but we've got two units in Houston and one unit in Louisiana. The precursor is called Terraforge — it's the energetics precursor at scale. It does roughly 240,000 drones worth of precursor explosive. And then the Nitroforge is the distributed payload production part of it — roughly 48,000 drones per unit. So one Terraforge feeds five Nitroforges fundamentally. We actually built the Nitroforge technology in six months.

更好的炸药与 Kraken Kinetics 合作

How do we make a better energetic? Comp B was what our grandparents used to use. We need to make something much better. We designed these plants to produce higher density energetics that allow your blast radius to increase.

We partnered up with the premier warhead designer, Kraken Kinetics, and we actually built a fully CONUS advanced energetic supply chain in 247 days for $100 million. To give you some context, this would take a traditional chemical company five years to build up.

Fundamentally, we're going to need dozens of Terraforges and probably 100 to 150 Nitroforges. So we launched a company with Kraken Kinetics called Odin Energetics, focused solely on creating payloads that we can scale across multiple drones.

需要的支持

What we need to succeed is a MEAL — if you're listening, I just need someone, one lead on the R&E side, that can help us over the next 30 days to do a sprint. We're going to show you guys that we've solved this problem and now we need to scale it — and I can't do that by myself. Thank you.

三、Luther Lowe 介绍下一场 Fireside

Good morning. I'm Luther Lowe, the head of public policy for Y Combinator. So excited to see everybody here this morning. I'm going to be your part-time emcee.

I'm so excited to welcome to the stage Emil Michael and Jason Miller.

  • Emil Michael is the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, and the department's chief technology officer, leading its research, development and prototyping efforts. Before returning to government, he served as Uber's chief business officer and held leadership roles at Tellme Networks and D-Wave. He previously served as a White House Fellow and special assistant to the Secretary of Defense.
  • Jason Miller is a longtime senior advisor to President Donald Trump and a veteran political strategist and communications advisor. He's held senior roles across President Trump's presidential campaigns and transition efforts.

Please welcome Under Secretary Emil Michael in conversation with Jason Miller.

四、Fireside：Emil Michael × Jason Miller

白宫超智能承诺（Superintelligence Compact）

Jason Miller: Good morning. So it's great to be here this morning with one of the rising stars in President Trump's administration, Emil Michael, Under Secretary for Research and Engineering.

Yesterday, we were all watching on TV — Fox, CNBC — with all of the tech leaders and the President. The President made it very clear where he is on superintelligence with data centers. How does something like yesterday then immediately impact what you're doing in the Department of War starting today?

Emil Michael: It was an extraordinary collection of really some of the country's most important technology leaders. From Jensen to Elon to OpenAI's leadership, Anthropic's leadership, Google. It was really a collection of people who are going to drive the superintelligence race for the country and essentially for the world.

To get them to agree on a framework for how we develop these technologies for the benefit of the American people and do it safely, without sort of an overbearing regulatory scheme, was quite amazing. Having the president gather these people and get them to agree on core principles was a fantastic act. We'll look back on the moment where they signed this White House Compact for the Responsible Development of Superintelligence as a watershed moment.

对创业者的意义

Jason Miller: How will what happened yesterday impact founders in the early stages of their company's lifespan?

Emil Michael: I hope it ensures that we are not headed for regulatory capture by one or two companies in the SI world. We are headed for a world with a lot of competitors. We're going to promote open source. We're going to ensure that companies that are talking about risks internalize those externalities and make sure they're spending enough on the safety part of their model development and deployment process. That's good for the ecosystem. What you never want is one or two companies driving regulation that keeps small companies out.

与中国竞争的经验

Jason Miller: You're one of the few people I know who's actually gone into China and won, as the chief business officer for Uber — you went in there with approximately a $2 billion investment, and exited with a $7 billion valuation. What did you learn that now applies to competing head-to-head with the Chinese?

Emil Michael: One of the things I learned doing business in China during the Uber days (2014–2016): the Chinese are great at copying, using American IP. But there is this tipping point where they've run out of stuff to copy — they start inventing. And that's not to be underestimated. Even more so now, they are inventing things and they have spare capacity in their manufacturing base.

They have the ability to mass-produce things we don't here, which is why reshoring critical supply chain technologies is so important. If we don't have that, then we can't do mass either. That's why you see us doing critical minerals, reshoring batteries for drones, brushless motors. We're going to have to go after robot parts, actuators, all the things that go into the things we want to build up.

Don't underestimate their ability to invent — and they shouldn't underestimate our ability to reshore and ensure we have our own domestic supply chain.

美国创业者的独特优势

Jason Miller: What can founders in this room do that their contemporaries in China cannot right now?

Emil Michael: A few things are uniquely valuable about the American ecosystem:

  1. The entrepreneur class themselves — the ability to take risks. It is not shameful to try and fail in this country. It's a badge of honor. Sometimes VCs want to bet on you after you fail even more than your first thing. Not that you should be aiming to fail, but it shows you've got grit. There's still some social negative about failing over there.
  2. Our capital markets are five times as robust as theirs. Our VC community, they take risk on smaller companies. They bet on people. How quickly those dollars come out is a huge strategic advantage.

五角大楼的效率鸿沟

Jason Miller: What was the gap between what the Pentagon supply chain was producing versus what we actually needed?

Emil Michael: When we got in there, the sheer neglect was staggering. Neglect on critical minerals, supply chain, shipbuilding. We canceled hypersonic missiles. There was an allergy to business, an allergy to AI and technologies. When we got in there, we had less than 50,000 people out of a department of 3.5 million people using AI. When the rest of the world was using ChatGPT on your phone, we were just not using it at all. Today we have about 1.7 million out of our 3.5 million using AI.

We were single-threaded on one AI provider. If you're a defense contractor working on an important program where we were spending $50 billion of taxpayer money, you got one meeting every four years — and your program is failing. There was no way we were going to buy a low-cost cruise missile like we are from Anduril and a few others. Low-cost drone defense — we were producing hundreds, not millions like the Chinese.

成本/杀伤比与定向能

Jason Miller: When you talk about shooting down a rocket from Iran, how does the dollars-and-cents versus scale debate play out?

Emil Michael: My counterpart in acquisition and sustainment needs to build more Patriots, which are the expensive way to take these things down. I'm doing the cheaper way — directed energy, things that cost thousands of dollars, not millions. Otherwise, it's asymmetric. Iran could send a $50,000 drone; if you're spending millions, over time the math doesn't math.

We've launched and transitioned the joint weapons laser system. Golden Dome's architecture is built on directed energy, lasers, high-powered microwave — things that could take things down at a really cheap rate. That's critical not just because of the money, but because I could deploy these systems in a lot of places, and that deters the threat. If your systems are all expensive, bespoke and small in number, then the adversary is not deterred. If they're proliferated, small, cheap — then they're deterred.

简化规则、竞争性环境与 Drone Dominance

Jason Miller: Where do you look and say: this is wasteful, this is not going to work for the long haul?

Emil Michael: A lot of this is on us at the Pentagon. We've got a lot of rules, qualification standards, things written 20 years ago that haven't been modernized. We try to kill them when we find them. We also try to create competitive environments.

For example, we created this program called Drone Dominance. It's not you just applying with your drone product one-on-one. We have a competition, we invite companies, we take the top 20, we put you in a fly-off situation, we give you objective metrics, we measure you against other companies — and at the end, the top three get some money. We call them gauntlets, and at the end we have half a billion dollars of orders to give. You get transparency, objective metrics, and a financial order at the end. If I were the entrepreneur, I'd rather compete and know if my product works, rather than knocking on 20 doors at the Pentagon.

需求改革（Requirements Reform）

Jason Miller: What's your advice for founders trying to decide, am I solving a current need or is this a great transformative idea?

Emil Michael: We've done something called requirements reform. Typically the military would write a 300-page RFP designed for a lawyer, a lobbyist, and a prime contractor. Small companies read it and have to figure out what all these things mean — one thing wrong, you get kicked out.

The new way: here's my problem. I need to fly a missile 500 miles in this kind of environment. It's a one- or two-page description. You come back with solutions. That gives entrepreneurs a creative way to answer with different technologies we might not have thought of. And you get feedback right away — turning what used to be a two-year cycle into 90 days.

何时该在华盛顿聘请游说者

Jason Miller: At what point does a company look and say they should hire someone in DC?

Emil Michael: In theory you want it open so small companies aren't spending disproportionate dollars on lobbying. Congress every line item tries to prescribe where the budget goes. But early on it's not that useful. We consolidated the innovation ecosystem — SBIR, DIU, APFIT, Office of Strategic Capital — all in my world now. So whether you're a small company doing an initial thing, a medium company scaling up, a bigger company doing a prototype, or an established company with a product that works, now they're eligible for a big loan that's low cost. So maybe until you get closer to being a program of record, you could hold off hiring a lobbyist.

快速 Yes 与快速 No

Jason Miller: What have been the fast yeses and fast nos?

Emil Michael: One deficit was hypersonic weapons. The primes' cost was $50 million per unit, taking years. We essentially stopped during the last administration. We found a company, Castellan, doing low-cost high-volume ones — that was a fast yes.

From a no standpoint: there are so many drone manufacturers now, that if they're not in the Drone Dominance program and their capabilities are the same as others, it's tough unless they've done something unique.

Drone Dominance 的多轮迭代

Jason Miller: How does someone get into Drone Dominance if they're not already in?
