item.description:
## 一个被忽略的镜像结构：Jake Paul 的"帝国"其实只是同一套模板换了三次皮
表面上看，Jake Paul 是"网红→拳击手→投资人"的三段式蜕变。但如果你把三段业务的骨架剥开会发现——**它们是同一个商业模型**：
- **Team 10（20 位网红）** → 挖掘被主流低估的注意力资产，捆绑打包出售 - **MVP（400 位拳手）** → 挖掘被 UFC 剥削的搏击资产，捆绑打包出售 - **Anti Fund（100M 基金）** → 挖掘被传统 VC 忽视的创始人资产，用注意力当"利率补贴"注入
Jake 一辈子只学会了一件事：**在一个供给方被系统性低估的市场里，做那个愿意付合理价格的聚合器**。这就是为什么他一提到 UFC 只付选手 15% 收入（其他联赛 50%）时眼睛发亮——他嗅到的是 Vine 当年不肯分钱给创作者的同一种气味。**你以为他在多元化，其实他在做同一笔生意的第 N 次复利。**
## 一个跨领域的惊人巧合：Chainsmokers 2012 年干的事，就是 2026 年 AI 时代的"超个性化冷启动"
Alex 侵入 Hype M

item.title: [Latent Space] Inside OpenAI DevDay: Superhuman Computer Use, Decisions API, and the AI Cloud — Ari & Nikunj
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个反直觉的观察

1. 无障碍技术（Accessibility）意外地成为 AI 时代的关键基础设施

Ari 提到的一个被普遍低估的转折点：为视障人士设计的屏幕阅读器技术，竟然是让 LLM 高效使用电脑的核心接口之一。这是一个惊人的历史回响——数十年前为了"包容人类少数群体"而构建的技术冗余，如今变成了"包容非人类智能体"的关键通路。

这里有个跨领域的连接值得深思：这与生物学中的外适应（exaptation）现象惊人相似——恐龙的羽毛最初是为保温进化的，后来才被用于飞行。软件的可访问性 API 就是数字世界的"羽毛"：一个为 A 目的设计的能力，被 B 用途彻底激活。这暗示着：一个技术栈中最"边缘"、"合规性"的部分，可能是下一个范式的入口。 想想还有哪些"合规冗余"正在等待被 AI 重新定义？审计日志、API 版本控制、i18n 国际化框架……这些可能都是下一波价值的暗物质。

2. Decisions API 揭示了 OpenAI 的一个隐秘转变：从"训练文化"回归"黑客文化"

最容易被忽略的一句话是 Nikunj 的坦白："We haven't trained a new model for this. We're building this purely on top of the same Luna weights."

四周前 Groq 的 Jev 出现，OpenAI 没有启动一个庞大的训练项目来"回应"，而是让"推理团队的一个哥们"和"基础设施团队的另一个哥们"周末黑一个原型出来，然后开始 hill climbing。

这里有个隐藏的系统性真相：Frontier Lab 的护城河正在从"我们能训练更好的模型"悄悄迁移到"我们能围绕同一个模型榨出更多形态"。同一份 Luna 权重，通过约束解码 + 并行批处理 + 结构化输出，就变成了一个新产品品类。这与制造业中的"平台化战略"如出一辙——丰田 TNGA 平台、大众 MQB 平台——一个底盘衍生数十款车型。AI 行业正在进入"权重平台化"时代，而不是每个新能力都对应一次新训练。这对创业者的启示是：不要总想着"能不能超越 GPT"，而要想"能不能围绕同一份权重构建新的产品形态"。

3. Computer Use 的真正瓶颈不是模型，而是……DoorDash 加载页面的速度

这是访谈里最容易被跳过的一句话，但可能是未来两年最重要的架构约束：Ari 说，"a non-trivial amount of time in our benchmarks is actually waiting for doordash.com itself to load."

当 agent 变得比人类更快时，瓶颈从"智能"迁移到了"环境"。这产生了一个惊人的推论：互联网的整个前端架构，是围绕"人类反应时间（约 200ms）+ 阅读时间（数秒）"设计的。而 agent 的反应时间是 20ms，阅读时间是 0。

跨领域连接来了：这与高频交易（HFT）改造金融基础设施的历史几乎完全同构。当 HFT 出现，纽交所必须重建整个 colocation 数据中心，因为光在光纤中的传播速度成了瓶颈。同样地： - 未来的 SaaS 会出现"agent-optimized rendering"，跳过所有为人类设计的过渡动画 - 会出现"agent DNS"——预加载常见任务链路 - 甚至可能出现"agent-only 服务器端点"，绕开整个前端

这也解释了为什么 OpenAI 要给 dots 分配一整台 Linux 云主机——他们不只是在做 agent，他们在做为 agent 而生的操作系统层。Roman 演示中"agent 在拍你屏幕截图，你在做其他事情"这个细节，实际上宣告了一个新范式：人和 agent 从"顺序共享一台计算机"变成"并行共享一台计算机"。这是自 Unix 分时系统以来最重要的操作系统语义变化。

一个额外的暗线：为什么 Ari 会说"我让它给我配 DNS、付账单，几万美元就 YOLO 出去"？

三年前我们害怕把 LLM 接到网络上；今天 OpenAI 的产品负责人在用 agent 配 DNS。信任的建立不是通过工程验证，而是通过日常暴露带来的脱敏。 这与心理学中的暴露疗法（exposure therapy）完全同构——恐惧不是被论证消除的，是被反复接触消除的。这意味着 agent 的用户教育路径可能不需要"证明它安全"，而只需要"让它做很多小事"。产品设计的启示是：先给用户 100 次无害的成功，再引导他做一次高价值任务。

📝 转录文本

冷开场：Superhuman Computer Use 的下一个前沿

"Now computer use is like faster at accomplishing tasks than the average human probably in most cases. And I think that the next frontier is to have computer use be literally superhuman in its performance where it actually is as fast or faster at using software than expert computer users like us."

Um, and I think that'll be really consequential and exciting when that happens because I think we'll be able to all of a sudden build products that provide just much more real-time experiences.

主持人： Like 4 weeks ago, this was not at all —

Ari： No, this is Jev-inspired.

主持人： I think you're officially the first Frontier Lab to clone/adopt this.

Ari： Yeah. Yeah. I feel like OpenAI has such a strong hacker culture — people just get excited about things. So a guy from inference, this one awesome guy from the infra team — they're like "uh, this is amazing, we're going to hack on it." They build a prototype, it works, and now we're just hill-climbing on latency and trying to make this as fast as possible. We want to launch it in the coming days. As soon as we hit our latency target, we'll try to get this out.

一、DevDay 主题回顾：Dots、GPT 6.1 Soul、Agents API

主持人： Okay, we're very excited to be here. Today is OpenAI DevDay special after-podcast. We have Ari here who leads the product and engineering team for computer use agents. Before we kick in and dive deep on computer use, you want to give a quick recap what was announced?

Ari： Yeah, it was a super exciting day. We just got out of the keynote — it was really sick. There were a bunch of computer use announcements that I think are worth thinking about.

  • Dots — the new sort of personal-assistant product, with some really exciting computer use features.
  • GPT 6.1 Soul — this amazing new model, particularly great for computer use because of the cost and speed advantages. We shared that it's a fifth of the cost of Astra, and a seventh of the cost if you're looking at computer use specifically — which is really amazing.
  • Agents API — now has computer use in it, which is really cool because developers can build on the same computer use that is part of Codex and ChatGPT.
  • App Shot demos — you can take the context of something you're doing on your computer and bring it into Codex and ChatGPT really fast.
  • Native computer use on Mac — Roman had it taking screenshots of his app automatically, and he could do other things on his computer while computer use was using his applications.

主持人： And not to mention this Decisions API.

二、Decisions API：与 Computer Use 的关系

主持人： Off the bat, are they all the same model — this is or the same dataset distilled to different models? Is computer use using Decisions API, or are they kind of separate?

Ari： What's really cool about the Decisions API is it has all these new capabilities — it does inference in parallel, it doesn't have reasoning, it's a smaller model than the ones we use for computer use. So those capabilities make it really fast. They also make it a little bit less good at doing long-horizon sophisticated tasks. It's still an open area of research for how we bring those approaches together. But yeah, I'm really excited to see what people build with the Decisions API.

三、Dots 与云端 Linux 计算机

主持人： One of the interesting things is Dots now have attached personal computers — so it seems like they're very much more persistent. You've been using them for a while. How should people push the bounds? What should people aim for? What should they try? Personally, right now I use it for a lot of customer service: "oh, this was wrong, I don't want to sign in, I don't want to authenticate — find whatever and just get it fixed." How should we push further?

Ari： Dots are a really cool product because each Dot has access to its own Linux virtual computer in the cloud — which is different from our other products. Traditionally we have access to a browser in the cloud, or it has access to your own computer, but now you get your own entire Linux computer in the cloud. So it can run full desktop applications, and it can also use a web browser.

The powerful thing about computer use — and the reason why I think it's so exciting — is because it makes it so that the agent can do anything you as a person can do. All the software in the world was designed for humans, and now agents can use that same software, and you can delegate to the agent. So anything you would do on a computer, you can ask a Dot to do.

What's particularly useful is going to depend on who the end user is and what's valuable in their life. But yeah, I would just start by thinking about: what are the things that you spend time on, and how could you delegate those to an agent?

一个真实案例：Meal-prep 订餐

主持人： Yeah, a lot of flight booking, and shopping, and honestly even like playing a game or whatever, right?

Ari： Totally. For me — something I did recently — I've subscribed to a meal-prep service because I was trying to eat healthy, you know. I really like this meal-prep service because it lets me customize the meals I order to a high degree of granularity — I can say "I want this many grams of chicken and this many grams of rice." But it was so complicated it took me two hours to do an order. I found that I could ask computer use to do it for me and it did it in 15 minutes. I actually saved two hours — it both did it eight times faster than I could, and it saved me two hours, on GPT-6.1 Soul. Those are the kinds of tasks that are really powerful.

创作者用例：自动化 YouTube

主持人： As a creator, I can tell you automatically immediately my number one use case is automating YouTube — because YouTube doesn't expose a lot of things via API, and you have to just put it in a VM and just run it. Let's say their A/B testing feature, or making community posts — none of this is available by API because they hate developers.

Ari： I've heard that from our developer-experience team — they use it with YouTube a lot.

四、"Computer Use 两年没进步"？

主持人： So I want to draw for you know — let's say I want to get a little bit spicy. One of the leading AI podcasts — our friends — is famous for saying that computer use hasn't advanced in the last two years, which is a very interesting statement. And I think you're one of the best people in the world to talk about this. How have things progressed?

Ari： You know, they said that a few months ago, I think, and I hope they have a different perspective now, because computer use is like 180 degrees different.

主持人： He's a tough guy to impress.

Ari 的职业主线

主持人： You've basically spent your whole career working on some kind of computer automation, right? Shortcuts at Apple, then Sky, and then joining OpenAI. Can you draw what your through-line is — what is driving you, what wasn't possible back then, and what your milestones were?

主持人： I guess to add on to that as a follow-up — what's the major change from using Codex computer use from last week through to today? Is it model? Is it Dots? Is it harness? So all the history plus what really just changed in today's announcements?

Ari： On the through-line — I guess I've always been excited about automation and helping people automate tasks, because then you can save time in your life and focus on things more important to you than operating a computer very intricately. That was why we worked on some of those products. I was at Apple before. We made a company called Sky. We ended up joining OpenAI, which is really exciting.

主持人： Almost like you had to hack around Apple until Apple was like "fine, we'll just hire you and you can just work on the inside," right?

Ari： It was a cool place to get to work. It was really interesting looking back at Sky — as we were working on computer use there as well, and the models were so much less capable. Now the models — just in the last one year — have become extraordinarily capable at computer use.

最大的 delta：从"启动任务"到"调试自己"

I think the biggest delta I see is: before, they could reliably start tasks but then run into problems. Now they're really good at debugging — really good at trying again, introspecting what is and isn't working.

The computer-use field itself has moved forward. We're using more techniques. Now computer use often writes code. If you look at it in Codex and expand the tool calls manually, you can see that it's not just doing one action at a time — it's actually writing JavaScript code that the computer executes to perform sometimes many actions at once. That's a great speed-up and a great capability.

We use more accessibility / multimodal interfaces. The model may use screenshots, it may use accessibility, it may use Playwright — it can use a lot of different mechanisms based on the task at hand.

And then the model acceleration has been just amazing.

今天与昨天的差别

What's different today? We're making capabilities better all the time — so one day's difference is probably a little bit less consequential than the past month or the past two months. But the computer use in Dot is really exciting, as well as the new model.

五、如何衡量 Computer Use 的进步

主持人： On the keynote, Tejal was mentioning 7× improvements in computer-use speed, a lot better on a few benchmarks. How do you guys think about measuring it? Computer use is one of those things where — as you say — it's improvements over time. Is it harness? Is it model? Is it post-training? How do you look at it internally? And what were the changes with the new model?

Ari： We actually have a bunch of different ways of measuring it — some of which are on different permutations and configurations of the harness. It's a bit of a complicated story, because our production products have some more safety checks, and those are configured differently based on the needs of the task at hand. So there's a lot of ways to measure it. But regardless of how we measure it, we find pretty consistent gains — sometimes in the harness, sometimes in the model.

I was really excited by this result: GPT 6.1 is even more cost-effective for computer use than its baseline cost improvement as compared to Astra. Really cool to see.

Aha moments：多模态与 DOM 直连

主持人： One of the visuals I really liked from the livestream was that you're improving the Pareto frontier of your curve, and there was a lot of talk about how you're improving it together with the harness. Can you give some examples of aha moments — whether on model driving the harness, harness driving the model, whatever?

Ari： I don't mean to repeat myself, but introducing more modalities has been really powerful. One specific example: in the past, computer-use products had to spend a lot of time scrolling — take a screenshot, try to do something, "oh I got to scroll down to the next page of results," screenshot again, try again, scroll down again…

Now with accessibility, direct access to the DOM, and other things like that, the language model can actually see an entire page or an entire application. It can write code that does multiple steps at once. Those have probably been the biggest single aha moments. There are a lot of tiny ones that are less exciting in comparison — but actually a lot of speed improvements are driven by a lot of little paper cuts that we had to go in and introspect. A lot of really hard engineering.

六、App Shots 到底是什么

主持人： Appshots in general, right? People don't quite get the difference — because there's a nice visual in Codex when you take a snapshot, but maybe they get the difference: you are able to actually drive each button, and you have each text in a very optimal representation.

Ari： Yeah, exactly. It's kind of fun actually if you want to be really nerdy about it. You can go into Codex, take an app shot by hitting the two command keys — you grab the content from whatever app you're working with, bring it into Codex or ChatGPT. If you click on the attachment and click on this little tiny button in the top-right, you can see the raw text and the raw accessibility representation. We've put a lot of work into dumping everything out — but also making it token-efficient. There's a bit of an art to it.

It turns out that the same technology that was invented for humans who maybe have accessibility needs — who want to use a screen reader — that technology is really helpful for LLMs to be able to use computers. That's been really fun to get to work on.

主持人： For context — I feel like a lot of people don't understand appshots, they don't even know it's a feature. It's when you double-hit Command, it pulls in what looks like a screenshot, and you're like "oh, why have I opened up just a screenshot and thrown it in?" No — it's actually pulling all the metadata, all the code, everything.

Ari： Exactly. If you take a screenshot of a webpage that has a link, the screenshot doesn't include where the link goes. If you take a screenshot of your calendar, the event titles are truncated. But when you take an app shot, it gives the language model full context about everything — and that lets it do much more.

主持人： For those who want to see more — Jason Louu, I invited him to do a full workshop on this at AI Engineer.

Ari： He did a great job.

七、未来两年：瓶颈到底在哪？

主持人： I have a broader vision question on computer use agents. Your example of "take a screenshot, scroll page, take a screenshot" — where we were today, they can automate a lot. What are the bottlenecks? Is it models? Is it harnesses? Where do you see it going in like 2 years? Do you see it just running for hours? Any predictions?

Ari： What's really crazy — that I think the team's accomplished over the past couple months — is that now computer use is faster at accomplishing tasks than the average human, probably in most cases.

The next frontier is to have computer use be literally superhuman in its performance — as fast or faster at using software than expert computer users like us. That'll be really consequential and exciting, because we'll be able to build products that provide much more real-time experiences. Lowering the barrier to entry — or the activation energy — of using computer use, I think will make us start to default to doing certain things in agents that we've become accustomed to doing manually. And that'll save us a ton of time.

真正的瓶颈：网站加载速度

There are a lot of little paper cuts and bottlenecks standing in the way. There's things on the model side, on the inference side, on the harness side, on the representation. As computer use gets faster, we're increasingly bottlenecked by just the speed of doing an operation.

For example — a non-trivial amount of time in our benchmarks of computer-use tasks is actually waiting for doordash.com itself to load. You want as little delay as possible between when it finally finishes loading and when you go and trigger the LLM to do the next action — which is itself a statistical science.

主持人： Like an event-driven way maybe to do that.

Ari： When possible, you want it to be event-driven. JavaScript has load events, the web browser has load events for web navigation, but there are other types of events that really can't be event-driven. So there's a lot of complexity.

主持人： The one that comes to mind is chatting with customer service — replies could take 30 seconds, could take 3 minutes.

Bot 遇上 Bot

主持人： Oh, right. I have dealt with so many bots with Codex. It's great, but I also wonder if the other side knows that they're talking to a bot — because I'm answering in complete sentences, capitalizing correctly, giving full reference numbers and everything. It's clearly too good. I don't care — I'm just trying to get my [issue fixed].

主持人： I prompted it: "you know, don't pretend you're a bot — be a very annoyed human, short one-liners, push it, do all this." I also tell it: while you're waiting for responses, use sub-agents to research better ways to figure out what we need. It's just like human little intervention.

Ari： That's awesome.

主持人： I also feel like half the time it's a bot on the other end. So now you got the bots talking to each other.

八、从"害怕"到"YOLO 几万美元"

Ari： One milestone of computer use we're at now: three or four years ago we were scared of hooking up LLMs to the web and to our devices. And now — I'm having it configure DNS for me. I'm having it pay my bills. Really — tens of thousands of dollars of stuff I'm just sending it over and YOLO-ing with computer use. Like — what's the worst thing that can happen?

九、给 API 开发者的建议

主持人： Now that you've released this in the API — what are some pitfalls or tips you want to tell developers?

Ari： First of all, I'm really excited that we brought computer use into the Agents API. A lot of developers are building applications that want to work with third-party websites and services — and computer use has this universality to it. It can work with anything. So now developers can build using the same computer use implementation that we're building on.

There's great work to be done if you want to build your own computer-use harness — but it's hard, and we train our models on our computer-use harness. There's an advantage to using the one that's in distribution for the model: there might actually be a speed, cost, and accuracy advantage.

信任的建立需要时间

We're all sort of still in the process — and maybe some of us are ahead of many people in the world — of getting comfortable with this technology and trusting it. It's incumbent on us to build that trust over time by:

  • Making sure we're building things that are reliable
  • Building the right kinds of safety checks
  • Asking for the user's consent before doing something consequential like making a payment
  • Depending on the application, making sure you're only letting it access the websites or applications it actually needs

I'd really encourage people to try the new Agents API — build all kinds of cool stuff on it. We'd love to hear your feedback.

十、Computer Use 改变开发者工作流

主持人： Have you seen any changes in the way it affects dev workflows? With Dots, you're seeing it in Slack, people using voice and build, Roman's example of "change this app and send me screenshots along the way." Anything you're seeing in adoption about how people are using computer use for coding workflows?

Ari： One of my favorite use cases for computer use — and one we see a lot in the wild — is computer use letting the agent actually test the software the agent has built. Which is far more consequential than it sounds.

Traditionally you'd build something in Codex — the Codex builds it for you — and then you have to test it. You are now QA for the agent, right? With computer use you can complete the software development life cycle: the agent can build software, and it can test it. I have a lot of fun building stuff, having the agent test it — by the time it comes to me, it's already working.

I have extra fun because sometimes I'm developing computer use itself — so now I have a computer use agent that's using my computer use agent that's using something else.

主持人： I have a visual play-test skill that I've developed that really catches a lot of design issues — that normally when you just look at code, you wouldn't really pick up. It's also really good for cloning apps. If you're using a shitty SaaS and you want to kill the SaaS, you just clone it screen by screen by screen. Computer use can completely drive everything, take screenshots, note it down, and then clone everything with Codex.

主持人： Thanks for all your progress. I think that is our time. This is not the last we're going to talk.

Ari： Cool. This has been really fun. Thank you guys for having me.

第二部分：与 Nikunj 的对话——API 团队

主持人： Okay, so — Nikunj, we're very excited to have you. You've shipped a lot on the API side. Anything you want to highlight on the API-side of changes, and introduce yourself a little on what you do.

Nikunj： Yeah, for sure. My name is Nick. I lead product for the API team — been here for roughly 3 years. I've been working on launching models — that's just been a constant thing throughout my time at OpenAI. With every new model we try to work super closely with the post-training team, the research team, to figure out what's new in it. Then we expose those capabilities in the API. That's the basic way of putting it.

GPT-6 时代的新 API 能力

If you look at everything that's new with GPT-6, the cool new capabilities we launched were:

  • Async function calling — with things like Codex and Dots, tool calls take so long that you don't have to pause the model's execution while the tool is running. You can kick off a tool call, keep running, keep reasoning, then check back in.
  • Mid-turn steering — you can inject messages while the model is reasoning in the middle. As your tool call finishes, you can put in that instruction.

主持人： And that's also partially a model-alignment capability, right? They have to train in the ability to be steered.

Nikunj： I feel like we've had it in the app — you could always steer as it's reasoning, but it wasn't the best. It's gotten much better.

主持人： Excited to see how it does this.

Nikunj： Our main goal in the API is to put things in the API once it's trained into the harness. We kind of wait for that moment — until it's good enough. A lot of that is actually being powered by websockets, which we launched a few months ago. Websockets just opens this whole bidirectional communication thing with the model. (This is not the GPT Live thing — I'm just talking about GPT-6.) You can do all these async tool calling, async reasoning, injecting messages. It's a really fun API to work on.

十一、Ultra Fast：极速 Frontier 智能

主持人： This is why we're the engineering podcast — because we get to talk about websockets. This also pairs very well with Ultra Fast, right? That is now, I think for the first time ever, available in the API — which is basically the theoretical fastest speed you can ever get. Frontier intelligence.

Nikunj： Yes. It's been so exciting to work on that project. Before I go into the API — the most fun part of Ultra Fast has been just watching the inference team cook with Astra. They're constantly having these Codex agents running, trying to squeeze out more performance.

For at least a couple of months, a lot of it was focused on efficiency and driving cost down — which is how we were able to cut the Luna price by like 80%. A lot of that was driven by all the inference improvements they landed. Now they've shifted gears toward: how can we make this run as fast as possible? Ultra Fast has been amazing to see on a model like Astra — to go that fast has been really cool.

Websockets — the first time we launched websockets was for GPT 5.3 Codex Spark. Can't believe we named a model that, but you know, that's what we launched it for. Obviously it helps so much because you've got to have the tool calls — you've got to really reduce the overhead of going back and forth with tools. So websockets is awesome for that.

主持人： It's always cute to see — like I have my Reset usage limit and my Spark usage limit that I never use. It's there if I want it.

Nikunj： I think it's gone finally. So —

主持人： You're slowly killing off all the old ones.

Nikunj： It was a great week. I mean, it was the first time we had frontier intelligence at extreme speeds.

主持人： People really liked it.

Nikunj： Yeah.

主持人： So first time — it comes back.

Nikunj： Yeah.

主持人： And for 5.3 Spark — is explicitly attributed to Cerebras. You guys are not confirming or denying that Ultra Fast is related to Cerebras, but people are — I'll just say that people do care and are wondering about it. And you have your own silicon as well.

十二、房间里的大象：Decisions API

主持人： Elephant in the room — decision models. Decisions API. We were the first podcast to do a big Jev deep dive with Dogo, and I featured him at AI Engineer. How quickly did you see Jev and go like —

Nikunj： Firstly — huge props to Dogo and the Jev team for really inspiring a whole segment in the market. Obviously Jev comes out, everyone's losing their minds over it. Our users are hitting us up, but also our internal teams are like: we need a much faster classification system.

I don't want to get ahead of some of the Dots features that are going to come, but you're going to see some cool really-snappy fast things built on top of the Decisions API.

Props to Jev for inspiring this whole thing. A bunch of people at OpenAI got nerd-sniped by it, and they're like: how can we make this work? We're not going to train a new model, but —

主持人： Like four weeks ago, this was not on.

Nikunj： Not at all. No, this is Jev-inspired.

主持人： I think you're officially the first Frontier Lab to clone and adopt this.

Nikunj： Yeah. I feel like OpenAI has such a strong hacker culture — people just get excited about things. So a guy from inference, this one awesome guy from the infra team — they're like "uh, this is amazing, we're going to hack on it." They build a prototype, it works, and now we're hill-climbing on latency and trying to make this as fast as possible. We want to launch it in the coming days — as soon as we hit our latency target.

Decisions API 到底是什么？

主持人： It's interesting — at the same time of hacker culture, you also — as Sam said — like 99% one of the most reliable APIs with I think probably the most usage, which is your team directly. How should people see Decisions API? A lot of people saw Jev, heard the buzz, haven't built with it. You're making it very mainstream. What should people see it as? How should they use it?

Nikunj： The main use cases we've seen: really fast classification. All the computer-use demos have been amazing and really cool. There will be limitations of course — in terms of having Astra write a JavaScript script to control your computer versus having Luna pick one action at a time. It's not going to be at the same intelligence level — but maybe there's some computer-use tasks that this is good enough for. Excited to see that come through.

The other cool prototype I've seen internally is people hooking it up with GPT Live. GPT Live is our bidirectional realtime API — it's built on this model of front-end models and back-end models. GPT Live is the talker — super fast, really good at delegation — and you have something like Astra sitting at the back. But tool-calling has always felt really slow in GPT Live. People have been putting together these tool-calling demos of GPT Live controlling a computer, and it just feels so much more snappy and natural. So I'm kind of excited to see what people do with Live and Luna on Decisions API.

澄清：这不是"关掉推理 + 结构化输出"

主持人： So I want to iron this out for people, especially from the product side, because a lot of people have been putting out Jev clones — there's been about 100 in the last two weeks.

Nikunj： Oh really? That's amazing.

主持人： First. But like — they can clone the Jev API, which is honestly structured outputs, which OpenAI was first to. Right? So let's iron out for people: what is a decision model as far as what is important. It is not just latency, it's not just structured output. Because I could just have Luna — and Decisions models are priced the same as Luna — turn off reasoning and have structured output. Do I have a Jev? No, right? There's a confidence there.

Nikunj： Yeah, totally. The way we haven't trained a new model for this — we're building this purely on top of the same Luna weights that we have. This is really just Luna. On top of that what you're doing is you're constraining. Structured output is a big part of it. You're really optimizing the inference stack to get very fast on TDF. Because you can have multiple questions, you basically run those in parallel — as a batch. All sorts of inference techniques people are working on to try to make it as fast as possible.

At least our implementation of it at the start — this first version — is like zeroing this on top of Luna to see how it goes. Obviously you want to put it out there — this is open, classic iterative deployment. Put it out there, see what people think, and we'll make more model improvements as needed.

视觉能力：Luna 免费带来

主持人： And obviously as a benefit you have vision — they don't have vision, right?

Nikunj： True. We get it for free with Luna.

主持人： I do think that some of the innovations — it sounds like it's still to come, if it's still the same Luna weights — which is like the confidence stuff and calibration. This is something we've talked about on the podcast with benchmarking calibration. The whole point is that RLHF kind of collapses you towards what you want to hear — but not actually what the amount of confidence is.

Nikunj： Yeah, totally. I'm eager to see how it pans out. These may be the key areas where we may have to hill-climb with a future model release.

架构猜测：Diffusion？中间层？

主持人： Architecture-wise — the other thing that's in the debate: obviously nobody knows because Jev doesn't talk about it, but the two speculations are — one, maybe a diffusion model instead of autoregressive — but you are able to achieve the parallel generation in your way. And then the other one is some mech-interp type thing — that you're analyzing the activations and just outputting the weights — which you guys have all done the research on this.

There have been demos on both. Gemini shared a Gemini Diffusion — Gemma Diffusion — on a Jev-style output. Interp people have also pulled out interp from a middle layer. But this is all speculation. It's just: what are you trying to aim for? Because you can achieve the API — everyone can achieve the API, it's actually pretty trivial. But then there's the speed, then there's the accuracy, then the calibration features.

Nikunj： It's so cool that this whole space has been kicked off now, and people are going to do so much cool stuff, and everyone's going to learn from each other.

十三、平台团队的哲学：赋能构建者

主持人： I feel like being on the platform team, a lot of your job is to empower builders. What do you think people should build with Decisions API and computer-use agents? Any stuff you've been building with internally that you think really opens up after the new changes?

Nikunj： Decisions API use cases internally have been pretty obvious. The user-ops team was jumping on it — "we've got to classify all of our support tickets." Obviously there were the really cool GPT Live demos. The Codex app team might pick this up and try to do something cool with it. This whole thing started a week ago, so it's very very early.

主持人： There was a big push in Evals — LLM-as-a-judge — having really low latency there.

Nikunj： Yeah, that'll be interesting to see.

Agents API：内部产品全线接入

With the Agents API, we're having a bunch of first-party products at OpenAI built fully on top of it. The CoC security stuff that just went out is fully built on top of the Agents API. We have sort of the meetings type of thing launching today — do you remember the plug-in extensions when Sam was showing it? There was a demo of "you're in a calendar, you can have your meeting notes drop into a Granola type thing." All of that is fully built on top of the Agents API.

I'm just excited to see — we're getting this out, let's see what people build on top of.

主持人： You showed it off very well — the whole edit spaces, pages, collaborate, add in your Dot. That's a lot. So there's a lot of inspiration people can build from.

Nikunj： All possible with Astra. Things just move so fast now — people go from idea to execution so quickly. It's amazing.

十四、给 API 开发者的重点：性能、缓存、预热

主持人： Is there something you want people to focus on to give you feedback — like, you're just putting this out there, there's a fork in the road, and you want developers to help you decide?

Nikunj： Agents API and Decisions API — these are our newest products. Would love any and all feedback on that.

Over here we're very open on Responses API, which is sort of our workhorse. Really focused on performance right now. Performance comes in two main ways:

1) 延迟优化

We've been rewriting the whole Responses API stack to make it as fast as possible from a TTFT (time-to-first-token) / DBD perspective. That continues to be a main area of focus.

2) 缓存优化

Really going deep on caching — particularly with these personal agents that are basically a single thread that goes on and on forever. We provide guarantees of cache hits within 30 minutes. For one of our users, we just launched a much longer cache window: a 12-hour caching guarantee — you have guaranteed cache hits for that period.

主持人： Is there a public API?

Nikunj： Not yet — that's in preview. We're going to try to get that out to everyone as soon as possible. Just pay a little bit more for the cache, right? We guarantee cache reads for a much longer period. So even if your instance/thread — you do something on it, then come back to it 3–4 hours later — you're still getting the caching performance out of it.

主持人： Cut the cost there quite a bit too, right, with the new model.

Nikunj： Oh yeah. We're driving down cache reads.

主持人： For builders — they should implement, because it's significantly cheaper.

Nikunj： Yeah. Just building your apps to be very cache-aware, and use our prompt diagnostics or cache diagnostics tool to figure out where things are dropping off. The caching part is really important.

3) 预热（Pre-warming）

I also want to talk about pre-warming — we have that in the API now. If you know "hey, I'm going to get this prompt, I just want to pre-warm the cache," you pay the cache-write fee right now and then have it ready to go for the next 30 minutes.

主持人： And I can spawn many instances of that thread.

Nikunj： Exactly — you can just keep going.

I'm very excited about getting feedback on the low-level performance things — so we can keep making Responses API the most performant and reliable way to build on top of an LLM. And then you basically have our new products where I'm just looking for any and all feedback.

主持人： Yeah, just use it — just tell us. Yeah, define our roadmap for us please.

十五、上下文压缩：Compaction

主持人： I think for me the caching thing — great, right? Obviously very needed. But at the end of the day, you're still bumping up against a million-token context, and that's probably not going to change for the foreseeable future. You still need good compression, right? What is the best practice there?

Nikunj： Yeah, totally. Firstly — OpenAI has its own proprietary compression which is —

主持人： Comp — it's in the Agents API — you decide for us, right?

Nikunj： Exactly. In the Agents API, it comes built into the harness. If you're in Responses API, there are two ways of doing it:

  • Server-side compaction — you basically tell Responses API: "if you ever hit this threshold of tokens, just auto-compact and reduce the context being used."
  • /compact — if you want full control, you can /compact at any time and have your own logic on when to.

主持人： It's the manual override.

Nikunj： It is the manual way. A lot of the big coding agents like to do it manually. If you look at the Codex implementation in the open-source Codex harness, you can see that they use /compact and do it.

There are also new compaction techniques we're working on — some of which you'll be able to see in the Codex harness. It's already implemented in the Codex harness. Some file-based systems we're experimenting with. Lots of cool stuff going on around compaction.

十六、平台愿景：AI Cloud 与"正确的抽象层级"

主持人： We are running out of time. You've talked a lot about performance and about the new APIs. Can you give us any other hints as to things you're interested in — the future of the platform?

Nikunj： We're obviously very low-level. I used to work at Stripe before this — at Stripe a lot of the game was building higher-level primitives and products on top of the core payments primitives. I'm always curious about what the best way of doing that is in AI.

We've had a couple of attempts at that. We launched Assistants API way back in the day — it wasn't really the right fit. We're going off with this Agents API — it gives you the Codex harness, but where's the right amount of flexibility to give?

That's an open question. How should we have memory vaults and all these higher-level API objects — to abstract away more storage concepts? There's a whole space I'm very curious about — figuring out how we design that.

A lot of things in AI are just: have a low-level API primitive, see an example harness, and have your coding agent implement that. But how much should be built into the API is a constant question I'm thinking about. If anyone has ideas — it'll be super interesting to hear.

主持人： The analogy I always bring back to — and to end there — is: you're building an AI cloud, right? Which is something Sam said a year ago. It's almost like you're doing the AWS invention — "this is EC2, this is S3, this is —" but you're doing the AI-native versions of each of these. There are a lot of analogies. So you're pre-warming caches for stuff that you know. And it's nice that it's all exposed to builders, because it just opens up ways you can build new things.

Nikunj： Yeah, absolutely.

主持人： Okay — awesome. Thank you guys.

Nikunj： Thank you. Yeah.

item.description:
## 三个反直觉的观察
### 1. 无障碍技术（Accessibility）意外地成为 AI 时代的关键基础设施
Ari 提到的一个被普遍低估的转折点：**为视障人士设计的屏幕阅读器技术，竟然是让 LLM 高效使用电脑的核心接口之一**。这是一个惊人的历史回响——数十年前为了"包容人类少数群体"而构建的技术冗余，如今变成了"包容非人类智能体"的关键通路。
这里有个跨领域的连接值得深思：这与生物学中的**外适应（exaptation）**现象惊人相似——恐龙的羽毛最初是为保温进化的，后来才被用于飞行。软件的可访问性 API 就是数字世界的"羽毛"：一个为 A 目的设计的能力，被 B 用途彻底激活。**这暗示着：一个技术栈中最"边缘"、"合规性"的部分，可能是下一个范式的入口。** 想想还有哪些"合规冗余"正在等待被 AI 重新定义？审计日志、API 版本控制、i18n 国际化框架……这些可能都是下一波价值的暗物质。
### 2. Decisions API 揭示了 OpenAI 的一个隐秘转变：从"训练文化"回归"黑客文化"
最容易被忽略的一句话是 Nikunj 的坦白："*

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Regime-Change Wars Are So Hard to Win - Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"死地悖论"：政治目标越极端，军事执行越自败

克劳塞维茨说"政治目的第一"，孙子说"陷之死地然后生"——把两人拼在一起会看到一个几乎从未被明说的悖论结构：你所设定的政治目标的"雄心度"，会通过对方的心理机制反过来决定你所面对的军事难度。

一旦你宣示"政权更迭"这样的无限目标，你等于替对方做了一次决策简化——你亲手把敌方的策略空间从"投降/谈判/抵抗"三选一，压缩到只剩"死战"这一条。也就是说：你越是把政治目标推向极端，敌方就越只剩下那唯一一种对你伤害最大的应对方式。这是战略上的"己方乌龙"。乌克兰不是"神奇地"守住了，而是俄罗斯替他们清空了投降的选项。

跨领域联想：这在免疫学里叫"细胞因子风暴"——身体对入侵者的反应过度，最终把宿主自己搞死；在谈判理论里，这叫"替对方烧了他自己的桥"，你不是让自己 no way back，你是让对方 no way back，而这在博弈论上通常是最糟糕的一手。

二、复杂性反转：概念简单的最难执行，概念复杂的最好执行

这是这段访谈里最反直觉、也最容易被忽略的一句话——无限战争"conceptually simple, hard to execute"，有限战争"conceptually difficult, easy to execute"。

大多数人对"难"的直觉是线性的：概念复杂 = 执行复杂。但战争、产品、组织，甚至个人决策里普遍存在这种难度反转： - "把公司卖了"概念上极其简单，执行时会撕开你所有隐藏的股权、文化、身份裂缝； - "重构这个模块的一部分"概念上很难说清边界，但一旦定义好就能干净地做完； - "分手"两个字最容易说，但要执行到"两个人各自能过好"是漫长的；"改善这段关系的某一个具体互动模式"听起来含糊，反而更可操作。

凡是把目标推到"总体性/无限"的层次，你就在放大所有耦合项——政治、经济、心理、身份、合法性全部纠缠进来。凡是把目标切成"某一段前沿地区""某一个季度的KPI""某一次对话"——耦合项被隔离了，执行才有对象。

一个意外的观察：美国越战、伊战、阿富汗的失败，一半是"选择了无限目标却按有限战争的资源规模投入"造成的。它不是"投入不够"，而是目标—资源的类型不匹配：无限的目标撞上有限的意志，这在克劳塞维茨那里叫作范畴错误。

三、"傀儡吸血术"：留下裕仁不是仁慈，是萃取合法性

美国没杀裕仁，Paine 一句话带过，但这里藏着战略史上最狡猾的一步棋——战胜方把战败方的合法性人格留下来，当作自己改革方案的"背书签字机"。

宪法要有人签，改革要有人宣布，占领要有一张原住民的脸——征服者最缺的从来不是武力，而是合法性。合法性只能从被征服者那里榨取。这就是为什么马基雅维利在《君主论》里叫你"斩草除根"，而 20 世纪美国治国术恰恰反着来：不杀君主，让他成为你政策的"翻译层"。

跨领域连接：这在企业并购里叫"保留创始人"策略——收购方最怕的不是资产整合，而是被收购公司员工把新东家视为"外来入侵者"。留下老 CEO 几年，作为过渡合法性载体，一模一样的动作。殖民统治里的"间接统治"（Lugard 在尼日利亚的做法）也是同构的——你不废掉酋长，你让他成为你征税命令的"最后一公里"。

所以裕仁这个案例给出的真正教训是：无限战争的"无限"不在于杀了多少人，而在于你能否在物理胜利之后，制造出一个"由被征服者自己发声"的合法性回路。做不到这一点的无限战争（伊拉克拆掉复兴党、去军事化，等于把所有能签字的人赶跑），最后都变成占领者独自站在废墟上说话——没有回声，也没有正当性。

四、朝鲜的"摇摆"为什么是最糟的选择

顺带说一句常被漏掉的：Paine 说朝鲜的"waffling"（摇摆）代价惨重——因为摇摆本身是第三类战争，比纯粹的有限或纯粹的无限都更差。

摇摆做了两件蠢事： 1. 向对方释放了"我可能要灭你"的信号（把中国推到了死地判断的门槛上）； 2. 却没有匹配"我真的要灭你"的资源与意志（所以真的越过三八线时，志愿军过江了）。

这在博弈论里叫"未承诺的升级"（uncommitted escalation）——你付出了让对方紧张的所有成本，却没有获得让对方屈服的任何收益。这是战略上最贵、回报最低的一档姿态。放到今天读，几乎是所有"半吊子制裁""半吊子威慑""半吊子谈判"的通用病理学。

📝 转录文本

Korea: The Cost of Indecision

In Korea, the United States couldn't decide — do we want just half the peninsula, like the Gulf War, where we're just going to return to the territorial lines prior to the whole thing? Or, if we're on a roll militarily, maybe we should take the entire peninsula — the unlimited objective. And this waffling was really costly.

Clausewitz: The Political Objective Is Always Primary

Clausewitz has real comments about this. His idea is: the political objective is always primary. It is never the military objective. The United States is going, "Oh, maybe we can take the whole peninsula. Let's go for it." That's where you're letting the military objective [drive things]. It's like, "Why are you even in Korea? What is it you want to achieve here?"

And Clausewitz says: "No other possibility exists than to subordinate the military point of view to the political. The degree of force that must be used against the enemy depends on the scale of the political objective on either side. The political object — the original motive for the war — will thus determine both the military objective to be reached" — like how far up the peninsula you need to go — "and the amount of effort it requires."

Ends vs. Means: The Real Discriminator

One of the reasons this man is considered brilliant is because he believed that the primary discriminator determining what type of war you're dealing with is not the amount of effort — how many resources you're pouring into it. He argues that no, that's about means. What's key are the goals, your ends — whether it's limited or unlimited. So unlimited is regime change; limited is something else.

Here's his comment: "Wars have all degrees of importance and intensity, ranging from a war of extermination down to a simple observation." So you've got this long continuum — but he believes on that continuum, ultimately there really are only two types of wars: limited and unlimited.

Here's his take: "War can be of two kinds, in the sense that either the objective is to overthrow the enemy" — right, regime change — "to render him politically helpless or militarily impotent, thus forcing him to sign whatever peace we please." That's an unlimited objective. "Or merely to occupy some of his frontier districts, so that we can annex them or use them for bargaining at the peace negotiations." Those are limited objectives.

There's much argument about where on this continuum you want to be.

Sun Tzu's "Death Ground": Why Unlimited Wars Backfire

I think it's helpful, for the unlimited objectives, to pair this with Sun Tzu — much earlier work by several millennia. There's a concept of death ground. And what's that? "Ground in which the army survives only if it fights with the courage of desperation is called death [ground]." Soldiers fight to the death when there's no alternative.

The idea: if you have an unlimited objective, that means at minimum the regime that's on the receiving end of this is slated for annihilation — and then, if you have genocidal ambitions against the population, that affects them too. People in that situation tend to fight to the death. And you've seen it in your own lives in Ukraine, where they have defied all expectations of people who don't get death ground. The Russians have put them on death ground, and the Ukrainians aren't giving up if they can possibly avoid it, because they're dead men — many of them.

The Paradox: Unlimited Is Simple to Conceive, Hard to Execute

So unlimited wars are conceptually simple — it's regime change, everyone can get that. But executing them is really difficult, because you put people on death ground and they fight with incredible desperation. Then you can transform a failed state into a lethal adversary.

Limited wars are conceptually difficult, because you're going to be arguing about what the optimal limited objective is going to be, and that's troublesome. But they're much easier to execute, particularly if you have a very limited objective — maybe your enemy doesn't regard giving it up as too terrible.

Summary: The Hirohito Example

Anyway, to sum up on this limited/unlimited — because it's counterintuitive, but it's really helpful for analyzing wars:

  • An unlimited policy objective generally concludes with regime change. The key is that the defeated has no choices. So yes, the United States kept Emperor Hirohito around — the United States could have executed him at the end of World War II, but kept him around because he was useful. He would sign things like the Constitution, so that the United States could implement its political reform program, and Hirohito gave it some legitimacy. But it's an unlimited war against Japan.
  • A limited war is something less — and it means that the defeated government is going to be around. You're going to be negotiating with them, whether you like it or not, and they may come back to cause you problems later.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.description:
## 一、"死地悖论"：政治目标越极端，军事执行越自败
克劳塞维茨说"政治目的第一"，孙子说"陷之死地然后生"——把两人拼在一起会看到一个几乎从未被明说的**悖论结构**：**你所设定的政治目标的"雄心度"，会通过对方的心理机制反过来决定你所面对的军事难度**。
一旦你宣示"政权更迭"这样的无限目标，你等于替对方做了一次决策简化——你亲手把敌方的策略空间从"投降/谈判/抵抗"三选一，压缩到只剩"死战"这一条。也就是说：**你越是把政治目标推向极端，敌方就越只剩下那唯一一种对你伤害最大的应对方式。**这是战略上的"己方乌龙"。乌克兰不是"神奇地"守住了，而是俄罗斯替他们清空了投降的选项。
跨领域联想：这在**免疫学**里叫"细胞因子风暴"——身体对入侵者的反应过度，最终把宿主自己搞死；在**谈判理论**里，这叫"替对方烧了他自己的桥"，你不是让自己 no way back，你是让**对方** no way back，而这在博弈论上通常是最糟糕的一手。
## 二、复杂性反转：概念简单的最难执行，概念复杂的最好执行
这是这段访谈里最反直觉、也最容易被忽略的一句话——**无限战争"c

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Can THORChain Stay Neutral After the $388M Bitget Hack?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：ThorChain 不是"去中心化过头"，而是"去中心化的可证伪性"被自己亲手推翻

大多数评论者把这次事件读成"去中心化 vs. 中心化"的老掉牙争论，但真正的关键点在 Michael Perklin 那句极短的话里："没有主动签署的选择，却有主动关闭机器的选择。"

这句话把 ThorChain 推入了一个哲学困境——它一旦证明过自己能停机（May exit 事件），就永远失去了"我停不下来"这个抗辩权。这在密码学里叫"承诺方案"（commitment scheme）：你一旦对世界公开过某种能力，就无法再声称你没有。ThorChain 的问题不是它做了或没做什么，而是它在过去用一次停机，为未来所有"不停机"都盖上了自愿的印章。

换句话说：每一个曾经声称过 kill switch 的去中心化协议，都在为自己未来的每一次"不作为"预先签下了法律意义上的自愿声明。 这是一个反身性陷阱——透明度本身把"技术不能"转化成了"选择不为"。

二、跨领域连接：这不是加密行业问题，是"点破客"（Point Break）式的道德结构问题

Austin 半开玩笑地引用《惊爆点》，其实无意中触到了本质。这部 1991 年的电影讲的是抢银行的冲浪者以"体制反叛"包装犯罪的浪漫化叙事。今天的加密安全事故正是同一个心理结构的重演：用"意识形态纯度"（decentralization）为财务损失做美学辩护。

更深的跨领域连接——这和中世纪的"教会庇护权"（sanctuary rights）如出一辙。中世纪欧洲，罪犯只要跑进教堂就能获得神圣豁免，因为教会声称自己是"另一种主权"。这个制度最终因为被系统性滥用（尤其被有组织犯罪利用）而在 16-17 世纪被各国废除。ThorChain 现在扮演的正是"数字教堂"——但历史已经演算过一次这个博弈的终局：当庇护结构被证明可以被少数群体系统性利用，社会最终会摧毁这个庇护结构本身，而不是修补它。

再补一个更冷的连接：保险精算学里有一个概念叫"道德风险的可观测性"（observability of moral hazard）。你能观测到的坏行为越多，保险产品就越贵——最终贵到不可持续。ThorChain 每一笔链上可追溯的洗币，都在为整个 DeFi 板块的"隐性风险溢价"计价。你以为你在看 388M 的损失，其实市场在悄悄把整个 permissionless swap 赛道的估值 discount 上调。

三、被所有人忽略的一层：量子威胁与本次事件的隐秘同构

Chris 在结尾抛出量子威胁看似跑题，其实是这场讨论最尖锐的一根刺，只是没人接住。

注意这个不对称结构： - BitGet 攻击：坏人伪造交易数据，让好人的授权系统自己签署了坏交易 - 量子攻击（Harvest Now, Decrypt Later）：坏人今天收集加密数据，等未来算力成熟后用你自己发布过的公钥破解你

这两者在结构上是同一件事——都是"利用防御方自己主动暴露过的东西反过来攻击防御方"。BitGet 暴露的是授权流程，ThorChain 暴露的是停机能力，公钥密码学暴露的是数学上的可预知性。

加密行业真正的系统性弱点，不是安全预算不够，而是它比任何其他行业都更依赖"透明性"作为信任基础——而透明性正在被 AI + 量子武器化。 这才是 Chris 那句"我们已经看到了 harvest now, decrypt later"背后没说完的话：加密行业正在为自己"一切公开可验证"的建筑美学，支付一笔我们还没开始计价的费用。

一个真正让人不安的推论：未来 5 年内，"选择性透明"（selective transparency，如 ZK 系）会从加密的技术分支跃升为整个行业的默认生存策略——不是因为隐私更好，而是因为完全透明已经成了不可承受的安全债务。ThorChain 事件之所以重要，是因为它可能是"完全透明公链"这一叙事最后的高光时刻之一。

📝 转录文本

开场与频道迁移提示

If you've enjoyed Bits and Bips these last few years, be sure to subscribe to its dedicated channels. All Bits and Bips content has now moved to the Bits and Bips channel and no longer plays on Unchained. Search Bits plus sign Bips wherever you listen and subscribe. We'll see you there.

一、BitGet 被黑事件概述

BitGet got hacked. On September 24th, attackers took roughly $388 million from BitGet, largely the contents of the hot wallets — not by stealing their private keys, but by spoofing transaction data. So BitGet's own approval process signed off on the withdrawals.

The hack reopened some of the neutrality debate around crypto after ThorChain refused to block the hacker's addresses while stolen ETH kept swapping into Bitcoin through the protocol.

So, one: the loss is about $388 million. No private keys were accessed, according to Gracie Chen, CEO of BitGet. And the attacker, quote, "used it to spoof transaction data and triggered our own authorization process to move funds out." She says it's, quote, "consistent with techniques used by DPRK-linked hacker groups." And it is currently the largest reported crypto theft of 2026.

BitGet's $464 million user protection fund covers the losses. BTC withdrawals reopened today. ETH is on the 29th, Tether is on the 30th, and everything else is on 10-2.

二、ThorChain 的回应与业内交锋

ThorChain. Gracie said, quote, "decentralization is a design principle, not a shield for facilitating known stolen funds. The industry is watching."

ThorChain responded: "ThorChain is permissionless. It doesn't censor by design."

To which Star of OKEx said: "ThorChain paused its own network after its May exit. Bitcoin cannot be stopped, but ThorChain can. It simply chooses when to do so."

And Michael Perklin said: "There's no active choice to sign. There is an active choice to turn off the machine."

Reminder for those who are not paying attention: 1.2 billion of Bybit's 1.46 billion path also ran through ThorChain.

A middle path was taken by Near with Intents, where of the 50 million hackers tried to route, about 166K got through, but 503K was frozen. And it says Near Intents are "permissionless infrastructure, but not with no boundaries," according to Alex Shevchenko.

三、Chris Perkins：安全是行业的根本瓶颈

So, I have a couple of thoughts here. We'll come back to the ThorChain part because I want to start with the bigger point, Chris. This is something you've been talking about for a while. When we see these attacks happen right now, the framework is either the attacker succeeds and gets away with the funds or they don't. But that just means they failed with regard to effort. And that's kind of the end of the story. That's a pretty favorable landscape for attacks to continue indefinitely because they either win or have very low cost. What do you think needs to change? Because this remains a theme that's really sapping the space.

It's kind of mind blowing where you have a new technology and people think that the rule of law, like laws just go out the window. It's like it doesn't matter because we have this new technology. It's crazy. I would argue that security is the one thing that is holding us back from — in this industry. I'll continue to argue it.

I really enjoyed the Near post. I retweeted it because they said, look, we moved as quickly as we could. We took the actions that we could because we know how detrimental it is to the system. This is like human nature 101. If you don't have security, guys, you've got nothing. Trust me, you can't have anything. There's no applications of anything else. So we got to solve for it. It's insane.

Look, I welcome — please, I'm begging you with tears in my eyes — if you have solutions, bring them forth. The only thing I could think of is to increase the surface area of the defenders and the counter attackers. Went back to the Constitution. Christian, Carlo and I published it. By the way, Crypto Dad's got a book coming out. I'm going to plug it because he talks about this throughout his book. There you go, Chris.

But the point is, we just don't have the surface area or the sophistication. The great thing about things on-chain is we know where those assets are going. We're starting to see some actors perhaps not doing the right thing, e.g. ThorChain — we'll address that here in a second. But you can trace these things, and if you can trace them, then you can hack them back.

And I'm very hopeful that the president — he put forth an EO that talked about leveraging the skills of the private sector. It was actually embedded in CLARITY. We'll see how that comes out with the sausage making. I'm going to be in Europe this week. I'll see Patrick Witt. Very excited to hear what he has to say about it. I'll report back next week. But we need to solve security or we've got nothing. Rules of law apply. Governance needs to get serious about it and they need to hold people accountable who allow the law to be broken.

Last thing I'll say about decentralization: either you're decentralized or you're not. If you're decentralized, you can't stop something. It's out there. The code is working. You just can't touch it. If you can stop it and you don't, maybe you're not decentralized. My two cents. Austin, back to you.

四、Austin Campbell：ThorChain 陷入自证困境

Yeah, I think — so to pick up on your last thread before I get to some of the other points — this is where I think the ThorChain folks have now got themselves in a serious pickle. You showed that you have the capability to stop your chain when you choose to do so, and you chose not to do so here. That is very different than infrastructure that has no off switch, right?

If you got exploited yourself and there was no way to fix it and it just happened, okay, you know what, I buy your claim of decentralization then. Because the point at which you really would use it is when you yourself are being harmed. And if you don't, that's pretty good evidence you can't.

However, ThorChain did. They transparently did. They stopped the chain when there was an exploit. They've done it. They showed they have the capability. And here they voluntarily chose to launder sanctioned funds for the North Koreans. There are consequences for that.

So, you know, to me, this is actually a much cleaner case for people at the DOJ than something like Tornado Cash, right? Where it was never turned off. This one's clearly — you have elective control over the network and you're choosing when to use it and choosing when not to use it. That's an obvious case, I think.

五、抢劫案 vs. 逃跑司机：法律责任的类比

Sorry, go ahead.

No, I was thinking about this. And again, I don't know every detail, in fact, and circumstance, but let's just do an analogy. If there are a bunch of bad guys that roll into a bank and they rob it and they take a bunch of money out of the vaults and they run off into a car and the getaway driver is there to take them away into the land of safety, usually the guy or the lady who's driving that getaway car is culpable as well. They get in trouble. Is that not the case here?

I don't know — and again, I don't know all the detailed facts and circumstances — but even if you don't rob the bank, but you're driving the getaway car, usually there's some liability there.

And there are some layers to it too, right? There's like knowing involvement and then there's gross negligence, right? If you're the guy at the rental car place and these folks roll up in like the dead-president's masks with guns, and they're like, "hey, we want to rent a car," and you rent it to them, you probably also have a problem. On the other hand, if they pretended to be relatively normal customers and you had no way to know, you probably don't.

So the other point of "well, we process all transactions" is — that is not the standard, to be very clear. Like you said, the law just doesn't go out the window. You can't just la la la la la la about these things.

So one way or another, I think there's going to be a reckoning coming for the people who are — call it the "DINOs," right, where you're claiming decentralization without actually having it. That's going to be a problem.

六、博弈论视角：没有惩罚，就没有威慑

Number two here, Chris, to your privateer's point: until we start inflicting consequences on the people doing this, they're going to continue doing it. This is just a classic game theory principle. If anybody is familiar with this, if you could defect in a game with no consequences to yourself for greater rewards, you will just do that over and over and over and over. And the way you stop that from happening is by punishing people for defecting.

You know, I was recently on stage at the Philadelphia Fed and I said this same thing, which is: to cause this to stop, we need to start allowing people to inflict consequences on the hackers. And there's two ways to do that.

We can do that through allowing companies to counter-hack them, which we are now working on. I believe it was on August 12th, President Trump signed a national security presidential memorandum about expanding capabilities to combat transnational cyber-enabled crime. And it lets participating companies run operations against them. Like we've talked about this — but you need to be able to counter-hack them and disrupt them.

The other, and call it more extreme version of this, is kinetic warfare against these people, right? If you knew every time I hack a crypto exchange there's a 5% chance a drone with a bomb on it comes through my window and ends me, that greatly changes whether you're going to be willing to hack a crypto exchange or not. And so consequences matter.

I think, given the persistence of the adversaries and their structure, this is not three dudes in a basement somewhere. These are nation-state actors or organizations of hundreds to thousands of people. We need to start inflicting consequences.

七、《惊爆点》梗与市场感知

Okay, can I just say: respect for the Point Break reference for the old people that were listening — with the president's mask and robbing banks. I caught that. Just wanted to say it's a great movie. Great movie. If you haven't watched Point Break, it is actually genuinely worth a watch.

But now, Ram, as a markets observer, you're an investor, you're trying to assess risk in this space. How does this change your perception of crypto if we don't fix anything?

It's 2026. It's embarrassing. Imagine going back to 2021. We said five years from now, would we have these issues? And here we are. What if we have these issues two years from now or four years from now or five years from now? Probability that probably is going to be there because of more social engineering, especially these AI-related capabilities which can impersonate humans really well. It's going to drive more adoption to ETFs away from the on-chain ecosystem.

八、中介化的反讽：去中心化理想被自身伤害

Yeah, it's more than that, right? We see it at my current firm. It's really sad, actually. And I don't think enough people are angry. People should really get angry about the way that our industry is getting abused. And I don't think they're angry enough, because a lot of people enter into our space because of the ideals — the ideals of holding on and controlling their own keys and holding their own assets and believing in decentralization in a world without intermediaries. And I totally get that.

But what the security situation is forcing — it's forcing intermediation, to Ram's point. It's forcing — and I don't mean to talk against my own book — but it's forcing folks to trust a big institution to safeguard assets. And look, I've said this all along, intermediaries do offer value. And that's the thing that we do. We provide safety and soundness. Maybe we can do it a little bit more robustly. We've got professionals doing it.

But what gets me angry is that it's really taking away choice for people. I mean, look at the Coldcard hack. You know, these are like OGs who did everything they thought was right. And it's getting very, very dangerous to self-custody. And I know so many people are in this space because that's what they want. That's what they believe in.

So I would like to see — you know, I thought the Near post, Illia and crew, well done. And I'd like to see more people taking that type of proactive action. And I'd like to see people get more angry and really take steps to fix the situation. Otherwise, we're going to be stuck in the land of intermediaries forever without that choice.

Yeah, I mean, if we idealistically built a decentralized system to prevent people from being abused by centralized actors, and the main outcome of that is people having all their money stolen by centralized actors — I do not think we achieved what we were going for.

九、社会契约与金融史的重复课

Yeah, it's like getting back to like core political theory — like social contract, you know. I'm going to use a government to provide me security and I'm going to hand over some of my rights, or I'm going to hand over some of my rights to an intermediary and I'm going to trust them. It forces this sort of social contract.

I think, you know, we've talked on this show before about how crypto is relearning some of the lessons of financial history. This is why centralized intermediaries and regulations were created in the first place. If the core feature of your system is that whoever is the most morally bankrupt and steals the most money becomes the richest, people are not going to use that system to transact. It just becomes something that's pointless.

And Chris, I think you're right. Actually, it should be a combination of being angry and also being disappointed at a lot of the current actors in this space for not having worked harder on this problem already. You know, ThorChain's a great example. If your response to this hack is to just throw your hands up and be like, "whatever, we're gonna collect some fees" — quite frankly, you should be blacklisted from this industry by everybody. Every single crypto exchange should blacklist a wallet that interacts with ThorChain ever, if that's going to be their response. Because that exact attitude will destroy this space over time.

Yeah, like it reminds me of my days in Iraq. Back in the day, every house was allowed to have three AKs, and that was fair because they needed it for security. Is that really the world that we want to go back to? It's not working. We got to fix it. We need more of a grassroots effort to stop it.

十、公链 vs. 半私有链：BIS 论点的隐忧

I would also say: if your goal is for public blockchain infrastructure to win, you cannot keep making the case for semi-private blockchain infrastructure, right? Because we're not seeing these sorts of hacks on the networks that have very strict in-and-out controls. Like Connexus at JP Morgan is not having this happen. We haven't seen it with Canton. We haven't seen it with all of the internal chains. You're making the BIS's argument for them if you won't control this stuff. And to me, I really think that's a second-order effect that the industry needs to grapple with.

Gracie calling out ThorChain — I think, obviously from the personal position of BitGet, I get that. But Star piling on, I think, was correct, right? Like this is the industry starting to grow up and be like, "no, you really do need to do better here." Because, Ram, to go back to the point you were making, which I think you were right about, kind of makes it hard for you to think this space is investable if this is going to be the security posture, right?

Yeah, it comes under confidence. Markets come under confidence.

Yeah. How much money would you guys leave at State Street if they were constantly letting your securities be stolen?

十一、量子威胁：地平线上的下一场风暴

Yeah, and then I think — I told you guys I've been spending a lot of time on quantum. Yes. Quantum's coming and AI is accelerating it. And we're already seeing — what are the bad guys doing? Harvesting now, decrypt later. And, you know, this is — we really got to get our act together, because that's real and it's scary.

Good news is: I think that crypto is going to actually lead us out of this challenge. The $500 trillion in post-quantum cryptography — that's about right now, $500 trillion in assets are being secured by public key encryption. That could be undermined. I do think that crypto will actually lead us out of that, because if only there was a concentration of cryptographers in an industry, probably know what they're doing.

But I feel like AI was the first real tool that the bad guys got. The good guys got it too. I think in the long term, we'll be fine, better off. But I think quantum is also lurking on the horizon. Now, I don't know if the bad guys are going to get it out of the gate — it'll probably stay controlled. But that's the problem: it's been state-controlled actors that have been ravaging our startups. So it could get worse in the future.

十二、节目结尾与赞助信息

If you like this segment, please like, subscribe, and tune in every Monday at 4:30 PM Eastern time. I'm Austin Campbell, the host of Bits and Bips, along with my friends, Ram Aluwalia and Chris Perkins, and our slate of exceptional guests. Every week, we're going to discuss macro, crypto, and the collision of worlds, covering topics that move markets and shape the financial landscape.

One more thing. We've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes, it's anonymous, and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

Sponsor — 1inch Aqua:

$540 million. That's how much concentrated liquidity sat idle in a given week in the first half of this year. About 30% of the DeFi TVL, if you're wondering. That's according to Dune Research commissioned by 1inch.

But there's a solution. 1inch Aqua is the new shared liquidity platform. It lets LPs back multiple positions with the same token balance and keep their tokens in their wallet till a swap comes. Why does that help? Because LPs don't have to split their tokens across positions. They can cover more market conditions and pairs with their full balance. That means more activity across deeper liquidity.

See how it works at oneinch.com/aqua. Remember that providing liquidity carries risk and fees aren't guaranteed.
