item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：ThorChain 不是"去中心化过头"，而是"去中心化的可证伪性"被自己亲手推翻
大多数评论者把这次事件读成"去中心化 vs. 中心化"的老掉牙争论，但真正的关键点在 Michael Perklin 那句极短的话里：**"没有主动签署的选择，却有主动关闭机器的选择。"**
这句话把 ThorChain 推入了一个哲学困境——**它一旦证明过自己能停机（May exit 事件），就永远失去了"我停不下来"这个抗辩权**。这在密码学里叫"承诺方案"（commitment scheme）：你一旦对世界公开过某种能力，就无法再声称你没有。ThorChain 的问题不是它做了或没做什么，而是它**在过去用一次停机，为未来所有"不停机"都盖上了自愿的印章**。
换句话说：**每一个曾经声称过 kill switch 的去中心化协议，都在为自己未来的每一次"不作为"预先签下了法律意义上的自愿声明。** 这是一个反身性陷阱——透明度本身把"技术不能"转化成了"选择不为"。
## 二、跨领域连接：这不是加密行业问题，是"点破客"（Point Break）式的道德结构问

item.title: [a16z] AI, Infrastructure, and the Next Investment Cycle
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的信号：不是"增长"在说话，而是"倍数"在沉默

大多数人看到"标普四年涨90%"就本能地喊泡沫。但这份 presentation 里藏着一个几乎被主持人一带而过、却极具颠覆性的观察：股价涨了20%，估值倍数反而跌了20%。也就是说，这一轮涨幅完全由 earnings 撑起来，而不是由"叙事溢价"撑起来。

这与2000年、2021年是根本反向的两种物理定律。2000年是"倍数扩张 + 增长扩张"（双击估值），本轮却是"倍数收缩 + 增长扩张"（估值在冷却、基本面在加速）。这意味着市场其实一直在"半信半疑"地为AI定价——这恰恰是最健康的一种繁荣：怀疑越多，泡沫越少。真正危险的信号会是有一天 P/E 冲到 40，那时才该逃。

二、被彻底忽视的隐性经济学：数据中心正在补贴普通家庭的电费

这是全场最出人意料的一段：美国研究显示，数据中心容量每增加10%，居民电价反而下降40个基点。为什么？因为电网是一种"共享固定成本"——杆、线、变电站的成本是摊薄的。一个稳定、24/7、大体量的"客户"接入，等于把每千瓦时的分母做大。

这个逻辑值得跨领域联想：它其实是"Costco 会员模型"套用到能源基础设施上——大客户不是掠夺者，而是共同成本的稀释器。同样的原理可以解释：为什么高铁开通反而降低了周边货运价格；为什么亚马逊的物流反而压低了美国邮政的边际成本。"AI 抢电、抢水"的舆论叙事，可能是这个周期里被误导得最深的一件事。

三、真正的"贝叶斯信号"藏在一个几乎没人报的数字里：Carta tender 参与率只有 58%

主流媒体喜欢报"员工套现"，但这份数据反过来讲了一个隐藏的故事——42%的员工在有机会卖股时选择了不卖。这个数字比任何分析师评级都值钱，因为它是最接近内部信息的"用真金白银投票"。

跨域比较：在公开市场，学界公认最强的一类α信号是"insider buying"（内部人买入）。私募市场里，"tender 拒绝参与"就是它的镜像形态——员工放弃的是流动性溢价，赌的是延迟满足的复利。当58%的私募员工在做和Zuck、Musk一样的选择（拒绝短期市场纪律），你其实是在观察一个关于"耐心资本重新定价"的宏观现象。

四、一个几乎无人指出的悖论：AI 让"屏幕时间"这个指标本身死亡

Facebook、Instagram、TikTok 全靠"日均使用时长"定义消费者规模。但主持人无意间说出一句极重的话：deep research 任务在后台跑的时候，你可能正在开车、正在做饭。AI 时代最好的产品可能是"你几乎不打开的产品"——它在你不在场时替你工作。

这在跨领域意义上非常重大：整个数字广告的估值框架（CPM、DAU、engagement）建立在"人类注意力可被中介"这一前提上。当 agent 成为消费的中介人，广告业的估值锚点会从"眼球时间"迁移到"agent 决策权重"。Meta 与 Google 在此周期的分野，本质上不是"谁做得好 AI"，而是"谁的核心资产在 agent 世界里还有意义"。搜索广告可能会活下来（意图明确、直接可变现），而信息流广告则可能面对哲学层面的挑战——因为 agent 不会被"闲逛"。

五、被埋没的最反常识的一句话："the factory is the product"

Elon 多年前的这句话被 Alex 随口引用了一下，但它其实是整个 presentation 的暗线。AI 投资的正统叙事是"软件吞噬世界"，可这一轮的实质是"物理世界正在反向吞噬软件"：$90 trillion 的基础设施缺口、football field 尺度的工厂、SpaceX 100 亿投资路易斯安那——AI 让"原子经济"重新变性感。

一个跨领域的意外连接：这轮浪潮里最好的创业者，很多都来自 Tesla / SpaceX 体系。他们带来的不是"如何做产品"的知识，而是"如何管理物理复杂性"的直觉——供应链、资本调度、产能预测、工程进度。这个技能集在过去二十年被硅谷系统性地贬低（"我们不搞制造"），而现在成了最稀缺的α。这意味着未来10年最贵的招聘岗位，可能不是ML研究员，而是"能把工厂投产提前六个月的运营天才"。

📝 转录文本

AI, Infrastructure, and the Next Investment Cycle

a16z Podcast — 25 Key Slides from the State of Markets Presentation

Cold Open

"Eight of the top 10 valued companies in the world are US tech companies."

"Since ChatGPT came out almost 4 years ago, the market's up 90%, which is 17% annualized. The natural instinct is: well, that's got to come down. We're definitely in a hot period."

"This puts us in a new age of atoms. Global infrastructure investment needs are estimated at $90 trillion through 2040. This goes way beyond AI and data centers. It includes power, water, roads, transit."

"Live deployments at S&P 500 companies — that's at 69%. Now, if you go to the ultimate barometer, which is a metric tracked over time, that's actually only at 2%. AI is generating major revenue and savings. On the other hand, adoption is still extremely early."

"Today's opportunity is so much around taking these capabilities and harnessing them to build reliable services."

"That's all great, but is it a bubble? Um… um… um…"

Introduction

Welcome back to the a16z podcast. I'm David George. I'm here with my colleagues Sarah Wang, Alex Emerman, and Santiago Rodriguez.

Today we are walking through 25 key slides from our latest state of markets presentation: the earnings behind the market's rise, the scale of the AI buildout, the evidence of growing adoption, and what this cycle means for hardware, software, and the next generation of private companies. We'll explain what the charts show and discuss what we're seeing inside businesses along the way, so you can follow along whether you're watching or listening.

David: So, Sarah, Alex, Santi, thanks for joining me.

All: Of course.

David: The day this podcast goes live, we will be releasing our state of markets presentation. This is a now yearly tradition from our growth team where we synthesize the biggest trends in tech, AI, infra, and markets. Today we're just picking out a subset of interesting slides and having a discussion about them. So I would direct you to look at the whole version, which is filled with a lot of nuggets. The areas that we're going to discuss today are: macro — where we'll talk about capex, data centers, accelerating demand at a high level — and then on-the-ground takeaways, where we will discuss models, apps, and some vertical deep dives.

Macro Setup

Technology is driving an economy-wide investment boom, with rising earnings supporting market gains and AI demand pushing infrastructure spending far beyond earlier forecasts. Hyperscalers are investing all of their near-term operating cash flow to build out this capacity for demand that continues to outstrip supply in almost every case that we see. They are channeling this investment into chips, power, cooling, construction, skilled labor, and much more. This expansion coincides with a broader need to modernize physical infrastructure, creating opportunities across industries and potentially lowering shared costs for businesses and households.

So with that, let's jump in.

Slide 1 — Tech Is the Everything Cycle

David: First slide: tech is the everything cycle. Some of this may be a little bit obvious, but the numbers are somewhat striking at this point. High-tech equipment, software, and R&D now account for roughly 55% of US capital spending, which is just a staggering number. Tech is driving the investment cycle obviously across all areas of the economy — from software and models to power, construction, and industrial capacity. Tech is almost 40% of the aggregate value of the whole stock market in the US, and eight of the top 10 valued companies in the world are US tech companies.

So this is a broad story. You're seeing it in capex — this is heavily covered in the data center buildout. It's obviously heavily covered in the amount of capital that's been going into the model companies — together raising I think over $350 billion at this point. And just to put it into very deep historical context, because this is probably the analogy that we've seen the most of: this buildout just surpassed railroads as a percentage of GDP.

So, exciting times, massive buildout. We all happen to think that if you fast forward five to seven, maybe 10 years from now, we'll be looking at these numbers and they'll probably be 20x higher cumulatively.

Santi: Yeah, this does feel like the next chapter of Marc's software is eating the world. Over the last 15 years, software has transformed all these industries, but only a small fraction of the population could build it. None of us could. But today, look at us — we all have like a handful of automations running every night. So if you think about the software demand, that means a lot more compute, chips, power, construction. So it's no surprise to see the majority of investment now covered in tech.

Slide 2 — Is It a Bubble?

David: One of the questions that we get all the time from various audiences is: okay, that's all great, but is it a bubble? So the market has reached new highs, and at the same time that it has reached new highs, the trading multiples of the market are actually down. Stocks are up about 20% while multiples are down about 20%. What that means is the performance is driven by fundamental earnings, not by increased multiples. The S&P 500 earnings multiple is below 20 times.

So, if you just start with that — these are, in most cases, very high-quality businesses. It's nothing like the dot-com boom in that way, where some of the highest market cap companies in the world had their massive stock runups based on increases in their trading multiples and would trade in many cases for like a 100 times PE. That's not what's happening here. In contrast, some of the memory companies — which again are very cyclical — are trading, you know, for call it six times, seven times forward earnings. So very, very different.

Santi: And I think there's an important double click here where — since ChatGPT came out almost four years ago, the market's up 90%, which is 17% annualized. And I think anytime there's been 17% annualized growth for four years, the natural instinct is: well, that's got to come down, right? We're definitely in a hot period. But when you compare that to, as you said, the market trading for below 20 times earnings, growing 15% — this definitely feels a little different than maybe the 2021 period that was recent, or the 2000 period when multiples and growth were not really going together.

Slide 3 — Hyperscaler Capex Scale

David: So I mentioned the scale of the capex buildout in the context of the railroads. If you just look at the hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle — their capex in 2026 is about $780 billion. That's up from $416 billion in 2025, and all expectations point to them spending over a trillion dollars annually from 2027.

The pattern recognition is: each of these computing platforms has supported a much larger population of users and uses. In this case, this buildout can happen so quickly and demand can still outstrip supply because the amount of users is driven by the fact that there's already existing distribution. This trend is built on top of the internet and cloud computing, obviously, and mobile phones — and so it's sort of immediately could reach billions of users, in contrast to previous technology cycles.

Sarah: Yeah, and I think it's an important point to double click on, just because we've moved well beyond this model of occasional queries, right? If you think about the rise of agents, you have parallel tasks, you have long-running tasks. And so — I mean, Alex, you mentioned this previously — you have tasks going into the evening, during the day when you're doing other things. And so if you think about agents autonomously writing code, searching, carrying out these tasks, it just gives these platforms a much larger compute requirement than ever thought before.

Slide 4 — Successive Forecasts Keep Moving Higher

David: Absolutely, totally agree. This one is another one that just points to what is happening on the capex side of things. Successive forecasts for the five largest hyperscalers' capex have moved sharply higher in pretty short succession. So spending that once looked like a ceiling — a number of quarters or years out — has become near-term as the demand for the compute keeps expanding.

Santi: Look, if you look at the chart here, I think at any point in time, the natural instinct is just to say: like, the investment will kind of flatline from here. Yet for the last four years, as an economy, we keep underestimating just the strength of the trend. And as Sarah said, with model developments, usage of our installed capacity keeps being taken up. So right now, the numbers that David pointed to are the current estimates.

Sarah: Yeah, I mean, maybe to use DG's language, I think we'd all call the demand for compute a "model buster" at this point. One anecdote that's telling that we've all experienced is — you know, Sam Altman, Sarah Friar, they got a lot of flak a year or so ago for their massive compute commitments. They were being reckless and aggressive. And I think at this point, everyone would say they're incredibly prescient with that decision. Even so, two weeks ago, we all saw that they had to pause new subscriptions on their pro plans — showing up with a $2,000 service — no, no thanks. Pretty amazing, insatiable demand that we're experiencing here.

Slide 5 — Demand Outstrips Supply Everywhere

David: Absolutely. Pretty much every one we talk to at every stage of the supply chain is telling us the same thing — some version of the same thing — that demand outstrips supply. There are certain elements in the data center supply chain where you can't get access to materials or products until 2028. So this is not softening.

At the same time, you can look to the hyperscalers and see some evidence of high-quality business on the demand side that you can hang your hat on. So Microsoft, Google, and Amazon have about $1.7 trillion of combined cloud backlog together. Those customer commitments are building rapidly while the platforms invest heavily in the capacity to serve them.

So while right now free cash flow is depressed during this buildout, consensus forecasts are showing a recovery from 2028 and substantial growth thereafter. You could look to Amazon's latest earnings call, where they did a really good job of explaining this sort of J-curve dynamic — where the useful life of GPUs (or TPUs) is actually pretty long. You have to build out the shell, the data center — that's a certain amount of time. You have to buy the chips. But those will have a very useful economic life for a long period of time, and it's been longer than I think any of us expected.

Santi: Yeah, and I know some of the hyperscalers have frankly gotten dinged for raising debt for capex, but similar to the model lab dynamic, I think the ones who have blinked and been less aggressive have regretted it. I know on the podcast recently that you did with Gavin, Microsoft came up. But I think this is an issue across the board.

David: Yeah. The other dynamic that's been spoken about a lot is pricing on the spot markets for existing GPUs, which is just another signal that any GPU that you can bring online is being priced at an attractive rate where the hyperscalers earn an attractive return. It's a key point. This is one of the things that we talk about all the time — each one of these successive waves just creates a tremendous amount of user or consumer surplus. What's actually happening right now, at least as far as we can tell, is: consumers and users get a tremendous amount of value out of this. That's why they're using it so much. The vendors who are serving those users are making very good money. And then you go all the way down every level of the stack to the chips, where you have to pay much higher than you did 12, 18, 24 months ago to get access to them — and yet you could still make very high margins and create a tremendous amount of surplus out of the users.

Santi: And as we talk about this capex for the hyperscalers, we should think of it as someone else's order books. So these big platforms with historically the largest profits are pouring their cash back into AI infrastructure. That's putting pressure on their free cash flow short term as we just talked about, but it's been a boon for chip orders, for power, for construction — and that's why this broader technology boom has become an industrial boom. We've been spending more of our time looking at businesses serving this industrial boom, and everywhere along the data center supply chain.

I think it's interesting because traditionally our world was more about monetizing existing IP — build once and then sell infinitely. But with these businesses, there's many more complexities that the companies need to manage: financing, managing vendor relationships, predicting capacity, and predicting demand. And we've seen — there are some teams that excel at that, and some teams that have struggled or kind of taken a pause. And it's a little bit of a different expertise than we typically spend our time with.

Slide 6 — A New Age of Atoms

Santi: This puts us in a new age of atoms. Big numbers on this page: global infrastructure investment needs are estimated at $90 trillion through 2040. Importantly though, this goes way beyond AI and data centers. It includes power, water, roads, transit. We're seeing this across our portfolio. You can see this at Anduril with their massive manufacturing facility — the scale of it is 87 football fields. Waymo — they're aggressively expanding their depots. And of course, SpaceX with their $100 billion investment in Louisiana.

Betting on the future today, from our perspective, isn't what it exactly was in the past. As Santi said, it means building factories, expanding infrastructure, more skilled jobs, across the country at large.

Santi: And I mean, similar to what we just said on data centers, I think investing in physical infrastructure is very different than investing in software. Elon coined the term many years ago, the factory is the product. It's no surprise that a lot of the great founders that we've backed have come out of Tesla or SpaceX, because they just learned that executing on the factory ends up being a massive competitive advantage as they scale.

Slide 7 — Debunking Data Center Myths

Santi: So there are many myths that we hear all the time about data centers: they're draining all of America's water; rich people don't want to live near them; and then, one of our favorites, my electricity bill is going to go through the roof.

It may seem counterintuitive, but a data center can help lower your electricity rate. A recent US study showed that for every 10% increase in data center capacity, residential rates went down by 40 bips. You should think about it as: a power grid is a shared fixed-cost space — poles, wires, substations. And so a large, stable customer like a data center can help spread those costs across more units of electricity. Simply put, more demand across a shared system is a positive.

David: Yeah, I mean, totally agree with what you're saying. Investment in shared infrastructure can also improve the economics for the households and businesses connected to it.

Santi: And I don't think that point gets enough media attention. Dina Powell went on a podcast recently from Meta and talked about the Louisiana site that they did, where they worked with the community to lower electricity costs. So there's real examples of that today. It's not just lip service.

David: Totally agreed.

The Model and Application Layer

Slide 8 — Costs Plummet, Adoption Still Early

David: So now we're going to talk about the trends that we're seeing at the model and application layer. On the one hand, as we've sort of previewed, AI is generating major revenue and savings. On the other hand, adoption is still extremely early. And then I think on top of this, the trend is very much so that costs are plummeting. We previewed agents already, but agents are actually economical now for a much wider range of work. And of course this is changing even as we speak, right? New innovations like Jev by newer labs like Typesafe are taking this to a greater extreme. You're starting to see things like two orders of magnitude cost differences really impact the number of use cases. It's sort of classic Jevons paradox — which is why it's very aptly named.

All in all, this is an awesome setup for both the model layer and the app layer. These improvements are creating real opportunities for both growth and profitability among software companies. And that's not to say that everyone will win, but it's no surprise that AI is attracting venture dollars into a very much expanding range of industries. We're also seeing more companies just reach enormous scale in the private markets.

Slide 9 — OpenAI + Anthropic Revenue Scale

David: So this is not a new chart, but it is one of my favorite charts, which is the combined scale of revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. This is one that we've had sort of in every GP offsite as far as I can remember the last few years. And we have to keep updating it every month because it just sort of gets out of date that quickly.

I think the point here — you can see in the numbers — OpenAI + Anthropic: their combined annualized revenue has climbed to an extraordinary degree. We love to show this relative to the greatest software companies in history. You can see that on the right: if you look at the estimates for revenue added for the best software companies ever built, the estimates for net-new for the leading labs has well surpassed that. So it's really a striking combination of not only scale but also speed to get there.

Santi: But we're still pretty early. Relative to other platform shifts, the interesting thing about the AI shift is we're not only early in terms of percentage of population or percentage of users that use AI, but still very early on in kind of the share of wallet gains within those users. So it's a little bit different than, in 2008 we would model percentage of people with an iPhone; here we need to think about percentage of people that will use AI products, and then to what extent they're using the products.

Slide 10 — Enterprise Deployments: The Real Barometer

Sarah: Yeah, I think that point that we're still so early is such an important one, and there's a bunch of metrics in here that I think elucidate that. One is — if you think about live deployments at S&P 500 companies, that's at 69%. So, if you're AI-pilled as we all are, maybe something close to what we would all expect. But then if you move toward quantifiable impact, which is probably a good metric of how far along they are in their deployment, that's 30%. Now if you go to the ultimate barometer, which is a metric tracked over time, that's actually only at 2%.

So we believe that AI is delivering results, but there is a huge amount of room to actually deepen its use inside the organization and track those results over time. Moving from these individual deployments that you're seeing to really deeply influential recurring workflows is the next stage, frankly. And I would just say that most of the enterprises that we speak with anecdotally — their exposure to AI is still mostly with Microsoft Copilot, which just shows you how far they have to go.

Santi: Yeah. This gap between what the models can do and how they're being used is what makes me so excited about the application layer. Sarah, you did this great conversation with Ali Ghodsi at Databricks with Martin, and he talked about how the AI can know a lot about the world but know very little about your company. And we're seeing this in our application layer companies where they're bridging this gap.

One example that has stuck out to me over the last few months: if you were to take Revolut, who has a really sophisticated engineering team, they still had to partner with 11 Labs, and take 11's best-in-class voice model and harness it to connect securely with customer accounts and banking workflows, so that when I as a customer call, I can have my problem resolved smoothly, efficiently, and securely. Today's opportunity is so much around taking these capabilities and harnessing them to build reliable services.

Slide 11 — Power Users Pull Away

David: So in addition to the fact that enterprise adoption is still quite early for AI, the other really remarkable trend that we wanted to put some stats to is just that the power users are totally pulling away. You can think of AI spending rising generally across companies, but the power users — as we talked about, the most intensive users — are spending much, much more. We looked at some Yipit data for this. If you look at sort of median AI vendor spending in the top 1%, that's roughly 8 times the level of the top 10%.

Santi: What's impressive about that is it's almost as much as the 2 to 10% combined — is basically the 1%. So you got these power users that are clearly early adopters.

Sarah: Yeah, absolutely. And I mean, anecdotally, even inside our own portfolio companies, which you could say are pretty much fully AI-native or AI-pilled — you're seeing the top users spend anywhere from call it $7,500 to $9,000 a month. And the median users, again for the most AI-native companies, probably closer to the cost of a monthly subscription of $200, maybe you're stacking two subscriptions on top — so $200 to $400. Over 20 times the spend if you think about median versus top users.

David: Yeah. We talk to our own portfolio companies and one of the questions that we discuss is: how much adoption do they have, and how do you measure that? And if you just look at the percentage of money that they're spending on AI tools compared to headcount, as an example — relatively forward-leaning large Fortune 500 type companies are probably today at like 1%. And the most forward-leaning AI-build companies in our portfolio can be as high as like 10%. So all of these are just questions of: how early are we into diffusion, and how deep will that diffusion go?

Sarah: Yeah. Another example we've seen within our portfolio — many enterprises are really excited when they buy Cursor or Cognition for the first time, but the reality is that's just like the beginning of the journey. The runway from just procuring and trying these tools to full adoption is massive.

Slide 12 — Quantifiable Case Studies

Santi: And I mean Sarah, you touched on this early, but we're starting to see quantifiable case studies. And we've highlighted a couple here of public companies that actually report on the metrics where they've seen meaningful improvements with AI.

Two that we call out — one on the cost side: for example, Chime has reported that they've reduced their cost to serve by over 10% a year for the last four years, compounded. We're talking about almost a 50% reduction in cost to serve. Happily supported by one of our portfolio companies, Decagon. But just in general, many initiatives to lower the cost to serve.

On the revenue side, an interesting one that I found was Shopify here, who launched their AI sidekick. This AI sidekick helps merchants get up to speed much, much faster — so the percentage of customers that reach five orders within 15 days after onboarding has grown 8%. And that is kind of a metric that Shopify tracks: once you reach five orders, you're going to stick around and you're going to retain on Shopify. So it's been a meaningful tailwind to their business as well.

Sarah: Yeah, absolutely. And I think to your point on just the cost to serve coming down — if you think about the advantages that lower cost to serve gives you, you just have more room to compete. So you have better pricing, maybe broader service, you can reinvest in growth. The benefits are reaching the customers, but also the margins, and then they rotate that back in.

And then I think the other thing that's been really fascinating to see is — of course they vary, so you can't throw everything into one bucket, but the incumbents have done a pretty nice job on monetizing this as well. ServiceNow is a good example, right? They've reported more than a billion in AI ACV, and actually a 9x increase in agentic deployments. So you're kind of seeing it across the stack, incumbents to newer companies.

David: Yeah, one of the interesting things that we've talked about a lot — and again, some of our most forward-leaning companies like Stripe have discussed with us — is: where are they actually putting their incremental AI investment dollars? Are they putting it toward things like building new products for customers that could drive higher revenue, or are they putting it toward optimization or efficiency gains on the cost side?

This is sort of a litmus test for us of: where are the founders or CEOs of these companies seeing the most amount of opportunity? The opportunity to drive revenue growth is unbounded to the upside. Whereas the opportunity for cost improvement — yes, you could take that and reinvest it, but that's sort of a latent opportunity that will continue to exist. And if you think that the best and highest use of your dollars today is to optimize your cost structure, what does that say about the revenue new opportunity for you?

Santi: And even within cost optimizations, there's different flavors, right? One is lowering your cost to serve, which allows you to reinvest and makes you a better business. I think six months ago our industry was really focused on rebuilding systems of record internally — and if your engineers are focused on rebuilding a system of record to save a couple thousand, a couple hundred thousand dollars, I expect there to be better uses of those resources.

David: Yeah, totally agree.

Slide 13 — Agents, Tokens, and Falling Costs

Santi: So Sarah referenced with ServiceNow seeing massive agentic usage. Agents are here. They are performing tasks. Tasks require multiple steps, which require multiple model calls. That helps explain the 14x growth in agent token usage on OpenRouter.

Those steps though are becoming more affordable. We're seeing caching — so the system can reuse background information instead of processing it from scratch each time. I've seen Hebbia take advantage of this: they've seen their financial chat workloads become 10x cheaper to run. The same budget that they had before can now support more work.

David: Yeah. I think your broader point is just that lower costs make it practical now for an agent to try, check its work, try again — and you can just open up a ton of tasks where maybe reasoning or tool use would have been just prohibitively expensive. And I think this is especially important in cases where reliability is maybe the de facto reason you would or would not use an agent. Again, we sort of talked about Typesafe previously — but imagine what happens when you go an order of magnitude cheaper, two orders of magnitude cheaper. I think the amount of use cases that open up are actually unimaginable.

Santi: Yeah, totally. And with much greater improvement in latency.

David: Yeah, absolutely.

Slide 14 — Optimizing Latency, Cost, and Performance

Santi: So companies are definitely thinking more and more today about how to optimize latency or performance at large with cost. Take Databricks as an example. They're leveraging routing — choosing the appropriate model for each specific task to improve performance and cost. Their smart router performed better: it solves more problems at 35% lower cost than the strongest individual model.

Another approach we're seeing a lot of right now is fine-tuning. We've seen this with Harvey. We've seen this with EliseAI. In the case of Elise, they fine-tuned a smaller model, so it became much more affordable — 60% cheaper — but also had way lower latency. So live use cases from an audio perspective became tenable. These engineering gains are making AI more useful but also more affordable.

David: Yeah. And I think, if you roll that up and think about for application business, the relevant unit for them is really the cost of getting the customer's job done. If you can decouple that — you get the customer's job done, you charge for that, and you can use better routing to make the product more economical — that's pretty magical. Because now you're not using the most expensive model for each step, but you are getting the job done. And I think we're going to see more margin improvements in the best app companies.

Consumer AI

Slide 15 — Only 2% of US Households Pay for AI

Santi: It's a nice segue. We've been talking mostly about usage inside of the enterprise, but important to talk about consumer given obviously that's the place where we've had some of the largest outcomes and where we spend a lot of our time.

We think it's still pretty early. There was a recent survey that showed that only just over 2% of US households actually have a paying subscription for AI. Maybe subscription is not going to be the best place to monetize the majority of households, but it has been so far. And the interesting thing about the subscription revenue is it has some of the best retention we've ever seen in consumer. Alex likes to talk about smile curves, and it's really, really rare to see a retention profile that not only flatlines but actually smiles as the product improves and people come back to it. But that's what we've seen with AI, which just demonstrates the value that the subscription is being able to deliver to the person who pays.

Sarah: By the way, just on subscription — what struck me about these numbers, especially if you look at the bottom right chart, is just how small they are. Like think about Amazon Prime — that's over 200 million households. Netflix is a great one — 70 million households, right? I had to look it up — I'm like, is that K correct? So totally agree that it's just getting started.

Alex: Yeah, I mean, our partner Josh Elman does have a definition I like that would be counter to that a little bit, which is: consumer AI is what I use for my daily life and not necessarily what I expense. So in his view, he would say it's maybe not super surprising that 97% of households that are using AI aren't yet paying for it.

You are right, Santi, I do like smiling retention curves. We do like to see users coming back more and more. Another common characteristic of large consumer platforms is time spent. If you were to look at Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snap — they all get 60, or 30 to 60 minutes per day from their active users. And while the best AI assistants — and there's many up and coming right now — all aspire to be my go-to application, I hope that they are going to be incredibly persistent and always on and super proactive, such that they may not be the place where I spend the most time in the future.

Santi: Yeah, it's going to make our job harder when we can't look at engagement via outside-in data, because the agents are working in the background instead of us just looking at like screen time on a social media application. But it is important. I remember, when the newest models come out — in December, even in our workloads — we would set off a deep research task or an agent task and then drive up to the city or something. That's not driving Tesla. That's not screen time being tracked as would have been in prior generations of consumer.

Alex: Yeah, totally agreed.

Slide 16 — Muse, Instinct, and the Marketplace Question

Alex: It's early, but it is a really new and exciting time in consumer. Muse and Instinct are no doubt the new kids on the block, but they've grown really quickly. Those, along with ChatGPT, are taking more and more of my queries away from traditional search.

But it's really a dynamic time. So if you are an existing consumer discovery platform, an existing marketplace, you really need to be thinking about your chess moves right now. There's a couple questions I'd be asking:

  1. How much incremental demand can I get from an AI agent? How many more orders can they bring me?
  2. How much of my business, how much of my profit pool comes from owning the customer relationship and discovery?

Last week there was a lot of news where Amazon said no thank you to Muse, but Instacart said yes please. If you think about Amazon × AWS and Instacart, and look at their advertising revenue — it outpaces all of their operating profit. So advertising revenue, owning the customer relationship, is incredibly important. But for Amazon, how many incremental new orders or certainly customers am I going to get from connecting to Muse? Not that many. Whereas if you look at Instacart, online penetration of grocery is still relatively early — a lot more orders to go get.

So the optimistic possibility here is that there's going to be a lot more orders coming from these applications. Historically I've had to click all these different ways through to process an order. If I offload that to an agent, all of a sudden there's no clicks and hopefully more GMV. The trip I once wanted to book but didn't gets booked. The order that we all wanted to place for dinner tonight happens. So I'm optimistic there's going to be a lot more GMV, and that'll make up for some of this lost advertising revenue.

David: Yeah, it's sort of this question, though, that's open of how does it get compensated for? To your point, Amazon has an over $70 billion advertising business that's extremely high-margin flow-through that is totally predicated on the fact that consumers go to the website and click on the ads. And if they don't do that anymore, what happens?

Today, Meta and Google famously advertise probably best out of any of the internet platforms. They each make call it $200-plus per user in the US, in developed world. In the case of Meta, it's an entertainment application — we'll see what happens with that. It's probably a little bit safer in the case of Google. It's funny, the whole talk track around Google two years ago when all of this just happened was: oh my gosh, what's going to happen to Google's search business? And it turns out it's been really resilient. Part of the reason it's been really resilient is because their very high-monetizing ad terms were somewhat safe — because they were things like "I need to buy insurance," or "find me a hotel in this city," things like that that you can very directly monetize. But that the AI was not yet capable of going to take action for on your behalf. If that changes, that could be a very different dynamic.

Santi: Yeah. The other thing, just to add — I think the narrative last week was a little bit like negative-sum, where it was very negative: like, look, these marketplaces are going to be impacted. I do think the positive-sum view of this is: number one, maybe that $70 billion that's spent on advertising on Amazon just finds a different channel — goes elsewhere, maybe spent directly on the agents through a different form factor, or just finds better ways to target people. And then two, with the lower friction, we might just see more consumption — people might buy more, and that's just like a positive flywheel that drives economic growth. I think a little bit, we're locked into this "oh this is bad for profit pools," but actually might be just good.

David: Yeah, totally. Both could be true, by the way.

Sarah: Yeah.

David: There might be profit pools, but it could be additive overall to the economy. I think we all would be disappointed if we looked back three years from now and there's not a meaningful productivity improvement actually at the overall macroeconomic level, which would drive consumer spending higher in the case of advertising. But it might just be that profit pools disappear from certain places and get reallocated.

Santi: The immediate reaction has been net market-cap-positive across the ecosystem. The Meta gains have far exceeded any of the losses from the marketplaces.

David: Yeah, it's a great point.

Software: Winners, Losers, and Verticals

Slide 17 — The Public Software Divergence

David: Going back to our discussion on software and moving maybe more to the public side — I think the big trend that jumps out at you from these charts is that the mix has really shifted toward slower-growing, more profitable companies. Roughly 75% of the public software sample here is profitable, and only 30% is growing at 20% or more.

Santi: Which is a staggering number, that only 30% of the public software companies are growing at 20% plus.

David: And not only 20% — I mean, that's 30%. If you draw the line at 30%, we've discussed like the absolute number of companies is less than five, when in the private markets basically every company we see and spend time with is growing at well in excess of 30%.

Look, this is somewhat obvious actually if you just talk to IT managers, CIOs, etc. If you look at the growth that they're experiencing and what they spend on AI — the easiest place for those dollars to come from is not spending incremental new dollars on new SaaS software projects.

Santi: Yeah, exactly.

David: So, you know, I think we're investors in some of the SaaS software companies including in the public markets, and the conversations that we're having with them and the founders are very focused on: okay, how do I take my existing distribution, which in many cases is very, very strong — locked-in customers who wouldn't go anywhere — and apply really interesting new AI products to them, where I can drive my revenue growth higher?

In order to dispel the greatest fears around the SaaS apocalypse: I think we just need to see a period of time where the software companies continue to post things like 98% gross dollar retention, which was kind of always the sticking point for why they were so attractive as investments; continue to drive efficiency like we've talked about; but most importantly, drive revenue growth acceleration. Which shows that they're safe from a defensive standpoint, but that the offensive investments that they're making are actually going to drive their business to be better.

Santi: I thought your point in the blog post that you wrote a couple months ago on two paths was really interesting as a rule of thumb. Maybe share more on the finer point of the percentages.

David: Yeah, the more I talked to founders after it, the more I felt like almost everyone that we talked to is like: yeah, I'm trying to drive revenue growth higher. It's clearly, I think, the predominant path for the types of companies that we're investors in and that we've backed over the years. Again, I think maybe relative to a year ago when the fear was like — okay, everyone's going to vibe-code their software systems — that is clearly not what's happening in the market. But the onus is high on delivering revenue growth acceleration. And so we had said: let's target 10% plus acceleration, which is a high number, but with a magical product given the budgets that are available to AI, seemingly doable. And so we'll see — I think that there are a few of them that we are close to where we'll see that over the next 12 to 18 months.

Slide 18 — Cybersecurity, Observability, and Vertical Software Stand Out

Sarah: Yeah, absolutely. And as with all things, you can't lump every company into the software bucket — sort of talk about multiples coming down and sort of growth decline as well. In fact, software has been very differentiated. If you look at this chart here, you can see that cybersecurity, observability have really stood out, and vertical software as well has generally held up much better than the horizontal applications.

The framework for how we think about what's held up, or even gone up nicely, versus what is in more secular decline, if you will, is that: really you think about how AI changes the customer's need for that product. And I think the cybersecurity risk associated with AI has been well publicized. But as you think about more software and agents creating new security and new monitoring needs, this is creating greater demand honestly for the incumbents in these markets. And you can see the callout on CrowdStrike on the right-hand.

And then of course, on the flip side, applications are facing different degrees of workflow change. It's sort of — if you think about, one of our top CEOs Ali Ghodsi likes to talk about this "chopping block of AI" and what's first on the chopping block. On the flip side, what is actually needed for AI? You pair those dynamics together, and I think it explains a lot of what we're seeing in the public markets.

Santi: Yeah, I think a lot of this is pretty intuitive with what we're seeing on the private market side. As you alluded to Sarah, on the security front, agents are accessing more and more systems, taking more actions. The OpenAI–Hugging Face incident was an eye-opening event for many. So security is paramount.

And then as we look at the vertical AI companies — these are some of the fastest-growing companies we're seeing in the private markets, right? Harvey, Abridge, Elise — they are growing faster than any of the precedents ever have in their industry. And that's a reflection of the customers recognizing it's not just the model, which we talked about earlier, but how you orchestrate that, how you build the application around it — and vertical-specific workflows command these needs.

And I mean, we spend a lot of time looking at public markets, less so for investments — but we underwrite exit multiples, right? So we track that pretty closely. And I think if we were to recap the year, what's happened: first couple months, there was the SaaS apocalypse. We wrote a blog post about what kind of businesses would do well. And if you fast forward to today, the software index is actually back to where it started the year, but it's really bifurcated into some companies that are deemed AI losers and some companies that are deemed winners. And the public market sometimes simplifies things a bit too much — but to your point, the AI winners are not just the ones that can improve their cost structures. They're the ones that are actually accelerating and capturing some of this net-new dollars up for grabs. If you're not really capturing, then you're probably not riding the wave.

David: Yep.

Slide 19 — Stripe's SaaS Renaissance

Sarah: Yeah. On the flip side, we wanted to showcase some private-company operating data that gives us a view of what customers are actually doing. There's a little bit of a narrative violation in Stripe's SaaS customer data, which actually shows growth accelerating into 2026 across both young and mature businesses.

Santi: Stripe calls it the renaissance.

Sarah: Oh, the renaissance. I actually quite like the renaissance.

Santi: I like renaissance. Yeah, it's very good. It's very good.

Private Markets: Staying Private for Longer

Slide 20 — Six Companies, $2.4 Trillion

Santi: If we talk — we've been talking about public markets a bit; Sarah talked about private market SaaS acceleration. We get a lot of questions around companies staying private for longer. So if you actually look at the top six companies today — Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut — by last-round valuation, they add up to about $2.4 trillion. This is more than the combined market cap of IPOs we've seen in the last 10 years excluding SpaceX, which adds up to $1.7 trillion.

So just the amount of activity that happens within our market — again, six companies, $2.4 trillion — it's almost as big as the Russell 2000, which is a big index in the public markets where there's hundreds of public managers that spend most of their time in. So it's increasingly exciting to just spend time in these late-stage champions that can keep investing in growth more so than maybe maximize short-term profit.

But David, you can talk a little bit about how we advise companies on the IPO — and when to stay private versus public.

David: Yeah, look, I mean, the IPO — especially for founder-led companies, one of the things that we've talked about and that I've written about is that the founder is the asset class at this point. So the bet that we make — and part of the reason that it's been a benefit for some of these companies to remain private — is they can many times take bigger swings in the private markets that have longer-duration paybacks.

Zuck and Elon are kind of obvious exceptions to the rule in the public markets. But the way you see it manifest in the numbers in companies like Databricks or Stripe is massive, massive new bets in new product areas. You can see revenue acceleration that happens as a result. You can do that in the public markets, but it's going to catch greater scrutiny. Obviously, Meta's stock price at the nadir got below $100 a share, when people were very, very skeptical about their investments in AR/VR.

For us, the way we talk about it with our founders is: just the IPO is another financing event. And what do you get out of being a public company, relative to what do you get out of being a private company? But clearly you can reach big scale in the private markets.

Santi: And there's some other companies that already talked about running themselves like they were a public company — with high focus on efficiency, and just basically every metric being tracked. There's also some companies that benefit from maybe public disclosing of financials and earning customer trust, both at the enterprise level and on a consumer level. I mean, Navan went public and we've seen a reacceleration just on the basis of some of the larger enterprises actually trusting them more because they're a public business.

David: Yeah. And then of course there are examples where capital needs over time could be very, very large. The capital pools in the private markets are very large and can serve the needs of many of these companies. But at some point, the capital needs may even get too big for the private markets — that's the public markets.

Slide 21 — Secondaries and Tender Offers

Santi: In the private markets, one of the things that we spend a lot of time in too is secondaries. There's two dynamics at play. One is: we see an increasing amount of companies holding tenders for their employees. So if they choose to stay private, allowing employees to get liquidity outside of the public markets.

And an interesting data point shown here is — participation in tenders tracked by Carta has only been 58%. So this is employees choosing not to take liquidity because they have so much conviction in the performance of their business. It's the opposite of — I think sometimes there's a narrative of like "employees cashing out" — and what we're seeing is actually employees choosing not to cash out because they believe in their company so much.

David: Imagine SF home prices if that was 100%.

Santi: Exactly.

David: It'd be hard. Exactly. Yeah. The tender offers that happen — we're obviously participating in these and leading these pretty frequently. So we think they're a good thing. They do serve two purposes.

One: for employees and prospective employees, it is sometimes hard to compete with the liquidity appeal of public-markets RSUs that hit your account on a net-tax basis every quarter. So it is a weapon of competition for the private markets that want to compete for employees, or retain their employees, with the public-market companies.

The other side of it is: we're advocates of sort of more-frequent resetting of your valuation. That keeps your private stock price fresh for a number of reasons. One, it's easier to talk about that with employees and prospective employees. But two, in the event that you want to do M&A like many of our companies have done, you have fresh currency that you can use.

Santi: Yeah, no, maybe just the other dynamic. I think people talk about the "secondary discount" quite a bit, because that's a dynamic that we've seen over the last five years. Where maybe coming out of 2021 and '22, '23, '24, the median discount to the last-round price in secondary markets was meaningful, because there was maybe like a round that was priced too high and it was out of date. But actually what you're seeing today is: when there are transactions in secondary markets, the discount to the last-round price is basically zero. Which just speaks to these valuations at which companies have raised that are fresh, and there's always net-new investors willing to pay that same price — which wasn't the case for the last couple of years.

David: Yeah, great point.

Everything Is AI

Slide 22 — AI = 86% of VC Deal Activity

David: So this is a fun slide that says everything is AI, computer. AI-related companies account for 86% of US VC deal activity in this 2026 snapshot, up from 65% in 2025. Obviously AI has become the dominant destination for venture dollars.

Santi: Yeah. But beneath that AI label, the opportunity has broadened a lot, right? So enterprise apps, consumer apps, but also services, semiconductors, power, defense. A lot of the attention goes to OpenAI, SpaceX AI, and Anthropic — but beyond that, our opportunity set has never been deeper and broader.

Slide 23 — Areas of Excitement

David: Last, we thought it would be fun just to talk about some of the areas that we're very excited about right now.

Consumer agents. Obviously we touched on some of the consumer work that will now be done by agents. You could call it long-running agents, you can call it autonomous agents, heavy-use consumer. If you take the perspective that you could have consumer agents do all the tasks that you wouldn't want to do, to give you things that you otherwise wouldn't have spent time or money on — it's very appealing. And I think that the distribution of this could happen pretty quickly.

Robotics. Robotics is an area where we're spending a lot of time and attention. We happen to think that it could be even larger than LLMs — but probably 3 to 5 years earlier. So we think over the next 5 years this is going to be a massive area of investment and excitement.

Autonomy. Autonomy is here. Self-driving works. It's a very exciting time. If you just take a step back and talk about the auto industry and transportation industry — this is one of the biggest industries in the world that we probably don't talk about as much, because we spend so much time talking about AI right now. But if you look at miles traveled by Uber and Lyft, or in Ubers and Lyfts, it represents about 1% of miles traveled in the US. I think with full networks of autonomous driving cars that are 14 times safer than human drivers, we expect that to expand by at least an order of magnitude in the coming years. Plus, there's 17 million new cars sold per year in the US, and I think over the next 10 years those will all be autonomous.

AI × Bio. This is a super exciting area. Obviously, the folks in the labs are talking about this. But new drug discovery, solving some of the most debilitating illnesses or diseases in the world, I think is a promise that we all are very hopeful for — that we'll see a lot of progress over the next 10 years.

Personal health. This is another one that I'm very excited about, for myself as a "healthmaxer." There's not been a great place or avenue to take all of the information about yourself, put it into somewhere, and get very hyper-personalized advice.

Enterprise diffusion beyond coding. And then lastly, diffusion into the enterprise beyond coding. This is one that, Sarah, you were talking about — we're so early in actual diffusion of the technology into the enterprise that I think it's going to be super, super exciting.

American dynamism. And then lastly, there's another area that is not inside the AI bucket, which is what we call American dynamism — the retooling of the entire American dynamism stack. We've been large investors in this area for a while. It's still just a small fraction — less than 5% of overall dollars spent in the military is sort of newer vendors like Anduril, Saronic, Castellan — and we expect that to grow dramatically as needs change.

Closing

So many areas of excitement. Obviously, we've been very active in this AI space, and we're optimistic about the effect that it's going to have on the overall economy. The buildout is massive, but we think it's going to be massively productivity-enhancing in the US.

So — it's a blast to hang out with you guys. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的信号：不是"增长"在说话，而是"倍数"在沉默
大多数人看到"标普四年涨90%"就本能地喊泡沫。但这份 presentation 里藏着一个几乎被主持人一带而过、却极具颠覆性的观察：**股价涨了20%，估值倍数反而跌了20%**。也就是说，这一轮涨幅**完全由 earnings 撑起来**，而不是由"叙事溢价"撑起来。
这与2000年、2021年是根本反向的两种物理定律。2000年是"倍数扩张 + 增长扩张"（双击估值），本轮却是"倍数收缩 + 增长扩张"（估值在冷却、基本面在加速）。**这意味着市场其实一直在"半信半疑"地为AI定价**——这恰恰是最健康的一种繁荣：怀疑越多，泡沫越少。真正危险的信号会是有一天 P/E 冲到 40，那时才该逃。
## 二、被彻底忽视的隐性经济学：数据中心正在**补贴**普通家庭的电费
这是全场最出人意料的一段：美国研究显示，数据中心容量每增加10%，居民电价反而**下降40个基点**。为什么？因为电网是一种"共享固定成本"——杆、线、变电站的成本是摊薄的。一个稳定、24/7、大体量的"客户"接入，等于把每千瓦时的分母做大。

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 毒品毒駕零容忍！邁阿密市長給台灣人的啟發：沒治安，談什麼拚經濟？Steven Meiner【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：他把「治安」当作最高级的经济基础设施

大多数人以为的因果链是：经济发展 → 城市繁荣 → 治安改善。 Meiner 悄悄把这条链条反向重排：治安 → 资本流入 → 财政盈余 → 更好的治安。

他不是在"平衡"治安和经济，而是把治安当成最底层的资产类别——一种城市的"无风险利率"。他对商会说的那句"我还没为商业做任何事，但我会是最亲商的市长，因为你们需要的是安全"，其实是在宣告一种资本定价逻辑：当一个城市能保证物权、人身与秩序的确定性，它就能以低"折现率"收割全球高净值人群。

Ken Griffin 移出芝加哥的公开理由不是税，而是犯罪——这条数据点被大部分评论者忽略了。税率是终点线上的博弈；治安是入场券。Miami Beach 卖的不是阳光和沙滩（那是佛州每个城市都有），而是"你的孩子夜里可以在街上走"这份底层信用。

二、跨领域连接：Broken Windows Theory × Capital Flows

Meiner 的策略本质上是把 1980 年代 James Wilson 和 George Kelling 提出的"破窗理论"扩容到跨州资本迁徙的宏观层面。

  • 微观版：一扇破窗不修，社区秩序信号崩溃，犯罪加剧。
  • 宏观版：一次未被起诉的重犯（"turnstyle"回旋门），资本对该司法辖区的信心崩溃，HNW 逃离加剧。

有趣的是，他还把治安的"边际收益"数字化了——度假税创纪录、酒店房价领先第二名 150 美元——这是把"秩序"折算成 P&L 的操作。城市治理正在被证券化：一个市长本质是在管理一支"城市 ETF"，居民和资本是流动性提供者，警察和许可制度是风险控制模块。

而他作为前 SEC 执法律师 17 年的背景，让这个类比不再是比喻——他真的用监管者的思路在为一座城市做信息披露和合规套利。

三、藏在最深处的一条线索：大屠杀记忆如何编码成城市规划

访谈里最容易被略过、但最具解释力的一段是他说自己"祖辈死于大屠杀"。

大多数听众会把这当作情感段落一笑而过。但如果你追踪他所有政策选择的共同底层结构，会发现——

他真正害怕的不是犯罪，而是"政府对人民失灵"的那一瞬间。

  • 增加警力 = 政府履行唯一不可外包的功能
  • 反对安全注射屋 = 政府不能给"缓慢的自毁"背书
  • 反对财富税 = 政府不能靠没收创造正当性
  • 精简许可 = 政府不能用摩擦惩罚生产者
  • 免费水上出租 = 政府应补贴流动性，而不是补贴消费

这套体系不是右翼保守主义模板，而是一种"创伤后的极简政府观"：政府要极其强大地履行极少数职能（人身安全），并在其他所有领域退出。犹太历史记忆里"我们相信过政府，然后被清算"的教训，被转译成了 21 世纪一座迈阿密海滩城市的施政哲学。

四、一个隐藏的战略双层结构

Miami Beach 表面在做"金融科技中心"转型，但仔细看它的现金流： - 旅游税 & 酒店税（老经济）→ 支付警力和基础设施 - 警力和秩序（护城河）→ 吸引对冲基金和 HNW（新经济） - 新经济人口→ 拉高房价，但不直接贡献市政营收（无州所得税）

这是一种"用旧经济的现金流补贴新经济的入场成本"的两层套娃结构。他反复强调酒店房价创纪录，其实是在提醒选民：别忘了游客还在为你们的低税生活买单。这层机制一旦松动（比如春假失控赶走游客），整个金融中心叙事的财政基础就会塌方。

五、一个"啊哈"预测

如果我的分析成立，Meiner 未来两年最大的政治风险不是税收、不是移民、不是华尔街回流—— 而是教育。

他自己都承认："如果学校跟不上，资本流入会被卡住。"

因为他建立的是一座为 CEO 迁徙服务的城市，而 CEO 不迁徙孩子的学校。当 Ken Griffin 已经在公开谈论"需要建新学校"时，这其实是资本对城市投的第一张不信任票的前兆——不是财政的，而是再生产的。

一座城市是否成功，最终不看它吸引了多少亿万富翁，而看亿万富翁是否愿意让他们的孙子在这里长大。Miami Beach 目前赢在"迁入"，下一场胜负在"扎根"。

六、歡迎哪類企業？水上計程車政策

Bonnie: It's like this "I'm open for business" type of attitude, but what type of businesses do you prefer?

免費水上計程車

That's something that we're trying to offer people so that they can be able to move quickly between their jobs, their homes. We're also trying to ease regulations. For example, I called a special commission meeting — that's when we sit together as a body and vote. David: Well, businesses, hedge funds, corporate entities, tech companies — they want to move here to Miami. But what about the average employee and salary man? Why should they move to Miami? What business incentives and job incentives are you providing to the average day worker?

住房負擔

As far as housing, there's still pockets. David: Can you give us some examples? Surely developers are probably approaching you and your office to say, "Hey, Citadel is moving, XYZ tech company's moving. We need houses now. 十三、最大挑戰：教育系統

Bonnie: What is the number one challenge you have right now attracting capital?

Miner: I think it's keeping up with the educational system — the universities certainly, but also really starting with first grade. Because the schools have waiting lists. The top tier schools — public schools actually have lost some students because a lot of students have gone to private schools and charter schools, but the high-end sort of the "have have."

So I think we really need to keep up with that. I've heard Ken Griffin and others talk about the need to create new schooling. But that to me — if we don't get that done, that could impede the capital flowing in.

David: That's the long-term vision. What about short term? What could impede it right now?

Miner: Right now, I think we are in a sweet spot in Miami Beach and in South Florida. I actually don't see... I only see growing momentum. It's taking off. It's exponential at this point.

Obviously everything is an unknown. I've been meeting — interestingly — not just nationally, I've had capital and also residents from foreign countries who've met with me saying they're looking to move their base of operations here. And sometimes they ask me the same question you just asked me: "Is there anything — are we safe here? Is this the place?" You're seeing other parts of our country, other parts of the world that unfortunately when political leaders make decisions could have severe consequences — for the negative or the positive. Right now in South Florida, we're big-time positive.

十四、回應反對聲音：企業進來會不會讓小人物更苦？

David: Now, we're talking about the benefits of businesses coming to a city. But there's a lot of people out there — not just in Miami, but New York and other places — who would probably say: "We don't want these big businesses to come. We don't want the super wealthy to come because they're just going to drive up living costs on a very small piece of property and land like Miami Beach that's already built up. Our living costs are going to go up. Why should we care? Why should you welcome the businesses and hurt the little guys?" How would you respond to that?

Miner: I did hear that actually, shortly after I got reelected as mayor this past November. I put out a social media post — and they ended up having a billboard on Times Square from me saying "We are open for business in Miami Beach." And there were people who had that reaction like, "Why are you trying to bring these businesses down here? We're busy enough. We have enough traffic down here."

To me, the businesses creates jobs. So that is an incentive. And I'm always looking at everything from a lens of safety and law and order. And right now things are really good. But things can change too. To me, when you have good businesses, you have good jobs — that helps everyone and it creates a safety net. And that's one of the reasons I think why you're seeing Miami Beach becoming one of the safest cities in America.

免費交通 vs. 免費雜貨？

Bonnie: Okay. So let's say things get more expensive — I'm not saying they will, but let's say they do. Groceries go up, rent goes up, etc. Would you do anything in the New York playbook? Would you make the metro and buses free, for example? Are you going to go that route?

Miner: Well, for example, the water taxi — that was my initiative. I worked on it for 5 years before launch, and I had a lot of pushback. It's free, and I continue to have pushback because I'm looking to expand this and I keep hearing, "Well, you're going to have to charge this, you're going to have to charge that." And I've been resisting that. I think it needs to be free for people to want to utilize it.

So our residents are utilizing it. Our tourists are utilizing it. I mean, maybe if you charge a dollar, it wouldn't make a difference. But if you start charging $5, $10, people are not going to use it.

So yes, there are certain things. Free grocery stores? No. I don't think you're going to see that under my leadership in Miami Beach. No, you're definitely not going to see that. But I think free transportation, especially because in comparison to other means of transportation, it's really cheap. And I think it's something that we can utilize and help people.

十五、下一步大計劃：基礎設施與交通

Bonnie: What else would you want to work on? Like, what is the next big plan you have in mind?

Miner: So infrastructure — it doesn't sound exciting, but we're a 110-year-old city and some of our pipes are 78 years old. So we're working on that. We've actually completed several world-class parks recently, which our residents and tourists can enjoy.

But transportation is a biggie because traffic — we've become so popular and it's not just Miami Beach, it's really all over South Florida. Traffic is pretty severe. So the transportation mobility is certainly high on the list.

But I am very focused on the business and the capital flow here because I do believe the job creation and the job growth is essential for Miami Beach. And like you said, our moment is now. It's happening and we need to capitalize on it.

十六、溫哥華來的問題：毒品怎麼管？

David: Let me present to you a problem a little bit farther from Miami. I just want to see how you approach it. I'm from Vancouver. One of the biggest issues in Vancouver, BC is the drug use problem. No doubt you've heard about it. How do you approach that problem? Walk us through A to Z.

Miner: Well —

David: And obviously I'm not saying it's happening in Miami, but let's say you're mayor of a city that has this problem.

Miner: Sure. I've actually read up on this a bit. One is to try to stop the flow of illegal drugs into our country. You're never going to eradicate it completely. Certainly, I would never condone drug use to begin with — it is illegal. But unfortunately what happens is some of these drugs are laced and create a compounding effect and they're just lethal. So certainly if somebody's going to use drugs, you just don't want them to have an overdose from it.

I think partly it's also enforcing our laws. For example, when I became mayor, I wouldn't say we had a major drug problem, but we had pockets in our city where there were drug dealers. I'd hear it from our residents. That was something that I worked closely with our police department to make sure that we were able to arrest those drug dealers, move them off our street, and make sure they're prosecuted — because often that was happening too, they weren't prosecuted. So we're making sure all that's done.

I also brought an initiative that we're going to be rolling out fairly soon to have canine dogs because they can sniff out the drugs. It's very hard — you have to have undercover officers try to buy, but the canines can actually just smell the drugs. So it's very important to move the drug dealers. If you don't give them an avenue to make their income and their livelihood, then you're going to get them off the streets.

安全注射屋：明確反對

David: One more question. What is your view on safe injection sites? If the government supplies some drug — doesn't matter what it is — then you eradicate the need for illegal dealing.

Miner: I am not in favor of that. I am not in favor of that.

David: Are you? Personal opinion, but that is happening in Canada.

Miner: Yeah, I am not in favor of that. Unfortunately, there's always going to be some level of illegal drug use. People are going to have the need. We're all human beings. That being said, I look at it as not a healthy recreation. It is not good for someone. And we shouldn't as a government be promoting it and utilizing it.

I think the better source is to try to help people who have that addiction and try to wean them off of it. And certainly if somebody is selling it, then they're committing an illegal act and they should be prosecuted for selling it. The user is a little different — I think there you're trying to get them the help they need so they don't continue to become addicted to something that is harmful to their health.

十七、對亞洲企業家的邀請

Bonnie: For someone in Asia watching that owns businesses, should they move to Miami Beach?

Miner: Come on down! [laughter]

Bonnie: Should they?

Miner: I obviously — I'm mayor of Miami Beach, so you could say that I'm biased, but I'll tell you: when I have people coming here... I was in Israel recently for a mayor's conference. It was actually mostly non-Jewish mayors from 13 different countries around the world. And I'll tell you, there's something special about Miami Beach.

Every time we'd meet either residents there or diplomats or elected officials, people would go around the room, and when I would introduce myself — Miami Beach — the whole room would smile. There's a recognition that something special is happening here.

It's a very safe city. Literally, every group considers it to be a safe haven because we take it very seriously if someone commits a hate crime here, which is very rare. But also the capital flow, the income that's happening here, the paradise, we're right next to the beach. You literally have everything that you want here. People are happy. People are enjoying life and making money doing it.

十八、稅收哲學：政府是納稅人的信託人

Bonnie: Is tax something you focus on?

Miner: Yes. So in Miami Beach, there's state taxes, there's county taxes, and then there's Miami Beach. We control, as I mentioned, a portion of the millage — the property tax rate. We want to make sure that we're being efficient with our residents' funds. It's their money.

And like I said, I was very proud that we were able to return money — first time in 20 years — lowered the tax rate for the first time in 10 years. I was very proud of that. I think that shows you the direction that we're heading.

Somebody actually called me — it was $500 that we returned. Somebody said to me, "Does it really matter?" For some people it does matter — $500. But either way, I said, "You know what? Yes, it does matter, but we're also making a statement." We're making a statement here that it's your money and we're the trustees of it. We're going to utilize it to the best we can, but then we're going to return it to you if we have a surplus.

Because we are looking to lower regulations, make it easier for people to live their life, to open a business, and also to enjoy the wealth that they're creating. We don't create wealth in government. It's entrepreneurs. It's people. It's small businesses. And we have incentive programs for small businesses. It's very important to us. We're not just looking for the big player. We're looking for the mom-and-pop store as well. And we're seeing that thrive in Miami Beach.

十九、教育：全美警訊，邁阿密如何應對？

David: You mentioned education earlier. Let me just give you a few statistics. This is from 2025.

American schools got a big fat F on the report card this week. Reading proficiency for eighth graders hit the lowest level in the 32 years that the federal government has been tracking. US high school seniors are performing at the worst levels in decades. 45% score below basic in math. 22% are proficient in math. And only 35% are proficient in reading.

I know this is a nationwide statistic. Bringing it to the city level, what can Miami do to make education good for the public sector?

Miner: Yeah, fortunately our schools here — we have a lot of private schools, public schools — we're actually doing pretty well, better than the national average.

But we also in Miami Beach, even though the school board (which is a county entity) runs the public schools here, we actually spend several million dollars a year in after-school programs in STEAM Plus. We're offering programs in science and technology and engineering because we feel it's so important. It's an incentive for families to move to Miami Beach or stay in Miami Beach when they're looking at other options.

Also, we are offering Pre-K. We are the only city in the entire state of Florida that supplements VPK, which is something the state of Florida offers. We actually offer a stipend as well for Pre-K students, which is so valuable. The studies all show that is an integral age for higher education.

Our schools are doing well. If you look at our schooling and what our students are doing after they leave high school and going on to college, we are definitely educating our kids. And it's something we have to continue doing because that's the future of our country.

AI 如何改變教育與政府？

Bonnie: How is AI changing the education system?

Miner: That's a good question. I think it's changing everything. I see my kids utilizing it, although they are very careful. The schools tell the students that they check it. They have programs that check their work to make sure they're not utilizing AI. That being said, it's still a great resource for education.

I mean, everyone uses it. I've started using it a lot more. I do check my work though to make sure — because I want to create my own content and not have to rely. But AI is changing the world. It's only going to continue.

Just on ourselves, I brought legislation last year that we should incorporate AI in every level of our government. I actually was meeting with — I hope he doesn't mind me saying — Jack Hidary, used to be with Google and Eric Schmidt. He's actually offered to spearhead and help out incorporating AI into our government, because that's his expertise. It's something we can utilize — like I said with the permitting, I want it done in hours.

二十、最引以為傲的政績會是什麼？

David: My final question to you before I pass it back to Bonnie: if in the future when you leave office you'll look back at your time and people will ask you, what is your proudest accomplishment as mayor of Miami Beach — what would that answer be?

Miner: That I created the environment for people to enjoy their quality of life and for businesses to grow here.

And to me, the first step was the safety. I remember I spoke with the Chamber of Commerce shortly after I was elected and I was already putting in all these different law and order initiatives, and I said, "I will be the most friendly business elected official you will ever meet." And they looked at me like... because I hadn't done anything yet specifically for business. I said: "Because you need the safety. If people don't feel safe and don't see the safety, they're not going to want to live here. They're not going to want to invest here."

I think that has created the environment that people are excited to be here. They're spending money. Our hotels — as I said, our hotel room rates through the roof. We're breaking records on resort taxes. Businesses and capital is flowing in here. And pretty much I think everyone's happy with that. Even though the house has come up — but think about it, people own homes, their house in the last four or five years has doubled or something like that. So pretty much everyone's excited about that.

二十一、大屠殺記憶與治安執念

Bonnie: I love what you're doing, but what I like to do is understanding why people do what they do. What is that personal story that is so important to you that you keep on emphasizing safety?

Miner: It's interesting. I grew up, I guess, when a level where my parents — we'd walk down the street and we'd see a police officer, they would say, "Can you please go over to the officer and say thank you?"

I guess it was always a recognition to me — and I'm a big student of history — that unfortunately governments can turn on a people. I have ancestors who were murdered during the Holocaust. So I know that you need a good government and a good police force to keep people safe.

And that's what happened. I'm going to turn 55 next month. If you told me 10 years ago that I'd be the mayor of Miami Beach, I would have looked at you like, "What?" It was not on my radar. But literally, it started that in my little neighborhood in Miami Beach, I wanted to see more police and I wanted more lighting so people would feel more comfortable. And I just tried to do it without running for office and I couldn't get it done. And that led me down this path that I ended up saying, "You know what? I'm going to run for office."

And that was the first thing I did — make sure there was more police out, which you're seeing if you drive around Miami Beach and you walk around Miami Beach. And in many parts of our areas, I brought initiatives to have better lighting so people could feel safer at night to be able to walk their dog, to walk their kids in a stroller, or to go to a business and enjoy a dinner.

二十二、結尾：別抱怨，就去當市長

Bonnie: I love that. Don't complain. Just be the mayor. Like, run for—

Miner: Yeah. Take action.

Bonnie: Be the solution. Just be the mayor, guys. What are you waiting for? Why are you sitting at home doing nothing? Complaining. Anyway, thank you so much, Mayor Miner. It was an honor to meet you. Appreciate it.

## 一、最反直觉的观察：他把「治安」当作最高级的经济基础设施
大多数人以为的因果链是：**经济发展 → 城市繁荣 → 治安改善**。 Meiner 悄悄把这条链条**反向重排**：**治安 → 资本流入 → 财政盈余 → 更好的治安**。
他不是在"平衡"治安和经济，而是把治安当成**最底层的资产类别**——一种城市的"无风险利率"。他对商会说的那句"我还没为商业做任何事，但我会是最亲商的市长，因为你们需要的是安全"，其实是在宣告一种**资本定价逻辑**：当一个城市能保证物权、人身与秩序的确定性，它就能以低"折现率"收割全球高净值人群。
Ken Griffin 移出芝加哥的公开理由不是税，而是犯罪——这条数据点被大部分评论者忽略了。**税率是终点线上的博弈；治安是入场券**。Miami Beach 卖的不是阳光和沙滩（那是佛州每个城市都有），而是"你的孩子夜里可以在街上走"这份底层信用。
