item.title: [Bits + Bips] Did THORChain Just Hand the DOJ an Easier Case Than Tornado Cash?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Thor Chain 的困境：不是"去中心化不够"，而是"太诚实地暴露了半中心化"

主持人 Austin 抓住了一个极其锋利的悖论：Thor Chain 之所以比 Tornado Cash 更容易被 DOJ 起诉，恰恰因为它在 5 月的漏洞事件中"证明了自己有暂停能力"。这构成了法律上的"能力即义务"陷阱——你一旦向世界演示过刹车踏板存在，此后每一次"选择不踩"，都从"技术无能"变成了"主观故意"。

这里有一个反直觉的观察：Thor Chain 通过一次自救行为，把自己从"代码即法律"的庇护区，永久性地推进了"运营主体责任"的司法管辖。这是一种典型的证据自证陷阱（evidentiary self-incrimination trap）——去中心化项目最危险的时刻，不是被黑，而是被黑之后成功自救的那一刻。从此以后，它每一秒不作为都在累积法律敞口。

二、跨领域连接：加密安全困局 = 免疫学中的"自身免疫悖论"

Chris 反复呼吁"要愤怒起来"，但从系统论角度看，加密行业正在经历的其实是免疫系统的重新校准——而这在生物学里有精确对应。

一个免疫系统若过于开放（无边界识别），就会被病原体反复入侵（当前的 DeFi）；若过于封闭（强识别、强排斥），就会走向自身免疫疾病，攻击自己的正常细胞（BIS 主张的 permissioned chain 模型）。行业当下讨论的"能否黑回去 / 动能打击 / 交易所黑名单"，本质上是在给一个先天缺乏适应性免疫的婴儿系统，人为植入 T 细胞。

更意外的一层：Chris 提到"每家伊拉克家庭可持三把 AK"作为无政府状态的隐喻——这与加密的"自我托管理想"是同构的政治哲学困境。当洛克式的社会契约论（放弃部分权利以换取安全）被强行套用到密码学空间，得到的必然结果是：理想主义者最终会为了不被抢劫，主动把资产交给最大的中心化保管人。这是一个自我毁灭型的哲学循环。

三、隐藏关联：Oracle-OpenAI 的债务危机 与 Thor Chain 的洗钱事件，其实是同一种病

表面上一个是 AI 泡沫、一个是加密安全，但两者共享一个深层结构性缺陷：责任主体的刻意模糊化。

  • Oracle 用 CDS 飙至 227bp 的代价，为一家没上市、不盈利的公司提供 2.45GW 电力承诺，本质是"我不承担风险，因为下游会有人接盘"；
  • Thor Chain 说"我们只是协议"，本质也是"我不承担责任，因为代码在跑"。

两者都在做同一件事：用"技术叙事"稀释"法律主体"。 而 Bessant 拒绝给 AI 实验室责任盾牌，与 DOJ 可能起诉 Thor Chain，是同一波监管钟摆的两端——监管者正在系统性地拒绝"技术例外论"。

最出人意料的洞见：本期节目里 Rahm 反复推荐买公用事业股 XLU 作为利率敏感资产的反弹标的，同时又极度看好 AI 数据中心——他没有明说但已浮现的一层是：公用事业股与 AI 数据中心的融合，正在悄悄创造一种新的"准主权信用"资产。当 Blackstone + Nvidia 联合做数据中心的 senior secured lending，当电力公司变成 AI 基础设施的收租方，一种介于国债和企业债之间的新债券品类正在诞生。这可能比 Bitcoin ETF 的资金流入更深刻地重塑固收市场——AI 时代的"新长久期资产"，其实是电力合同证券化。

四、一个容易被忽略的信号

Rahm 提到 Alexander Wang 从 MIT 辍学、通过 YC 融资、最终被 Meta 数十亿美元"aqua-hire"——他用一句话总结："YC 现在比 Harvard + MIT 加起来更像一所机构"。

这句话被节目一带而过，但它其实是本期最大的宏观预警：当风险投资机构取代大学成为社会顶级人才的筛选器，同时 AI 又开始取代大学的知识传递功能，那么支撑美国 GDP 的"人力资本折旧"计算方式将彻底失效。这意味着 Austin 讨论的"debt/GDP 会不会爆炸"命题，其实缺少一个变量：如果 GDP 的计算范式本身在 AI 时代过时了，那么"债务危机"可能不是数字问题，而是会计范式问题——这是市场里几乎没人在定价的风险。

📝 转录文本

开场：利率、AI 与生产力之争

"So now we're in this race between less people more AI to see where productivity goes. And if you're on the AI skeptic side of things, you're looking at this and saying, 'Ah, debt to GDP is going to explode from here.' So if we're trying to read the tea leaves for rates because rates markets are filled with grouchy people who doubt the future. That is the nature of being a rates trader. I think this is the classic sort of conflict between rates and equities and one of them is wrong."

Hey everyone, welcome to Bits and Bips where we explore how crypto and macro collide one basis point at a time. We're here to discuss the latest stories in the worlds of crypto and macro. But remember one, we have our own channels now.

And before we begin, a quick commercial break.

广告：1inch Aqua & 听众调查

This episode is brought to you by 1inch Aqua, the shared liquidity layer from 1inch. Back multiple liquidity positions with one wallet balance and keep your tokens in your wallet until a swap fills. See how it works at 1inch.com/aqua.

Before we get started, I want to ask you for something. We're making a bunch of decisions right now about Unchained — what we make next, when we go live, what we should be doing more of — and I'd rather hear from you before we make them than after. So we put together a survey. It takes just a few minutes. It's anonymous, and there's a box where you can tell me what we could be doing better. I read all the responses. The link is in the show notes, or you can snap the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. Thanks.

主持人与嘉宾介绍

All right, as always, I'm your host Austin Campbell, high scholar of Zero Knowledge Group. I'm here with my two usual co-hosts aka co-conspirators Rahm Alawalia, Maester of Wealth, leader of Lumida, and Chris Perkins, the golden hand of Franklin Crypto.

第一部分：BitGet 被盗 3.88 亿美元 与 Thor Chain 争议

事件回顾

So, let's start with one of the big news items over the weekend. BitGet got hacked. On September 24th, attackers took roughly $388 million from BitGet, largely the contents of the hot wallets — not by stealing their private keys, but by spoofing transaction data. So BitGet's own approval process signed off on the withdrawals.

The hack reopened some of the neutrality debate around crypto after Thor Chain refused to block the hacker's addresses while stolen ETH kept swapping into Bitcoin through the protocol.

So, one, the loss is about $388 million. No private keys were accessed according to Gracie Chen, CEO of BitGet, and the attacker quote "used it to spoof transaction data and triggered our own authorization process to move funds out." She says it's quote "consistent with techniques used by DPRK-linked hacker groups," and it is currently the largest reported crypto theft of 2026. BitGet's $464 million user protection fund covers the losses. BTC withdrawals reopen today. ETH is on the 29th. Tether is on the 30th, and everything else is on 10/2.

Thor Chain 各方表态

Gracie said, quote: "Decentralization is a design principle, not a shield for facilitating known stolen funds. The industry is watching."

Thor Chain responded: "Thorchain is permissionless. It doesn't censor by design."

To which Star of OKX said, quote: "Thorchain paused its own network after its May. Bitcoin cannot be stopped, but Thorchain can. It simply chooses when to do so."

And Michael Perkland said: "There's no active choice to sign. There is an active choice to turn off the machine."

Reminder for those who are not paying attention — $1.2 billion of Bybit's $1.46 billion path also ran through Thor Chain.

A middle path was taken by NEAR with Intents, where of the $50 million hackers tried to route, about $166k got through but $53k was frozen. It says NEAR Intents are permissionless infrastructure but not with no boundaries, according to Alex Chevco.

Chris Perkins：安全是行业的头号命门

Austin: So I have a couple of thoughts here. We'll come back to the Thor Chain part because I want to start with the bigger point. Chris, this is something you've been talking about for a while. When we see these attacks happen, right now the framework is either the attacker succeeds and gets away with the funds, or they don't — but that just means they failed with regard to effort and that's kind of the end of the story. That's a pretty favorable landscape for attacks to continue indefinitely because they either win or have very low cost. What do you think needs to change?

Chris: It's kind of mind-blowing where you have a new technology and people think that the rule of law — like laws just go out the window. It's crazy. I would argue that security is the one thing that is holding us back from in this industry. I'll continue to argue it.

I really enjoyed the NEAR post. I retweeted it because they said, "Look, we moved as quickly as we could. We took the actions that we could because we know how detrimental it is to the system." If security — like this is like human nature 101 — if you don't have security, guys, you've got nothing. Trust me, you can't have anything. There's no applications, nothing else. So we got to solve for it.

Look, I welcome — please, I'm begging you with tears in my eyes — if you have solutions, bring them forth. The only thing I could think of is to increase the surface area of the defenders and the counter-attackers. Went back to the Constitution. Christian Carlo and I published it. By the way, Crypto Dad's got a book coming out — I'm going to plug it because he talks about this throughout his book.

The great thing about things on chain is we know where those assets are going. We're starting to see some actors perhaps not doing the right thing — e.g. Thor Chain. But you can trace these things, and if you can trace them, then you can hack them back.

I'm very hopeful about the president's EO on leveraging the skills of the private sector — it was actually embedded in Clarity. We'll see how that comes out with the sausage-making. I'm going to be in Europe this week. I'll see Patrick Wit — very excited to hear what he has to say. I'll report back next week.

But we need to solve security or we've got nothing. Rules of law apply. Governance needs to get serious about it and they need to hold people accountable who allow the law to be broken.

Last thing about decentralization: Either you're decentralized or you're not. If you're decentralized, you can't stop something. It's out there. The code is working. You just can't touch it. If you can stop it and you don't — maybe you're not decentralized. My two cents. Austin, back to you.

Austin：Thor Chain 比 Tornado Cash 更容易被起诉

Austin: To pick up on your last thread — this is where I think the Thor Chain folks have now got themselves in a serious pickle. You showed that you have the capability to stop your chain when you choose to do so, and you chose not to do so here. That is very different than infrastructure that has no off switch.

If you got exploited yourself and there was no way to fix it and it just happened — okay, you know what? I buy your claim of decentralization then, because the point at which you really would use it is when you yourself are being harmed. And if you don't, that's pretty good evidence you can't.

However, Thorchain did. They transparently did. They stopped the chain when there was an exploit. They've done it. They showed they have the capability. And here they voluntarily chose to launder sanctioned funds for the North Koreans. There are consequences for that.

So to me, this is actually a much cleaner case for people at the DOJ than something like Tornado Cash, right? Where it was never turned off. This one's clearly: you have elective control over the network and you're choosing when to use it and choosing when not to use it. That's an obvious case.

银行抢劫的类比

Chris: I was thinking about this — and I don't know every detail in fact and circumstance, but let's just do an analogy. If there are a bunch of bad guys that roll into a bank and they rob it and they take a bunch of money out of the vaults, and they run off into a car and the getaway driver is there to take them away into the land of safety — usually the guy or the lady who's driving that getaway car is culpable as well. They get in trouble. Is that not the case here?

Austin: And there are some layers to it, too. There's like knowing involvement, and then there's gross negligence. If you're the guy at the rental car place and these folks roll up in like the dead-president's masks with guns and are like, "Hey, we want to rent a car," and you rent it to them — you probably also have a problem. Now, on the other hand, if they pretended to be relatively normal customers and you had no way to know, you probably don't.

So the other point of like "well, we process all transactions" — that is not the standard, to be very clear. Like you said, the law just doesn't go out the window. You can't just LARP about these things.

One way or another, I think there's going to be a reckoning coming for the "DINOs" — decentralized-in-name-only — where you're claiming decentralization without actually having it.

用博弈论谈如何终结攻击循环

Austin: Number two, Chris, to your privateers's point — until we start inflicting consequences on the people doing this, they're going to continue doing it. This is classic game theory. If you can defect in a game with no consequences to yourself for greater rewards, you will just do that over and over. And the way you stop that is by punishing people for defecting.

I was recently on stage at the Philadelphia Fed and I said this same thing: to cause this to stop, we need to start allowing people to inflict consequences on the hackers. Two ways to do that:

  1. Allow companies to counter-hack them. On August 12th, President Trump signed a national security presidential memorandum about expanding capabilities to combat transnational cyber-enabled crime, and it lets participating companies run operations against them.
  2. Kinetic warfare — the more extreme version. If you knew every time I hack a crypto exchange, there's a 5% chance a drone with a bomb on it comes through my window and ends me, that greatly changes whether you're going to be willing to hack a crypto exchange.

These are not three dudes in a basement. These are nation-state actors or organizations of hundreds to thousands of people. We need to start inflicting consequences.

Chris: Can I just say — respect for the Point Break reference for the old people that were listening. With the president's mask and robbing banks. I caught that.

Austin: Great movie. If you haven't watched Point Break, it's genuinely worth a watch.

Rahm 与 Chris：安全危机正在反向逼迫"中介化"

Austin: Now Rahm, as a markets observer, you're an investor. You're trying to assess risk in this space. How does this change your perception of crypto if we don't fix anything?

Rahm: It's 2026. It's embarrassing. Imagine going back to 2021 and saying five years from now would we have these issues — and here we are. The probability is going to be there because of more social engineering, especially these AI-related capabilities which can impersonate humans really well. And it's going to drive more adoption to ETFs, away from the on-chain ecosystem.

Chris: It's more than that. We see it at my current firm. It's really sad actually and I don't think enough people are angry. People should really get angry about the way that our industry is getting abused. A lot of people enter into our space because of the ideals — holding on and controlling their own keys, believing in decentralization in a world without intermediaries. I totally get that.

But what this security situation is forcing — it's forcing intermediation. To Rahm's point, it's forcing folks to trust a big institution to safeguard assets. I've said this all along: intermediaries do offer value. We provide safety and soundness. But what gets me angry is that it's really taking away choice for people.

Look at the Cold Card hack. These are OGs who did everything they thought was right. And it's getting very, very dangerous to self-custody. I'd like to see more people taking that type of proactive action, get more angry and take steps to fix the situation. Otherwise, we're going to be stuck in the land of intermediaries forever without that choice.

Austin: If we idealistically built a decentralized system to prevent people from being abused by centralized actors, and the main outcome of that is people having all their money stolen by centralized actors — I do not think we achieved what we were going for.

Chris: It's getting back to core political theory — like the social contract. I'm going to use a government to provide me security and I'm going to hand over some of my rights, or I'm going to hand over some rights to an intermediary and trust them. It forces this sort of social contract.

加密行业正在"重学"金融史的教训

Austin: We've talked on this show before about how crypto is relearning some of the lessons of financial history. This is why centralized intermediaries and regulations were created in the first place. If the core feature of your system is that whoever is the most morally bankrupt and steals the most money becomes the richest, people are not going to use that system.

Chris, I think you're right — it should be a combination of being angry and also being disappointed at a lot of the current actors for not having worked harder on this problem. Thor Chain's a great example. If your response to this hack is to just throw your hands up and be like, "Whatever, we're going to collect some fees" — quite frankly, you should be blacklisted from this industry by everybody. Every single crypto exchange should blacklist a wallet that interacts with Thor Chain ever, if that's going to be their response.

Chris: It reminds me of my days in Iraq. Back in the day, every house was allowed to have three AKs — and that was fair because they needed it for security. Is that really the world that we want to go back to? It's not working. We need more of a grassroots effort to stop it.

Austin: I would also say — if your goal is for public blockchain infrastructure to win, you cannot keep making the case for semi-private blockchain infrastructure. We're not seeing these sorts of hacks on the networks that have very strict in-and-out controls. Kexus at JP Morgan is not having this happen. We haven't seen it with Canton. We haven't seen it with all of the internal chains. You're making the BIS's argument for them if you won't control this stuff.

Gracie calling out Thor Chain — from the personal position of BitGet, I get that. But Star piling on, I think was correct. This is the industry starting to grow up and be like, "No, you really do need to do better here." Because — Rahm, to go back to your point — this makes it hard to think this space is investable if this is going to be the security posture.

Rahm: It comes down to confidence, Marcus. Comes down to confidence.

Austin: How much money would you guys leave at State Street if they were constantly letting your securities be stolen?

量子威胁与加密的救赎角色

Chris: I told you guys I've been spending a lot of time on quantum. Quantum's coming and AI is accelerating it, and we're already seeing what the bad guys are doing — "harvest now, decrypt later". We really got to get our act together.

Good news: I think that crypto is going to actually lead us out of this challenge. $500 trillion in postquantum cryptography — right now $500 trillion in assets are being secured by public-key encryption that could be undermined. I do think crypto will actually lead us out of that, because if only there was a concentration of cryptographers in an industry — [laughs] probably know what they're doing.

I feel like AI was the first real tool that the bad guys got. The good guys got it too. In the long term we'll be fine and better off. But quantum is also lurking on the horizon. I don't know if the bad guys are going to get it out of the gate — it'll probably be state-controlled. But that's the problem: it's been state-controlled actors that have been ravaging our startups. So it could get worse.

广告：1inch Aqua 数据 & 听众调查

$540 million. That's how much concentrated liquidity sat idle in a given week in the first half of this year — about 30% of the DeFi TVL, according to Dune Research commissioned by 1inch. But there's a solution: 1inch Aqua is the new shared liquidity platform. It lets LPs back multiple positions with the same token balance and keep their tokens in their wallet till a swap comes. LPs don't have to split their tokens across positions — they can cover more market conditions and pairs with their full balance. See how it works at 1inch.com/aqua. Remember that providing liquidity carries risk and fees aren't guaranteed.

One more thing — we've got a listener survey open. Anonymous, few minutes, changes what we make next. QR code on screen or unchainedcrypto.com/survey.

第二部分：全球利率走高 与 债券市场的关键时刻

宏观背景

Central banks are tightening as energy-driven inflation from the Iran conflict spreads — maybe not just energy. The 10-year yield in the US is at its highest since 2007, while Japan's 10-year is at levels last seen in the 1990s. Against that backdrop, spot Bitcoin ETFs had their biggest week since October 2025. And as of me speaking these words, it's still around $83,500 for price.

  • Norway hiked, the Riksbank hiked, and Hungary held.
  • RBA is deciding tomorrow with an 80–90% chance of a hike priced in.
  • BOJ hiked to 1.25 on September 18th.
  • Fed just hiked on September 16th to 3.75–4.0, with Polymarket currently giving around 67% odds of another hike October 28–29, a week before midterms.

Kevin Warsh said: "The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."

Despite these hikes, longer-dated bonds continue to sell off. US 10-year cleared 5.25% briefly and as of me saying these words I see it at 5.236. Japan's 10-year is at 3.1, the highest since 1996. And while Treasury buybacks are at least $4 billion per operation, the sell-off kept going. In fact, supply continues to come online in even larger amounts.

Bitcoin ETFs are now a buy. We saw $2.4 billion in weekly inflows — the biggest since the week of October 10th, 2025. Spot Bitcoin ETFs are now almost a billion positive for 2026. Nate Geraci said they've taken in $4.6 billion since Treasury said it would increase buybacks of long-dated bonds. And Lacy Zong from BitGet said that BTC's near-zero correlation with yield suggests it's not simply trading as a duration or rates asset.

Rahm：不要买国债，买公用事业与金融股

Austin: Rahm, we saw hikes from the Fed. What are you thinking specifically about the 10-year? Is this the point? Start buying bonds?

Rahm: I've been a hater of owning sovereign debt for many years. Why are you owning government paper where your upside is capped? The best you get is your principal back plus a coupon, and the debt and fiscal situation is such that the incentives are to print.

That said — if you were to buy bonds, I would not judge you at this moment in time. The 10-year is at 5.2%. Inflation's clocking around 3.5% (depends on the metric — true inflation actually has an even lower rate). This is just getting to like technical panic selling of bonds. I don't think rates are going to blow out. The US is the least dirty shirt in the world.

But the better thing to do is instead of buying bonds, look at rate-sensitive securities such as utilities and financials. Those categories sold off as rates went up. Utilities are bond proxies — a long-term stream of predictable cash flows. When rates go up, discounting those cash flows drops the price of the security.

The XLU ETF — when rates topped out around 5% in October '23, or in 1982 — in all those moments, you were always better off buying equities. Here's the XLU: the earnings from these companies haven't dropped, it's just rates. And these are linked to the data-center trend as well. So you get a win there. When rates top off, this should have a snapback rally. History is going to repeat here.

Chris：非美市场怎么办？

Austin: Chris, given your previous experience at the big bank — how would you be thinking about this rate setup for non-US markets? Rahm's "cleanest dirty shirt" argument necessarily implies others are dirtier.

Chris: Rahm is 100% right. The US remains the strongest economy in the world. There are issues all over the place:

  • Asia is facing a very severe oil and fuel shortage right now. Hormuz is a big issue.
  • Europe — sitting in Europe right now — has issues in and of itself.
  • The Saudis also have energy issues, dependency on Russia.

Where do these folks go? There's a lot of political ambition to decouple from the United States. You've been seeing a lot of sovereigns dumping US Treasuries where they can. But where do you go? Do you go to Bitcoin? I had a chat with a sovereign not too long ago thinking about going deeper into that space. Or gold? Also a very difficult asset to store.

I think a lot of this decoupling is probably temporary. Midterms are going to be really interesting — leading up to them, it feels like the president's trying to get a deal with Iran. Bessent has been focused on the 10-year his entire administration. The 10-year has gotten a little bit out of his control. I think the president's trying to lower the stress heading into midterms.

Once midterms are through, though, it could get a little bit nutty. He'll be a lame duck — less constrained by worrying about elections. If there's a Democratic shift, he could face more scrutiny — impeachments and things like that.

Rahm, what do you think? If you're outside the US, where do you go? Gold?

Rahm: Gold is selling off now. You buy from the United States. That's it. And if you buy from the United States, it helps — you sell merchandise as well. It can actually improve your trade flows in terms of balance of payments. That's the move. I know Scott Bessent would appreciate it.

Austin：两大同时到来的宏观压力

Austin: As I've been paying attention to this, there are a couple of things happening simultaneously finally coming to a head. People have been gesturing at them for a long time, but now instead of being far in the future, they are near in the future.

One: The US is starting to head to a point where we're going to need to restructure our spending in a meaningful way. One of the temptations for politicians in those moments is always to just shoot cash out of a fire hose and cause inflation. If you look at the financial repression of the post-war era or the 1970s, there's definitely a chance inflation could run significantly hotter while they don't run rates hotter. Things like Social Security — do we really think when the Social Security trust runs out of money they'll have the fortitude to cut payments, or are they just going to spend more and cause inflation?

Two: We're at a demographic shift. If we don't get significant productivity growth out of AI, we're going to be in a world pretty soon where we have a declining number of two-legged humans working — which starts bringing your GDP down. Even without increasing debt any, your debt-to-GDP is going up.

So now we're in this race between less people, more AI to see where productivity goes. If you're on the AI-skeptic side of things: "Ah, debt-to-GDP is going to explode from here." Rates markets are filled with grouchy people who doubt the future — that is the nature of being a rates trader. This is the classic conflict between rates and equities, and one of them is wrong.

Rahm: I agree. It's just technical overshoot. Happens every few years — you get some kind of ban in a rates market. I wouldn't read too much into it. There is a case for higher long-run rates:

  1. Inflation — look at the price of beef, semiconductors, chicken, tighter labor markets.
  2. House prices remain stubbornly high.
  3. Higher returns on capital — the bull story. AI investment (adding something like a point and a half to GDP) is inflationary in the short run — not enough electricians to go around. But that's a bullish story: you're going to get productivity growth. Hyperscalers also issuing a lot of debt, which will boost rates.

Rates are going up for the right reasons overall.

第三部分：数据中心、Oracle 与 AI 泡沫的信用风险

AI 时代的政治与信贷张力

Austin: Do you think that's going to self-modulate, because what's the one thing Democrats and Republicans are agreeing on going into midterms? Data centers are bad — the NIMBY trade. Do you think that may slow down?

Rahm: Have you all seen any of these debates play out? How prominent is the topic — is it going to truly move polls?

Austin: I suspect yes. It becomes a very thorny risk-reward situation for most politicians to support it. Nuclear is a good example — a small minority really hated nuclear power, but they were loud and pointy enough that it actually pretty much stopped nuclear development in the US. This is the tyranny of the loud minority problem in political theory.

But I'm going to raise a different point: is this going to naturally slow itself down? There are a couple of interesting things moving together.

  • Treasury Secretary Bessent, to his credit, brushed off some of the AI labs — called a slow frontier development — even as those labs are investigating tens of thousands of self-generated security incidents.
  • On the other hand, the debt financing of the buildout is starting to strain at what is probably its weakest link right now: Oracle.
  • Yields are at multi-decade highs. Is it going to be credit that becomes the problem here?

Key data points: - Bessent said if the frontier development is a problem, they can stop their progress anytime they want. He urged Congress not to give AI developers a liability shield. - Dario at Anthropic said: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." - OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents of models bypassing rails. - Meta and Microsoft have come out against both the slowdown and some proposed fixes. - Other AI labs don't seem to be having these levels of security incidents — some criticism: it's not that there's any problem with AI, it's that you don't know basic InfoSec. - Oracle has sent notice on its 2.45 GW Project Jupiter campus in New Mexico, preserving the right to defer their lease payments. Those loans are trading below 90 cents on the dollar. Oracle's 5-year CDS hit 227 basis points — a record high, with S&P rating them one notch above junk.

Bernie Margles from American Compute says: if you have a deal with Anthropic, will 50 basis points really stop you? But the counterpoint is that Oracle seems to be trying to stop, and Michael Burry is pointing out that betting everything on this as free cash flow turns negative is quite dangerous.

Rahm：信贷市场没问题，但主权救助不该发生

Austin: Is it actually the credit market that might discipline things here?

Rahm: The credit markets are going to do just fine with AI. These are quality underwriters — you have Blackstone, you have Nvidia — and they're taking senior and secured positions on their loans. They know how to make good lending decisions. Credit markets as it relates to data centers are going to be more than healthy.

The issue around Oracle is they have the counterparty risk with OpenAI. So it's a proxy for Oracle stock. And OpenAI deferred their IPO process, meaning they have less liquidity — paper money, not liquid money, to backstop their obligations.

One level deeper: is there a buyer for those data-center contracts? Oracle has a contract with OpenAI — a promise to pay for delivering cloud services. Yes, there's going to be a buyer because GPU rental prices keep going up. The H100s were already accounting-wise depreciated. They still have economic value. If OpenAI defaults on their trillion dollars in capex obligations versus their $50 billion in revenue (less than that), someone else will step in and pick up that data-center contract. So Oracle will be fine too.

I certainly hope we don't have a sovereign bailout. That is what people are talking about — does the US get in there and bail out Oracle?

Chris：真正扼杀 AI 繁荣的是"责任与诉讼"

Chris: But how do you have a sovereign bailout? What I think is going to end this boom is liability and litigation. If you're creating technology — we talked about this earlier with the rule of law — technology doesn't change the law. The law is the law. If you have technology breaking the law and you're centralized, the amount of litigation piles up. Litigators see these big honeypots. We're a very litigious society in our country.

My concern is: it's not about slowing down. It's about accelerating to make sure you conform to the rule of law. If you want to destroy your balance sheet, get litigation after litigation up. That's the problem.

Rahm: Product liabilities is a great point. There are product liability statutes on the books and everyone's accountable. If you have a Tesla and you're using FSD mode, you as the driver are still liable even though you're using technology that Tesla created. So maybe OpenAI isn't going to be liable for agents behaving badly.

Chris: This is why decentralization gets so interesting. Does a cell phone company get in trouble when you do something bad on your cell phone? No. But if I'm a company and I build technology and that technology does something bad, then I'm accountable.

Austin: So what I would like to see is a situation where the technology is the technology, and the people using it have the liability for using it right or wrong.

Chris: But we're not there right now. These agents are getting spun up — if you spin up an agent and the agent does something wrong and it's your agent — I'm not a lawyer, but someone's going to have liability. Just because it's an agent doesn't mean no one gets in trouble.

Rahm 强推 Muse，Austin 提出锋利质疑

Rahm: So Muse has like a million downloads on their app. It's saving people money in an inflationary context. You're getting mainlining of consumer AI. This political issue is going to go away. People are applying for jobs with AI, updating their resumes, getting more work done.

Austin: You haven't seen Muse have an accidental bot go rogue on a million downloads and tens of millions of user interactions. We haven't seen that from Grok bot either. We haven't seen it from Anthropic to my knowledge. Microsoft Copilot?

Chris: Oh, here we go, Austin. Here we go. You gave me the soft pitch.

Austin: Every week. It's selling by fear — like it's an OpenAI thing. "How do we get in the headlines again?" Because Anthropic has pulled ahead on revenue. Remember, OpenAI was the chosen one — $86 billion valuation. Anthropic was raising at 5–10-ish, and they pulled way ahead.

Part of it is like a strange form of sales: it's saying "we are a systemically important institution" — like the SIFIs in banks. If you can operate in the regulated perimeter and be seen as a leader, then pull up the ladder so competitors can't enter — you're in a good spot. That's what it looks like.

Why is it that we don't see these issues anywhere else?

Austin 的产品责任分析框架

Austin: To pull a few threads together:

1. Agents are not legal persons. If you're using a computer and instructing it, the computer is not a legal person. That would be like saying "my shovel should be liable if I hit somebody with it." It's not part of law.

Two types of product liability distribution — the Tesla example is really good:

  • Type 1: User fault. If I'm the owner of a Tesla and using it dangerously — FSD, not paying attention, hit somebody — I am liable. So if you deploy an agent, don't sandbox it, and give it some query like "go get this information no matter the cost" and it hacks something — that is on me. It's like firing the Tesla down the highway at 100 mph blindfolded. What did you expect?
  • Type 2: Manufacturer fault. I'm using the product responsibly — going the speed limit, observing road laws — and then my car explodes and kills everybody. That's a Tesla problem: a horrible design flaw, not fit for purpose, probably wasn't disclosed. Product liability goes to the manufacturer.

So if an OpenAI or an Anthropic is making false claims about safety or being grossly negligent in design and the agents start doing things — that's on them. If not, it's probably on the user. Product liability 101.

Muse 的产品哲学：把护栏放在 LLM 外面

Austin: However, Muse is a really good example of how you don't just have to let these things do anything they want. Mark Zuckerberg and Alexander Wang deserve a huge amount of credit for what Meta did with Muse.

Where a lot of people were zigging, they zagged. They looked at Open Claw but understood the core security vulnerability: LLMs, lacking internal state or reason, cannot provide their own guardrails.

So what did they do? - Provisioned people a VM. - Gave them access to Muse Spark, the LLM. - Put a very nice UI/UX wrapper around it — the Steve Jobs lesson: user experience distribution dominates tech every single time. - Importantly, they put guardrails outside of the LLM. If you look at the Sentinel setup requiring people to click through for the agent to take various tasks — that is not the agent throwing that up. That is a thing outside of the agent serving as guardrails.

Chris, we've learned this lesson in algorithmic trading at the big banks. You don't let the algos police themselves. You always have some controls layer outside so it doesn't try to buy more than all the Apple stock in the world.

Result: I'm having tons of people who are not AI experts and not coders talking to me about Muse in a way that is just not happening with Anthropic or OpenAI. The only thing that's come close is Grok bots — that's more of a power-user thing. Muse is so much more easy for, say, my own mother to download on the phone. And if they don't have it, Sentinel is like, "Hey, do you really want to let it send that message on Facebook Marketplace that gives people your address?"

Meta got a pretty decent pop when Muse came out. Rahm — is what we're seeing the start of frontier model companies selling on technical capability, but Muse being the first time we've seen somebody run the distribution play hard in this space?

Rahm：Alexander Wang 与 YC 取代常春藤的时代

Rahm: It's impressive what Meta has done. The big players have distribution, they have the data, they know how to code. Lessons here:

One is around leadership. Alexander Wang stepped in after Mark put Yann LeCun (who won the Turing Prize) out to pasture. In a few short months, look what he delivered. He's effectively paid Alexander Wang billions of dollars by acquiring half of Scale AI — a multi-billion-dollar aqua-hire — and he's added at least $500 billion in market cap to Meta.

Second: Alexander Wang dropped out of MIT at 19, then went to Y Combinator, and started building. Y Combinator is a more significant institution now than Harvard and MIT and all these Ivy League schools. YC gave him the capital to succeed. It wasn't Alexander Wang paying MIT to get an education — it was the other way around.

I hope my kids take that kind of path.

Chris: Is your wife on board with that?

Rahm: Oh, 100%. My son is getting into games now, 7 and 8 years old. He's like, "I want to build a game." AI can build you a game — his eyes lit up. We're trying to find a path to get him onboarded while you can be a creator while you still preserve critical thinking.

But what's the point of school? Look at Alexander Wang. OpenAI came out of YC. Prior generation: Bill Gates went to Harvard, dropped out. Steve Jobs went to Rice, dropped out. Elon in South Africa. It's not a prerequisite anymore. If you go to the Ivy League schools, you're going to work for the Y Combinator kids. May as well just go directly to YC.

Austin：大学在 AI 上的姿态是"重演 Excel 之战"

Austin: Universities are having a harder and harder time staying current. I teach at a business school, taught at another one in New York. Universities were very negative about AI — and my thinking is that's backwards. This is like back when we were trying to keep kids from using Microsoft Excel. What did that fundamentally do? Made it harder for them to get into a lot of fields where being really good with Excel became extremely valuable.

People need to understand this is just a tool, and you are responsible for the understanding and the output and the usage of the tool. Speaking as a professor: if my student uses AI and gives me a bad answer, I should fail them and hold them accountable for understanding what that answer means. I don't care if you have AI write it or AI tutor you. I care whether you, the two-legged human being, understand the thing you were confronted with. It's just the distinction of "do I care if you wrote it with a pencil or typed it?" No.

Rahm, you're getting at the Nassim Taleb point of you can learn a lot more from tinkering than rote memorization. There's no substitute to just get out there and do it with your hands. This is part of why I'm so excited about Muse — if you really want to turn perception of AI and things like data centers, you've got to show people how it's useful for them.

Rahm：Alpha School 与新的教育模型

Rahm: Parents are disappointed in public education and tired of the high cost of university education. Students graduate with a lot of student debt, then blame the system because they can't get a job, then resent capitalism. That's why you have these tensions.

Look at what's happened with Alpha School: private K–12, micro-teaching, 2-hour learning model, the rest is real-time mastery mentorship. We need to see more of these Alpha School campuses all over. Hopefully now for the first time, AI can create a more disruptive education model — an alternative to public education.

Chris: Not all universities are anti-AI. I walked into Carnegie Mellon a few weeks ago and they're like, "We invented it in 1956. Everybody take a look."

Rom — gaming really helps kids with a lot of skills. It's not all bad. Gateway to computer science.

Getting back to Zuck: of all the companies in the world that understand liability, it's these guys. They've been dealing with liability since they started. As that company's matured, they're learning to manage liabilities in the release of their products. That's their edge. Let's see where it goes — they're so sensitive to it because they've been through it so many times, and frankly they've succeeded through it.

Meta 的另一个隐形优势：分发

Austin: One element is that, but Chris — something else Facebook understands better than almost anybody other than maybe Apple is user experience. Look at Facebook and Instagram globally. Those are some of the products in the world with the most consumers, and most things beyond them are physical: yeah, more people drink water than use Facebook, but you have to get into that stratosphere.

What that also means: they've learned the very important lesson of "we can make a product 10% better OR we can make the user experience 10% better." Technical capability versus how it feels to use it. They focused on the latter, and that seems to be driving a lot right now.

Chris: And they also have distribution already. You can have a great product, and it takes time to get distribution. OpenAI, Anthropic — they've had to create distribution from scratch. That's not easy. Then they pivoted to institutions because that was a better model.

Meta had the benefit of ubiquitous retail distribution, and that allowed them to build a product because they knew distribution wasn't going to disappear overnight. That's been a distinct difference.

第四部分：VC 世界的重塑

Austin: They're getting to enterprise now. A lot of things are changing with AI. Venture is changing. Execution's changing. Let's talk about venture — Chris, would love your take as a venture investor.

You've got this consumer app Granola that comes out. Then Instinct — multi-billion dollar valuation, personal agent that does tasks, raises at a couple billion. Then Muse shows up two weeks later and it's so good.

I think now is one of the hardest times ever to be a venture investor. The joke used to be in the 2010s: "What if Google does this?" And Google never did it — Google's focused on search. Now, yeah, Meta did it. Here it is.

Chris: The AI venture space is really, really, really hard. You better have a real edge. You probably need to be sitting there in SF if that's all you're focused on. That said, I think the venture landscape right now is as good as it's ever been. Couldn't be more excited. Here's why.

You got crypto — democratizing global finance, institutional adoption happening, institutions have problems that need to be solved. A lot of infrastructure stack things to happen, not to mention apps.

Then you get AI. Crypto and AI are friends — very important. AI, is it disrupting crypto a little bit? It's found some vulnerabilities. But fundamentally, crypto rails and the machine economy go hand in hand. There's value accrual you can find along that intersection.

And the last civilization-defining technology is quantum. It's coming. I just published a piece in Fortune. Quantum will disrupt $500 trillion in public-key encryption. If only there was a concentration of cryptographers — crypto is going to lead the world across this initial challenge, post-quantum cryptography.

Then you get into the app layer. When you look at the intersection of those three technologies — I hate being hand-wavy — but that's the niche you need to focus on.

Austin: If you're just looking for the next prediction market, the next mention market — how many thousands of those I've seen. It has to be unique and differentiated.

Rahm: We should dig into venture next week. It's extraordinary. Harry Stebbings coming out saying it's insane. Nicole Wischoff from her venture fund saying the valuations are nuts. But the revenue ramps in AI have also never been seen before. And if you raised money before ChatGPT, you're out in the cold. If you're not in the AI theme, no one cares.

Chris: AI is a tough vertical — you better have an edge. But there's plenty of edge out there if you know where to look. I've been seeing very reasonable valuations.

Rahm: What are you seeing for seed round valuations?

Chris: I've seen stuff around 25. Not crazy. And it's not in these saturated spaces. Crypto is not cool anymore — it's all supply and demand. So you can find really good crypto projects out there at reasonable valuations. Or you find that intersection no one's thinking about — not saturated with VCs because they're missing it. It's all supply and demand — more buyers than sellers, price goes up. You have to have an edge, find those holes. They're out there. I'm excited.

结束语

Austin: They are definitely out there. I think a lot of the VC world is looking at the frontier labs model and really underestimating the vertical integration and data integration in the way Chris is talking about in conjunction with AI. But on that note, we're going to have to table that for next week if we want to have this argument, because we are at time.

As always, thank you for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips. As a reminder, we're on our own feeds on X, on YouTube, all the podcast platforms. And this week we are no longer going to have short segments on the Unchained feed — so subscribe to Bits and Bips on the platform of your choice.

Otherwise, we'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding. Until then, everybody, thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips.

Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice, and please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.
