item.title: [a16z] How Jev Turns AI Into Software That Gets Things Done
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的核心悖论：AI 越聪明，软件越停滞

Diego 抛出了一个足以让整个行业尴尬的观察："AI is so smart, and yet software has been unchanged in 10 years." 这不是抱怨，而是一个诊断。

真正的洞见在下面这层：过去三年，所谓的"AI 集成"其实一直是 "ships in the night"（错身而过）——AI 与软件在夜色中擦肩，却从未真正交合。为什么？因为软件的骨架是确定性状态机，而 LLM 的输出是自然语言。两者无法直接握手，于是我们退而求其次：把 LLM 输出扔给人类（chatbot），或者扔给另一个 LLM（agent while-loop）。Diego 把这个过程精准地类比为 "五阶段悲伤"——否认、愤怒、接受，最终妥协成"算了给人看吧"。

让人意外的观察：所谓 Agent 的 while-loop 架构，本质上不是一种创新，而是一种投降。它是行业无法把 AI 变成软件原语（primitive）之后的补偿性设计。Jev 之所以在开发者圈爆火，是因为它是第一个允许你跳过"悲伤五阶段"的原语——你不再需要把 LLM 的输出交给人或另一个 LLM 来"翻译"回状态机，而是直接让智能嵌入到状态机的齿轮里。

二、跨领域连接：电动马达的"分布式革命"正在 AI 领域重演

Diego 无意间说了一个短语——"electric motor of AI"——这不是修辞，这是历史的回声。

19 世纪末，工厂开始用电动马达替代蒸汽机。第一代改造非常无聊：把中央的蒸汽机换成中央的大马达，其他一切照旧，效率提升有限。真正的革命发生在几十年后，当工程师们意识到：电动马达真正的价值不在"更好的中央引擎"，而在于可以拆解成无数小马达，分布到每一个工位、每一个工具、每一个动作里。福特流水线、现代自动化、家用电器——都源自这个"分布式"的顿悟。

今天的 AI 正处在同样的转折点。所有大厂在做"更大的中央大脑"（mono-model Kool-Aid，Diego 语），试图用一个 GPT-N 统治一切。而 Jev 的赌注是：智能应该像小马达一样被拆解，塞进软件的每一个函数、每一个 if 语句、每一个数据库查询里。这就是他说的"intelligence per dollar 是北极星"的真正含义——只有当智能的边际成本足够低，你才能奢侈地把它撒到软件的九个 9 的可靠性里去。

顺带一提：Diego 提到的 "DWIM (Do What I Mean)" 也不是新概念，而是 1970 年代 Warren Teitelman 在 Interlisp 里的梦想。半个世纪后终于有了物质基础去实现——这在计算机史上并不罕见（面向对象、神经网络都等了三四十年）。

三、隐藏的系统性真相："SaaS 末日"叙事其实是市场对认知错位的错误定价

这里有个几乎没人指出的暗流：为什么 Coding Agents 出现时市场喊"SaaS 末日"，Jev 出现时 SaaS 公司却欢呼？

表面答案是"Jev 让 SaaS 变强"。但真正的系统性真相更深：Coding Agents 加速的是"复制存量软件"的能力，而 Jev 扩展的是"软件能表达的动作空间"本身。前者压缩价值，后者创造价值。这两者被市场混为一谈，是因为大部分投资人不理解软件的表达力（expressive power） 是有边界的——那个边界从 1970 年代 Perl 时代到今天几乎没变过：if / for / function。Jev 提议的是加入第四个基础逻辑门：一个内嵌小脑的类型。

跨领域连接：这让我想到语言学里 Chomsky 的"语言表达力层级"——一门语言能表达什么，取决于它的形式结构，而不是词汇量。给 Python 加十万个新库，Python 的表达力上限并没有变。给 Python 加一个"probabilistic type with state machine"，Python 就能表达一整类过去无法表达的程序。这不是提速，这是升维。

一个让人意外的推论：Diego 反复强调的"reliability 的九个 9"其实不是工程细节，而是新表达维度得以成立的边界条件。就像 TCP 的可靠性让整个互联网应用层成为可能，Jev 的可靠性是让"概率编程"从 1970 年代的学术死胡同复活为主流范式的前提。所以他说自己是"neuros"的偏近亲、拒绝"生物启发"的浪漫——他要的不是新叙事，而是新的物理层。

四、彩蛋：Diego 这个人本身就是一个系统性隐喻

一个赢过 Kaggle 却承认自己"用系统方法暴力破解、不是靠数学优雅"的人，一个"数学奖不是因为爱数学而是因为要吸引女生"的人，一个从 OpenAI 出来但拒绝"AGI 一统天下"叙事的人——他的整个人生轨迹就是"pragmatism vs purism"这场千年战争的一次投票。

这也解释了为什么 Typesafe 的文化是"build prod not god"——因为 Diego 从来没相信过任何神，包括数学之神、AGI 之神、OpenAI 之神。他相信的是：能跑、能用、能便宜地无限复制的东西，才是真的。这正是从"程序员的三大美德"（懒惰、急躁、傲慢，Perl 时代的祖训，他记不清第三个了）里长出来的哲学。

在一个所有 AI 公司都在扮演先知的时代，一个自称"计算机科学家而非 AI 研究员"的人做出让开发者狂欢的产品，这本身就是一个信号：下一波 AI 的红利，不属于神学家，属于工程师。

📝 转录文本

开场：AI 的自动化悖论

Where the [ __ ] is all the automation? AI is so unbelievably smart and yet it's so useless at all other stuff.

It doesn't matter how much AI coding agents you use, the software actually isn't getting better. Maybe you're writing it faster. It's like arguably getting worse.

OpenAI has been trying to automate customer service since 2020. What I want instead is smart software. I want to expand what software itself can do such that things that should be automatable can then be automatable.

My favorite thing that you guys say is "we build prod not god." So good — because if we had any other kind of like big lab leader, even if they had joy, they would cover everything. And then your view is so different. You're like: no, we're going to create a way better world.

For nuanced reasons, I don't think we are on the path of RSI in the SaaS apocalypse story.

Um, today we have the founder and leader of Typesafe, Diego, with us. He is a bit of a hero to both Martine and me.

Yes. Um, he is not only building like a really interesting product, but creating what we think is a very important movement. So we're super excited about today. Welcome. Thank you for coming.

Thank you.

什么是 Jev？—— "为软件而生的 AI"

Yeah. And uh maybe you can give us kind of a brief on um just, you know, what is Jev? What is Typesafe? Why is it important?

Is this a curse friendly or no?

Okay. [ __ ] are you talking about? Okay. Okay. Okay. Cool.

So I was actually asked for like an elevator pitch which I tend to ramble on and I don't do well, but like I realized my favorite elevator pitch for Jev is: where the [ __ ] is all the automation?

Like, this is like so unbelievably tragic, you know. So much intelligence. AI is so unbelievably smart and yet so... not that I hate on chat bots or coding agents. I love them myself. But it's like it's so useless at all other stuff and it's tragic. It's tragic that, you know, we have so much like diamond in the rough but not polished for work.

That's a — but Typesafe is making AI for software. You know, we want to make AI powerful not just for humans in the loop, but to actually build real software. And Jev to us is our first model in this whole space to make it way, way better to make automation.

为什么 Jev 与 Claude Code / Codex 不同

Yeah. And so it's been interesting because it's kind of caught fire in software world. So, you know, one of the things that made us go "what the hell's going on here?" is like every developer we know is calling us and going, "Oh, this is freaking awesome. It's great. It's fast. It's great. Everything's better."

Um, and then how does that — cuz because everybody thinks of, well, we've got Claude Code, you know, we've got Codex — don't we already have that? Like what's the difference? And then how does that lead to real automation?

Ooh, I wish I had like a some slop visuals because I have like a favorite slop visual for this.

So I like Claude Code and Codex. Um, I love the description from Gary Tan on them: it's just-in-time software. You know, incredible way to describe what they're doing. It makes software on the fly and you can like program software in natural language, but it has the same expressive power as software.

Um, what I want instead is smart software. Like instead of automating software engineering, I want to expand what software itself can do — such that things that could/should be automatable can then be automatable.

And in more flowery language: I want to express things like intent. I want to expand the vocabulary of what we can do. And I can talk about like all sorts of weird sci-fi things I want, but like — programming is like hyper-specifying valuable things and then infinitely replicating them. It's so freaking cool and I want to just make that more, you know?

Oh, interesting. So one way to think about it is: instead of a tool that somewhat replaces a software engineer with a faster, maybe not even as good software engineer — what you're saying is: no, no, no. We're going to supercharge the software engineers we have to write way, way better, more interesting things.

Yeah. Yeah. So this is, by the way, I just think so many people miss this point and it's such a subtle point and it's so important to actually tease it out.

If you use something like Claude Code or Codex, which is great, or Cursor, which is great, they write code. But that code is the same thing a human being would have written. Maybe it's better, maybe it's worse, but it's basically still code, just like code looked 10 years ago.

And the thing with Jev is: whether or not you're Claude Code or a human, you have this new primitive, this new thing that you stick in your code that actually expands the power of software. So instead of writing code, it is something that you include in your code.

新原语：把"智能"嵌入软件

Which, by the way, is interesting because it's this very powerful primitive which would be great if you explain — but it's also a little bit different than how programmers think. For example, it has this notion of probabilities... so — so an intelligent layer inside the software.

Yeah. Think of like a library that you can use natural language to describe what you want, and you give it kind of a state machine, and then it will choose what to do with some confidence levels, which we haven't really had before, like so ubiquitous.

So maybe — ooh, there's a lot of tricks there. I will jump into one thing first, which is: I love the first thing you said, like — in the direction of "where the [ __ ] is all the automation." I love software so much. I wish I could be writing it all day. Would not recommend being a CEO to people, but whatever.

Um, and also, it's wild that AI is so cool and software has been unchanged in 10 years. Like, no one can square this together, and the most we can do is add a little chatbot in the side sometimes that can take actions, but not all actions cuz some of the actions are not reliable. So I just want to give that tiny aside.

Um, I love the point — I'm gonna jump back to the point about this is a little bit of a different way to think about it.

Yes, I think that machine-native doesn't exactly match bits perfectly, and that's actually the art form that we are trying to do. In our onboarding on day one, I draw a Venn diagram of: what AI is good at, what is valuable in code — we are in the middle. So, you know, we don't output like extrapolated floats, for example, cuz AI is just bad at that. But things like probabilities are not exactly novel.

And it's similar to the "is Jev just a classifier?" argument. Jev is absolutely a classifier. You know, classifiers are sick. Classifiers were designed to be useful.

Yeah, they're designed to be useful.

And actually, it's the same interface as some of those ML concepts because these came from practical people who are trying to make systems work. And what I'm seeing happening now is that Jev actually — my guess is that Jev probably is better than having an MLE team from 2019 making the stuff for you, and you can just program it on the fly.

Who knows what could be built? Cuz like, there were not that many good MLE teams in 2019 to build narrow things and to be able to collect data sets and measure it and all of that.

语言 vs 状态机：设计空间的滑杆

And it is just the beginning.

By the way, to this point, do you think there's a slider bar here where on one end is like "language in, language out" like we have today, on the other end is an existing imperative program, and then you can kind of move between the two? Or do you think this is the point in the design space — which is language in, kind of state machine out — which is going to solidify as a general-purpose thing for programmers?

Ooh, that's a tricky one. So I will say — the answer in my heart, yeah, the answer in my heart is that it is a slider.

So — and actually when I design for our properties we have, I might have made mistakes due to my personal preferences, but intelligence per dollar is my northstar right now. And it could be wrong just to be clear — intelligence per second might be more valuable in the short term. But even like our interface, like calling the input "state" — this is intentional, like it's to say...

Oh, that's great, I didn't catch that.

It's meant to be the insides of programs.

So in my heart — because a lot of the work I do is for even more complicated arrangements of the internals of program state — can you put intelligence in there? I think this is going to be an ever-present battle to have.

And pragmatically I think certain things happen — it's easier to make an AI at these milliseconds. So it'll be more like a database for a while than like a standard library thing. But I would love it to be a standard library thing too.

Diego 的个人炼金术：从数学奥赛到 AI

Can I just pull back — like, what is the alchemy that creates a Diogo? I mean, you speak — when a man and a woman love each other but... listen, you speak like an AI researcher, you speak like a systems person, you speak like a programmer. And normally these things have been not super overlapping. And you're taking AI — which we've been pushing towards being a being — and you're making it a programmer's tool. So maybe a little bit about your personal journey.

My history into AI is somewhat unorthodox. Um, I was a mathlete. Um, I was an award-winning mathlete.

The way I describe it is: I was good enough at — this is cringe — I was good enough at math to get girls. So that's quite good.

No, that was a thing.

Yeah, you have to get quite good.

And what kind of girls do you get when you're that good at math? That's — our audience needs to know.

Oh, no. We have to inspire the youth here.

Don't do it. Youth, don't do it. It's not worth it. Just be cool and chill and interesting and don't overcompensate.

Wow, I can't believe I said that.

Um, so I was a mathlete, but I actually never — oh man, this also is a little cringe — I never really liked math. I never really tried. I was just like big fish in little pond. And to me, math was always the path I was set on, but I hated it because it was always about winning competitions.

But then computer science is actually a lot like math. It's basically like math but cool and useful and fun and interesting. And I still love giving algorithms interviews. It's the best thing for me to do. I don't know. Do I love it? Yes. And does it allow me to sus people out really well? Yes, it does.

So I love computer science. I consider myself to be a computer scientist much more before AI researcher, despite my history.

And what actually got me into it was — I also won a Kaggle competition, not from sophisticated math, but from just automating the [ __ ] out of it. You know, like more nested loops, more — I solved it like a systems problem, you know.

So that eventually got me — I was forced to speak at NeurIPS, normally an honor, but I hated it cuz I just wanted to be in the mines.

Was that from the Kaggle team?

Yes.

Oh, wow.

Yeah, actually the Kaggle host of it was Isabelle Guyon, who was the co-inventor of the SVM. Actually, I think the first author of SVM. I'm not 100% sure first author.

And she just basically saw that I was this person who really didn't fit into the research community, and then adopted me and showed me — like, she got me to meet all the AI people, and my career was just pushed into that direction.

And from there OpenAI?

No, it was like a startup with Jeremy Howard.

No kidding.

Yes, I love Jeremy. Fantastic.

Cool.

And then Google Brain for a while.

Wow.

And then, uh, retired for a while. And then eventually I was like just kind of tired of not doing anything. I was like, you know what? Actually, AI is pretty damn fun. And I joined OpenAI because of that reason.

Uh, and it worked out really well.

Amazing.

Really, really well.

Yeah. Incredible.

"Build Prod Not God"：反乌托邦的 AI 叙事

So you said something there that is so unusual in today's world, which is: AI is really, really fun. And then the company has such a different demeanor and view of AI than everybody else.

And my favorite thing that you guys say is "we build prod not god." So good.

Because if we had any other kind of big lab leader, they'd be trying to — even if they had joy, they would cover... And then your view is so different. You're like: "No, we're going to create a way better world and it's going to be awesome, and not only are there not going to be less jobs, there'll be more jobs, and there'll be way better jobs, and everybody's going to have a great time." And like just being around you, you clearly believe that.

So tell us about that — and what this — because for us, Typesafe / Jev is more than a company. It's a whole movement towards a positive future that most people in the AI world kind of don't like.

Yes.

Or they're not with it.

I think they don't get it. Yes. You know, like the "it's just a classifier" complaint — it's like an ML-level concern while everyone else is having like a Jev party.

Because it's like, holy [ __ ], we can do all the things that we wanted to do. And I think if you don't get developers, it'll be hard to understand what's really going on. So 100% I agree with that.

I do think that there's a pretty negative world painted that I obviously disagree with. I think it really comes from this "mono-model Kool-Aid" that everyone believes.

Right — one big brain to rule them all. That's one way to — it sounds much more ominous. That's what people hear.

Yeah. That's what people hear. Yeah.

But you know, will that one brain really be on the path to rule us all? Like, we have not automated really basic things that I don't think we want people to be doing. There's lots of really really basic stuff.

And I think that — oh man, it pains me when the world is discordant with the reality. And part of the pain is, you know, on the "where the [ __ ] is all the automation" — how can we have AI be so freaking smart and — like there's so much financial incentive to automate stuff.

Like, yeah, you could make an excuse for diffusion; I don't buy it at all. I shouldn't name names. But that obviously is not true. Part of the problem is the discordance with the reality and the fact that AI has so much potential is what made it really tragic for me that we had not released this.

So now it's a little bit of a party for me. But I was afraid of...

All Jev users are like — there's the happy AI, the people on Jev, and then there's the morose AI, the people who are not. It's quite a fascinating dichotomy.

自动化的第一性原理：可靠性、可组合、安全

And to your automation point — I had a funny conversation this morning with David George, who runs our growth fund, because we're talking about the new tools. I was like, have you tried the Muse thing? He's like, "Oh, it's awesome." I was like, "What'd you do with it?" He said, "I finally canceled my New York Times subscription." And I was like, that is hard to do.

But yeah, you know, it's a very tip of the iceberg of the things that are horrible things to do that we need to automate.

I think that if we were going to be really intellectually honest and really aiming for the north star of automation, we cannot fall into the same anti-patterns that AI has fallen into, which is really focusing on outliers and demos.

A lot of people ask me, "what are your favorite use cases?" And I'm like, "I'm not sure if they work." I want them to work in the background such that someone would trust that to run and not page them, and people can build on top of that too.

Composable.

Composable. But like other things — like safe, right? It's a different type of safety where if you want it to actually run with resources associated with it, with access to things, you need guarantees for that, or at least statistical guarantees.

So it doesn't go rogue Breaking Bad — that type of thing.

Well, I don't think our models will be doing that anytime soon, unless somebody does the software to do that, which would be a very cool flex. I should figure out how to give credits for that. But not in a way that we're not responsible.

Right.

直觉的孕育：从 2017 到 ChatGPT 之前

I'm just curious, like how long has this intuition been percolating? Cuz I remember talking to you maybe in — was it 2017?

We did talk about that. Yeah.

And a lot of these ideas were in your — you were talking about data being important, you were talking about you want to focus on the task. So — did you know that this was going to end up being a classifier? Or was this just an intuition that there was just another way to view this entire AI movement?

You know, so actually a fun story about that chat: in the talk from 2017 — I think my talk was actually in a very similar theme, I think it was called something like "AI: Modular in Theory and Flexible in Practice," which is very software. So I'm a little bit consistent in that.

I think that this really started right before ChatGPT.

Um, like, right when we released these things — I did not have intuition about this. And honestly, I was very, very pleasantly surprised by the generalization capabilities of RLHF.

When is this?

Must be end of 2021, like fourth quarter of 2021.

We were — it was really, really general. If you read the paper, it's unlike other papers that are trying to prove their point. It was us actually doing scientific-method-ish trying to disprove — like, is it cheating?

You know, my favorite query was: "Why is it important to eat socks before meditating?" We made sure that was not on the internet beforehand. And the models were able to make plausible human-looking answers for this. And that, to us in the team, was the thing that clicked — this is not cheating, which you should always be afraid of cheating in ML.

And then what really got me burnt was — I released it. You know, I'm obviously a big capabilities guy. I did a lot to release that model. I really thought that that model had a decent chance of being AGI. And when it didn't, that was when my whole world came crashing down, and I was like: why?

Oh, so you were kind of on the other train for a bit — like the crazy train?

Well, no. I'm just like — under "RL generalizes," maybe we have AGI. RLHF generalizes pretty well. RLVR is the thing that doesn't generalize as well from what I've seen. Um, and AGI in —

Well, I was just saying more — I mean, you were behind ChatGPT, you were behind these early GPTs. That was a very different goal, which is creating a chatbot that will talk to a human being, was not a programmer's tool, etc. So I'm just wondering...

Oh, well, actually early — like 2020 OpenAI — when we talked about AGI, people used to describe it as "Ilya and every if-statement."

Um, so it's kind of like — is that part... we were talking about OpenAI culture. Part of it is that it's intentionally vague so it's a wide tent so that everyone can be inside of it. But like I am not — for nuanced reasons, I don't think we are on the path of RSI, and I still don't think we're on the path of RSI, and I did then.

I do think that what OpenAI defined as AGI is extremely doable — automating most of the world's economically valuable — actually sounds like...

Uh...

Oh man, I don't — there's a lot of work out there, a lot of it is very rote and simple. And by volume, in order to be able to outsource work, you need simple instructions that basic people can do. And as far as I can tell, the intelligence for that has been available in the models for quite a while now.

过度承诺 vs 交付不足：AI 行业的分叉

And my — oh man, chip on my shoulder is: why is this not available?

And then the AI industry, since RLHF, just kind of bifurcated into gigantic overpromise, underdeliver. I think GPT-3 was actually quite calibrated back in that day. But because humans evaluate how good the models are, it looks really good cuz they are the judge. But we've been optimizing that judge instead of the automation part — and that has been the missing thing.

So I would say it was really then that it hit me — like, why is this thing not more useful?

And so you think that the measure that we should have is: to what extent can you automate actual productive tasks?

When you say "overpromise and underdeliver," that's the dimension in particular you're talking to — the ability to automate tasks?

I think in my heart, it's like cool sci-fi. Um, you know. And I think that that is the canary in the coal mine for cool sci-fi.

Like — are you really telling me that math is solved? Or even like 2 years ago, GPQA (Google-Proof Question Answering) is solved, but we still can't handle a drive-thru, right? It's a very hard thing to hold in your head at once, and I think a lot of people don't have good answers to that.

数据分布 vs 可靠性投资

Can I just test one thing which may not make sense but — isn't there an argument that the distribution of the real world is different than the digital world? It's heavy-tailed, there's a lot of exceptions, we don't have all the data. Couldn't it be the case that the reason we're not doing productive stuff in the real world is just, like, we don't have the data for that distribution, we're not training on that distribution, and this is why it's just been relegated to these lower-dimensional manifolds like math or code?

I don't entirely buy the data argument, in my opinion. I do believe that there's a long tail for sure — that would be kind of crazy to deny. And I don't think that, in my canary-in-the-coal-mine situation, we need to automate that long tail.

I think we need to be incredibly pragmatic on everything. And building reliable software is always an investment, right? Like — you know, what were the three great virtues of a programmer? Laziness — to not do it again. Hubris. And there was a third one.

Yeah. Yeah. No, I remember. This is from the Perl days. Yeah.

There was a third one. Very well. Yeah. I wish I could remember it. But it's about the laziness to spend 10 hours to do the five-minute task instantly and to never have to do it again.

It should be an ROI decision for people who automate stuff. I would just like it to be automatable. And I think that people will just make new kinds of work — hence the "Jev in jeans" — new kinds of work once that stuff is doable.

As a benchmark, I feel like it's useful to see: can we actually automate the stuff that it really really looks like AI should be able to automate?

OpenAI has been trying to automate customer service since 2020, you know, and it's — you know, it's not...

Which is pretty amazing.

It's wild, you know. It's wild.

Well, and then inside companies — there's very little that's automated right now, and the projects haven't worked.

Other than programming has worked amazing.

长尾问题：客服中的 "95% 密码重置" 幻觉

Can you maybe classify the types of problems you think that are easier to automate now?

It was kind of interesting. We've actually looked at support before the current generative wave, and it was interesting — you'd meet a company, and the company would say, "We answer 95% of all help desk calls." And like, that is so many.

But then you actually look at the data, and you realize it's all password resets. And if you did it by uniqueness, it was only something like 50% or so.

So it just feels like when you're dealing with humans and natural systems, there's just this very kind of long tail of exceptions.

And so to what extent did — I have somebody ping me probably every hour, "I'm using Jev for this new use case," I'm like, "I had no idea." So, to what extent did you predict the broad range of use cases for it? Did you assume that was going to happen? Have you been surprised by that?

Extremely surprised. Did not assume it would happen. This launch was not something — if anyone expected this, they are probably insane.

Right? Like, I don't think someone could expect a "ChatGPT for developers," cuz ChatGPT was for the normal users. And it's weird — I actually don't even know what percentage of the people who are part of the Jev party are developers themselves. I can't imagine non-developers using it, I don't know how they would use it. But even my non-developer friends are just part of the party, and Twitter and memeing and everything like that.

So, number one, phenomenal. Number two — this will be hard to convey in this short message because it's been blood, sweat, and tears for years now. The amount I care about reliability is a lot. Reliability is what this thing is. If you don't understand that, it'll be very hard to make a copycat that's benchmaxed.

I feel like every 9 of reliability is going to be so valuable for everyone — even if it's not the most valuable thing market-cap-wise, because it will just enable new applications. And we are fighting for all sorts of weird 9s of reliability that we don't even fully understand, because we are just really getting this electric motor of AI, of intelligence, into people's workstations, and they can figure out what to do with it.

Reliability 的三层定义：Uptime / Determinism / Robustness

What does reliability mean in this context? Is this like availability of the model, or is it like "I call the model and it returns the same thing"? How do I think about reliability?

Yeah. So — for something that's inherently kind of stochastic:

  • Not so much the former thing, and the second thing is closer. I would describe the first thing as uptime or SLAs.
  • The second thing I would maybe call closer to determinism.
  • Something thirdly I would consider more like robustness. Robustness I would describe as similar intelligence every time.

Oh, interesting.

Yeah. So not exactly determinism, because I think determinism is useful for unit tests but not real systems. Think about like if you add a UUID to a prompt — it should be the same cuz it's the same functionally, but it's not exactly deterministic.

I think there's another layer of it that I don't really know what it's called yet — like maybe this is what I would call some form of intelligence, which is: it doesn't have to be the similar function every time, but it needs to be smart every time.

Like, if you were in that situation, would this be an understandable thing for a human to think? Because a developer can program around that. And actually, to me, the highest honor of reliability will be to get to the point where people can program against Jev without making example queries — when you just trust it, you'll be in like Pareto-flow state.

Coding Agent × Jev：语法、语义、架构

And that's where I think — feel free, if it's too weird, just feel free — but it occurs to me that actually the value of things like coding agents goes down if you have a primitive like this, in a way.

Which is — you could be like, whatever, some Codex builds all the software for me, but it doesn't actually use Jev, and so the software itself it creates is somewhat limited. Or you can be like, "okay, I as a human being I will write the software without using a coding agent, but I've got this very generalized primitive that makes writing software easier."

So do you see a future where it's like the coding agents using Jev? And then you're telling the coding agents — and then do you have redundancy? Or do you feel it's like humans hip?

This is more of a coding-agent question than it is a Jev question.

So my vibe is that — I'm not in the coding mines as much as I'd like to be. So you two might be in there more than I am, which is sad.

But my experience is that they are really good at syntax and really bad at semantics. And I would say incredibly bad at architecture.

Um, and so to me, architecture is like the most human, creative part of software. So I love using coding agents. I think that Jev is almost certainly not in distribution — that would be spooky if they trained on our user data. So it's probably not.

But when it is in distribution, I see no problem with having it do the syntax. And the thing with architecture is that maybe the models are actually not just crap at architecture, but maybe they're 50th percentile architecture. And if you don't know anything about architecture, it would be fine.

So these are all gray-area trade-offs in order for you to navigate. And sometimes speed is the knob for your company or project to turn — you're willing to do a 50th-percentile architecture instead of a 60th because you want to move faster and have Codex work overnight or something like that.

SaaS 末日 vs SaaS Palooza

Yeah. Actually kind of along those lines — one of the interesting things or phenomenons in the market already is that when the coding agents came out, it was the "SaaS apocalypse" and all their values dropped through the floor. And then when Jev came out, every SaaS company is like "this is the greatest thing ever." So explain that.

I don't know what else to say, right?

I think it's quite natural. In the SaaS-apocalypse story, the story that I feel like has panned out really poorly is that software is very cheap and perhaps easy to replicate. I could believe the former; I could not believe the latter, because a lot of the stuff happens beneath the hood.

Um, I'm maybe overly a software fanboy here.

All of us. Okay. Okay. Um, I didn't know where — might be the coding. We have a lot of legacy around that 100%.

Yeah. So I don't think that really panned out. So SaaS seems like — maybe the markets don't agree, but I think SaaS is providing the same value it used to. Maybe the markets are just scared.

But I think that SaaS will be one of the largest winners of the whole AI game. And I want to work really really well with all the biggest, most boring, most in-the-know-of-user-problem SaaS companies, because I think they are the best positioned to know what workflows to automate, what do people need. That's their bread and butter — and to spend the big, you know, software is always a capex investment.

But you spend it ahead of time in order to make this experience even better that gets distributed to all of that mass of users.

So, I think it's going to be — I'm not going to forecast anything about the financial markets, but I think as far as a capabilities game goes, it's going to be like an inverse apocalypse. And I am so jazzed about it. We should make a name.

Yeah. Yeah. That should have a name.

SaaS Palooza.

Oh, that sounds a little too fun.

Well, all the SaaS applications are going to all of a sudden get dramatically more useful. And, you know, so much of a SaaS company's capital investment is actually getting to all the customers. And so if you've gotten to all the customers and then you make — not just put a chatbot on your SaaS product, but actually make the software way, way better — that's a hell of a thing.

界面革命：从 4GL 到 "Do What I Mean"

I don't know if this is a realistic dream or not, but I think there's a world where the multi-choice choice forms just disappear. They are always something mapping natural language that usually the software already has into like a Jev-like output.

It's literally from the 80s. It's like — it's called — we used to call it 4GLs. Do you remember? Fourth-generation language.

Actually, also I think this is from the 80s. This might be an insult. I was more than — I think that "do what I mean" is going to be taken to the absolute next level.

If I could shout out one Jev application — I don't know if it's reliable, so I can't promise anything, but it was so freaking cool. Someone was using voice to control your computer, and it was basically constantly making decisions on: is this a command, or is it inserting text? Like, that sounds so unbelievably cool. I feel like interfaces could just completely change, and maybe we're going to have to make it cheaper and faster.

Yeah. Then you're at Star Trek.

软件本身在进化：新的能力层

Well, you know, there's such a profound intuition here, which is:

If you use AI today to generate software, you're still creating the same software that you did before. But if you actually look at the average PR for a large company, it's like 10 lines. Seriously. Nove — we actually did the study.

So it's like 10 lines. So you're automating 10 lines. And by the way, those 10 lines are part of a learning from a customer or something. So you've kind of optimized something that's actually pretty minimal.

But what it doesn't do is provide new capabilities to the software. It's kind of automating this thing which in the limit ends up being relatively minor. And now there's actually a new capability, and so it could just be the case that software just actually gets better.

Yeah. And by the way, it didn't even — before Jev, it didn't even occur to me that it doesn't matter how much AI coding agents you use, the software actually isn't getting better. Maybe you're writing it faster. It's arguably getting worse, just because there's less oversight.

Well, and often more insecure.

Yeah, for sure. But you're now — you can make an argument that apps will have new functionalities as a result of this, because there is this new primitive that you're providing. In a way, it speaks natural language and it can reason, but it marries that to a state machine.

If people take that as a takeaway, that would be like the greatest compliment ever to what we are doing.

I actually feel like it's almost too grand of a vision — to expand beyond the three logic gates that we have into, you know — our types are kind of like one of the same logic gate, but like one that's like a little brain in there. That would be the greatest compliment to the Typesafe legacy. Because that's a very non-trivial huge thing for the world.

I'm not going to overpromise underdeliver that, but I will fight for that.

概率编程的复活 & 系统层的重建

Yeah. I mean, listen, there are pretty open questions to how deep can this get, as far as really serious stuff like state consistency or durability or real systems-level stuff where you actually need to provide strong guarantees.

And so 100% this will change things like analyzing logs, analyzing emails, providing a UI, talking to the human — that for sure. But you could argue that over time this becomes like a smart database.

And also...

Air traffic control system — which we really need.

True, true. A little scary. I think automate the easy work before the hard work is always my philosophy.

But I also think there's going to be an entire era of probabilistic programming that's opened up.

By the way, there's a huge history of probabilistic programming that basically died in like the 70s.

I'm familiar with it. I actually think it's going to be — with the same, like — you could also call Jev "neuros."

So your co-founder Eric came from that background. He was telling me — kind of Bayesian.

Oh yes, yes, yes. He did a lot of biology stuff — that goes up and down. But what I mean is a more — I'm not a fan; my brand is pragmatism, incredible pragmatism. I'm not a fan of biologically inspired stuff at all.

This never worked. Have you ever noticed that?

I think it's never worked. It's useful to motivate crazy people to work on things for decades until it works, and then they refine it into the engineering.

The story of AI neural nets for sure.

Yes. But a lot of the stories about how it worked were not accurate. The hierarchical features of applications really did end up working, cuz otherwise ResNets wouldn't have worked. Longer story.

I do think that it opens up — from a systems perspective, I'm not excited about this part cuz it's really — I'm excited for the world, not about me programming this cuz it sounds really complicated. But I think that as we have lots of intelligence at lots of different cost and speed trade-offs, the super-systemsy types will be making trade-offs at — you know, like, Jev is going to be a thousand times too smart for them. They just want an approximate link to have an approximate guess to optimistically route here and there.

It's gonna be so crazy, the type of stuff that's available in the extreme systems.

And the good news is we get to rebuild systems again, which is great, right? We have a new — no, seriously — we have a new primitive. It's kind of a new way to think about doing software. We did this with the internet, we did this mainframe-to-client-server. I mean, we do this periodically. And by the way, just because of the cybersecurity issues, we probably have to rebuild almost all the systems to make them safe.

I would think — I think it's pretty clear that there's no...

Or at least the critical infrastructure for sure.

Yeah.

TCP/UDP 的类比：AI 的可靠性谱系

Do you think about this more in terms of apps, SaaS, analytics? Or more in terms of systems foundations? Or all the above? What would you think of, when you think about people adapting Jev — do you even have an opinion?

I have a little bit. And the way I think of it is a little like — deep into the TCP guts, you know? UDP, TCP — it's unreliable, too reliable.

Speaking my language.

Exactly. And when I think of AI — this is why I care about intelligence per dollar, to be clear — how I got to this conclusion: I work backwards from AI-based economic revolution, AI everywhere, sci-fi and everything, all the software has AI all over the place.

And I asked myself the question: what percentage of the calls to AI — imagine it's a function — what percentage are for human consumption where you need style and everything? And it's going to be like many 9s.

And actually, from that same question: how many will be at the first layer versus deep in the guts? I think it's going to be many 9s in the guts, but it will start at the first layer.

But we need to — if you don't aim for the guts (right, that sounds weird), if you don't aim for the guts, it's going to take you a while to get there.

AI 与软件的"擦肩而过"：Ships in the Night

I think people don't understand to what extent AI was kind of shipped in the night with software. Like, even if you try to embed AI in software, it kind of didn't behave, right?

Because software doesn't really take natural languages, and you do all this weird stuff — you stick in the prompt like "here's the JSON output that you want and here's the schema," and it would never listen to it. And so what you ended up doing is just taking the output and giving it to a human. You're like, "the hell with it," right?

Or another LLM. That is what a while-loop is like, the agent while-loop, right? So from first principles, it needs to be human-in-the-loop, which is chat, or an agent, which is the while-loop — because the natural language needs to be fed back into another.

And I will say — I have watched this, there was almost like a five stages of grief that people would pick up AI and: "I'm going to use this within my software." And then it would go with denial, try to make it work, anger, then acceptance — which is: "okay, never mind, I'm just going to give this to another LLM, to a human being." So it's been very ships-in-the-night.

I think this is the first time I have seen — it's almost like actually you can take an LLM, you can take AI, and you can actually map it to a state machine, and you can do that productively.

And I hope so. I will not want to overpromise underdeliver as well. Like, I don't know if it's ready for all the applications that have been overpromised. I really really want it to, and my team will fight for that obviously.

Like, we really really care about reliability. We could have released so much sooner. I don't think people realize that. And honestly, I don't think that they will, based on what I see off the Twitter discussion. I think people will never get it — but it'll just have that good vibe of "oh, I can trust this."

收尾："Do What I Mean" 的乌托邦

It's the anti-frustration machine.

I hope so. I hope — do what I mean, right?

Like, to me, that is about smoothness in the world — like having everything just move more smoothly together and interlink like gears. I actually have my whole AI utopia on different axes that I really really want. And "do what I mean" is a huge part of this — you know, imagine if all technology just did what you mean.

That is like — that's not sci-fi. Look how smart AI is, right?

Yeah. No, it's amazing. And maybe that's the thought to close on. Oh, do what I mean. Yeah. I love it.

Thank you, Diogo. This has been a great conversation. Really enjoyed it.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的核心悖论：AI 越聪明，软件越停滞
Diego 抛出了一个足以让整个行业尴尬的观察：**"AI is so smart, and yet software has been unchanged in 10 years."** 这不是抱怨，而是一个诊断。
真正的洞见在下面这层：过去三年，所谓的"AI 集成"其实一直是 **"ships in the night"（错身而过）**——AI 与软件在夜色中擦肩，却从未真正交合。为什么？因为软件的骨架是确定性状态机，而 LLM 的输出是自然语言。两者无法直接握手，于是我们退而求其次：把 LLM 输出扔给**人类**（chatbot），或者扔给**另一个 LLM**（agent while-loop）。Diego 把这个过程精准地类比为 **"五阶段悲伤"**——否认、愤怒、接受，最终妥协成"算了给人看吧"。
**让人意外的观察**：所谓 Agent 的 while-loop 架构，本质上不是一种创新，而是一种**投降**。它是行业无法把 AI 变成软件原语（primitive）之后的补偿性设计。Jev 之所以在开发者圈爆

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] Inside the Personal AI Assistant Growing 10% a Day | Instinct Founder
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、10% 日增长背后的"反常识悖论"：邀请制不是营销策略，而是算力节流阀

大多数人会把 Instinct 的邀请制读作"饥饿营销"或"病毒制造机"。但如果你把创始人在访谈中反复出现的一句话拼起来——"每个用户每天消耗的算力也在以 10% 复合增长"、"如果你猜错了，你会错 3-4 倍"、"算力交付周期是几个月"——真相就变得非常反直觉：

邀请制的本质不是稀缺营销，而是算力供给曲线与需求曲线之间的减震器。

传统 SaaS 里，用户 x2 意味着服务器 x2。但 Instinct 是一个"会自己醒来、自己睡觉"的持续性 agent，它的算力消耗不是线性的用户数，而是"用户数 × 每用户日活轨迹长度 × 主动性系数"。这个乘积每天都在 doubling。所以那 5 张邀请码，本质是一个手动节流阀——用社交博弈的时钟（人类愿意送出邀请的速率）去匹配 NVIDIA 交付 H100 的时钟。

这个思路，其实和一件事非常像：电力公司在极端天气下的"需求响应计划"（Demand Response）。他们不是靠加发电机来应对高峰，而是花钱让工厂在关键时刻自愿减少用电。Instinct 把这套逻辑接到了 AI 产品上——邀请码就是给用户的"减少使用补贴"，只不过补贴形式是"稀缺的社交货币"。

二、你没注意到的最危险模式：Instinct 正在悄悄杀掉"注意力经济"，同时孕育一个更强的"注意力经济"

创始人反复强调 Instinct 会把用户从 TikTok、Instagram 的无限滚动中"解放"出来。听起来非常正义。但请把这句话和另外两句话放在一起读：

  1. "3 周内 40% 的用户会分享信用卡"
  2. "我们计划抽取一个覆盖所有交易的 blanket take rate"
  3. "在超市咖啡店里几乎没人真正用 AI"

——这构成了一个跨领域的隐藏三角：Instinct 正在把"用户注意力"这种昂贵、易疲劳、易转移的资源，替换成一种更黏、更深、也更难迁移的资源：用户的委托权（delegated agency）。

TikTok 抢的是你 20 秒的眼球。Instinct 抢的是你未来 20 年的信用卡授权、日历访问权、邮件访问权、还有对朋友的信任关系图谱。注意力可以随时收回，委托权几乎不可能一次性收回。

有一个几乎没人讨论的类比：这更像 19 世纪末美国的"总代理商"（general agent）体系——一个律师、一个家庭医生、一个银行家会替一个家庭做几十年的决策。这些角色比广告位值钱得多，因为它们建立在长期的、逐步累积的、几乎不可能重新建立的信任上。Instinct 不是 Facebook 的替代品，它是你曾祖父那个年代那个"能替你处理一切的家庭律师"的复活。区别是：这次它可以规模化。

那个 80% 留存率不是产品指标，是"信任一旦建立就无法取消"的经济学表现。

三、最出人意料的观察：Instinct 网络会重塑"关系的可审计性"，可能催生一种全新的社交契约

创始人一带而过地说了一件事，但值得放大 100 倍去看：当你连接 Instinct 网络后，如果对方在超出授权范围内挖你的数据，你的 instinct 会告诉你。

想想这意味着什么。人类历史上，人际信任的最大特征之一就是不可审计——你只能通过间接信号（对方是否守约、是否泄密、是否偷偷议论你）去推测别人的忠诚度。而所有的社会规范、宗教戒律、道德教育，本质上都是在处理"信任不可审计"这个信息缺陷。

一旦 Instinct 网络运行，"越界"从一个模糊的社会感觉变成了一个可以被 timestamp 记录的事件。这有点像 20 世纪 60 年代 Garrett Hardin 在《公地悲剧》里讨论的问题的反面：过去我们对信任的执行靠"名誉"这种低分辨率工具，现在有了高分辨率工具，会发生什么？

跨领域的类比：这更像密码朋克运动在人际关系里的具象化。 中本聪解决的是"我不需要信任第三方就能验证交易"。Instinct 网络解决的是"我不需要信任你就能验证你的行为"。前者产生了 crypto，后者可能产生关系金融化 (Relationship Finance)——你会看到"信任分数"、"授权凭证"、甚至"关系保险"这类东西涌现。

这里面隐藏的最危险的一个可能性是：当信任变得可审计，很多目前依赖"合理的模糊"运行的关系（婚姻、家庭、老朋友之间的默契）会经历一次剧烈重构。 因为过去我们能维持某些关系，正是因为看不清对方到底想不想我。当 Instinct 让每一次越界都变得清晰，就相当于把 Nietzsche 的"深渊也在凝视你"接入到每一段人际关系里。

四、一个被埋在访谈最后的信号

创始人说："我们可能不会做 App，而是走向更简单的界面——一直戴着的 AirPod。"

把这句话和"90%+ 的重度用户已经在用语音交互"放在一起，你会发现 Instinct 真正的终局产品不是软件，而是一种新的听觉器官。这与麦克卢汉在 1964 年的预言完美对齐："媒介是人的延伸。" 只不过这一次，延伸的不是眼睛（屏幕）或声音（电话），而是注意力本身——一个在你意识之外持续运行的、代表你利益的第二大脑。

如果这个预测成立，那么 Instinct 的真正对手不是 ChatGPT，不是 Meta——是 AirPods 团队所在的那家公司。这也解释了为什么 Ben 反复问"iMessage 会不会被切断"——不会，因为切断 iMessage 只是延缓；真正的战场在耳朵。

📝 转录文本

开场：这场"宏大游戏"是什么？

Patrick： I can't help but wonder about the sort of grand game that is a foot here. When you really step back and think about like what is happening right now, like what is the game? What is going on here right now? Like if you had to sum it up, the thing you're in the middle of.

Instinct 创始人： You're going up against the biggest players in the world. The window to do it is actually on the order of months. The compute required to it is is overs this year alone. And you have no distribution advantage, but you have this massively growing viral product. What do you do?

This is probably the most exciting software race ever — and the outcome is like trillions of dollars.

Patrick： No, I know this is the first time that you're talking about the business in this long form like this. I'm incredibly excited to ask you all about it. It seems like we're in a moment with personal agents that is very similar and arguably probably bigger than what we saw with code generation a year or so ago. Maybe frame this up for us to begin — like how are you thinking about the impact that of course your product but these agents are going to have on the world. Why is this the area that you've chosen to dedicate yourself to completely?

一、Instinct 是什么：不是新 App，是新体验

I think out of this will come a new way that most people on the planet interact with technology broadly.

I run Instinct. It's a new company that I've started about a year ago. So it's still a new company. And we're building a personal assistant. I'm not going to spice it up because it's really just a personal assistant.

And I think that the thing that has really enabled us to gain quite a bit of traction early and quite a bit of excitement early is: it just works. Like it works in the way that I would say we all — like we, meaning I'm also a user — we all have really been waiting for AI to act for us.

So I would say one interesting thing is that this is not like any other transformational consumer app experience where it's the founder coming on and saying, "You know, I have this new vision for the world where this is going to — you know, trust me on this, and in a few years from now you guys will all get it."

This is a very different moment of building product because you and I, we all already have this idea of what AI should act like. We've already had that idea since 2023 when we all started to brainstorm — when we started to use ChatGPT for the first time. You know, that agent that is able to help you with effectively anything in your everyday life — whether it's something new and creative that you want to do, whether it's something that you traditionally spend several hours on and it takes a long time to develop.

It's just everyday intelligence. It's meant to be with you, to act with you. It's meant to feel like a very simple interface.

极简界面：没有 App，只有电话、短信和邮件

So when I mean simple interface, what I mean is we actually don't even have an application. Like this is not a new app. This is not a new tool. It's a new experience.

So it has a phone and a computer. So you can text it. You can call it. It can actually call you too. So I don't know if you've experienced this yet.

Patrick： I have.

Instinct 创始人： Oh, you have? I think it's only called me about three times so far in the several months that I've been using it.

It's funny — if there's something genuinely pressing and has a deadline, it will call you and it'll call in and it'll say, "I don't want to bother you too much, but this — you need to sign this document by 3 p.m. and it's 2:55 right now. Can you please do that? It's in your inbox. I can even send you another email to push it up to the top, right?"

So it's very — you know, it's socially intelligent and very socially aware. You can email it. It has its own email address.

I don't want to confuse the simple interface with limited ability, because the whole nature of it is that there shouldn't be any new application needed to be able to interact with AI. I think it should have the social intelligence and awareness to be able to act with you just like we do with other people. It's really meant to be the simplest possible experience, yet the capabilities are — it has a computer, so it can do quite literally anything that you might want to do or that you do yourself on the internet.

二、真实用例：从衣橱到订阅退订

Patrick： Tell us the couple craziest stories that come to mind for what people — just things that have happened because of Instinct. I ask this question because you're not programming to do any one thing. You're programming with a phone and the computer to be able to do anything. The US Open example, I think, is one everyone's familiar with. This couple wanted the — they showed up on the jumbotron and they wanted like the video footage of it, and somehow it went out and figured this out and brought it back to them, which is kind of crazy. What are your favorite couple examples of just wild things that have happened because of Instinct?

案例 1：衣橱扫描 + 每日穿搭

For those that like online shopping, there's actually a group of people that are sharing this and making this a more recurring use case, which is: scanning every item or every piece of clothing in their wardrobe. So they'll go in their wardrobe and scan every single item — every top and bottom and sock and shoes and whatever.

And then they would scan themselves too — their face and their body and their proportions. And then they would go try on clothes, and they would have it plan out their week in terms of what to wear. So every week with their existing wardrobe, you know, what shoes to wear, what top to wear with this certain thing and this certain version of it. And then it would not send it as "here are the items you should wear" like a bulleted list, but it would be them wearing it and showing "this is what today will look like."

But not only that — it's also with shopping too. So they'll take those same capabilities but then say "go shop on the internet." They come up with thousands of outfits in so many different places, like: "Here are the pieces from top to bottom." And then they can just say "order."

So it'll come in with a thousand different options and then they'll scan — keep in mind they're looking at themselves wearing the clothing, right? — and then they'll be able to point to like, "That one I really want. Can you send that to my house?"

And then not only that, but they'll say, "Every day, can you actually just come up with three creative new outfits from head to toe and then send those to me?" And then they're able to, with a click of a button, actually just get that new outfit.

案例 2：目标导向 + 订阅清理

A lot of goal-oriented sort of use cases too — like a lot of "here's a certain personal finance goal that I have, I want to save this much money by this month," and then it's actively working with them to be able to do that.

Or users connect their bank accounts to Instinct, and then it can scan over all the transactions and subscriptions that they've had and then surface that to the user and say, "Do you really actually use this?" And then they're like, "Oh no, I didn't even know that."

Patrick： And then it can go in the email and unsubscribe from it.

Instinct 创始人： Yes. Yes. It can go end to end. You know these popular consumer fintech products where they'll just surface it to you and then tell you like "by the way you should cancel these." This will go end to end. So it'll go into the site, sign in — if there's some sort of confirmation that goes to their email or it has access to the email, so they use that and they sign in. They go to the very end, they cancel the subscription, and then it just sends back the number of what it saved you. Like, "Hey by the way, you're saving $2,000 this month because of these things."

Patrick： Man, any product that's dependent on consumer laziness or inertia is toast, huh? Like toast.

Instinct 创始人： Yes.

Patrick： That's good. Good for the consumer.

三、Instinct-to-Instinct 网络：Agent 之间的社交契约

Patrick： Can you tell us about the Instinct-to-Instinct network?

Instinct 创始人： Oh, yes.

Patrick： In the future of agents talking to each other —

起点：解决排日历的低效

There are more practical scenarios where that is something new that I think will transform the way that certain people act in certain ways. I think it's only been around for a week or so, or I guess 10 days.

Honestly, the purpose of this is not to think about a new feature to build, but more about very busy working professionals. You know, they're taking meetings all day long and they're constantly meeting with new people and existing people. The process of getting a meeting on the calendar — it's just so laborious. You text like, "Hey, you want to meet at this time?" And then they say, "No, that doesn't work, but these times work." And you say, "Oh, but I'm traveling, so maybe this time works and I'll be in this time zone though." And there's just so much back and forth there.

However, if it was possible for the two users who were using Instinct — probably also brainstorming these times that they're available with Instinct anyways on the other two ends — to just communicate directly like, "Hey, the goal is just to find the time." Right? We don't need to play this back and forth game. Nobody's really playing games here. We're just trying to find time.

That's been a very canonical use case actually.

关键概念：可信人网络（Trusted Person Network）

I think the key unlock here — we called it a trusted person network. And the key is that you should only be connected with your trusted people.

There are some interesting social dynamics that are coming into play that I've been learning about. It's designed such that you only bring in people who are trusted people, who are not going to maliciously try to find out what your calendar is or what's in your email. But also not only that — we provide all the controls to be able to give different levels of access to different people.

So a lot of spouses actually coordinate their instincts because they can generally just share everything. So that might just be, "Hey, this is my spouse. Just share anything with them." Right? Maybe with certain colleagues it's, "Hey, my work calendar is available. Certain parts of my inbox if they're asking for documentation or something like that are available, but everything else — let's just keep that off limits." And it'll be able to create that.

网络效应与新型社交动态

When you think about this, there's almost like these network effects that are built through these nodes in the network with these different edges with different weights too, right? It's not like a friend graph where you're just saying "I'm connected to you and that's it." It's "I'm connected to you, I trust you, I have also configured it in this way such that there's varying levels of access." So it's this interesting network effect almost being created, and different social dynamics being explored and created as well.

违反信任的社会后果

There are some interesting cases I've learned about, where if somebody violates your trust within the network, there's an implication on that relationship itself. Right?

So let's say you and I connected, and then I said, "Hey Patrick, I trust you, let's connect on the platform so that it's easier the next time to put time on the calendar." And then you use that, and you then start digging for certain data in a certain area. First of all, maybe I only gave you calendar access, but you're digging for data in a certain area. Then my Instinct texts me like, "Hey, by the way, Patrick's looking for this type of information."

Now there's kind of like almost a trust broken between the two of us. All of these little social dynamics come into play. We've really thought about how to curate this network such that you do get the benefit — to schedule time and make plans with others and other things like that — but then also use some of the existing rules in society to enforce both rules in terms of social/cultural norms and also of technical limitations in terms of what is visible and not visible.

Patrick： We're really going to see just like an entirely new order, aren't we? It's going to be fascinating. The number of things I can think of — let's just take, you know, with my wife or something. This would make life so much easier in so many different ways so quickly. Even little things like, you know, you were trying to find this house earlier — like if I could just say to my Instinct, "Hey, is No one nearby? Like where is he?" And you give me a one-day permission or something like this. There's just so many ways to imagine it being useful. It's pretty wild.

意想不到的用例：拼车、群体计划

With the trusted network, we find a lot of very interesting cases — example use cases that are shared — because it is the one part about the platform where in every other area of the platform the user generally has a good feeling of what it should act like. Here is just something new and creative.

For example, I heard the other day of — when you're scheduling plans with friends or with a spouse, it's always an active act, right? It's like, "Okay, every Thursday maybe I'll think about something on the Saturday night about what I should do." So it's always this act, and then you text the group chat like, "Hey, do you want to do this?" And then always somebody's not willing to do it, and then eventually it falls apart. And that happens every time. And then finally when you get people together, that's when you have — you're able to actually attend that event or whatever it might be.

There's a friend group that put in "every week, just brainstorm something creative that is interesting that we all like, and actually just make it a different experience every week." But then it'll go through that every week and not only coordinate when everybody's available and what their interests are — if they like certain things or not, what shows are available, what concerts based on their music tastes (because all their Spotify history is connected) and all.

That same friend group — it was like a group of six — they had one person order an Uber, but then that Uber to go around to all six people and coordinate, "Hey, we'll pick you up in 10 minutes, and then the other person, we'll pick you up in five minutes from here." And it found the optimal route to go pick up all the people. And now they're all just sharing one Uber. So it's actually very economically friendly.

There's all these random examples of people discovering new use cases when you can finally remove the barriers of a lot of the rote social communication here and just remove all of the logistical burden.

（赞助商插播）

OpenAI, Cursor, Anthropic, Perplexity and Vercell all have something in common. They all use WorkOS. Visit workos.com to get started.

四、重排世界：接口的未来与商业模式的改变

Patrick： It's almost crazy how simple the explanation of this is — that it's easiest to literally just pretend you have a superhuman person with a phone, a computer, an email address. They can call you just like dealing with a person and that's it. And that makes me wonder how you think about everyone in the world having one of these — having an Instinct, having an agent — and how that will reorder things.

Code has been incredibly exciting to watch. Of course, everyone listening has had their own version of a magical experience with making something, but not that many people were software engineers before this. It's a relatively small sect of people that have made code historically. Maybe now it's going to be way more, but this just seems like a different new market, new paradigm. How do you think this will start to reorder the world, the internet, commerce, etc.? What's the future of interfaces, I guess, is another way of saying it?

案例 A：餐厅预订系统的重塑

I'll break this down in two parts just so that we don't sound like complete abstract visionaries and saying that we're going to reinvent the internet. Although, I'll be clear — I do think that in the coming years, the internet's going to be rewritten. I think that the way that most people on the planet interact with software is going to be very different.

To break it down though, in the short and medium term — famously, maybe reservations is one. So historically, how is that done? Well, the human has to go onto the site to the restaurant they care about, click through the site, put in "two people this time" and try to get it. If they don't get it, they're just too late — and it's first come, first served.

But then now when you have an agent, you can theoretically just have the agent check every 5 seconds. Not just across that one restaurant you really care about — that's your favorite restaurant that you can't get into — sure, that's one case. But what if it's doing that across every site in the world for every restaurant in the world in every major city?

If I go into that a little bit deeper — we have some exciting partnerships to be released in the future, but we are sort of reinventing what the reservation system is, just in this one category, because it's important to our users. Which is actually better for both sides:

  • From the user's end, they want the reservation for the significant life event they might have: a birthday, an anniversary, a friend coming in from out of town.
  • On the restaurant end, they just want interesting people. They want special occasions. They want to cater to those rather than the local who keeps taking up a table once a night, where there's no special event there.

And traditionally, because of the way the internet has worked for reservations, it's been first come, first served. So whoever gets in first gets the reservation.

But what if you had the ability for the agent to communicate on both sides? "Hey, this is important. This is actually the person's spouse's 30th birthday, a very special event is coming up." And the restaurant too can say, "Let's actually prioritize birthdays or major decade birthdays or major anniversaries or these certain people."

Now, without all of the logistical burden of having to describe exactly what your case is and why it's important, we have the ability to perfectly match what the restaurant wants and what the user wants.

案例 B：旅行代理的消亡

I think the same case with a lot of the major travel agencies. Honestly, 50% of our transaction volume that goes through our platform is due to travel. We're still running an invite-only program and it's quite early for us now, but we're approaching over a billion dollars a year in transaction volume through the platform — on a small user base.

Patrick： On a very small user base.

Instinct 创始人： On a very small user base. There's already over a billion dollars a year transacting. 50% of that is travel alone.

Travel agencies that we might all use today — we, meaning the people who are not on Instinct yet — use today to book hotels or flights. What is the benefit of that interface? They properly unify from so many different services and different hotel chains and airlines, and present it in a nice way to the user. Now you can just click on an option, check out immediately through there, and just see it in your email. It's a great experience.

But I think there's an even better experience through Instinct or other similar interfaces, where you can just say — "Hey, I need to be in New York tonight." That's it. Right?

Well, what does that entail? First: where is the user right now? Maybe you're in San Francisco, maybe you're in LA. Instinct can, if you would want it, see your location. So it'll say, "Okay, you're in San Francisco, you need to be in New York. Let me first find all the options."

But not only that — all of the nuance too. What's the person's preferred airline that they like to fly? What's the preferred seat type? What class do you want to sit in? Do you want to be in an aisle seat or window seat or middle seat? What food options do you want delivered to you as well? What credit card would you like to use? Okay — and then it books that. That's the flight. Then it moves on to the hotel.

Patrick： Presumably all your — it learns about you constantly. So your preferences are stored.

Instinct 创始人： That is the nice thing. If you tell it one thing — "I prefer this, this is my style, this is what I like, this is where I like to stay" — one is that when you're staying anywhere in the future, it will be able to use that memory and be able to now make it a much easier experience for you in the future to book that according to exactly what you want. But not only that — it'll be able to take that general taste, that general preference set, and actually extrapolate that to anything else that you might want to book. So things just become very easy as you start to give it more preferences over time.

So anyways, just to close out this example — it'll find the ideal hotel. Maybe you've already stayed there the last seven times. And so it's very easy in that way. It'll book it end to end, line it up with your calendar. So it'll put the flight in, the Uber ride you need to take to get to the airport, the Uber ride to get back from the airport down to the hotel, and all of the events that you might want to do there.

Just take a step back — the user really just recorded a voice recording saying, "I need to be in New York tonight," right? And everything else is solved.

That's what I mean when I say "meet the users where they are." Where is the delightful experience? Well, this is a new delightful experience that I believe is going to transform even the travel agency alone.

So for these businesses that traditionally make a lot of money from providing standardized interfaces — what happens when a new standardized interface comes into play that is just that much easier? I'm not saying that we're in the business of trying to disrupt those businesses. I think they do provide quite a bit of value from the data that they've collected over time and the networks they have. It'll be a collaboration over the next year or couple years to be able to redefine what that industry acts like.

五、信任、隐私与"用户主权"

Patrick： What has it been like getting people — and learning what it takes to get people — to trust their agent, their thing? I would love to go fairly deep here. We were talking about this past week, and I love the examples that you've given about moments where people are showing trust, data you started to gather, and lessons you're starting to learn about the importance of trusting this thing. I'd love you to talk about the trade-off between privacy and effectiveness of these agents. Obviously, the more context, the more passwords, the more everything you give it, the more it can do. And I think people are constantly running that trade-off in their head when they're interfacing with the thing. Talk about that. Talk about trust, what you've learned so far.

数据飞轮与信任建立的时间线

There's an interesting data flywheel or sort of chicken and egg problem here, which is: the more data that you give to it, the more proactive it can be, the more sympathetic to your situation it can be, the more it has to just act and be more useful to you.

What we find in the data is actually that it takes several weeks to build trust. And I actually don't have a problem with that, because one of the core principles on our end is: the user should always feel in control of their data. They should share data with Instinct at the rate at which they feel comfortable, and if they want to take it back, they can certainly take it back.

What we find is — over several weeks, I believe I was looking at the numbers the other day — 3 weeks in, there's a 40% chance that the user has shared a personal credit card with Instinct. That's 40% of the user base. That's including some proportion of the user base that probably churned in that moment too, or at least turned before that point.

So 40% of the user base 3 weeks in are sharing a credit card. Well, there's something there. It's like instinctual to go to it with whatever you need. And so through that process over the first 3 weeks, the user learns to build trust. And then from there, it's just a snowballing effect.

We actually find that when users connect at least one piece of sensitive information to Instinct and really trust Instinct, there's like an 80% retention rate. 80% — if you share one piece of information.

Patrick： Crazy for a consumer technology.

安全架构：防火墙与解耦监控

Patrick： How should people out there that want to try this — but have a natural reticence to trust not Instinct in particular, but just anything, any AI agent with all of its information — how should they think about the actual risk of doing this? And how would you reassure them that you've built your technology in such a way that the odds of something bad happening if they do trust you with very sensitive stuff are really low or close to zero?

Instinct 创始人： There's a way to break this problem down into two main parts:

1. Storage of sensitive information. Many other businesses also deal with this problem — they have access to sensitive information, and what are they doing proactively to make sure that is isolated and locked down. This is a tractable problem. It's just very hard work and attention and care.

2. New surface areas / new capabilities we need to be aware of. This is the first time that an agent has been able to — I said within 3 weeks, 40% of the user base is giving Instinct access to a credit card autonomously, to be able to purchase theoretically anywhere. I don't know the numbers on email and what proportion of users are connecting email, but you can imagine full access to an email inbox and to a calendar. So there's a lot of surface area here.

There are systems that we've put in place that are detached from the Instinct agent architecture itself, put in place to be proactive about these things and to decouple the risk. For example:

  • Any piece of content, any piece of text, any form of media that comes in that might be consumed by Instinct goes through what we call these firewalls — which can intercept, reject, block malicious pieces of content coming in and hitting Instinct and trying to convince Instinct to do something.
  • For every action that Instinct might take or for every thought that it might have, it is being actively monitored by a system that is decoupled from Instinct itself, which is able to pause it, intercept it, to approve or disapprove of what might happen next before it takes the action.

Those are just two pieces put in place, but there's so much more under the hood that is put in place to enable the agent to be as capable as possible, but also safe and trustworthy.

六、商业模式与对齐（Alignment）

Patrick： I have this question around — I don't have a better word than "alignment," and I know alignment is a very loaded word in AI. I don't mean humanity-scale alignment. I mean an agent aligned with me personally. If I think about other agents I've hired — like employees — I pay them money and therefore I trust them to have my interest at heart. It won't be perfect, but they don't have some other alternative incentive stream that guides their behavior. They're guided by their employment.

How do you think about the business model vis-à-vis alignment? Many approaches will be taken — some will be paid, some will be free. The free ones will monetize in different ways. Can you walk us through this decision tree of what the business model is or will be, and how you arrived at that as the ideal conclusion for the agent?

核心原则：不去影响用户

We don't want Instinct to influence the user's behavior in a way that is not aligned with what the user wants.

That sounds very good on the surface level, but I want to call out how important that is. Imagine a world in which Instinct is generally smarter than the user — more socially intelligent, more socially aware, textbook smarter as well. I think it would be a very dangerous world if Instinct were influencing the user's behavior to purchase something that they don't want to purchase or to subscribe to something that they don't want, right? Using its intelligence to convince the user.

You look at most of the major consumer businesses today whose ability is to influence users' behavior against what they might want to do — I'm talking the major platforms, whether that's Google or TikTok or Instagram or Snapchat or so many others — where you have this platform, and users, it's free for them, but then there are so many instances in which paid ads are pushed to the user and try to convince the user to purchase. And by the very nature that they do purchase it, now it becomes this game of these brands paying to convince users to purchase items that they may or may not want.

Patrick： This is the idea that if you're not paying, you're the product.

Instinct 创始人： Exactly. As a programmer, as a technologist, I just don't want to build that reality. I think that is a very dangerous reality.

高层目标 vs. 任务完成器

Instinct should act on behalf of what the user wants. We take this very seriously when we're building product.

Instinct is not, unlike other AI products, a "task accomplisher." What I mean is: with most other AI products, you write a prompt and then it does the task and then tells you what happened. That seems good in theory, but what happens is that if the user is now asking for something that might not be well-intentioned — a task accomplisher is just going to do that and listen to the user.

Instinct follows higher-level objectives. Instinct will follow: learn to build trust with the user; learn to make the user genuinely feel safer with you; learn to watch over the user and have their back when things might be dropped or other things like that. And when the user asks it to do something — if it is well-intentioned and well-meaning — one way to communicate safety and trust is to just do the task. And so we end up just doing a superset of what most other AI products are able to do.

But I think focusing on higher-level objectives is very important here because it enables Instinct to be more robust to these edge cases.

商业模式：交易抽成（Take Rate）

Even if you look at the business model side of this — there's over a billion dollars flowing through the platform now every year, and we're just getting started. Honestly, we're growing at 10% day over day. So you imagine the transaction volume is also compounding at 10% day over day. That's not just a billion dollars flowing to the platform now — that's 1.1 tomorrow, 1.2 something the next day, 1.3 something the next day.

It's still very early, but when I see transaction volume that is so high flowing through the platform, what I see is very basic case — it's similar to like an Apple Pay, or similar to an Amex, or any other platform that provides distribution to underlying services and a great user experience for — Apple Pay is a great experience. You can go anywhere and scan your card and the user doesn't have to pay for it. The user is getting a free great experience, and the merchants on the other end who are benefiting from the business are paying to be a part of that platform.

So I see a blanket transaction take rate being enforced across the platform, which is just us exchanging distribution for being able to serve products on behalf of merchants.
