七、支付栈的重构与与既有玩家的博弈

Patrick： Can you say a little bit more about how that runs into the existing world? I can imagine the layers being — you could be a card issuer, you could be something like Stripe, you could be Visa/Mastercard. There are sort of rails that have been built in the payments world that create convenience and reduce friction and take a vig as a percent of the transaction. Those are some amazing businesses to be sure. How do you think about which of those are partners, which are potential things you would displace? How does that vision of a small take rate on the transaction volume on Instinct — because it's a free product — slot into the existing world?

Take Rate 的天花板在哪里？

Just to put that into context — those are very great businesses. There are so many people along the line where you make one digital transaction: there are like 40 people along the line that make money on that. And just to take a step back — those 40 people making money at each line of the stack are really sharing what, 2 and a half percent, 2%? Depends on where the transaction's coming from. So it's actually a very small piece of the pie.

We're not primarily interested in doing what Amex does best and has the network to do, or what even Stripe does on the internet or some of the underlying payment infrastructure — because it's such a small piece of the pie, and I think they're providing real value.

Where I see the majority of the value — just thinking on the business side — is: if you look at most of the other major platforms in the world and what take rates that they're able to achieve. It's free for the user, it's a great free experience for the user, and the merchant now is recognizing the distribution source.

  • Shopify — I believe is between 2.5 and 3% — providing their services and taking some take rate from those businesses.
  • Stripe — maybe on the lower end.
  • Amazon — has a great platform and taking upwards of 10%.
  • Apple — and then of course the premiere, you have Apple, where you make any in-app purchase, which is 30%.

I'm not saying we're going to be 30% — I think it's very unrealistic for a lot of businesses. But what I'm saying is that we still don't know where along this curve of distribution power versus take rate we're going to be.

I just want to call this out again because I don't want it to be misunderstood: it's a free experience for the user. It's a great free service that we're providing to all of the underlying providers. I'm not focused on finding 30 bips on the 2.5 with some partnership with some payment provider. I'm looking at: can we provide so much value that we're on the upper end of this scale?

The reason why I think this is possible — very practically, 50% of the transaction volume flowing through the platform is travel alone. And we all know the travel industry and some of the rates that —

Patrick： Yeah, the OTA rates are high.

Instinct 创始人： It's very high. For flights, maybe it's on the lower scale — you know, how many single-digit percentages can you take off of a flight? Or for hotels — some of these boutique hotels are offering to pay up to upwards of 30% for every transaction you're able to deliver for them. And I'm not saying again we're going to be at 30%, but you can see the range.

These are existing business models that we can bootstrap off of in the early days. But then, what would it be like to take that and extend it to effectively every major industry? This is only the case if it is true that most digital behavior then moves to these new types of interfaces — which is well, again, "no interface." But it is only the case if there's significant distribution power. So I think it's actually a quite interesting intellectual question about how this evolves over time.

Uber Eats、DoorDash 会站在你的对立面吗？

Patrick： It seems to me like there's going to be a serious corporate agent war — you've already seen this with Amazon and Muse. You've got all these established players with tremendous vested interests and relationships with customers, that both Instinct and other agents could really disrupt in a major way. What are you thinking about that? Like, how do you interface with the other great services out there? I'll pick a random one — I use Uber Eats a lot. It's kind of a pain to click through the thing. I can imagine a lot better experience on a snappy WhatsApp connection with Instinct or something saying, "Hey, I want my usual from this restaurant." And that's it — it's got its computer and it goes on to Uber Eats and orders. At what point does Uber Eats not like that anymore?

Instinct 创始人： So I'm serious when I say — I mean, you're alluding to this too — that I think most digital services or industries are going to be not disrupted, but just changed and transformed.

I was running through an exercise the other day of pulling effectively every digital service or business or application from various different verticals and industries, and sort of plotting it along the line of saying: what proportion is the user's attention experience on the product as a proportion of revenue, and what proportion of it is delivering the underlying service (meaning if the user didn't use the app, what proportion of that transaction or revenue is due to the underlying good/service being provided)?

Your question is of that upper end of the scale — where let's say the majority or some significant amount of revenue is due to attention on the application or advertisement. So yes, that's Uber. I actually don't know what Uber's number is. That's a lot of the restaurant or food delivery services. That's the travel agencies. That's even Amazon themselves, with the upselling that they do on their platform.

Okay, there's one simple way to look at this — which is: okay, well, it's 70% ads, 30% good, and so therefore you're going to slash the 70% and they're going to be a 30% business moving forward.

There's another way to look at it, which is — take any business, let's take Uber Eats or DoorDash. I don't know the numbers, but they know the numbers: as they reduce the number of clicks needed to check out to order food to your house or order an Uber, as they reduce that time to check out, the transaction volume increases because it's reduced friction to get the same underlying good.

And we're taking something like Instinct and making that friction to do anything almost zero. It is literally zero in the case that there is proactive behavior.

Example — ride sharing: if Instinct has access to your calendar and owns your calendar and is booking all these events and knows where you need to be in person here and in person there — what if Instinct just always had a car lined up for you at every time where you need to be, so that it's out of your mind to know "oh, in 5 minutes I need to order this Uber because I need to be in this place in 45 minutes and there might be traffic"? Instead, what if it was just proactive behavior — a car will always be lined up and you will never be late because it's going to calculate traffic?

What would that do to Uber's business or any ride share business if now the default, for existing riders that love Uber or Lyft, is to have proactivity now make the friction to experience that good/service nearly zero? I think that will result in that 30% looking a lot bigger.

Example — food delivery: maybe you're coming home late off of an airplane and you need to be at your house and you haven't eaten yet. And it just texts you and says, "Are you hungry? Do you want the same thing you ordered yesterday or 5 days ago? I can send it to your house if you'd really like it. I know you're in the Uber — I ordered the Uber too — and you'll get here at this time." And then the user just says, "Yeah, please order that." So with very little friction, now — what will that do to the total transaction volume or the amount of times a user interacts with the business? I actually think it'll go up.

So it's this interesting game. This interesting transition period between users spending a lot of time on apps — painfully spending a lot of time on apps — and that being a monetizable surface, because that's where the user's attention is, to the user actually interacting with the business even more, which is counterintuitive, because the friction to do so is much less.

与既有玩家合作的路径

I think the way to approach any big change like this is not to come in hot. We're still a new company, we're just getting started. Not to come in hot and immediately just start disrupting certain businesses, but go to them and just say, "Hey, this is what we think your business looks like. You guys certainly know what your business looks like. This is how users on Instinct are interacting with your business now already. What can we do in collaboration to make that a better experience for both sides, where it makes sense for your business, it makes sense for our business, and certainly it's just a much better experience for the end user?"

That is something that we're exploring and learning across so many different industries right now.

传统企业该如何准备？

Patrick： If you think about the things that traditional companies could be doing now to prepare themselves for an agent-rich world — let's just pretend half of Americans have an agent doing all the stuff you just described, which sounds incredible and magical and very democratizing. I think that's maybe something to highlight — this is going to bring to everyone capabilities that have been rare or expensive. What kinds of businesses are going to thrive in that world? What should businesses think about doing to prepare for that world to be successful in it?

Instinct 创始人： I think it comes again back to that breakdown — where is your revenue coming from? What proportion of that is the user spending time in your application? What proportion is the user having access to the underlying service?

If your business benefits from more transaction volume, not at the cost of less time on the application, then you're going to be in a really great spot, because Instinct is going to make it 100 times easier to do that.

If you're in a spot where nearly 100% of your revenue is due to the user's attention — I think that, even in a lot of cases against the will of the user and what they want to do — there are so many games or malicious product building of trying to convince the user against their will to use the application more. A lot of these social media companies where the user doesn't feel happy when they're on the app, they're unwillingly giving their time to the app and they can't get off and they keep scrolling — but it's because that underlying business is benefiting from the user's attention.

It's almost like liberating for the user. This is why it's so important for Instinct to act on behalf of what's best for the user, because it's able to deliver experiences like this — where you can actually liberate the user from being sucked into these infinite scrolling moments.

Any blanket advice is probably just not well thought out. It's a case-by-case basis, and certainly different within different industries.

Very practically — we're finding, there are early partners with very innovative CEOs or other executives that are really thinking ahead, and they're willing to be early partners. What we're discovering is almost like a playbook: how every business, no matter where they exist along that risk curve, can discover what are the risks, so they have some data to work with, and then we can work together on finding ways to land in a happier spot for both sides.

One of those things is: you don't have to go all-in. You can mitigate the risk, scale down the experiment. They can run A/B tests to figure out — okay, if we enable this certain thing across 1% of users, how do they interact with the business? Does the user like it more? Is it a more enjoyable experience for the brand side too? Does the transaction volume go up? Does the willingness to buy the product go up? There's a lot of work in product discovery too — a lot of times the user doesn't know they want to buy something, they can't find it, right? Does that actually increase the user being able to find exactly what they want?

Doing scaled experiments here is a really great playbook to run, because you can scale the risk accordingly. You get proportional data, so you don't have to run it across your entire user base. That's what we're finding is really working so far. It's still very early, so we're still discovering this in real time.

八、Side Quest：算力、基础设施与产品"手感"

Patrick： Before I ask more questions about the world-reordering nature of personal agents, I'd love to take a little side quest in the conversation and talk about what it takes to do all this — to provide all this. I want to hear about what's been hard about building this — the technology itself. I want to hear about compute. I think you said to me at some point that you spend, I don't know, a big chunk of your time just thinking about compute right now. And maybe that's different 5 years from now, but certainly in the moment when you're growing fast, this is a really important thing. I'd love to hear your thoughts on that.

Maybe before we do that — just because I'm remembering all of our conversations, it would be helpful for you first to frame up what you want it to feel like and why it's so important to you that it sort of has this distinctive quality and performance, before we talk about then how you deliver those things.

从"能力"转向"可理解性"

I could talk all day about this because I think that is just so important. Honestly, as a product builder, it's a new muscle to flex and to build. But really thinking beyond capabilities is something I really want to push here.

Over the last 3 years, we've seen all these different product launches and new products saying "AI can now do this" or "AI can now do that" — and "did you know it can do this thing because of this small technical thing that happened under the hood?" I think the consumer is first fatigued by all this — they don't know how to access it. And then second, I think we're missing the point.

Early on, one principle that we held was: let's not focus on capability. Let's only focus on understandability. How much does the user understand about what's happening? What is their ability to predict what will happen when they ask this or when they do this or when they interact with it in this way?

Honestly, I think that is one of the major angles or factors that has led to engagement numbers that are completely off the charts, or the viral word-of-mouth growth happening at 10% a day.

关注细节：文字如何"呈现"

It's understandable. It just feels — if I were to describe it, for lack of a better word — it should just feel good in some way, in the way that it communicates to you. The purpose of communicating or sending a text message is not just the meaning of the text itself. It's down to underlying — even, what is the shape of the text message itself? And how will the user feel when they see that?

If you see a big blob of text that requires the user to scroll a little bit to find the next message, versus maybe you frontload some of the information so that the user really gets it in the first 30% and then can optionally read the rest. Thinking about how the user might read — even read patterns where the user might read 80% of the first line, and then maybe 50% of the next line, and then it tapers off, so it looks like a flag. That's a consideration that should be made.

If Instinct has the ability to think about things like this — okay, the user is going to spend most of their time reading the first two lines, and certainly the first part of each line. So how does it craft its message to deliver in the lowest-fatigue way, or with the least amount of cognitive load placed on the user?

There's a lot of consideration put into this in terms of product building. There's quite a bit of work we do on the infrastructure side to make it fast and affordable to serve — but this is another area that is just so important, and is going to be a differentiator.

品味 vs. 数据驱动

Patrick： How much of that is your personal and the team's taste versus it being the result of a quantitative type process — like iterative quantitative process of "okay, we did A/B/C testing of all — you know — emoji reaction versus short versus long, and this is the thing that is optimal"? Like, how much of it is an optimization exercise that's data driven versus your own sensibility and your team sensibility?

Instinct 创始人： Honestly, it's just all of the above. When you're thinking about building evals or evaluation or other testing frameworks to be able to test for these very soft qualities — or actually very long-term qualities — two or three weeks in, does a user trust Instinct? How do you measure that? How do you run simulated evaluations to test if the user is going to feel trust in 2 or 3 weeks from now?

A lot of it is staged rollouts over time. So I might come in and build a slightly different experience, and then I'll release it to myself and I'll play around with it for a little bit and see how I feel about it — I'm just very opinionated about these types of things. And then if I feel comfortable with it, I'll send it out to the team. I'll say, "Hey, you guys should try this." We'll see how they feel about it. Then they'll send it out to our smaller early access group, and they'll play around with it, see how it feels, and then if we're confident, if there are any tweaks we need to make, we'll do that, and then eventually roll it out to the general public.

This is very important because Instinct is quite capable and is one of the most capable products out there. But I'm not saying that over the next couple months or years others aren't going to come and deliver the seemingly same experience. But I think this deep focus and priority on how the user feels — and how to make it the most enjoyable experience beyond just the words that it's saying, just the way that it feels — is just so important.

九、增长曲线、算力扩容与生死时速

Patrick： One of the great things about the history of technology is this race between incumbents getting quality and innovation versus upstarts like you getting distribution. 邀请制的原点

Instinct 创始人： Well, I think you just described everything all at once in about 20 seconds there.

If we think about the growth story so far — we are, I guess famously or infamously, serving an invite-only product, which is honestly not meant to be an exclusive thing. Although some users are treating it like that — but that's really not the intention.

The goal is: I'm ambitious. I want to scale this thing as fast as possible, but I also want to do it in a responsible way that enables us to not wake up one morning and have 10 times the number of users, and then 80% of them actually can't talk to it because there's not enough compute.

We first started this program — we gave it to about 200 people. It was close friends and family members, and we just said "go try it out." And then the next day, like five people came onto the platform because they just referred it to somebody. Just to describe a little bit more — it's an invite-only platform, and every user has 5 invites. So just 5 invites.

So we rolled it out to 200 people. Next day it was like 205, and then the next day it was 210. So it's like, "Okay cool, a couple people are sharing it to like one person." But then that just started to accelerate. It was very odd. It was like, "Okay, it's like not 1%, 2%," and then it started to be like 3%, 4%. And then once we hit a couple thousand users, some people just started to share it online too — natively share some cool use case that they had with it. And then that accelerated the growth even more. It started to turn into 6%, 7%, 8%, 9% — and now I believe we're like 10 or 11% day-over-day.

Just to call that out — it's not that we're doing some sort of creative marketing event every — we spent $0 on marketing so far. It's not that we're doing something every single day to support this growth. Every day about 10% of the audience — or slightly less because you can refer multiple people — are making a decision to give up one of their 5 valuable invites to somebody else. But that is happening every single day at a 10% rate.

There's something very significant there when I talk about strength of word of mouth. It's honestly a little bit surprising. It's one of the strongest cases of word-of-mouth growth. I find all these stories of people saying — hey, they'll actually be ashamed. They'll email me and say, "Hey, can I please get an invite? I think I have a friend that has it, but I don't know if I make it into his 5 friends." Right? And then there are also people who are bragging, "Oh, I got three invites left, and I'm just holding onto them right now." So there's so much happening — people that want access to the product, but these odd social games happening of people using their invites. I was seeing the other day there were some invites selling on eBay too. It's like 300 bucks — people were buying these invites on eBay.

算力问题：如果你猜错，就错 3-4 倍

So the big question comes — the thing that most people are asking right now: yeah, I mean, you have much bigger players that are able to distribute to a billion or two billion people on the planet immediately. Maybe they might not be compounding naturally as fast, but they have such a great top-funnel distribution. And then you have us — compounding at a very very fast clip every day, but we don't own a major service that has two or three billion people to distribute to immediately that day. So it's this interesting question — where does the curve line up? Where's the inflection point?

There's another problem that comes with this too, which is that it's an interesting scaling problem. This is what is, I think, the core of the problem — that I spend like 40% of my time just worrying about.

It's not like the traditional other consumer products that grew very fast, where to double the number of users on Instagram or Facebook, it would be this many number of other requests going through the platform — and yes, there's a scaling story there, and it's certainly hard infrastructure work; we also have that, to be fair. But what do you do when the underlying compute also needs to — you know, 10% every day?

We've been doing this for several weeks now. What does it mean when the amount of compute you need access to is doubling effectively every week? Do we buy compute, you know, 2x of what we have right now? Well, we're going to consume that in a week. So then do you buy 5x? Well, we're going to consume that in less than 3 weeks. Do you buy 10x? So now it's like you're 10x leveraged — right? If you can even stomach what it's like to buy 10x ahead. But then you're going to consume that in a couple weeks from now.

That is the hard problem. It's thinking about how far ahead — how far ahead do you buy? It's going at a faster rate than Claude Code or Codex or some of those other applications, where they also had to reason about other similar exponential-type problems.

The other subtlety here is that it's not like a certain business where when you double the number of users you can buy 2x more resources in order to power it. It's that the resource has a lead time of several months. So you can't just go out tomorrow and start buying compute — because honestly, you get taxed like 3 or 4x what it is if you're wrong. You're wrong by 3 or 4x.

Say we don't actually do 10% for a very long sustainable period. Let's just say it's 5 to 8%. But 5 to 8% compounding day-over-day for 3-4 months, which is the lead time to bring compute online, and that's even aggressive itself — that's 100 million users. So then do you buy compute for 100 million users?

Those are the types of questions I'm wrestling with. If you're wrong, you're very wrong. You get charged 3 or 4x.

单用户服务成本与推理优化

Patrick： What about if you zoom in on the individual user and the cost to serve them on a day-per-day basis? Do you have a — per week, I don't know what the right metric is — like how much me using my Instinct costs in inference per day or something like this? Do you have a sense of that scale? What is that scale?

Instinct 创始人： One thing that I think is to our advantage is we've figured out how to serve the product. When we run — no matter how you evaluate, whether it's A/B tests, whether it's internal evaluations, or tracking engagement across users that might be on one model or the other — we're able to deliver the same performance as, honestly, Opus 5 — which is now, I guess we're dating ourselves, Opus 5 is frontier-level intelligence.

We're able to serve — it's the same engagement rate, the same A/B test performance, the same internal evaluation performance — but at a cost that is very very low, and is actually very affordable. We're running this program — every user has the product for free — and our goal is really to deliver this product at affordable — I'm not going to commit to free for a lifetime for now, but that is my personal goal, to be able to deliver this product for free for everyone for a lifetime.

It's just hard infrastructure work. I don't know how deep we want to get on this, but — if I give one example — if you use frontier APIs from some of the main providers, you are taking a blanket cost on a certain request and for all of the requests that might be needed to power that product for that month.

But there's a lot of different work happening through productivity that is happening throughout the day that doesn't actually need to finish in hundreds of milliseconds. It needs to finish in minutes or even hours. There is batch work that is consuming a lot of content that can be served with deployment shapes that are 3x, 5x, 8x more efficient on the same underlying compute.

So when you customize these inference deployments to perfectly shape the data and the workloads that you're serving, you're able to find these 30% here, 5x there, 6x there, 10% here — and all of those compound to a rate where we were able to serve at a very low cost.

十亿用户级的算力需求

Patrick： How do you think about solving the bigger problem of how far ahead to buy? If I think about this at true scale, like you get to scale of a billion users or something — how much new compute demand do you think this will represent? It seems Codegen has obviously been an enormous amount, but ground us in some sense of scale — like, whether it's per user or some way of understanding just how much new compute this will require.

Instinct 创始人： I'm just saying it's going to be a lot. If you just think about — let's just ignore compute and just think about how many tokens are flowing through the platform.

The products that are, I would say, breakout products of a couple months ago — let's say in the code generation space — where it requires the user to prompt it, and then it goes and runs for something, and then it comes back to the user and then asks for something else, and then the user sends something again. Sure, a lot of that is background work, and so there's quite a bit of tokens consumed there.

But here — Instinct has the ability to wake up and to sleep at any moment in time during the day. That might sound a little odd, but its architecture is enabling it to do that, so that it can — if you have a meeting that you're running late to and you need to order an Uber, or if the — you know, if they ordered the Uber and the user is not showing up — help the user through those moments.

Proactivity is going to continue to expand over time. There's this big compute buildout with the earlier breakout products in the AI space that are just scratching the surface of productivity or of background work. Now we have something that is almost natively proactive. It is a smaller subset that is actually interactive.

So the amount of compute that is going to be needed is going to be honestly orders of magnitude more than what we thought we needed. With more productivity comes more care for the user, more time to think about certain things that could go wrong or not go wrong. There's just so much happening under the hood.

Maybe Instinct wakes up at 6:00 a.m. because it knows you wake up at 7 a.m. And then it goes and scans everything, makes sure that everything's ready for the day for you. And then it realizes, "Hey actually, now is not a great time. It should just go to sleep or do this one thing in the background and not notify the user." And then it realizes, "Oh, at 4 p.m. there's something that's coming up. There's value that could be provided." Maybe the user doesn't even know how to interact with Instinct in that way, and so Instinct thinks it's well-meaning and something valuable to the user — so it might wake up at 4 p.m., do the task, contact the user, and the user could lean into it and do that task.

You see how much work is going on in the background — that with coding products you don't really have. So yeah, I don't mean to quote a number here. I'm just saying that the shape of the product and of the workload that's going to be run — we're just scratching the surface in terms of how many tokens.

十、Meta 的 Muse、竞争与差异化

Patrick： What do you think of Muse? What do you think of the product?

Instinct 创始人： I think it's a great product. I was playing around with it for a little bit and I think it's interesting. It's a different take. Sure, you can say some of the underlying architecture might be similar, but I think it's fundamentally different. Instinct is meant to be simple and very easily accessible — of the soft qualities we were talking about earlier, of really thinking from the user standpoint about what's important and what's not, and how to make this task easier and easier to read. Versus a new application and a new interface.

Sure, maybe over time we have an application that also delivers on a different set of tasks, but I think it's a great product.

I just spend very little of my time thinking about competition and other players in the space, because — you walk outside, you go to the nearby cafe, and you think about how many people within that cafe are actually using AI in the way that they imagine they would, or the way that they want to be using it. And I would say very little. And that's here. You go over to other countries or other cities, and it's certainly less of a case.

So I think it's still an open space. It's still an exciting time. I think it's an interesting game that's going to be played and rolled out over the next coming months and years. I'm just focused on building the best product experience.

十一、失误、安全与主动防御

Patrick： What have been the blunders so far? What's gone wrong? What have you done about it? I'm sure more things will go — I mean, this is just going to be an explosion of emerging properties and mistakes, and the end's going to be really high. How do you think about things to guard against proactively, things to be reactive against? Yeah, talk us through the darker side of building this, or the harder side of building this.

Instinct 创始人： I think it's important to never be reactive and to always be proactive — to look ahead for what new surface areas are being introduced and what new risks might come.

This is the reason why we ran the early — well, this early access invite program — from the start. An earlier version of the product didn't have firewalls in place, didn't have these active monitors in place and so many other pieces of infrastructure that were meant to get ahead and be proactive about being able to provide that much control to the agent and existing system to be able to secure.

So yes, the early version of the product had some of these mistakes, and we addressed it. We went above and beyond and didn't just patch the problem — we built a different system to systematically solve these types of problems.

I said this earlier — the user should always be in control. The user should always be in control of their data. The user can share as much as they'd like or as little as they'd like, and if they ever change their mind at any point in time, they can always retract access to these certain services.

安全的哲学与幻觉过滤器

Patrick： Makes me wonder — what's the future of security? Even if you're the best in the world at this, which maybe you'll have to become, you're going to have so much information and context on so many people. Security is a big problem across the world. All these great hacking examples we've studied — it's wild what these things can do. The capabilities are going to get stronger. Do you have a general philosophy? I'm just curious for you to riff on the future of security and safety, and guarding against — I mean, early in technology revolutions of the past, there are these always — enormous hacks, enormous data breaches. It's hard to imagine this won't happen in this technology revolution too. How do you think about this and the responsibility of providing safety, given how much you'll know about people?

Instinct 创始人： It's the most important problem.

I think it comes to building security and safety and a mindset towards that into the core values of the company and the people and the way that you build product. This is topical because anytime — if you look in the past, the last 20-30 years, when any new breakout or new consumer experience has been revealed, there's always been immediate backlash of "whoa, this is different and confusing" — different being unsafe. And there's always this V-track. The last 20-30 years, seeing some of that now.

But also, just staying core to the principles that you hold — the user is always in control of their data, they should never feel out of control — and then being proactive about the systems you put in place to get ahead of these types of things.

If I call out one example — like a hallucination case that existed. First, language models hallucinate all the time. But with a product like this, you don't want a language model to be hallucinating. So we put in place a more systematic solution that will detect — before an action is taken, before a thinking trace is executed as a tool call, before any action might be taken — it is validated and scrutinized by something that is decoupled from the same incentive system as the underlying agent.

Patrick： It's like a watchdog.

Instinct 创始人： Yeah. A filter that's able to find, "Hey, this proper noun was just generated out of the — you know — due to some sampling error in the underlying model." And so it's very easy in hindsight to be able to capture these types of mistakes. And these are hardened.

We have world-class security teams that are constantly working proactively to find harder and harder adversarial cases, to try to find edge cases here and there. And it's becoming rarer and rarer over time.

One subtle part about building a platform like this is that it's getting better over time. As we continue to do more adversarial testing, as we continue to be more creative about certain edge cases, these models are just getting better and better over time towards being robust to these types of attacks.

十二、界面的未来：从 App 到"永远开着的耳机"

Patrick： On the other side of the ledger, everyone always shows that beautiful visual of each generation of the iPhone — you can see it getting better over time and more and more refined. What's that arc for you? It's so interesting because it's not an application. It's not a device. It's an interaction through existing communication channels — WhatsApp, iMessage, etc. What are the things that you're adding and envision adding over time that will make the platform and the product more powerful than it is today?

更简单，而不是更复杂

Instinct 创始人： The product experience right now is very simple, very very simple. Simplicity is one key that we focus on — but I actually think that it becomes even more simple over time.

We may roll out an application in the near future, but I actually think we're going to trend more towards a simpler interface. Do you even need to open the iMessage application and type in a certain piece of content and send the message out, and then look at what the response is after when it's done?

We have a certain subset of users that interact with Instinct only through voice — actually, more than 90% of the interaction, of the messages that they send to Instinct, is primarily through voice. I even have this action button on my phone, and it's paired to — I can click on the action button and I can say, "Hey, say hi to Patrick in two hours from now. I think you have his email address, you can go send him an email." And then I can just send. And then it goes and sends. I don't even need to unlock my phone and open the iMessage application and type the message in.

You can even imagine with real-time voice, with voice recognition that knows what your voice sounds like and has the discretion to know when you're addressing it and not addressing it — where you could have, let's say, an AirPod. Not a new type of AirPod, just an AirPod, because it's good enough. And it's just on. You might be going on a hike or bike ride or a walk or a run, and you're just catching up like:

  • "Hey, this contract needs your review." "Okay, I need to review that."
  • "Hey, this news article just came in — here's the headline, here's the takeaway."
  • "This new project was released, you should take a look at this."

And you're just in your ear like, "Okay, got it. Got it. Put that on my calendar. That's 15 minutes. Okay, yeah, that's not important, so go clear that part out. Oh, this person needs my help — I know the answer to that, so just tell them that it's this."

It's going to be much easier over time. I think in the long term the interfaces become much simpler. But in the short and medium term, maybe there are more expressive interfaces. We have a files feature that enables Instinct to send effectively entire sites — like full web applications — to you, to show more, whether it's a trip itinerary or a wedding plan or something that requires more creativity and more surface area. It can generate those on the fly and show that to you.

软件的坍缩

I think there's something interesting there. You look at the last 20 years of application building or product building — where anytime you needed a new interface to showcase some piece of information, you needed to build an application for it. It's this long software development lifecycle to produce the application, ship it out to people, and then you find some feedback like "hey, I wish it looked like this," and then you make the improvement and ship out a new version. This is on the order of months.

Over the last 20 years there have been all these applications built for so many different purposes, so many different things, and now the consumer is just fatigued. Every time I need something like, "Is there an app that does that?" — I don't need — I think that all of that collapses down in the future. I think that all of software is going to collapse down into, honestly, a single very very easy to use interface.

Don't get that confused with capability being limited. I think capability is going to expand.

从任务执行到高层目标

Patrick： What's the craziest thing you can imagine capabilities-wise?

Instinct 创始人： When we move away from these daily tasks like "I want to do this, can you do it" — that friction is going to go down to zero. It will start towards pursuing higher-level objectives that are aligned with the user, where the user is able to describe not just "hey, can you track this workout for me — I did this and I performed here and this is how I did," but more about "hey, in 3 or 4 months from now, over the next 3 or 4 months, can you work with me to make sure that I hit these certain goals?"

Actually, a lot of people are starting to experience or discover that today — of "you want to gain this many pounds, you want to lose this many pounds, you want to hit this certain mile time." Being able to specify objectives and goals, and then be able to work with it to achieve those goals and objectives.

I see small businesses being run now that are native to Instinct itself, meaning the entire business is run on Instinct — where the entire back office is now completely functioning on top of Instinct. And even parts of it are fully autonomous. Talk about high-level objectives — "in this certain area, make sure that this inventory level doesn't drop below this and doesn't go above this." So now it's not saying "hey please order this" as a static task — it's "pursue this higher-level objective and use the tools and devices that you have available to accomplish that."

I think that's the future. There are so many cases of objectives you could state and have it pursue for an unbounded amount of time. That's the meta-level picture — it's moving away from individual use cases over to higher-level objectives.

关于 "Her"、个性与关系

Patrick： Do you want it to have a personality that's distinctive for each person? I'm thinking now of the movie Her, where there's this relationship that forms between this omniscient, omni-capable agent and the user. What do you think about that aspect? I think of Instinct as this very seamless, almost quiet, extremely capable, reliable thing, but not as having a cheeky personality or something. How do you think about that component of the product?

Instinct 创始人： Well — you mentioned Her, I guess comically. Relationship building or anything in that area is not something that we want Instinct to do or to pursue or to develop with users.

If I describe more about what it should act like and feel like and represent within the person's life — it's almost like that socially aware operator that knows, no matter what room they're in, what is best for different people and what is the best interaction pattern. And it learns that over time.

I think it's possibly one of the most customizable — if you even call this an app — one of the most customizable apps ever. Because it's able to not just serve different versions of it — it's able to evolve over time. That's why we put so much care into the software pieces: pick up on when the user didn't like it being said in a certain way, or if there's a lower response rate in a certain way because it's just too much text, or they don't want to look into a huge file to know what you're talking about. It's going to learn those over time and just become easier and more delightful for the user to use.

We're not trying to impose certain experiences onto users. We want to solve this more from a higher level — it's just ability to adapt to exactly what is the best communication style and task execution style.

为什么叫 Instinct？

Patrick： Why is it called Instinct?

Instinct 创始人： I liked Instinct as a name for so many different reasons. The main thing is that Instinct should not be this playful thing that you might bully once in a while, that you think downward on, that it's this thing that only takes the dirty work off your plate.

I think it's this new, creative, exciting, competent actor — that there's mutual respect and trust, and they feel safe, and they trust that it has their back, that it's intelligent, competent, socially aware to know how to act in certain situations.

It's a bet. I like that Instinct is not named like someone's name or something like that to try to personify it into a human. It's more of — I don't even know what an Instinct is. I develop my feel for what it is and for what the brand is through just using it. Towards really thinking about this feeling of what it should be like.

I think it's a benefit that every user is able to come into it with a fresh slate. There's no prior in their mind about what it looks like or what it's named. It's purely through the product experience itself.

十三、盟友与对手：iMessage、WhatsApp 与渠道

Patrick： Who are your enemies and allies? I can imagine in WhatsApp or something you could get shut off — that's a Facebook product and it's a key channel for you. iMessage is an Apple-controlled product. Who are your friends? Who are your enemies? How do you think about some inevitable competitive realities here?

Instinct 创始人： I would focus less on "Instinct is an iMessage app" or "Instinct is a WhatsApp app," and more about — very grounded from first principles — what are the interfaces that users trust today, that they're familiar with interacting with today, and how can we deliver the experience of Instinct through the channels that they already interact with every day?

Primarily thinking: we're not pinned to iMessage. Actually, more than 50% of our traffic doesn't actually run on iMessage itself. But certainly users that are comfortable with iMessage are very familiar with it.

It's more about just thinking about what is most practical for the user, and we're going to shape-shift as we see towards just delivering that very simple, easily accessible, sort of zero-friction experience that it is today.

十四、融资、投资人与资本战略

Patrick： I know your latest round is something like a billion dollars at roughly a $10 billion valuation — some of the best investors in the world: Thrive, Benchmark, Coatue as the leaders of the round. How do you think about the future capital needs of the business alongside this? And how did you pick the partners that you picked?

Instinct 创始人： I'm just very lucky to work with some of the most supportive partners around the table — who have been through different but similarly shaped technology transformations in the past.

I would focus less on the numbers and more about the demand in the space — the demand for a product like this, or the demand for an experience like this. It's because it really is delivering on that AI experience or product experience that I think we've all really been waiting for.

It's also capital-intensive. We're a new company, trying to create something that's going to hopefully be distributed to billions of people on the planet every day, and at a very affordable cost. When I say affordable, I mean compute costs are high, and we're trying to deliver it in a very affordable way to our users.

So it's just very capital-intensive. There has to be some bootstrapping — especially if you think about the business model that we're chasing after. We could very easily just say, "Hey, it's going to be a certain subscription, and everybody on the platform needs to pay 100 bucks a month." There are shorter-term rewards that we can chase after. Or, we could raise a little bit of capital and use that towards — what is venture capital meant for? — to be able to take certain calculated risks, to prove transaction volume, or to prove experience across certain industries. That's how you escape these local optima of the subscription plan or other things like that.

十五、结语：最善良的事

Patrick： When I do these, I ask the same traditional closing question of everyone. What's the kindest thing that anyone's ever done for you?

Instinct 创始人： I've been able to surround myself and build such great relationships with so many different people — whether it's in the industry or outside the industry, where I work or in my personal life — that I'm very grateful to be around. And hopefully, certainly, I can also extend the same level of kindness and thoughtfulness towards them as well.

So I would say — I know I'm not answering your question. It's more on a higher level. It's just the qualities of things that I notice, that I really appreciate.

Patrick： No, you're building a fascinating company — maybe the most fascinating company of today's AI ecosystem in the world. Thanks so much for your time.

Instinct 创始人： Thank you so much.

（尾部赞助商）

You know how small advantages compound over time? That's true in investing and just as true in how you run your company. Your spending system is your capital allocation strategy. Ramp makes it smarter by default. See how at ramp.com/invest.

As your business grows, Vanta scales with you, automating compliance and giving you a single source of truth for security and risk. Learn more at vanta.com/invest.

item.description:
## 一、10% 日增长背后的"反常识悖论"：邀请制不是营销策略，而是算力节流阀
大多数人会把 Instinct 的邀请制读作"饥饿营销"或"病毒制造机"。但如果你把创始人在访谈中反复出现的一句话拼起来——"每个用户每天消耗的算力也在以 10% 复合增长"、"如果你猜错了，你会错 3-4 倍"、"算力交付周期是几个月"——真相就变得非常反直觉：
**邀请制的本质不是稀缺营销，而是算力供给曲线与需求曲线之间的减震器。**
传统 SaaS 里，用户 x2 意味着服务器 x2。但 Instinct 是一个"会自己醒来、自己睡觉"的持续性 agent，它的算力消耗不是线性的用户数，而是"用户数 × 每用户日活轨迹长度 × 主动性系数"。这个乘积每天都在 doubling。所以那 5 张邀请码，本质是一个**手动节流阀**——用社交博弈的时钟（人类愿意送出邀请的速率）去匹配 NVIDIA 交付 H100 的时钟。
这个思路，其实和一件事非常像：**电力公司在极端天气下的"需求响应计划"（Demand Response）**。他们不是靠加发电机来应对高峰，而是花钱让工厂在关键时刻自愿减少用

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] Trust Wallet 執行長：幣安 CZ 教我最重要的一件事！Felix Fan【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏在"持币两天"背后的注意力经济黑洞

Felix 提到最好的交易者"平均持币 2 天"就换仓——这不是交易策略的进化，而是金融正在被 TikTok 化。传统投资靠 P/E、DCF 这类"存量指标"定价，而链上顶级交易者已经在用注意力流速定价。这里有一个反直觉的洞察：当资产的定价锚点从"企业基本面"转向"社交讨论热度"，加密市场其实正在变成一个巨型的"注意力对冲工具"——你买的不是币，是"注意力涨落的期权"。

这解释了一个悖论：为什么 Bitcoin 价格没有创新高，Trust Wallet 的 DAU 却创下历史新高？因为用户不再需要"价格上涨"来产生活跃度，他们需要的是"轮动机会"。慢牛比快牛更能制造 DAU——这是所有加密交易平台从未公开承认的秘密。

二、CZ 的"我睡三小时"和 Felix 前女友的"你太穷"其实是同一件事

Felix 讲了两个看似无关的故事：大学时前女友因为他穷而分手，让他愤而创业；如今 CZ 睡 3 小时还去做 100×5 的俯卧撑，让他"没有借口"。这两件事的底层是同一个心理机制——"不对称参照系"。

这里有一个跨领域的连接：心理学上的"社会比较理论" + 神经科学的"损失厌恶"，在企业家身上被反向利用了。普通人被"别人比我好"击垮，企业家把它转化为燃料。前女友是"负向锚点"，CZ 是"正向锚点"，但两者产生的化学反应完全一样：制造一种"你不动就会消失"的存在焦虑。

真正惊人的是：Felix 说 CZ 作为投资人"从来不要求更高回报，反而要求赚少一点"——这是我在整段访谈中看到的最反常识的一句话。它意味着 CZ 已经把"钱"这个原本的最强激励，从系统里抽走了，然后用"文化"和"信任"填进去。这在管理学上叫做去激励化管理（demotivation management）——只有当创始人内在动机足够强时，外部激励反而会摧毁他。CZ 是在用"不施压"来施压。

三、Cyberport 的失败是理解香港的元隐喻

Felix 顺口提到一件事：Cyberport 原本要做半导体基地，最后变成了豪宅楼盘。这句话我认为是整段访谈最值得独立成篇的一句。

跨领域连接：这和 20 世纪 80 年代日本"广场协议"后资金涌入房地产而非半导体的路径几乎完全同构。当一个社会的资本流向"确定性收益"（房产）而非"不确定性创新"（芯片/科技），它就锁死了自己的未来。香港的低生育率、年轻人 YOLO 心态、Cyberport 变豪宅，其实是同一个系统的三个投影面——都是"当长期变得不可能，人们只能优化短期"的表现。

而这里藏着一个更深的悖论：Trust Wallet 的用户行为（持币 2 天、快速轮动）本质上是"金融领域的 YOLO"——当传统 hold 策略在信息过载时代变得低效，加密交易者也在"放弃长期"。Felix 一边惋惜香港年轻人不再存钱买房，一边在建设一个让全球用户不再"存币"的产品。他解决的问题和他叹息的问题，其实是同一个问题的两面——他自己可能都没意识到。

📝 转录文本

开场：市场信号与新一代交易者行为

This is a very good moment to build in crypto. The retail are coming back. The game is different right now. People rotate very often. We track the holding average on chain. The best traders hold a token at max 2 days.

Trading is becoming more social and social means attention economy and that become a very determining factor moving forward that traders have to adopt. They can't just look into some qualitative measures, how much the company make in profit, but also how people talk about it on social media.

It was very much the attention centralized to all the blue chips. But right now there are more and more selections. That's why we see the rotation become so rapid. People will have to move fast.

My investor never asked for more return. Oppositely, he always asked me to earn less.

嘉宾介绍与香港观察

I'm really excited to be joined by Phelix Fan. He is the CEO of Trust Wallet. He grew up in Hong Kong, so he knows firsthand how competitive Hong Kong is.

Off camera, we were talking about different industries. So, you mentioned property is a big thing here and finance,

but technology didn't really catch up. Is that what you said exactly?

When we look into one example, um, Cyberport, it was said to be a semiconductor site.

When was this?

Uh, it was like 20 years ago.

Oh, yes. Cyberport in, uh, Hong Kong Island. Uh, it's almost there. Uh, when a semiconductor uh, site could be set up in Hong Kong and it could bring like thousands um, job opportunities for locals. But it didn't pass. And eventually Cyberport transit into a property um a a property project.

No way.

Yes. Cyberport is part of it hub. Uh but also there are like a lot of properties people people a luxury building. Yeah.

Right. Residential apartments there.

So that kind of tell the story of Hong Kong. In Hong Kong, property is the the very big thing in everyone's asset uh portfolio. Even the property price is so skyhigh, um people still could afford it. So um yeah, I would I would say um it may be something that Hong Kong government will have to change.

Did you say people can afford it? Sorry, you said people can afford it.

Young people, people can afford. Oh, for youngsters, why not? Yeah.

So they shift their priorities, right?

They shift their wish. They no longer wish to buy house.

Yeah.

They will just enjoy life. YOLO.

I mean because even if you try hard, you can't afford it anymore.

Exactly. Exactly.

少子化与社会压力

So how does that shift a society from your observation?

I think one key factor we see is there are less people having babies.

Oh yes. I think that's a trouble and problem where a lot of the like leading cities would face. Um there are less babies, there are less populations and it is actually quite pressing. Elon Musk says we need more babies, we need more humans and I think that's what Hong Kong right now is facing. And hopefully I can contribute some personally.

How would you do that?

I have one baby right now. Maybe I can have more.

Right. So, the stats is um Hong Kong 0.84, Taiwan 0.89, South Korea 0.8.

People get married late. Uh maybe because of career, maybe because of societal uh or cultural uh standard that push them to like have their career first.

Felix 的创业起点：一段"被分手"引发的旅程

I read your profile. You have done so many different things. You have started your own business. Now you're the CEO of Trust Wallet. Take me through that journey maybe from when you're still studying.

I'm born and raised in Hong Kong. Um my parents are businessmen. So I watch them in action, how they strike a deal, how they pitch proposals and um that taught me a lot.

Uh and around 20 years old when I was in university, I want to put all these into action. I want to do something for myself. Um but the motivation would not be that high, right? Um because launching a business or founding a business would take a lot of courage and it has to be a little bit irrational.

So I took a leap of faith because my ex uh broke up with me uh because I was too poor. I just want to prove to her this is not me.

This was in college.

Yeah. This was in college.

Okay. Everybody was broke in college.

Everybody is broke.

Whatever.

Yes. But maybe because I gave her like high expectations, every entrepreneurs would say, "I will make millions. I will be a billionaire." Right. And she would have a sharp like reality check where I'm not that fancy. I'm just broke.

You were in college.

Exactly. But I try very hard. Uh she want to get out, right? She want to go out but I would prefer to like build products uh study and I'm broke. So uh it's pretty hard to maintain.

But uh after that I found my business with a very irrational motivation where I want to prove to her I can make it. But after a few months I'm still failed like I'm still very broke. Um but then I um like come up with such a motivation where I want to grind. I want to grind through this journey. Uh I have the business right now. I can't let it fail.

第一桶金：App 外包与冷 call 岁月

The business was uh simply a digital uh consultancy like uh I build apps because I have nothing. I just have my MacBook. Um I build apps and I sell my expertise.

So uh I reach out to listed companies who has budget who want to build mobile apps. Back then

amazing

back then uh iPhone was amazing. I think Steve Jobs was still alive and um everyone wants their own mobile app no matter what they want to do like they don't know what to do with the mobile app but they want one.

So there is a huge business opportunity where um like we can sell our service um but it turns out to be not as smooth as I imagined. Even everyone wants a mobile app it is pretty hard to find the clients. I try very hard. I call hundreds um cold calls and eventually I land one client uh China Paint which is a very well-established uh transitional companies in Hong Kong.

Um they call me back and say Felix yes we want a mobile app. Can you build one for us?

And start from there I establish a full cycle of how I sell a product, I sell my service, build that deliver it and then I can move on to the next client. So um starting from there I at that very year I get like 30 uh clients like that. That's a just a very humble start.

Did you go back to your ex-girlfriend and be like yo—

No, well actually yes I tried but yeah she moved on so I also moved on. So yeah uh I would say yeah that is like my university life.

从父母身上学到的：决心与坚持

Nice. Earlier you mentioned your parents were both in business.

Yes.

What did you learn from them? If you could summarize one big piece of business advice.

I think determination is the key cuz we never know the market. We never know the needs. We never know if the problem we solve right now will last forever. So you have to always adapt to changes. Business has up and downs. But what doesn't change is the entrepreneurs don't give up.

The perseverance to solve problems and to go through that journey is the utmost important thing that I carry forward till now.

从"服务"转向"产品"的关键跃迁

Yeah. And what happened after that business?

Well, I grow tired. If you could like imagine it is kind of a repeat cycle. Every single client is like I have to start again. The relationship. Maybe I got some referrals and maybe it could be smoother, but the whole process is almost the same. But I just asked myself, do I want to continue this repeated cycle for another 20 or 30 years?

And the answer was obviously no. Do I know what would happen in future? Back then I didn't know.

Can I explain it as in your previous business you were, you know, servicing one client at a time. So it's one-on-one but with your next company you could build something and it last for a long time.

So product and service are like quite different right. Service I might have 300 clients but if one big clients say no to us that would hurt our profit. But in product we try hard to serve millions users like hopefully they all enjoy the product but even if there's 1% users left us it's still okay. Can still plan ahead. That's a sharp difference and I chose that I want to build product.

When I start my business, it was just a very irrational motivation. But then when at time goes by, I realized my true motivation is to establish things for long run. So that is the leap of faith where I took that I understand my limitations back then. I didn't have that much resources to try building products that would serve millions. So I joined a company where they already have million users.

从 OKX 到 Trust Wallet：一场需要多次说"不"的邀约

How did you go from OKX to Trust Wallet?

So back then OKX wallet grow a lot because of the inscriptions mania like Audi and BDC and

2022 gen 2 or gen 3. Okay.

Yes. And um that's the first time she came to me and I said no because I thought I still have a lot of room to grow and the company is like the product is growing. I said no. And then the other time was I interact with CC on Twitter and she thought I'm ready to leave but that's not the case. I don't want to leave until last year.

We also talk about like philosophy and stuff. We are friends. Um and she again asked me how about coming—my baby just born like that. My life is like

chaotic.

Has a lot of things to do. I think like maybe this is the time even so chaotic. It's like a calling. I didn't expect she would ask me again because I reject her like two three times but she is just so insist and the article she wrote touch every part in my heart.

What was the article about?

The article was the philosophy of finance.

Okay.

The culture of finance. How they view Binance. I can't remember the exact wordings—she that products come and go. You can be a good craftsman, but culture is something you can't just replace. The relationship with your users, their hearts, you cannot replace and people can feel it. That is so much what I also think about.

CZ 的"放手式"信任

And what about CZ?

CZ is a visionary and I think he's a very good mentor. He's an investor for Trust Wallet. He's not hands-on. Whenever I came to him, literally he just say yes.

No way.

Like we are very aligned. Okay. I'm not sure if he treats other business leaders the same way I interact with him, but the trust level is tremendous and I really enjoy this kind of relationship where I could feel he gave me a lot of trust.

It doesn't mean he can't run this business. He can. But he choose to hands off so that I have the platform and freedom to do whatever I think would be the best for Trust Wallet.

I think that's the reason why he become so successful cuz he could run Binance and we all read his book. He had a lot of like startups before but the key things I think he is so different than others is uh how he evolved from a very hands-on entrepreneur to a cultural leader or a mentor and that draws all my motivations to serve Trust Wallet users.

Could you give an example of what he said to you or what he did that really inspired you?

Well, just like yesterday, he slept three four hours. He went to the like reading sections in the morning and in the afternoon there are four meetings. I went in the room. I said CC let's take some rest. Let's not talk anything. And he said no carry on. It's fine. It's fine.

And then after that he had two interviews. One on stage, another reading sessions and also dinner gathering and at night he tweet about I'm doing 100 push-up five seven sets. So like he's a very consistent person and he push to the limit of himself and I think this is truly inspiring to me.

So you're like, hey, the person that successful is pushing himself that hard. What is my excuse? No excuse. Okay.

Exactly that way.

Trust Wallet 的增长与市场变化

Okay. Well, now tell me about Trust Wallet and the progress you've made. Earlier you said you guys grew a lot recently.

I would say luckily because the market now become more bullish. When I first assumed this position, it was a bearish market back in February this year uh 2026. But right now as we see Bitcoin price goes up a little bit, memecoin vibe kind of come back, there are new innovations coming up. The regulatory framework is getting clearer and clearer.

So this is a very good moment to build in crypto and we are fortunate enough to have 30% increase. We reach all-time high in daily active users just in this week.

So is this just Bitcoin price raise?

I don't think so. I think that retail are coming back.

I think that is super interesting because right now Bitcoin price are still relatively low compared to all-time high.

Yes.

But you said the daily active users are all time. Why?

There are also innovations where over the past year people realize oh god crypto has so much new things. There are Hyperliquid, there are prediction market, there are ALPHAs, institutions are coming back. So that give people a kind of refresh to see crypto is not dead. Crypto moved on and it is time to come back to enjoy the very new crypto that is so different than last year.

新周期的三大变化：Perp、轮动、链上活跃度

What is different from last year?

So by the data we see people are trading per dex way more than before. We are now like despite we are now number one across all builders on Hyperliquid, people are trading more and more. People are relying more and more with perps and that's amazing.

The second part is yes memecoin—some previous memecoin might not have all-time high or the price might not go up but I think the game is different right now where people rotate very often. So the same set of users, more users coming in, they will not stick with one memecoin or the other. They follow the attention and that become more and more vibrant.

Like in the US, we can hold a meme coin and it goes up like 100 x, thousand x, right? This might be a little bit different or the pace goes so much faster to switch between one token to another. So, we didn't see the price action in previous meme, but we see a more vibrant activities on chain that's happening.

So I think the better metrics to track is the trading volume that right now it is exponentially growing and that's drive all the attention and users coming on chain right now.

新手入门 Trust Wallet：从下载到下单

For somebody that hasn't tried Trust Wallet before just for them to have a clearer picture of how it works. Let's say I want to, you know, go on Hyperliquid and trade Bitcoin perp, take me step by step. What will I have to do?

First, they create an account. They create a wallet and then on a fertile there's a Hyperliquid. If your city or countries is not restricted because there are like compliance and regulations. And once you land there, deposit funds. You can use Apple Pay, you can use your bank transfer, you can just transfer from any other exchanges or any other wallets and then you can start trading.

You have BDC pair, you have Ethereum, you have all these trading pairs right away waiting for you. So it is very convenient. You got push notifications to remind you maybe your margin is almost getting liquidated and you might want to refill it.

So the whole journey is very much step by step and all you need is just to download Trust Wallet.

Trust Wallet 的定位：Progressive Disclosure

But for somebody that is not an expert in this area, why don't they just go to Hyperliquid for example?

Right. So if they are sophisticated enough or advanced enough to use a website and check all the charts all the indicators and stuff, they will find the website Hyperliquid to their homeland.

But Trust Wallet stand for simplicity. It stand for easy entrance and convenience. You just take out your phone and you can trade. So if you look for a very advanced setup, you will go to the website of course. But if you look for convenience and when you see a news where you want to make an action right away on the go, you will prefer Trust Wallet.

So we also have order book but that is uh no more action. So we don't show you the order book right away cuz that would be too complicated for normies. We hide that. However, if you are advanced user and you want to look into the order book before you place trade, you are always welcome to click that button.

It's right beside the confirmation page before you click confirm. You can always check how deep is the liquidity and do I want to place market order or limit order. It's all on your palm but in a progressive disclosure way.

HODL 已死？——链上顶级交易者的两日周期

Yeah. And you were talking about trading volume going up and people are chasing narrative. The speed is a lot faster now. Does that mean the old HODL model is dead?

We track the holding average on chain. The best traders hold a token at max two days and they move on.

Yes. If you track friend deos, we are friend as well. But Frank Deos would hold just two days and move on and he made great fortune. So compared to people holding BDC for years that is a whole new investment thesis that people embrace and they are very successful.

And because they are successful they are on the leaderboard. People try to follow their trading behavior because they are successful. With social media and with all this influence, maybe trading is becoming more social and social means attention economy.

Right.

And that become a very determining factor moving forward that traders have to adopt. They can't just look into some qualitative measures how much the company make in profit but also how people talk about it on social media.

一个残酷现实：只有不到 3% 的人真的能做到

That is why Polymarket is working with traditional finance because you know traditional finance now realize that the real signal is now online in the communities. But here's the question now for viewers that are watching—not everybody is good at trading. So if we talk about you know the best performance is people rotating in and out of different areas, I think this could be a little misleading. Is there a metrics that tells you only a small percentage of people that could successfully execute this strategy?

Exactly. So the very harsh fact is people who adopt to this kind of strategy—they buy quick and sell quick—will only be less than 3% people who really make a fortune.

Traditionally if you find a good assets, if you find BDC valuable then hold it. By holding BDC over a decade it is always more and more, like so much higher ROI than you flip it.

I do relate a lot with what you just said because of all these traditionally crypto centralized exchanges now they do tokenized equity, they do commodities, so all the liquidity of you know retail traders are centralized in one area. Now you can rotate in and out of assets really quickly and we think it's the norm but it wasn't back then.

It wasn't back then cuz I think the key was there was not that much asset. It was very much the attention centralized to all the blue chips. But right now there are more and more selections.

Yes.

That's why we see the rotation become so rapid because there are more choice. When there are more supply with the same demand, people would have to move fast.

Mhm.

In the past, huge demand, very few supply. So everything concentrate to one thing. So I think that's a very different thing we see right now.

三年后的世界：不可知，但更透明

Yeah, it's a whole new world in like in three years. We don't even know what the world would look like.

I totally agree with that, Bonnie. We don't know what would happen after three years because blockchain is all about verify ledger. It is all about trusting yourself, safeguarding your own funds with your own private keys and cifase rather than trusting a black box that might in extreme case go bankrupt.

So with a fairer world, fairer and more transparent financial world, I think that would yield more and more innovations from ground up.

Cold Card 事件与自托管的安全边界

Well, you just mentioned self-custody and I really want to ask you about this unfortunate event that happened a couple months ago with Cold Card. What happened to Cold Card for somebody that is not technical? Can you break it down for us?

So technically they derive public address in a way that is wrong and for a very long time for years people didn't realize they derived in that way until someone jailbreak it. So if you still hold funds in the very traditional Coke address, you have to check it right now and move your funds immediately if that is still not yet got drained.

I would say that is a niche case where we definitely want to level up in the whole industry to level up the standard of how we derive public address and how we handle self-custody. Self-custody as a whole as we see from all these different wallet providers is still moving forward with a safer and more easier way to derive the public address. So that is a very unfortunate incident but that doesn't represent the full picture.

So people that are you know using self-custody products, they shouldn't be too worried.

They shouldn't be too worried. I would say most of the wallet providers right now, the leading ones are totally fine.

为什么要自托管？——不信任黑箱

Why don't we just use traditional finance? Why is self-custody such an important topic to you personally?

One thing I should admit is self-custody may be a niche demand for now. People still enjoy using bank. But to me personally I remember I set up 10 bank accounts just because I don't want my assets in one bank pass the threshold of that fund being insured, in extreme cases like bankruptcy of the bank—because it is a black box. I never know how much they lend my money to the others and I can't verify it until thing go south like Silicon Valley Bank.

So I always want to trust myself and self-custody provide the best alternative.

You mentioned insured and now I'm thinking if I were a viewer I would say well at least they're insured and second if they go if the banks go bankrupt the government might bail them out. So is that more protection for me?

Bail them out at a level—like we never know how much they will bail them out. I think when people start to study more and more into self-custody and blockchain, they realize why would you give your hard-earned money to someone else that might bail you out rather than you just safeguard your own funds on your own hand. You can always trust yourself.

CZ、Aster 与 Hyperliquid：一个出人意料的"Why not"

CZ was supporting a competition of Hyperliquid, Aster, and CZ is also an investor in Trust Wallet. Now, why is it okay for you to connect to Hyperliquid given this relationship?

Yes, I think publicly people are very surprised when we announce Hyperliquid integration is right now on Trust Wallet. The community from Hyperliquid welcome us a lot. We are now number one across all wallet and I appreciate all the blessing from the community.

But back then people thought how come CC would just accept us to support Hyperliquid? Why wouldn't we just stick with Aster? Back then I think that was February. I went to Abu Dhabi. I bring this topic to CC.

You said we want to integrate—

Hyperliquid. I said I want to integrate Hyperliquid. Is that okay? He said why not?

What?

Every single one publicly, internally, everyone say don't mention it to you. And you say why not? So this is really surprising to me. We all want to support the best builders.

And the key thing is from this very example it tells Trust Wallet will remain as a chain-agnostic wallet where we support the best builders no matter what backgrounds they are. As long as there is a real problems, as long as there is people needing something, we try our best to integrate it. We try our best to present them regardless of where they are or the competitions.

We are here for good. We are here for long term. I think that's most important thing when we make all the decisions. Is that beneficial to the industry? Is that beneficial to our users? If yes, do it. Some companies might have to go IPO or trace different track and they might want to maximize profit. We ain't.

投资人竟然要求"少赚一点"

How—that is a very interesting perspective. Before we wrap up this conversation, how do you balance out what you were saying, more of the philosophy, the vision versus your investors? They want to see numbers, right? They want to see returns. How do you balance those two things?

I think that is actually one thing Trust Wallet so unique is my investor never asked for more return. Oppositely he always asked me to earn less.

No way.

He always say can we make less profit? Yes. I really like that kind of flexibility he provide. It doesn't mean that we will make less profit. We make decent profit but for example yesterday we announced all the stable coins swap on the same chain is free right now. So we are giving up millions profit just by making that decisions.

给迷茫者的建议：先迈第一步

Earlier we mentioned how competitive you know Asian cities could be. One advice for people that cannot find their calling. They're struggling. All they want is to have a better future for them and their family.

I think always start from making your living. That's actually as you should be proud to make even just 20,000 Hong Kong dollars or you make millions. They are kind of the same. The achievement will come step by step.

So always start the journey. Don't think your friends or you see some big figures in this like Bonnie interview. You interview a lot of big players

like you.

No, no, no. I'm still a small potato. But they have been through a very long journey of ups and downs. So always start your journey. Always do the first step. And when you take that first step, eventually beautiful things would happen.

I love that.

Run through it.

I love that. A lot of people want to start a channel, start their own media company, start their business, but they're so afraid of people's opinion. What if I fail? But like what you just said, just start.

Yes.

I love that. Thank you.

Just do it.

Thank you. Thank you so much.

## 一、隐藏在"持币两天"背后的注意力经济黑洞
Felix 提到最好的交易者"平均持币 2 天"就换仓——这不是交易策略的进化，而是**金融正在被 TikTok 化**。传统投资靠 P/E、DCF 这类"存量指标"定价，而链上顶级交易者已经在用**注意力流速**定价。这里有一个反直觉的洞察：**当资产的定价锚点从"企业基本面"转向"社交讨论热度"，加密市场其实正在变成一个巨型的"注意力对冲工具"**——你买的不是币，是"注意力涨落的期权"。
这解释了一个悖论：为什么 Bitcoin 价格没有创新高，Trust Wallet 的 DAU 却创下历史新高？因为**用户不再需要"价格上涨"来产生活跃度，他们需要的是"轮动机会"**。慢牛比快牛更能制造 DAU——这是所有加密交易平台从未公开承认的秘密。

Felix 讲了两个看似无关的故事：大学时前女友因为他穷而分手，让他愤而创业；如今 CZ 睡 3 小时还去做 100×5 的俯卧撑，让他"没有借口"。这两件事的底层是**同一个心理机制——"不对称参照系

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏在通胀指标里的"反射弧"——市场其实在照镜子

视频提到核心PCE与CPI背离的原因之一是PCE中的"Portfolio Management"子项与美股指数挂钩。这个技术细节值得展开——它意味着美股上涨本身在推高通胀读数：股市涨 → PCE涨 → 美联储不敢降息 → 反噬股市。这是一个隐蔽的内生负反馈回路，市场以为自己在交易独立的宏观变量，实际上是在照镜子。

更深一层：贝森特之所以敦促美联储"保持开放态度"、强调CPI而非PCE，本质上是选择不把资产价格计入通胀——这正是Fisher到Bernanke数十年未解的经济学争论。政治施压的表象下，藏着的是货币政策哲学的根本分歧：通胀应该只衡量消费，还是应该同时衡量财富？

二、半导体的"情绪免疫"——生物学能解释金融现象

利率飙升的一周里，最该被砸的半导体反而涨7.4%，作者归因于"进入之前情绪已经极低"。这与免疫学的tolerance（耐受）机制几乎同构——反复暴露于同一刺激后，机体不再产生激烈反应。六月的周期股争论、七月抛售、八月二次探底，等于把弱手（susceptible cells）清洗殆尽，剩下的持仓者对"利率上涨"这种抗原已经产生免疫。

这解释了一个反直觉的规律：资产的抗跌性不是估值给的，是"卖压历史"给的。一只被市场遗忘了三个月的股票，比一只刚刚被追捧到情绪高点的股票更"安全"——尽管教科书告诉你后者估值可能更低。

三、市场的"时间地平线"——认知的天文学

一个作者带过但可能被低估的观察：每一年市场对"下下年"EPS增速的预期，几乎都固定在15%左右。今年年初预期2026是15%，现在已修正到32%；而市场对2027年的预期又"回归"到了15.4%。

这不是预测，是认知的地平线。就像天文学家观察遥远星系只能看到发光核心，看不到旋臂结构——市场对超过18个月的未来失去分辨率，只能fallback到"历史平均"。这带来一个可交易的规律：惊喜永远在"下一年"被定价，而不是在"后年"。所以2027年一旦跨过2026Q4的门槛，会经历一次剧烈重估——今年从15%到32%的历史极有可能重演。

一个语义值得留意的信号

作者全程使用"加息"来描述10月会议的66%概率事件——但结合上下文（当前处于降息周期、贝森特要求"开放态度"、MOVE恐慌），实际市场恐慌的是"降息被暂停"。这个反复出现的措辞混乱，本身可能是当前政策周期错位的一个心理标记：连专业分析师都开始弄混方向，说明这已经不是一个"标准的降息周期"。

跨领域连接：XLU的历史押韵与金融版Goodhart定律

XLU超卖到RSI=24，与2023年10月的耶伦Pivot前夜押韵——这本是漂亮的历史类比。但金融市场的规律一旦被广泛识别，就会自我否定（Goodhart's Law的金融变体）：当所有人都知道"XLU超卖后会反弹"，反弹本身就变成了空头进场信号，历史押韵的窗口会被前置吃掉。因此这次的抄底赔率，很可能比2023年那次要差——不是因为宏观不同，而是因为共识本身消耗了不对称性。
